1103 1109

Explanatory 

In sec. 343, after the quotation from Jarrell v. Com., the holding should read "Held no error" instead of "Held error."

In a note to sec. 1431, attention is called to State v. Ray, West 

Virginia, wherein an indictment for statutory rape is involved. 

It is there held that the form of indictment prescribed by the Code, and set out in sec. 1435 of this work, must allege that prosecutrix "was of previous chaste character" and that accused "is over sixteen years of age." Therefore, the indictment should read: "That A. B., a male person over the age of sixteen years. in the said County of ... in and upon one C. D., a female child, not his wife, under the age of sixteen years and of previous chaste character," (continue as in sec. 1435).

PART II 

[ 541 ]

The statutes of both Virginias prescribe a minimum and maximum sentence for the offenses herein treated. However, it will be observed that in West Virginia, by reason of Chapter 24, Acts of the Legislature, 1939, which amends Code 61-11-16 (sec. 

6128), every sentence to the penitentiary of a person convicted of a felony, where the maximum penalty is less than life imprisonment, shall be a general sentence of imprisonment in the penitentiary from the minimum to the maximum term of years. And where the trial court designates a definite term of years, the same is to be considered by the director of probation and parole only as a recommendation of the court as the appropriate term the convict should be required to serve, less the time allowed by law for good behavior. ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 788

ACCESSORIES. 

§ 787. Grades of offense. 

The offense of accessory is of two grades: Accessory before the fact, and accessory after the fact. The latter is a misdemeanor and is not considered in this work. § 788. Accessories before the fact defined. 

An accessory before the fact is not the principal actor in the crime, nor present at its commission, but is one who, being absent at the time of the crime, in some manner procures, counsels, commands, or instigates another to commit it. to commit it. Absence at the time and from the scene of the crime is an essential element. 

State v. Ellison, 49 W. Va. 70, 38 S. E. 574. 

State v. Roberts, 50 W. Va. 422, 40 S. E. 484. 

State v. Cremeans, 62 W. Va. 134, 57 S. E. 405. 

State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 668, 60 S. E. 785. 

Moore v. Lowe, 116 W. Va. 165, 180 S. E. 1. 

1 Wharton's Crim. Law (12th Ed.), sec. 263. 

1 R. C. L., p. 144. 

In State v. Roberts, supra, it is said: "An accessory before the fact is he that, being absent at the time of the actual perpetration of the crime procures, counsels, commands, incites or abets another to commit it. The crime of accessory before the fact is a particular one. The absence of the accessory at the time and place of the principal offense is an essential element of the crime. Sir Matthew Hale defines the accessory before the fact to be, 'One who, being absent at the time of the crime committed doth yet procure, counsel or command another to commit a crime. Wherein absence is necessary to make him an accessory.' 

Also in State v. Ellison, supra, it is said: 999 "The crime of accessory before the fact is a peculiar one. The absence of the accessory at the time and place of the principal offense is an essential element of the crime." 

And in Wharton on Homicide, 3rd Ed., p. 49, it is said:

$546 

"An accessory before the fact is one who is not the chief actor in the offense, nor present at its performance, but was in some way connected with it before the commission of the act." Citing, State v. Berger, 121 Iowa 581, 96 N. W. 1094. 

State v. Praeter, 52 W. Va. 132, 43 S. E. 230. 

Connaughty v. State, 1 Wis. 159, 60 Am. Dec. 370.

U. S. v. Hartwell, 3 Cliff. 221. 

§ 789. Manner of trial at common law.

Under the common law an accessory could not be tried until the principal felon had been convicted by the verdict of a jury, or outlawed, and upon the trial of such accessory the only admissible evidence to prove the principal's guilt was the record of his conviction by such verdict in a court of competent jurisdiction. 

790. Trial under the statutes.

Under the statutes of both Virginias it is no longer necessary to show that the principal felon has been convicted, but it is necessary to show that the substantive offense, to which the defendant is charged as having been an accessory, has been committed by the principal felon. 

Hatchett v. Com., 75 Va. 925. 

State v. Lilly, 47 W. Va. 496, 35 S. E. 837. 

The Virginia Code, secs. 4764 and 4766, and the West Virginia Code, 61-11-6 and 7 (secs. 6118-6119), are very similar, and provide: *. "In the case of every felony, every principal in the second degree and every accessory before the fact may be indicted, tried, convicted, and punished in all respects, as if a principal in the first degree, * "An accessory, either before or after the fact, may, whether the principal felon be convicted or not, or be amenable to justice or not, be indicted, convicted, and punished in the county (or corporation in Virginia) in which he became accessory, or in which the principal felon might be indicted. Any such accessory before the fact may be indicted either with such principal or sepa rately."

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 791 

That part of these statutes which authorize the indictment, trial and conviction of an accessory before the fact in the county in which the principal crime was committed, or in the county wherein the accessorial act took place (where such act took place in another county), has been upheld on the theory that the offense of an accessory is consummated at the time and place of the commission of the principal crime. 

State v. Ellison, supra. 

State v. Roberts, supra. 

Weil v. Black, 76 W. Va. 689, 86 S. E. 666. 

State v. Bland, 89 W. Va. 600, 109 S. E. 716. 

But in State v. Overholt, 111 W. Va. 417, 162 S. E. 317, it is held: "That insofar as it (the above statute) authorizes the indictment and trial of an accessory after the fact in the county where the principal crime is committed (unless the accessorial acts occurred therein) violates Article III, sec. 

14, of the constitution." § 791. Distinction between accessories and principals in first and second degrees.

An accessory before the fact must have been absent from the place at the time of the commission of the crime, and must have procured, counseled, commanded, or abetted another to commit the same.

Principals in the first degree are those who are actors, actual perpetrators of the crime, those who are the immediate perpetrators of the act, either acting personally, or through an innocent agent. But it is not necessary that a principal in the first degree in homicide should have committed the offense with his own hand, or been actually present when the offense was consummated. Either actual or constructive presence is sufficient. 

Principals in the second degree are those who did not with their own hands commit the act, but were present, aiding and abetting, encouraging or inciting the same by words, gestures, looks or signs, or who in any manner or by any means countenances or approves the same. To constitute one a principal in the second degree it must appear, 1. That he participated in the act committed.

§ 548 

2. That he was present, either actually or constructively, at the time of its commission.

State v. Watts, 5 W. Va. 532. 

Mitchell v. Com., 33 Gratt. 868. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 848, 38 S. E. 184. 

State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 668, 60 S. E. 785. 

State v. Roberts, 50 W. Va. 425, 40 S. E. 485. 

State v. Cook, 81 W. Va. 686, 95 S. E. 792. 

Brown v. Com., 130 Va. 733, 107 S. E. 809. 

Reynolds v. Com., 33 Gratt. 834. 

Kemp v. Com., 80 Va. 443. 

Wooden v. Com., 117 Va. 935, 86 S. E. 305. 

Hurd v. Com., 159 Va. 880, 165 S. E. 536. 

State v. Ellison, 49 W. Va. 73, 38 S. E. 574. 

Campbell v. Com., 130 Va. 741, 107 S. E. 812. 

Wharton on Homicide, 3rd Ed., secs. 42-45-58.

Wharton on Homicide, 3rd Ed., sec. 40, states the distinction between principal and accessory thus: "The distinction between principal and accessory is that the principal is the one who actually does the criminal act or participates in doing it, whether actually or only constructively present, or who is actually present at the time of doing it, aiding and abetting; while the accessory is one who has such connection with the crime by reason of preparation, procurement, advice, encouragement, or assistance, as to be deemed criminally liable therefor, though he does not participate in the actual commission of the crime, and is not present thereat." 

In State v. Cremeans, 62 W. Va. 137, 57 S. E. 406, it is said: "A principal in the second degree is one who is present aiding and abetting the principal actor in the commission of the crime, and actual physical presence is not necessary. 

A constructive presence is sufficient, as in the instance of a person keeping watch or guard at a convenient distance while the murder is being committed by the principal actor." 

In Sharswood's Blackstone, Book 4, p. 33, it is stated: “A man may be principal in an offense in two degrees. 

A principal in the first degree is he that is the actor or absolute perpetrator of the crime; and in the second degree is he who is present, aiding and abetting the fact to be done. Which principals need not always be an actor immediately standing by, within sight or hearing of the

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 793 

fact; but there may also be a constructive presence, as when one commits a robbery or murder and another keeps watch or guard at some convenient distance." See also, State v. Roberts, supra. § 792. Accessories bound by acts of associates, although not included in original design. 

In Boggs v. Com., 153 Va. 828, 149 S. E. 445, it is held: "Everyone connected with carrying out a common design to commit a criminal act is concluded and bound by the act of any member of the combination, perpetrated in the prosecution of the common design. But it is not necessary that the crime committed shall have been originally intended. Each is accountable for all the acts of the others done in carrying out the common purpose, whether such acts were originally contemplated or not, if they were the natural and proximate result of carrying out such purpose, and the question of whether the result is the natural and probable effect of the wrongful act intended is for the jury." 

See authorities cited in opinion. Also 

Brown v. Com., 130 Va. 733, 107 S. E. 809. 

State v. Belcher, W. Va. 2 S. E. 2d 259. 

And in Jones v. Com., 111 Va. 862, 69 S. E. 953, it is further held: "Any evidence tending to shed light upon the evidence of accomplices, or to affect their credibility, or the weight to which their testimony is entitled, by showing what influences, if any, have been brought to bear upon them is plainly admissible. If an accomplice has been promised immunity from prosecution, the jury are entitled to know it." 

Also in State v. Boswell, 107 W. Va. 216, 148 S. E. 1, it is held error to refuse to permit the defendant to show that a witness testifying against him had been promised immunity in the same or another criminal charge against him in return for his testimony. 

See authorities cited in opinion. § 793. Offense of principal and accessory may not be of same grade. 

In Hawley v. Com., 75 Va. 851, it is held:

§ 550 

"The offense of the instigator, or accessory before the fact, is not necessarily of the same grade of that of the perpetrator. An accessory before the fact, or instigator, may be guilty of murder, while the principal or perpetrator may be guilty of manslaughter. Or the accessory before the fact (instigator) acting in hot blood, may be guilty of manslaughter, while the perpetrator (principal), acting with deliberate malice, may be guilty of murder." § 794. Accessory may be indicted separately or with principal felon.

The last sentence of the statutes of both Virginia and West Virginia codes provides: "Any such accessory before the fact may be indicted either with such principal or separately." 

Virginia Code, sec. 4766. 

West Virginia Code, 61-11-7 (sec. 6119). 

And in Hawley v. Com., 75 Va. 851, syl. 1, it is held: "The same count may contain a charge of murder against one, and a charge of being an accessory against others." § 795. Same, must be indicted, tried and punished as an accessory and not as principal.

An accessory before the fact must be indicted, tried and punished as such and not as a principal. In Hatchett v. Com., 75 Va. 

925, it is held: "An accessory to a felony cannot be prosecuted for a substantive offense, but only as an accessory to the crime perpetrated by the principal felon. And, in order to his. conviction, although it is not necessary to show that the principal felon has been convicted, it is necessary to show that the substantive offense, to which he is charged as having been accessory, has been committed by the principal felon." 

Thornton v. Com., 24 Gratt. 657. 

Wren v. Com., 26 Gratt. 956. 

Rasnick v. Com., 2 Va. Cas. 356. 

Com. v. Williamson, 2 Va. Cas. 211. 

State v. Lilly, 47 W. Va. 496, 35 S. E. 837. 

State v. Powers, 91 W. Va. 737, 113 S. E. 912.

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 797 

Also in State v. Roberts, 50 W. Va. 425, 40 S. E. 484, it is held: "Such accessory (before the fact) may be indicted either with the principal or separately, but in either case he must be indicted as accessory and not as principal." 

Hatchett v. Com., 75 Va. 925. 

Hawley v. Com., 75 Va. 847. 

State v. Lilly, 47 W. Va. 496, 35 S. E. 837. 

State v. Cremeans, 62 W. Va. 136, 57 S. E. 406. § 796. Verdict of conviction in accessory to murder. 

It is true in both Virginias that a verdict which finds a person indicted as being accessory to murder, to be guilty thereof, but fails to specify whether he is guilty as accessory to murder in the first or second degree is fatally defective. 

Com. v. Williamson, 2 Va. Cas. 211.

And under the statutes of both Virginias, an indictment for accessory before the fact to murder will sustain a conviction of voluntary manslaughter. 

Moore v. Lowe, 116 W. Va. 165, 180 S. E. 1. 

State v. Martin, 112 W. Va. 88, 163 S. E. 764.

ACCOMPLICES. 

§ 797. Conviction may be had on uncorroborated evidence of accomplice.

It is the general rule that the fact that a state's witness was an accomplice may affect his credibility, but not his competency; he is a legal witness, and the jury must determine what credit his testimony is entitled to, whether corroborated or uncorroborated. 

Moreover an accused may be convicted upon the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice. 

In the early case of State v. Betsall, 11 W. Va. 704, this rule is thus stated: "A conviction may be had upon the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice, and in such case, if the judge who presided at the trial is satisfied with the verdict and refuses to set it aside, the appellate court will not reverse the judgment and set aside the verdict on the ground that it rested solely on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice." Affirmed in:

§ 552 

 State v. Thompson, 21 W. Va. 757. 

Jones v. Com., 111 Va. 862, 69 S. E. 953. 

Hunt v. Com., 126 Va. 815, 101 S. E. 896. 

Com. v. King, 9 Va. Law Reg. 653. 

And in the much later case of State v. Camp, 110 W. Va. 450, 158 S. E. 664, it is also said: "Long ago this Court, following the rules laid down by the Virginia courts, held that a conviction in a criminal case may be had upon the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice; and in such case, if the judge who presided at the trial is satisfied with the verdict, and refuses to set it aside, the appellate court will not reverse the judgment and set aside the verdict on the ground that it rested solely on such testimony." Citing, State v. Betsall, supra. 

Oliver v. Com., 77 Va. 590. 

Jones v. Com., supra. 

Crosby v. Com., 132 Va. 518, 110 S. E. 270. 

Simpson v. Com., 135 Va. 746, 115 S. E. 392. § 798. Same, but such evidence to be regarded with caution.

It is the general rule that in the trial of a criminal case the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice against the defendant is to be received with great caution, and the jury should, upon request, be so instructed. .State v. Hammond, 96 W. Va. 99, 122 S. E. 363. 

Simpson v. Com., 135 Va. 749, 115 S. E. 392. 

Hunt v. Com., 126 Va. 816, 101 S. E. 896. 

Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 483, 124 S. E. 240.

But, the above principle does not apply, nor should the jury be given such cautionary instructions where the testimony of such accomplice is fully corroborated by other evidence. 

State v. Hammond, supra. 

Draper v. Com., 132 Va. 659, 111 S. E. 471. 

Clark v. Com., 135 Va. 496, 115 S. E. 704.

State v. Thompson, 21 W. Va. 756. 

State v. Betsall, 11 W. Va. 704.

Jones v. Com., 111 Va. 862, 69 S. E. 953. 

Faulkner v. S. Boston, 139 Va. 569, 123 S. E. 358.

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 800 

§ 799. Rule as to corroboration of accomplices. 

In Jones v. Com., 111 Va. 862, 69 S. E. 953, it is held: "As to the extent of the corroboration of an accomplice, the general rule, and the one which is correct and safe is that if two or more accomplices are produced as witnesses, they are not deemed to corroborate each other, but the same rule is applied, and the same confirmations is required, as if there were but one. Moreover, the corroboration or confirmation must relate to some fact (or facts) which goes to establish the guilt of the accused." 

Draper v. Com., 132 Va. 648, 111 S. E. 471. § 800. Confessions or admissions of accomplices as evidence against associate in crime. 

In Hunter v. Com., 7 Gratt. 641, it is held: "Confessions or admissions of an accomplice in a felony, made after the commission and completion of the offense (prisoner was absent in this case), are not competent evidence against the prisoner, even though a previous conspiracy and combination between the prisoner and the accomplice to commit the felony has been proved. "The general rule in such cases is that such declarations are only admissible against the declarant, and are not competent evidence against his former associate." 

Garnett v. Com., 117 Va. 904, 83 S. E. 1083, and cases therein cited. 

See also, Oliver v. Com., 77 Va. 590. 

Jones v. Com., 31 Gratt. 836. 

State v. Hively, 103 W. Va. 237, 136 S. E. 862. 

Phillips v. Com., 143 Va. 504, 129 S. E. 257. 

Greenleaf on Ev. (16th Ed.), vol. 1, sec. 223. 

And in State v. Spurr, 100 W. Va. 121, 130 S. E. 81, it is said: "A confession or admission of an accomplice in a felony, made after the crime has been committed, and not a part of the res gestae, and not made in the presence of the accused on trial, is not evidence against the accused; and it is error to permit the persons who heard the confession or admission to detail the same to the jury."

§ 554 

And in State v. McCoy, 61 W. Va. 258, 57 S. E. 294, it is also held: "When two or more accomplices are tried together for felony, the declaration or confession of one made after the criminal act in the absence of the others, too long after it to be part of the res gestae, is admissible in evidence; but the court must instruct the jury that it is not to be considered as evidence against any one but the one making the confession.' 

Greenleaf, vol. 1 (16th Ed.), sec. 233. 

Jones v. Com., 31 Gratt. 830. 

Oliver v. Com., 77 Va. 590. 

Garnett v. Com., 117 Va. 902, 83 S. E. 1083. 

And in State v. Roby, 106 W. Va. 427, 145 S. E. 743, it is held that statements made by an accomplice after the completion of the crime, in the absence of the accused, and which are not a part of the res gestae cannot be introduced in evidence against the latter. § 801. Same, where the admission of such evidence constitutes harmless error. 

But in Hutchinson v. Com., 133 Va. 710, 112 S. E. 624, it is held that where the admission of such evidence (admissions of accomplice not in the presence of defendant) is not prejudicial to accused, such error is harmless. § 802. Where accomplice is promised immunity for his testimony against participants in the crime. 

In Belcher v. Com., 160 Va. 891, 168 S. E. 468, the evidence showed that defendant had made a confession to the commonwealth's attorney, and had previously testified against those jointly indicted with him. Later defendant was placed on trial and his prior confession admitted in evidence against him. It was shown that such confession was made while accused was under arrest charged with having committed the crime, by leading questions of the commonwealth's attorney and by both words and conduct causing defendant to believe that if he testified for the commonwealth he would not be prosecuted. The confession was held inadmissible by the appellate court, which said:

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS & 803 

"In view of what the commonwealth's attorney knew had taken place, he should not have permitted Belcher's testimony to have gone to the jury without any intimation. to it that he was testifying under the belief that by so doing he himself would escape punishment or receive only light punishment. If the practice followed in this case. should be indulged in by prosecuting attorneys and tolerated by the courts, it would jeopardize the lives and liberties of innocent men and women everywhere.” 

AIDERS AND ABETTORS. 

§ 803. Aiders and abettors defined. 

An aider and abettor is one who is present, actually or constructively, aiding and abetting the principal actor in the commission. of the crime. Actual physical presence is not necessary, a constructive presence is sufficient, as where one keeps watch or stands guard at a convenient distance while the crime is being committed by the principal actor. However, mere presence and consent alone are not sufficient to constitute one an aider and abettor in the commission of a crime. There must be something said. or done by him showing his consent to the felonious purpose and contribution to its execution. In other words, to make one an aider and abettor, he must be shown to have procured, encouraged, countenanced, or approved the commission of the crime, i. e. that he shared the criminal intent of the actual perpetrator of the offense, or in some manner committed an overt act. 

Wren v. Com., 26 Gratt. 952. 

Reynolds v. Com., 33 Gratt. 834. 

Kemp v. Com., 80 Va. 443. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 849, 38 S. E. 184. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 677, 115 S. E. 543. 

Brown v. Com., 130 Va. 733, 107 S. E. 809. 

Triplett v. Com., 141 Va. 577, 127 S. E. 486. 

Harold v. Com., 147 Va. 617, 136 S. E. 658. 

Gray v. Com., 150 Va. 571, 142 S. E. 397. 

Boggs v. Com., 153 Va. 828, 149 S. E. 445. 

Spratley v. Com., 154 Va. 854, 152 S. E. 362. 

Frazier v. Com., 155 Va. 1067, 156 S. E. 369. 

West v. Com., 156 Va. 975, 157 S. E. 538. 

Hurd v. Com., 159 Va. 880, 165 S. E. 536. 

Creasy v. Com., 166 Va. 721, 186 S. E. 63.

State v. Patterson, 109 W. Va. 588, 155 S. E. 661.

In West v. Com., supra, it is held: "To constitute one an aider and abettor it must be shown that he procured, encouraged, countenanced or approved the commission of the crime." 

And in Triplett v. Com., supra, it is also held: "To constitute one an aider and abettor, he must be guilty of some overt act, or he must share the criminal intent of the principal party who commits the crime." 

Wharton on Homicide, 3rd Ed., sec. 45. 

Daingerfield v. Thompson, 33 Gratt. 148. 

Hunt v. DiBacco, 69 W. Va. 449, 71 S. E. 584. § 804. Mere presence not sufficient to make one an aider and abettor.

But mere presence is not sufficient to render one guilty of aiding and abetting the commission of crime. There must be something done or said by him showing his consent to the felonious purpose and contributing to it.

Hurd v. Com., 159 Va. 882, 165 S. E. 536. § 805. To be aider and abettor, one must share criminal intent.

It is the universal rule that to constitute one an aider and abettor, it is essential that the aider and abetter share the criminal intent of the principal. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 848, 38 S. E. 184. 

State v. Clifford, 57 W. Va. 1, 52 S. E. 981.

Wharton's Crim. Law, sec. 258. § 807. Where crime is committed through an innocent agent. 

In State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 669, 60 S. E. 785, it is held: "If a person with felonious intent, through the instrumentality of an innocent agent, cause a crime to be committed, he, and not the agent, is the principal, and is pun- 2 CT-2

ishable accordingly, although he was not present at the time and place of the offense either actually or constructively, within the meaning of the law of aider and abettor, operative between principal and accessory before the fact. 

As between him and the innocent agent, there is no such relation. He alone is the guilty party. "Under such circumstances, an exception to the rules applicable to principals and accessories, in the trial of criminal cases, arises ex necessitate legis." 

See authorities cited in opinion. § 808. Whether one is aider and abettor may be determined by circumstantial evidence.

§ 809. Guilt of aider and abettor must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt. 

In Hurd v. Com., 159 Va. 892-3, 165 S. E. 536, it is held: * * * "The evidence introduced by the Commonwealth to convict the accused, considered collectively, as it must be when circumstantial evidence is relied upon, is just as consistent with his innocence as with his guilt, and when this is true that interpretation which acquits the accused must be accepted. 

It is true that after the jury have returned their verdict and the court is called upon to set it aside as contrary to the evidence, the motion is heard practically as on a demurrer to the evidence, and it is the duty of the court to consider whether or not the evidence is sufficient to sustain the verdict. But the rule does not leave the jury at liberty to guess, and where a fact is equally susceptible of two interpretations, one of which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, they cannot arbitrarily adopt that interpretation which incriminates him." Citing,

§ 810. Indictment of aider and abettor, principal must be named. 

In State v. Stone, 109 W. Va. 721, 156 S. E. 80, it is said: "The one who is the absolute perpetrator is principal in first degree. The other, who aids and abets, is principal in the second degree. To make a man principal in the second degree, there must be a principal in the first degree to do the principal fact-to perpetrate the main fact; failing in that, there can be no principal in the second degree. 

Therefore the full information of the character of the accusation which section 14, Article III of the Constitution requires, necessarily includes the name of the one, if known, whom the accused is charged with aiding and abetting. If the name is not known that fact should appear (in the indictment), and the facts of aiding and abetting set forth." Citing, * * * 

31 Corpus Juris., p. 738, sec. 288. 

Taylor v. Com., 28 Ky. L. Rep. 819, 90 S. W. 581. 

Mulligan v. Com., 84 Ky. 232. 

And in State v. Wamsley, 109 W. Va. 574, 156 S. E. 75, it is said: * * * "All persons who were present aiding and abetting the commission of the fact are principals in the second degree at common law and may be charged in the indictment as having done the act. 

Where several are present and abet the fact, an indictment may lay it generally as done by all, or specially, as done by one and abetted by the rest. Or if the punishment for principals in the first and second degrees is the same, all may be indicted as principals in the first degree." Citing, 1 Russell on Crimes, pp. 26-29. 

See other authorities cited in opinion.

CONSPIRACY. 

§ 811. General law. 

It is the general rule in the Virginias that where two or more

§ 560 

persons combine to do any unlawful act, if the act of one in furtherance of the common plan, terminates in a criminal result, though not the particular result intended, all are liable. That is, if a defendant and those indicted with him had a common design to do an unlawful act, then, in contemplation of law, whatever act any one of them did in furtherance of the original design, is the act of all, and all are guilty of whatever crime was committed. To illustrate: If two or more persons combine and conspire together to commit any unlawful act, and death occurs in the prosecution of the design, it is murder in law, although the death happened collaterally, or beside the criminal design. 

State v. Powers, 91 W. Va. 746, 113 S. E. 912. 

State v. Wisman, 93 W. Va. 187, 116 S. E. 698. 

State v. Phillips, 111 W. Va. 525, 163 S. E. 24. 

Also see authorities cited in these opinions. 

In Brown v. Com., 130 Va. 733, 107 S. E. 809, it is held: "All those who assemble themselves together with intent to commit a wrongful act, the execution whereof makes probable, in the very nature of things, a crime not specifically designed, but incidental to that which was the object of the confederacy, are responsible for such incidental crime."

Williamson v. Com., 4 Gratt. 547. 

Anthony v. Com., 88 Va. 850, 14 S. E. 834. 

Harris v. Com., 113 Va. 746, 73 S. E. 561. 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 549, 189 S. E. 329.

Werth v. Adj. Bureau, 160 Va. 845, 171 S. E. 255. 

In West Virginia, Code 61-6-7 (sec. 6033), under what is commonly known as the "Red Men's Act," the larceny of property as a result of a conspiracy is a felony. This statute contemplates the taking of property by physical force or threats, and against the owner's consent. It does not apply where the property is taken by false pretenses with the owner's consent and without force or threats. Virginia has no such statute. 

State v. Porter, 25 Va. 685. 

State v. Piscoineri, 68 W. Va. 76, 69 S. E. 375.

NOTE: In preparing an indictment under this statute refer to sec. 1143.

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 813 

§ 812. Mere knowledge of contemplated crime not sufficient to make one a conspirator. 

In State v. Naylor, 113 W. Va. 446, 168 S. E. 489, it is held: "Mere cognizance that another threatens the commission of a crime is not sufficient to make one a conspirator in the crime." § 813. Admissions and declarations of conspirators as evidence.

When a prima facie conspiracy has been established by evidence, the acts, admissions and declarations done and made by the parties, in pursuance thereof, not in the presence of one another, are admissible in evidence against all conspirators. And such evidence is not confined to cases in which the prosecution is for the conspiracy alone, but also extends to cases in which the prosecution is for the crime committed in pursuance of the conspiracy. 

Nor does it matter whether the prosecution be jointly against all, or severally against each, or one of the conspirators. But as a rule, before such evidence is admissible it must be shown that the person whose acts or declarations are sought to be made evidence, was, at the time of making or doing them, himself a conspirator; and also that they were done or said in furtherance of the object of the conspiracy. 

Sands v. Com., 21 Gratt. 871. 

Brown v. Com., 86 Va. 935, 11 S. E. 799. 

Cottrell v. Com., 134 Va. 554, 113 S. E. 728. 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 694. 

State v. Burnett, 47 W. Va. 731, 35 S. E. 983. 

State v. Grove, 61 W. Va. 697, 57 S. E. 296. 

State v. Robinson, 97 W. Va. 691, 127 S. E. 46. 

State v. Price, 114 W. Va. 736, 174 S. E. 518.

However, it would seem that the general rule that a prima facie case of conspiracy must be made out before evidence of acts, admissions and declarations of co-conspirators is offered in evidence, relates to the order of the introduction of testimony, and whether it is enforced or not is wholly immaterial, provided the conspiracy is finally proved. 

In State v. Prater, 52 W. Va. 132, 43 S. E. 230, it is held:

$562 

"While it is usual to first introduce the evidence of the conspiracy before the proof of such acts or declarations is offered, yet the order of introduction of the evidence is in the discretion of the court, and in such discretion the acts or declarations may be received subject to the production of subsequent proof of the conspiracy which will make them available as against the defendant.

Al- though such evidence of the declaration of an alleged coconspirator be admitted without such foundation being laid, yet the judgment will not be reversed for this reason, if the facts proved, or evidence certified, show that prima facie the fact of conspiracy had been established." * * * 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 679. 

Hatchett v. Com., 75 Va. 925. 

Gardner v. Com., 134 Va. 681, 114 S. E. 561. 

See secs. 460 and 462. § 814. Same, when made or done after the conspiracy or its unlawful purpose has been consummated.

It is also the rule that after the conspiracy has been consummated, and the common purpose carried fully into effect, subsequent acts and declarations of any of the co-conspirators, made in the absence of the others, are not admissible in evidence against the latter. But they are admissible against those who made them, as well as those present when they were made. In such cases the trial court, by proper instructions to the jury, should limit the consideration of such evidence as against those making the declarations or who were present when they were made. 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 680. 

State v. Goodwin, 32 W. Va. 177, 9 S. E. 85. 

State v. Baker, 84 W. Va. 151, 99 S. E. 252. 

Bank v. Waddill, 31 Gratt. 469. 

Oliver v. Com., 77 Va. 590. 

Burford v. Com., 132 Va. 551, 110 S. E. 428. 

Jarrell v. Com., 132 Va. 551, 110 S. E. 430. 

Garnett v. Com., 117 Va. 902, 83′ S. E. 1083. 

McCoy v. Com., 125 Va. 771, 99 S. E. 644. 

Seymour v. Com., 133 Va. 775, 112 S. E. 806. 

Ins. Co. v. Taylor (W. Va.), 254 Fed. 807. 

State v. Price, 114 W. Va. 736, 174 S. E. 518 

See secs. 460 and 462.

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 817 

§ 815. Same, where a part of the res gestae. 

In Willis v. Bank, 153 Va. 392, 149 S. E. 624, it is held: "A statement of a conspirator after the conspiracy is accomplished is generally inadmissible; but when the incident is so closely connected with the major purpose of the parties as to form a part of the res gestae, it is admissible." 

5 R. C. L., p. 1089. 

State v. Hively, 103 W. Va. 237, 136 S. E. 862. 

See sec. 462. § 816. Conspiracy may be shown by circumstantial evidence. 

In State v. Wisman, 93 S. E. 188, 116 S. E. 698, it is held: "In order to show a community of the unlawful purpose, it is not necessary to show an express agreement or an understanding between the parties. A conspiracy or common purpose may be inferred from the circumstances; preconcert may be shown by circumstances as well as by direct evidence." 

And in State v. Prater, 52 W. Va. 132, 43 S. E. 230, it is also held: "Proof of conspiracy or the existence of a common design on the part of two or more persons to commit a crime for which they are jointly indicted may be extracted from the circumstances connected with the transaction which forms the subject of the accusation; and when they are such as fairly tend to prove such conspiracy or common design, they constitute a sufficient foundation for the admission of the acts and declarations of the parties as evidence against the others." 

See authorities cited in these opinions. Also 

Coal Co. v. Mitchell, 245 U. S. 229, 38 S. Ct. 65, 62 L. 

Ed. 260.

See Chapter on Circumstantial Evidence. 

§ 817. Absent conspirator, degree of guilt. 

In State v. Roberts, 50 W. Va. 422, 40 S. E. 484, it is held: "A conspirator who is absent at the time the felony is committed, taking no part in the actual commission of the offense, is an accessory before the fact and can only be indicted and punished as such."

§ 564 

Hatchett v. Com., 75 Va. 925. 

State v. Lilly, 47 W. Va. 496, 35 S. E. 837. 

§ 818. Indictment for conspiracy. 

It is held that counts in an indictment charging both the conspiracy and the act committed as a result thereof may be joined. 

In State v. Wisman, 93′ W. Va. 185, 116 S. E. 698, it is held: "Counts charging a conspiracy and also the offense committed in pursuance thereof may be joined when both offenses are similar in nature and in mode of trial and punishment." 

See authorities cited in opinion.

But this practice is both cumbersome and unnecessary. Al- though the conspiracy is a complete offense by itself before it is carried into effect, yet if the act conspired to be done be a felony, and it is carried into effect, and the felony is committed, the conspiracy is merged in the felony, and the indictment should be for the felony, and not for both the conspiracy and the felony. 

Anthony v. Com., 88 Va. 850, 14 S. E. 834. 

State v. Wisman, supra.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

Accessories Before the Fact. 

Instructions Nos. 1 and 2 below are taken from the record in

State v. Snyder, who was indicted in Raleigh County, West Virginia, charged with being an accessory before the fact to an attempt to commit murder by Tony Stafford and others. Stafford, one of the principals, was convicted, State v. Stafford, 89 W. Va. 

301, 109 S. E. 326. Snyder, one of the accessories before the fact, secured a change of venue to Pocahontas County where he too was convicted; the Supreme Court denying a writ of error. § 824. Accessories before the fact defined. 

1. The court instructs the jury that under the law of this state the felonious killing of a person by another person or persons lying in wait is murder of the first degree, and that a felonious attempt by a person or persons to kill another person or persons by lying in wait is an attempt to commit murder of the first degree, and is a felony; and the jury is further instructed that under the law of this state for a person, before such last mentioned

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 824 

felony is committed, to feloniously and knowingly counsel, procure or abet another person or persons to commit the same, makes such person so counseling, abetting and procuring such offense to be committed, an accessory before the fact to such felony, provided that such person so counseling, abetting and procuring was absent at the time the offense was committed so as not to be able to render any immediate help, assistance, or encouragement in the actual commission of such offense; and every such accessory before the fact shall be punishable as if he were such person or persons who actually committed such felony. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case that Tony Stafford, (nine other principals named), or any or all of them, on the 16th day of November, 1917, in Raleigh County, West Virginia, by lying in wait, feloniously attempted to slay, kill and murder John Ranson, John

Spears, H. E. Nuckols, or either, any or all of them, and if the jury further believe from the evidence that Ed Snyder, prior to the commission of the said crime, feloniously, wilfully, maliciously, deliberately, premeditatedly, unlawfully and knowingly did counsel, abet and procure the said Tony Stafford, (nine other principals named), or either, any, or all of them, to commit such felony, and that the said Ed Snyder was so far absent at the time the said offense was committed as not to be able to render any immediate help, assistance or encouragement in the commission of such offense, then the court instructs the jury that the defendant, Ed Snyder, is an accessory before the fact to such felony, and the jury should so find. 

3. The jury is instructed that an accessory before the fact is one who is absent at the time of the actual perpetration of the crime, but procures, counsels, commands, incites or abets another to commit the crime. The crime of an accessory before the fact is a particular one. The absence of the accessory before the fact at the time and place of the principal offense is an essential element of the crime, and absence at the time the crime was committed is necessary to make him an accessory before the fact; and in this case, Grover Cremeans not being indicted as an accessory before the fact, therefore, if you do not believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that he killed John Smith,

§ 570 

as alleged in the indictment, or that he was present when the said John Smith was killed, aiding and abetting in the killing of said John Smith as alleged in the indictment, he cannot be convicted. 

But in order to constitute presence at the time and place of killing said John Smith, it is not necessary that it should be shown by the evidence in the case that Grover Cremeans was immediately standing by when the said Smith was killed, within sight or hearing, it is enough if the jury believe from the evidence in this case that said Grover Cremeans kept watch or guard at a convenient distance while Smith was being killed by the principal actor. A principal in the second degree is one who is present aiding and abetting the principal actor in the commission of the crime and actual physical presence is not necessary, a constructive presence is sufficient as in the instance of a person keeping watch or guard at a convenient distance while the murder is being committed by the principal actor. 

State v. Cremeans, 62 W. Va. 137, 57 S. E. 406. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that on the 16th day of November, 1917, that Tony

Stafford, (nine other defendants named), or either or all, or any of them, armed with rifles, guns and pistols, loaded with powder and leaden and steel balls and bullets, did go within range and shooting distance of the tipple of the Glen White mines, in which the cage that is used for bringing men up out of said mine, and that Carl Crim, (eight other defendants named), did then and there lie in wait until John Ranson and other persons mentioned in the indictment in this case came up on said cage, and did then and there shoot at the said John Ranson and said other persons mentioned in the indictment, or either, or any, or all of them, with said rifles, guns and pistols, loaded as aforesaid, with intent then and there to kill them, or either or any or all of them; and if the jury believe from the evidence that the said Tony Stafford was then and there present or within about three hundred yards of the said Carl Crim, (eight other defendants named), and watching to prevent surprise whilst the said Carl Crim, (eight other defendants named), were on the hillside committing said offense, or with the intention of giving assistance, should occasion arise, to the said Carl Crim, (eight other defendants named),

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 826 

and was near enough to afford it should the occasion arise, then the court instructs the jury that the defendant, Tony Stafford, would be guilty of an attempt to commit murder of the first degree. 

State v. Stafford, 89 W. Va. 307, 109 S. E. 326. 

5. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in the case that David Flaherty, Fry, and Bingham, or that David Flaherty and either Fry or Bingham, assaulted and injured R. B. Yowell, in said county, in pursuance of a combination, conspiracy, or understanding entered into by them either before they reached the place where said assault was committed, or after they reached there, to do said Yowell bodily harm or injury, then it is immaterial and makes no difference who struck the first blow, or who brought on said assault and conflict. 

State v. Flaherty, 42 W. Va. 241, 24 S. E. 885. § 825. Punishment of an accessory before the fact. 

1. The court instructs the jury in this case that, if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant, Grover Cremeans, is principal either in the first or second degree, he is liable to punishment as if he were principal in the first degree. 

State v. Cremeans, 62 W Va. 136, 57 S. E. 405. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that Eli Heller set fire to the building occupied by Max Heller as a store, as charged in the indictment, and that Max Heller, though not at Elkton at the time of the fire, planned, counseled or encouraged the firing of the building, then the said Max Heller is guilty as an accessory before the fact, as charged in the indictment, and liable to the same punishment as is prescribed by law for the principal actor. 

Heller v. Com., 137 Va. 788, 119 S. E. 69. 

§ 826. Corroboration of testimony of accomplice. 

1. The court instructs the jury that by corroboration of the testimony of an accomplice the court does not mean that he must be corroborated as to his whole testimony, but that if a portion of

$ 572 

his testimony, which is material to the issue, is confirmed in any material part of the case, or if it appears that he has testified truly in some material particulars, the jury may infer that he has in others, and that if the jury believe that an accomplice has testified truthfully as to matters which are material to the issue in this case they may convict on his uncorroborated testimony. 

2. The court instructs the jury that while it is dangerous to convict on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice, yet, when said testimony is corroborated by other evidence and circumstances such as finding the property and the testimony of other witnesses, they have a right to believe or disbelieve, according to the circumstances, the testimony of said accomplice. 

State v. May, 62 W. Va. 133, 57 S. E. 366. 

3. The court instructs the jury that although the testimony of an accomplice if unsupported is always received with great caution, yet an accomplice is unquestionably a competent witness, unless he has been previously sentenced for an infamous offense, and he is competent alone; that is, a prisoner may be convicted on the testimony of an accomplice uncorroborated by that of any other witness, it being the duty of the jury in all cases to consider the evidence and judge of the credit of the witnesses. 

Com. v. King, 9 Va. Law Reg. 653, 657.

Aiding and Abetting. 

§ 827. Aiders and abettors equally guilty with principal. 

1. The court instructs the jury, that though they believe that neither Samuel Burton nor Sylvanus Conquest actually fired at or upon the hack in which several people were riding as aforesaid, but that some other person or persons maliciously actually fired upon said hack in which the said people were riding, with guns and pistols, charged with deadly loads, and killed John Topping, who was passing by or standing near the scene of shooting, yet if they further believe the said Samuel Burton and Sylvanus Conquest were present and lending countenance, encouraging,

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 827 

aiding, abetting, counseling, advising or consenting to the firing upon said hack, as aforesaid, then they are guilty of murder. 

Burton, et al. v. Com., 108 Va. 900, 62 S. E. 376.

NOTE: This instruction was held to state a correct legal proposition of law, although held erroneous in above case because there was no evidence upon which to base it. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe, from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Jack Horton, wilfully, maliciously, deliberately, and premeditatedly, killed William T. Horton, in the County of Russell, and that the defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, or either of them, were present aiding, abetting, counseling, advising, or consenting to said crime, that then the said defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, or either one of them who were so present, aiding, abetting, counseling, advising, or consenting to said crime, that then the said defendants, Taylor Horton, and Henry Horton, or either one of them who were so present, aiding, abetting, counseling, advising, or consenting to said crime, are guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 848, 38 S. E. 184, and affirmed in 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 706, 115 S. E. 543. 

3. The court instructs the jury that unless they believe from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the shot which killed Dollard was fired by Madison Brown, the prisoner, with the wilful, deliberate, and premeditated design of killing, then the offense would not be murder in the first degree, unless you further believe that, though the shot was by another, such other was engaged jointly with the prisoner in the commission of a felonious act; that it was fired in the attempt to accomplish their common escape; and that the prisoner was present aiding and abetting the person who fired the shot. 

Brown v. Com., 90 Va. 676-7, 19 S. E. 447. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if they believe, from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt in this case, that Jack Horton killed William T. Horton, as charged in the indictment, and that the defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, or either of them, were present aiding, abetting, counseling, advising or 2 CT-3

§ 574 

consenting to said crime, that then the said defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, are equally guilty with Jack Horton in the said murder. 

Horton v. Com., supra. § 828. Must be a principal before there can be an aider and abettor.

The court instructs the jury that there can be no such thing as an aider and abettor unless there is a principal in the commission of a crime; and, it is, therefore, necessary for the Commonwealth to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the principal is guilty of the offense charged before the jury can consider the question as to whether there is an aider or abettor. And the jury is instructed that mere presence is not sufficient to constitute one an aider and abettor, and that whenever reasonable doubt exists as to the intentions of one charged as an aider and abettor, he cannot be found guilty as an aider and abettor; and the jury is further instructed that mere consent is not sufficient to constitute one an aider and abettor, but before a defendant charged as an aider and abettor in the commission of a criminal offense can be convicted, it is incumbent upon the Commonwealth to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant so charged as an aider and abettor was present and shared in the criminal intent of the principal. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 706-7, 115 S. E. 543. § 829. Principals in first and second degrees defined. 

1. The court instructs the jury that principals in the first degree in every murder or other crime are those who are the immediate perpetrators of the crime itself; that principals in the second degree are those persons who did not with their own hands commit the crime or act, but were present, aiding and abetting it in some way. It is not necessary, in order to make one a principal in the second degree, that he be actually present when the crime was committed, or that he actually participated in its commission. The test as to whether or not he is a principal in the second degree is, was he encouraging, inciting, or in some manner

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 829 

offering aid or consent to the crime. All persons present, lending countenance, or otherwise aiding, while another does the act, are principals in the second degree, and liable to the same punishment as if they were principals in the first degree, and actually committed the crime. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 853, 38 S. E. 184. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 707, 115 S. E. 543. 

2. The court instructs the jury that a principal in the second degree is one who is present aiding and abetting the principal in the commission of the crime and actual physical presence is not necessary, a constructive presence is sufficient as in the instance of a person keeping watch or guard at a convenient distance while. the murder is being committed by the principal actor. 

State v. Cremeans, 62 W. Va. 137, 57 S. E. 405. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that Toy Rasnake wilfully, maliciously, deliberately and premeditatedly shot and killed Rufus Sutherland in the County of Russell, and that the defendant, Ross Bumgardner, was present aiding, abetting, counseling, advising or consenting to said crime, that both Toy Rasnake and Ross Bumgardner are equally guilty of murder in the first degree in this case. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 706, 115 S. E. 543. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt in this case, that Jack Horton killed William T. Horton, as charged in the indictment, and that the defendants Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, or either of them, were present aiding, abetting, counseling, advising or consenting to said crime, that then the said defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, are equally guilty with Jack Horton in the said murder. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 854, 38 S. E. 184. 

5. The court instructs the jury that if they believe, from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Jack Horton, wilfully, maliciously, deliberately, premeditatedly, killed Wm.

T. Horton, in the County of Russell, and that the defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, or either of them, were

$ 576 

present aiding, abetting, counseling, advising, or consenting to said crime, that then the said defendants, Taylor Horton and Henry Horton, or either one of them who were so present, aiding, abetting, counseling, advising, or consenting to said crime, are guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 848, 38 S. E. 184. 

6. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant, Gilbert Nelson, killed Rogers Nelson, or that Jasper Nelson or Murrill Nelson killed him, and that Gilbert Nelson was present aiding, abetting, counseling, advising or consenting to said crime and that such killing was wilful, deliberate and premeditated, you should find the defendant guilty of murder in the first degree and fix his punishment at death, or by confinement in the penitentiary for life, or for any term not less than twenty years. If, however, you believe from the evidence that such killing was wilful and deliberate, but not premeditated, you should find the defendant guilty of murder in the second degree and fix his punishment at confinement in the penitentiary for not less than five nor more than twenty years. 

Nelson v. Com., 153 Va. 923, 150 S. E. 407. 

NOTE: In West Virginia the jury does not fix the punishment, and this instruction should be modified accordingly, and the punishment stated to accord with the statute. 

7. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that Sine Slyman came to his death by a gun shot wound inflicted by Burley Lamb, and that the defendant Paris May instigated and planned the killing from ambush, and by threats and menaces compelled the said Burley 

Lamb to fire the fatal shot which killed the deceased, and that said Paris May borrowed the gun with which the deceased was killed and gave it to the said Burley Lamb, and that the said Paris May was present at the shooting, aiding, counseling and abetting in the commission of the crime when the shot was fired, and cut the pack from the deceased and took his money, watch and pocket-book from the person of the deceased, at the time of the

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 830 

murder, then they will find the defendant, Paris May, guilty of murder in the first degree. 

State v. May, 62 W. Va. 133, 57 S. E. 366.

NOTE: If the defendant was guilty as charged in the instruction down to the asterisk, he was guilty of murder in the first degree. His interest was not affected by calling the attention of the jury to the other matters mentioned in the remainder of the instruction. 

8. The court instructs the jury that to constitute murder in the first degree, the prisoner, or Jasper Nelson and/or Murrill Nelson in concert with the prisoner must have been incited to the killing by malice, and the killing must have been a willful, deliberate and premeditated act on the part of the prisoner, or Jasper Nelson and/or Murrill Nelson in concert with the prisoner; that is to say, he, or they, must have willed, deliberated and premeditated that he, or they, should kill the deceased or do him some serious bodily injury, the necessary results of which would be his death, and from which he died; and to constitute a willful, deliberate and premeditated killing, it is not necessary that the intent to kill should exist for any particular length of time prior to the actual killing. It is only necessary that such intention should come into existence for the first time at the time of such killing or any time previously. 

Nelson v. Com., 153 Va. 924, 150 S. E. 407. § 830. Acts and declarations to be considered. 

The court instructs the jury that in considering whether or not 

Taylor Horton and Henry Horton are principals in the second degree in this case, aiding, abetting, counseling, advising, or consenting to said killing of Jack Horton, they may consider all the facts and declarations of the said Taylor Horton and Henry at the time of the said killing, both before and after the killing of the said William T. Horton, and if they believe from the whole evidence that they were so aiding and abetting in said crime, then they are guilty in this case. 

Horton v. Com., supra. Affirmed in 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 706, 115 S. E. 543.

$ 578 

§ 831. Principals in second degree.

The jury are instructed that if they believe from the evidence (in this case) that Robert Purdy, Dr. Lewis, or any other persons, at or in the said house of the accused, by the use of false pretenses, obtained from Joseph M. Fowlkes, the sum of $570.00, the jury cannot find the accused guilty of the larceny alleged in the indictment, unless they are satisfied from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the prisoner was present, aiding and abetting therein, or suffered or permitted the said persons so using the false pretenses, to use the said house with knowledge that such persons intended to use said house for the employing of such fraudulent pretense.

But if the prisoner was within easy call, to aid or assist them in their purpose, or in escaping, or in getting rid of, or misleading the person from whom such money was obtained, that is a presence, aiding and abetting, and the prisoner is as guilty as if he were personally present. 

Dull v. Com., 25 Gratt. 976. 

§ 832. Aiding and abetting robbery. 

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that Barney Cleaves robbed the prosecuting witness, William Meyers, as charged in the indictment, and that the prisoner, Henry Houston, was present aiding and abetting him therein, then the prisoner is guilty as principal in the second degree, although you may further believe that the prisoner neither beat nor struck the said William

Meyers, or that the prisoner after the robbing moved any portion. of the goods or articles carried away by the said Carney Cleaves, as the "fruits of said crime." 

Houston v. Com., 87 Va. 267-8, 12 S. E. 385. 

Boswell v. Com., 20 Gratt. 860.

NOTE: Under West Virginia Code, 61-11-6 (sec. 6118), and 

Virginia Code, sec. 4764, every principal in the second degree shall be punished as if he were the principal in the first degree. 

State v. Wamsley, 109 W. Va. 574, 156 S. E. 75.

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 833 

§ 833. Acts done after crime, not aiding and abetting. 

1. The court instructs the jury that any act done by either of the defendants, T. H. or H. H., after completion or consummation of the crime, and after the blow was struck that killed the deceased, cannot be considered as aiding and abetting the principal felon who struck the fatal blows and committed the crime, and unless the jury believe, from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the defendants, T. H. and H. H., aided or abetted the principal prior to the time the blows were struck that killed the deceased, and prior to the completion and consummation of the crime, the court tells the jury that the said defendants, T. H. and H. H., cannot be found guilty as aiders and abettors. 

Horton v. Com., supra. 

2. The court instructs the jury that any act done by T. H. after the completion or consummation of the crime, and after the blows were struck that killed the deceased, cannot be considered as aiding and abetting the principal felon who struck the fatal blows, and unless the jury believe, from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the defendant, T. H., aided or abetted the principal prior to the time the blows were struck that killed the deceased, and the completion of the crime, then the court tells the jury that the said defendant, T. H., cannot be found guilty as an aider or abettor. 

Horton v. Com., supra. 

3. The court further instructs the jury that any act done by the defendant, H. H., after the completion or consummation of the crime, and after the blows were struck that killed the deceased, cannot be considered as aiding and abetting the principal felon who struck the fatal blows, and unless the jury believe from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the defendant, H. H., aided or abetted the principal prior to the time the blows were struck that killed the deceased, and prior to the completion of the crime, then the court tells the jury that the said defendant, H. H., cannot be found guilty as an aider and abettor. 

Horton v. Com., supra.

 CONSPIRACY. 

§ 833a. Conspiracy to kill. 

1. The court instructs the jury that a conspiracy could be established by circumstantial evidence, and that such evidence was legally competent for that purpose; also as to whether an act which was committed was done by a member of the conspiracy could be established by circumstantial evidence, whether the identity of the individual who committed the act be established or not, and also whether the act was in pursuance of a common design could be ascertained by the same evidence. 

State v. McCoy, 61 W. Va. 260, 57 S. E. 294. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence, beyond any reasonable doubt, that a conspiracy was formed between the prisoner, Mary Jane Morgan, and other persons, whose names are unknown, that the purpose of that conspiracy was to murder Jacob Morgan, and that, pursuant to that conspiracy, the unknown members of the conspiracy, or some of them, killed Jacob Morgan, and that the killing was done with malice aforethought, either expressed or implied, and that the prisoner, Mary Jane Morgan, was present at the time Jacob Morgan was killed, and aided by acts, or encouraged by words or gestures, those actually engaged in said killing, then said prisoner was a principal in the killing and murder. 

State v. Morgan, 35 W. Va. 274, 13 S. E. 385. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if the three Praters had an understanding or agreement whereby Conley was to be killed, and, in pursuance of such understanding or agreement, they went to the place with deadly weapons in their possession and without any, or upon very slight provocation, either of them gave to Conley a mortal wound from which he died, the accused is prima facie guilty of murder in the first degree and the necessity rests upon him of showing extenuating circumstances. 

State v. Prater, 52 W. Va. 155, 43 S. E. 230. 

4. The jury is instructed by the court that even if you do believe before Friday, September 9, 1898, the deceased Charles Mc- 

Laughlin, the witness William Craig, the witness Frank Mc-

Laughlin and the witness James McLaughlin, had threatened, kicked, beat, bruised and assaulted the defendants; yet if you further believe from the evidence that the defendants followed the deceased and those who were with him, on the said Friday afternoon, down Market Street, from a point above Sixteenth Street to a point near the photograph gallery mentioned in evidence with the felonious intent to take the life of deceased and there without further provocation, justification or legal excuse shot and killed the deceased Charles McLaughlin as charged in the indictment then it is your duty to find them guilty of murder in the first degree. 

State v. Johnson, 49 W. Va. 692, 39 S. E. 665.

Accessory before the Fact. 

834. Jury cannot infer guilt of accessory from guilt of principal. The court instructs the jury in this case that although the jury may believe from the evidence in this case beyond all reasonable doubt that Tony Stafford and (name all the other principals in the crime) or one or more of them, did attempt to commit murder in the first degree as charged in the indictment in this case, the court instructs the jury that they cannot infer the guilt of the defendant, Ed. Snyder, as an accessory before the fact, from the guilty conduct of the said principals in said crime alone; the court further instructs the jury that they cannot find the defendant, Ed. 

Snyder, guilty as an accessory before the fact as charged in the indictment in this case unless they are convinced beyond all reasonable doubt, by the evidence in this case, that the defendant, Ed. Snyder, did counsel, aid, abet, procure, hire or command the said Tony Stafford and (name all principals), or one or more of them to commit the principal offense charged in the indictment in this case. In other words, the guilt of the accused in this case can in no way, under the law, be inferred from the guilt of the principal alone, but the guilt of the accused must be proven by the evidence in this case beyond all reasonable doubt. 

, State v. Snyder, writ of error refused.

The court instructs the jury that before they can find the defendant, Jacob Roberts, guilty as charged in the indictment, they must believe beyond all reasonable doubt, that he entered into a conspiracy and confederation with Thomas Hardin, Edmond Murphy, Malan Prater and James Roberts, or any one of them, for the purpose of robbing B. C. Bateman, and in pursuance of such conspiracy said Bateman was robbed, as charged in the indictment, and that such belief must be founded upon the evidence adduced before them in the trial of this case. 

State v. Roberts, 50 W. Va. 427, 40 S. E. 484. Accomplices. § 836. Uncorroborated testimony of accomplice ceived with caution. 

Also given in, State v. Snyder, writ of error refused. 

1. The court instructs the jury that the testimony of an accomplice in crime, that is, a person who actually commits or participates in a crime, is admissible in evidence, yet the evidence of an accomplice in crime, when not corroborated by some person or persons not implicated in the crime, as to matters material to the issue, that is, matters connecting the defendant with the commission of the crime as charged against him, ought to be received. with great caution by the jury before they should convict on such testimony. 

Simpson v. Com., 135 Va. 749, 115 S. E. 392. 

Hunt v. Com., 126 Va. 816, 101 S. E. 896. 

State v. Hammond, 96 W. Va. 99, 122 S. E. 363. re- 2. The court instructs the jury that the testimony of accomplices must be received with great care and caution, and if you believe the testimony of an alleged accomplice was false, and that he was induced to testify falsely either by fear of punishment or hope of reward, you must disregard that testimony in its entirety. 

Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 483-4, 124 S. E. 240.

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 836 

3. The court instructs the jury that while the rule of decision in this jurisdiction is that the jury, as triers of fact, may, if they see proper to do so, convict the accused upon the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice alone, nevertheless the principle is well settled that the evidence of an accomplice must be received and acted upon by the jury with great caution, and the jury are further instructed that if two or more accomplices are produced as witnesses, they are not deemed to corroborate each other, but the same rule is applied, and the same corroboration is required as if they were but one. 

Hunt v. Com., 126 Va. 819, 101 S. E. 896. 

4. The court instructs the jury that, while they may find a verdict upon the unsupported testimony of an accomplice, such evidence is to be received with great caution, and the court, in this case, warns the jury of the danger of basing a verdict on the unsupported testimony of an accomplice. 

Draper v. Com., 132 Va. 659, 111 S. E. 471. 

5. The court further instructs the jury that while you may convict the accused upon the uncorroborated evidence of accomplices (and Jones and Watson represent themselves as accomplices) yet the law is that their evidence must be received (by the jury) with great care and caution, for the source of such evidence is tainted with the danger of collusion between them, and the temptation to exculpate themselves by laying the crime upon another is so strong that the court warns the jury against convicting upon their uncorroborated testimony; and this is equally true if two or more accomplices testify to the same or nearly similar facts, for they are not deemed to corroborate each other; moreover, the corroboration or confirmation must relate to some fact or facts tending to establish independently, the guilt of the accused. 

, Clark v. Com., 135 Va. 496, 115 S. E. 704.

NOTE: Attention is called to the fact that in West Virginia it is held that the trial court cannot properly instruct the jury as to the weight to be given to the testimony of an accomplice. 

State v. Betsall, 11 W. Va. 704.

State v. Thompson, 21 W. Va. 756.

State v. Hammond, 96 W. Va. 99, 122 S. E. 363. 

Rex v. Tate, 15 Am. Cas. 698, note. § 837. Testimony of accomplice not corroborated by agreeing testimony of another accomplice. 

1. The court instructs the jury that if you believe from the evidence that the witnesses (name participants in the crime who have testified against the defendant) are accomplices in the crime. charged against the defendant in this case, then it is the law that the testimony of one accomplice cannot be considered as being corroborated by the agreeing testimony of another accomplice. 

, State v. Stafford, 89 W. Va. 301, 109 S. E. 326, and 

State v. Snyder, (writ of error refused). Given in 

Hunt v. Com., 126 Va. 819, 101 S. E. 896. 

2. The court instructs the jury that the testimony of one accomplice cannot be considered as being corroborated by the agreeing testimony of another accomplice. 

Jones v. Com., 111 Va. 868, 69 S. E. 953.

NOTE: It was held error in Jones' case to refuse instruction number 2 above. See also, 1 Greenleaf on Evidence (15th Ed.), sec. 381. 

Woods v. Com., 86 Va. 929, 11 S. E. 798. 

Byrd v. Com., 2 Va. Cases 490.

The accepted rule is that, if two or more accomplices are produced as witnesses, they are not deemed to corroborate each other, but the same rule is applied, and the same confirmation is required, as if there were but one. See also, Jones v. Com., supra, and cases there cited. 

3. The jury is instructed that if two or more accomplices are produced as witnesses, they are not deemed to corroborate each other, but the same rule is applied, and the same corroboration is required as if they were but one. 

Hunt v. Com., 126 Va. 819, 101 S. E. 896. § 838. Confession of accomplice, effect of. 

The court instructs the jury that although you may believe

ACCESSORIES, ACCOMPLICES, AIDERS AND ABETTORS § 840 

from the evidence that the witness, Alva Jones, may have made an alleged confession to the Prosecuting Attorney, and other statements as to the guilt of the defendant, Hively, of the charge against him in this case, still you cannot consider any of such statements or any part thereof as any evidence against the defendant, Hively, but such statements, if any were made by Alva Jones, can only be considered by you as going to the credibility of Alva Jones and not as to the guilt of Howard Hively. 

State v. Hively, 108 W. Va. 236, 150 S. E. 729.

Aiding and Abetting. 

§ 839. What constitutes aiding and abetting. 

1. The court instructs the jury that to constitute an aider and abettor it is essential that there should be: First, presence, actual or constructive; second, participation in the crime. But the court further tells the jury that any encouragement or act of assistance is a participation in the crime. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 856, 38 S. E. 184. 

2. The court instructs the jury that it is necessary, in order to make one an aider and abettor, that he should do something showing his consent to the felonious purpose, and contributing to its execution. 

Horton v. Com., supra. § 840. To constitute the crime of aiding and abetting, there must be a principal. 

1. The court instructs the jury that there can be no such thing as an aider and abettor unless there is a principal in the commission of a crime; and, it is, therefore, necessary for the Commonwealth to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the principal is guilty of the offense charged before the jury can consider the question as to whether there is an aider or abettor. And the jury is instructed that mere presence is not sufficient to constitute one an aider and abettor, and that whenever reasonable doubt exists as to the intentions of one charged as an aider and abettor, he cannot be found guilty as an aider and abettor; and the jury is

§ 586 

further instructed that mere consent is not sufficient to constitute one an aider and abettor, but before a defendant charged as an aider and abettor in the commission of a criminal offense can be convicted, it is incumbent upon the commonwealth to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant so charged as an aider and abettor was present and shared in the criminal intent of the principal. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 706, 115 S. E. 543. 

2. The court instructs the jury that to constitute an aider and abettor, it is essential that the aider and abettor should share in the criminal intent of the principal or party who committed the offense. The court also instructs the jury that wherever a reasonable doubt exists as to the person's intention, in interfering in the struggle or fight between two other persons, he cannot be found guilty as an aider and abettor, and if the jury shall believe, from the evidence in this case, that a fight or difficulty arose or occurred between J. H. and W. T. H., the deceased, in which the said J. H. was the aggressor, and that the said J. H. struck the said W. T. H. two blows upon the head, which resulted in his death, then the court tells the jury that unless they shall further believe (from the evidence), beyond all reasonable doubt, that T. H. and H. H. interfered or took part in said difficulty, and shared in the criminal intent of the said J. H., they cannot find the said T. H. and H. H. guilty as aiders and abettors in the crime. 

Horton v. Com., supra. See also, Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 707, 115 S. E. 543. 

3. The court instructs the jury that to constitute an aider and abettor it is essential that the aider and abettor should share in the criminal intent of the principal party who committed the crime. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 707, 115 S. E. 543.
