§ 841. Arson at common law. 

At common law arson was the malicious burning of the dwelling-house of another, either in the day or nighttime. And the term "dwelling-house" embraced the dwelling-house proper, kitchen, meathouse, dairy, barn, stable, office, and all other buildings within the curtilage of such dwelling-house. 

Com. v. Posey, 4 Call. 109. 

Curran v. Com., 7 Gratt. 619.

Page v. Com., 26 Gratt. 943. 

§ 842. Statutes compared. 

In 1932 Virginia amended its statute relating to arson, but for the most part these amendments were not procedural, except as to slight changes necessary in the forms of indictments. 

In 1935 West Virginia enacted an entirely new statute on the subject, Code 61-3-1 to 7 (secs. 5951 (1), 5951 (7)), inclusive.

This act abolishes the distinction between arson in the day and night, divides the crime into the first, second, third, and fourth degrees, greatly reduces the punishment, and makes necessary material changes in indictment forms. § 843. Statutory meaning of the term "dwelling-house", rule in Virginia.

In Virginia the common-law definition of the term "dwellinghouse" has been modified by statute. Code, sec. 4429, provides: "No out-house, not adjoining a dwelling-house nor under the same roof (although within the curtilage thereof) shall be deemed parcel of such dwelling-house within the meaning of this chapter, unless some person usually lodge therein at night." 

And in Page v. Com., 26 Gratt. 943, it is held that to make an out-house, not adjoining a dwelling-house nor under the same roof, parcel thereof, within the meaning of this statute, two things must appear:

ARSON § 846 

1. That such out-house is within the curtilage of the dwellinghouse, and occupied therewith; and 

2. That some person usually lodges therein at night. 

Daniels v. Com., 172 Va. 583, 1 S. E. 2d 333. § 844. Same, rule in West Virginia.

Formerly, West Virginia had an identical statute, but it was repealed by the act of 1935. The first section of the new act makes it arson in the first degree wilfully and maliciously to set fire to or burn or cause to be burned any occupied or vacant dwellinghouse, or any kitchen, shop, barn, stable or other out-house that is parcel thereof, or belonging to or adjoining thereto irrespective of whether any one lodges therein at night or not. 

845. Presumption. 

It is a general rule of law that "when a building is burned, the presumption is that the fire was caused by an accident, rather than by the act of the accused, accompanied by a deliberate intent." 

Jones v. Com., 103 Va. 1012, 49 S. E. 666. 

Stine v. Com., 162 Va. 856, 174 S. E. 760. § 846. Offense may be proved by circumstantial evidence. 

In Stine v. Com., supra, it is held: 

66* * * in the nature of things, it is generally extremely difficult to prove by direct testimony that an incendiary who sets fire to his neighbor's property actually started the conflagration, and this kind of proof is not required to convict of the crime of arson; but the coincidence of circumstances relied on to convict, however strong and numerous, must conclusively prove (1) the fact that the crime has been perpetrated, and (2) that the accused is the guilty party. "On the whole, the doctrine may be said to be that special care should be exercised as to the corpus delicti, and there should be no conviction except where this part of the case is proved with particular clearness and certainty." Citing, Bishop's Crim. Proc., secs. 1058, 1059. 

Brown v. Com., 89 Va. 379, 16 S. E. 251. 2 CT-4

§ 590 

847. Burning one's own property.

In the early case of Erskine v. Com., 8 Gratt. 644, it was held : "The malicious burning by the owner of a house on his own land, the house being in the legal occupancy of another, is a violation of this section." 

But the statutes of both Virginias now make it arson for one to set fire to and burn, or cause to be burned certain kinds of property "whether the property of himself or another." 

Virginia Code, sec. 4428.

West Virginia Code, 61-3-1 (sec. 5991 (1)). 

§ 848. Indictments, rule in West Virginia. 

In West Virginia, Code 62-9-8 (sec. 6270), prescribes a form of indictment for arson, but the re-enactment of the statute in 1935 makes it necessary to modify this form to comply with the new law. The first three sections of the new act use the words "wilfully and maliciously sets fire to or burns or causes to be burned" as descriptive of the intent with which the offense is committed, and they must be used in the indictment, changing the word "or" to "and" and the word "causes" to "cause." The fourth section deals with attempts to commit arson, and the statutory words descriptive of the intent must be used in the indictment. The fifth section uses the word "wilfully" only as descriptive of the intent, and it must be used in the indictment. In other words, an indictment for any of the several offenses under the present statute must strictly follow the language of the section under which it is drawn. § 849. Same, rule in Virginia.

The old Virginia statute used the words "maliciously burn” only as descriptive of the criminal intent with which the offense was committed, and they were essential in the indictment. In the early case of Howell v. Com., 5 Gratt. 664, it was held: "It is not sufficient to use the words 'set fire to' a house. 

The word 'burn' must be used, that being the word used in the statute."

§ 853 ARSON 

But the 1932 amendments to the statute also uses the words "cause to be burned," as a further description of the offense, and they must now be included in the indictment. § 850. Burning either in the day or nighttime, rule in Virginia.

The 1932 amendments to the Virginia statute in nowise changed the necessity of the indictment alleging whether the burning was done in either the day or nighttime. The early case of Curran v. 

Com., 7 Gratt. 619, held that it is necessary for the indictment to charge the offense to have been committed either in the day or nighttime, as the case may be. But where the time of the commission of the crime is uncertain, on page 626 of the opinion in this case, it is further held: "It seems to me advisable in all cases of doubt as to the time of the burning, whether in the night or daytime, to frame the indictment with two counts, so as to adapt the proof to either." 

§ 851. Description of property in the indictment. 

In Richards v. Com., 81 Va. 110, it is held: "An indictment must describe the building with such particularity as to inform accused what building is meant, and the mere allegation of the burning of 'a certain other building' is insufficient." § 852. Value of property need not be alleged. 

In Wolf v. Com., 30 Gratt. 833, it is held: "It is unnecessary to charge the value of the building and the property therein separately; and an indictment charging the value of the building and contents as a whole is good on demurrer." 

State v. Huffman, 69 W. Va. 770, 73 S. E. 292.

 both, State v. Huffman, 69 W. Va. 770, 73 S. E. 292.

§ 863. Circumstantial evidence in arson. 

The court instructs the jury that from the very nature of the crime of arson and the secrecy with which the same may be committed circumstantial evidence is often the only kind of evidence which can be produced against the party charged with its commission; that circumstantial evidence is to be regarded in all cases by the jury; that when it is strong and convincing the jury should so consider it, neither enlarging nor belittling its force. And if when taken as a whole and fairly and candidly weighed it convinces the guarded judgment, the jury should act on such conviction. The jury is not to fancy the situations and circumstances which do not appear in evidence, but are to make those just and reasonable inferences from the circumstances proven which they, with guarded judgment as reasonable men, ordinarily would make under like circumstances in the grave transactions of life. And if such circumstantial evidence satisfies the jury of the defendant's guilt, beyond a reasonable doubt, it is their duty to find him guilty.

Taken from the record in both, State v. Huffman, 69 W. Va. 770, 73 S. E. 292. 

State v. Gebhart, 70 W. Va. 232, 73 S. E. 964. 

§ 864. Circumstances pointing to defendant. 

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that a crime was committed as charged in the indictment, and that all the circumstances of time, place, motive, means, opportunity and conduct concur in pointing out the defendant, C. B. Huffman, and no one else, beyond a reasonable doubt, as the perpetrator of the crime charged in this indictment, they should find him guilty.

ARSON DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 871. Presumption that fire was caused by accident. 

The court instructs the jury that when a fire occurs the prima facie or first blush presumption is that it was caused by accident rather than by a criminal agency; and in order to (justify) the conviction of one accused of criminal guilt in causing the fire, the burden rests upon the commonwealth to prove such guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. 

Heller v. Com., 137 Va. 789, 119 S. E. 69. 

Jones v. Com., 103 Va. 1021, 49 S. E. 663. § 872. Knowledge by accused that property was insured necessary.

The court instructs the jury that before they can convict the accused of the offense charged in the indictment in this case, it is necessary for the jury to believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused, George O. Stine, knew that the Mineral Hotel was insured at the time it burned; that the jury are not allowed to speculate or guess that accused knew it was so insured at the time, but in order to find him guilty they must believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that he knew it.

, Stine v. Com., 162 Va. 856, 174 S. E. 760. § 873. Failure of evidence to disclose another criminal agent.

The court instructs the jury, that if the jury believe beyond all reasonable doubt that the hotel was set afire, then the failure of the evidence to disclose any other criminal agent than the accused is not a circumstance which may be considered by the jury in determining whether or not he was guilty of the crime wherewith he is charged, and he is not to be prejudiced by the inability of the commonwealth to point out any other criminal agent, nor is he called upon to vindicate his own innocence by naming the guilty party. 

Stine v. Com., supra.

DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS 

§ 901. Attempt to shoot. 

§ 879. Attempts in general. 

At common law an attempt to commit a felony was a misdemeanor, hence the crime is wholly statutory, and is an intended apparent unfinished crime. It consists of the intention to commit a felony which must clearly appear and not depend on speculation or conjecture; and the doing of some direct ineffectual act towards its commission without actually committing it. 

See authorities cited in 

Michie's Digest, vol. 1, pp. 846-7, also

§ 882  

Dixon v. Com., 162 Va. 798, 173 S. E. 521. 

Merritt v. Com., 164 Va. 653, 180 S. E. 395. 

§ 880. Statutes compared. 

The Virginia Code, sec. 4767, and the West Virginia Code, 6111-8 (sec. 6120), are similar, and provide that every person who attempts to commit an offense, but fails to commit or is prevented from committing it, where it is not otherwise provided, shall be punished as therein stated. However, the Virginia statute contains special provisions for punishing attempts to commit rape and larceny not found in the West Virginia law. 

§ 881. What constitutes an attempt. 

In Cates v. Com., 111 Va. 837, 69 S. E. 520, it was held: "The intention to commit a felony, and the doing of some act towards its commission without actually committing it, is an attempt and is, from its very nature, an offense of a lower grade than the consummated felony." 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 706. 

Glover v. Com., 86 Va. 382, 10 S. E. 420. 

And in West v. Com., 156 Va. 975, 157 S. E. 538, it is held: "The failure to consummate a crime is as much an element of an attempt to commit it as the intent and the performance of an overt act towards its commission. It is also true that when a crime has been actually consummated, there can be no prosecution for an attempt." § 882. Distinction between preparation and attempt.

Preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offense. Where the preparation is to kill, one may be held to keep the peace, but not for an attempt to kill. The attempt is a direct movement toward the commission after the preparations are made, and herein lies the crime. In other words, the attempt contemplated by the statute must be manifested by acts which would end in the consummation of the particular offense, but for the intervention of circumstances independent of the will of the party. 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 706. 2 CT-5

$606 

State v. Baller, 26 W. Va. 90, 53 Am. Rep. 66. 

State v. Hager, 50 W. Va. 370, 40 S. E. 393. 

Collins v. Radford, 134 Va. 518, 113 S. E. 735. 

West v. Com., 156 Va. 975, 157 S. E. 538. 

Wharton's Crim. Law, sec. 181. 

§ 883. Essential elements of offense. 

The statutes of neither of the Virginias define attempts to commit crime, but leave the common-law definition of the offense unchanged. However, the courts of both states are in accord that the essentials of the crime are: (1) The intent to commit it; (2) a direct, ineffectual act done toward its commission, which must reach far enough toward the accomplishment of the direct result to amount to a commencement of the consummation; and (3) the failure to consummate it. And such failure is as much an element of the crime as is the intent and the performance of the overt act, for if the crime is actually committed there can be no prosecution for an attempt. 

Com. v. Clark, 6 Gratt. 675. 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 706. 

Christian v. Com., 23 Gratt. 958. 

Hicks v. Com., 86 Va. 226, 9 S. E. 1024. 

Glover v. Com., 86 Va. 382, 10 S. E. 420. 

Cunningham v. Com., 88 Va. 39, 13 S. E. 309. 

Thacker v. Com., 134 Va. 767, 114 S. E. 404-5. 

Andrews v. Com., 135 Va. 451, 115 S. E. 558. 

West v. Com., 156 Va. 975, 157 S. E. 538. 

Dixon v. Com., 162 Va. 798, 173 S. E. 523. 

Merritt v. Com., 164 Va. 653, 180 S. E. 399. 

Bishop's Crim. Law (9th Ed.), vol. 1, p. 519. § 884. Intent must be proved, either by direct or circumstantial evidence. 

In Thacker v. Com., 134 Va. 767, 114 S. E. 404, it is said: "The law can presume the intention so far as realized in the act, but not an intention beyond what was so realized. 

The law does not presume, because an assault was made with a weapon likely to produce death, that it was an assault with the intent of murder. And where it takes a particular intent to constitute a crime, that particular intent must be proved either by direct or circumstantial evidence,

§ 886 

which would warrant the inference of the intent with which the act was done." "When a statute makes an offense to consist of an act combined with a particular intent, that intent is just as necessary to be proved as the act itself, and must be found as a matter of fact before a conviction can be had; and no intent in law or mere legal presumption, differing from the intent in fact, can be allowed to supply the place of the latter." See cases cited in the opinion. 

State v. Hager, 50 W. Va. 370, 40 S. E. 393. 

And in Merritt v. Com., 164 Va. 653, 180 S. E. 395, it is held that a person cannot be guilty of an intent to commit murder unless he has a specific intent to kill. § 885. Distinction between intent and attempt. 

In Merritt v. Com., 164 Va. 653, 180 S. E. 395, it is held: "Under this section (statute on attempts) "attempt" embraces the full meaning of "intent," the only distinction between "intent" and "attempt" being that the former implies purpose only, while the latter implies both purpose and the effort to carry that purpose into effect." 

Also in State v. Hager, 50 W. Va. 372, 40 S. E. 393, it is further held: "It seems impossible to doubt that the only distinction between an intent and an attempt to do a thing is that the former implies purpose only, while the latter implies both the purpose and an actual effort to carry that purpose into execution.' 99 

§ 886. Overt act defined. 

In Hicks v. Com., 86 Va. 223, 9 S. E. 1024, it is said: "The question as to what is an overt act is often difficult to determine, and no general rule which can be readily applied as a test to all cases can be laid down. Each case must, therefore, be determined upon its own facts, in the light of certain principles which appear to be well settled. 

The difficulty generally is in determining the proximity of the act in question to the offense in contemplation." Citing 

Lee v. Com., 144 Va. 594, 131 S. E. 212. 

State v. Baller, 26 W. Va. 90. 

Collins v. Radford, 134 Va. 540, 113 S. E. 735.

 § 887. Overt act must constitute an offense. 

In Thacker v. Com., 134 Va. 767, 114 S. E. 504, it is said: "The (overt) act must reach far enough towards the accomplishment of the desired results to amount to a commencement of the consummation.” 

Collins v. Radford, supra. 

But it is also held that: "The overt act composing one of the two essential elements of an attempt, need not be the last proximate act prior to the consummation of the felony attempted to be perpetrated." 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 706. 

Glover v. Com., 86 Va. 382, 10 S. E. 420. 

Lee v. Com., supra. 

State v. Baller, supra. § 888. Intent to murder need not be alleged in indictment. 

In State v. Hager, 50 W. Va. 371-2, 40 S. E. 393, it is held : 

"The better course is to charge both the intent and the overt act, (in the indictment) for both must co-exist. * 

But, *** the allegation of the attempt implies the intent to do the act attempted. In fact, the allegation of attempt implies both the intent and an actual offer to consummate the intent, and therefore such an allegation has been held in itself sufficient." Citing, 1 Bishop's Crim. Law, section 729. 

1 McClain's Crim. Law, section 228. 

Com. v. Clark, 6 Gratt. 675. 

In Fields v. Com., 129 Va. 779, 106 S. E. 333, syl. 5, it was held: "But, it is well settled law in this state that an indictment for murder need not expressly allege the intent to kill, and that an indictment for murder at common law, (which does not expressly charge the intent to kill), is valid * * *.

On the same principle, we are of opinion that an indictment for an attempt to commit murder is valid and sufficient to support the verdict, * *" § 889. Indictment must allege some act done by accused. 

An indictment for an attempt to commit an offense must allege

§ 890 

some act done by the defendant of such a nature as to constitute an attempt in a legal sense, to commit the contemplated offense, otherwise the indictment will not be sufficient. 

Com. v. Clark, 6 Gratt. 675. 

Hicks v. Com., 86 Va. 226, 9 S. E. 1024. 

Cunningham v. Com., 88 Va. 39, 13 S. E. 309. 

And in Merritt v. Com., 164 Va. 653, 180 S. E. 395, it is held that an indictment for an attempt to commit a crime should charge both the intent and the overt act. See also, Fields v. Com., 129 Va. 774, 106 S. E. 333. § 890. One indicted for a felony may be convicted of an attempt to commit such felony. 

One accused simply of an attempt to commit a crime usually is indicted for such attempt; but West Virginia Code, 62-3-18 (sec. 

6207), and Virginia Code, sec. 4922, are identical, and provide: "On an indictment for felony, the jury may find the accused not guilty of the felony, but guilty of an attempt to commit such felony; and a general verdict of not guilty, upon such indictment, shall be a bar to a subsequent prosecution for an attempt to commit such felony." 

This statute is construed in: 

State v. Cross, 44 W. Va. 315, 29 S. E. 527. 

Cates v. Com., 111 Va. 837, 69 S. E. 520. 

Mings v. Com., 85 Va. 638, 8 S. E. 474. 

Glover v. Com., 86 Va. 382, 10 S. E. 420. 

State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 673. 

Givens v. Com., 29 Gratt. 830. 

16 Corpus Juris, p. 271. 

And in State v. Collins, 108 W. Va. 98, 150 S. E. 369, all the evidence tended to prove the accused guilty of rape, but the jury returned a verdict finding him guilty of an attempt to commit rape. 

A motion was made to set aside the verdict as not being supported by the evidence, which was overruled by the trial court. In sustaining this ruling, the appellate court said: "Where a defendant in an indictment is charged with the commission of rape, he may be convicted of an attempt to commit the offense, such attempt being included in, or a part of, the offense charged by virtue of Code 62-3-18, (sec. 6207).

§  

610 "On a conviction for an attempt to commit rape, this Court will not set aside the verdict on the ground that there was no evidence to support it, if there was sufficient evidence to warrant a conviction of rape.” 

On page 102 of the opinion, the Court said: "The case of State v. Prater, 52 W. Va. 132, 43 S. E. 

230, is directly in point. There the jury found the defendant guilty of manslaughter where the evidence warranted a conviction of murder. Judge Poffenbarger, speaking for the Court, in his usual trenchant style, said: "They (the jury) illegally acquit and discharge the accused as to the higher degree of crime charged in the indictment, after having found him guilty. They have not exceeded the law but stopped short of the law and their duties. In other words, without warrant of law or moral right, they have exercised clemency, and dispensed what they conceived to be mercy.' The conclusion reached by the Court in that case upon the motion made by the defendant for a new trial was that the evidence and facts tending to prove murder were proper to be considered, and as it was found that there was sufficient evidence to have upheld a verdict of guilty of murder, had the jury rendered such a verdict, the verdict which the jury did find could not be set aside, unless for some error sufficient to reverse; consequently the case was affirmed. So we may conclude, in accord with both law and reason, that the defendant here cannot complain that the jury found him guilty of an attempt to commit the offense, where the evidence warranted a verdict of guilty of a commission of the offense." § 891. Verdict in attempt to commit murder must specify the degree, rule in West Virginia. 

In State v. Hager, 50 Va. 370, 40 S. E. 393, the court said: "Upon an indictment under this section for attempting to commit murder the verdict may convict of an attempt to commit murder in either the first or second degree, and the verdict not only may, but must specify the degree of the murder attempted." § 892. Same, rule in Virginia. 

In Fields v. Com., 129 Va. 774, 106 S. E. 333, it is said: "In a prosecution for an attempt to commit murder, the

$ 893 

jury found the accused guilty as charged in the indictment and fixed her punishment at two years confinement in the penitentiary. It was held that the verdict was not invalid. because it did not expressly appear therefrom that the jury found the accused guilty of the attempt to commit murder of the first degree.

§ 893. For attempt to commit murder.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 896. Elements of offense. 

The court instructs the jury that an attempt in criminal law is an apparent unfinished crime, and hence is a compound of two elements, viz: (1) The intent to commit the crime, and (2) a direct act done towards its commission, but falling short of the execution of the ultimate design. It need not, therefore, be the last proximate act to the consummation of the crime in contemplation, but is sufficient, if it be an act apparently adapted to produce the result intended. 

Hart v. Com., 131 Va. 733, 109 S. E. 582. § 897. Necessity for overt act.

The court instructs the jury, that to constitute the offense charged there must have been an actual overt act committed by the

§ 898 

defendants, or some one or more of them, to effect the burning of the barn, and that they failed in the attempt, or were prevented or intercepted in the execution of the same. But such actual overt act need not be the last proximate act prior to the consummation of the felony attempted to be perpetrated. 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 710. § 898. Attempt to commit murder. 

1. The court instructs the jury that under the law of this state any wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing of a human being by another is murder of the first degree, and that any felonious, wilful, malicious, deliberate and unlawful attempt by one human being to take the life of another is an attempt to commit murder of the first degree. 

NOTE: This instruction was objected to because abstract. 

Held: Where there is evidence to which an abstract instruction is applicable, but no particular reference is made to the evidence in the instruction, it will be presumed that the jury made the proper application. Citing, State v. Long, 88 W. Va. 669, 108 S. E. 279. 

See sections 402 and 403.

NOTE: This instruction is objected to and in passing upon such objection, the court said: "The evidence is conclusive and uncontradicted that the attempt was committed on November 16, 1917; and the indictment was found and returned at the March Term, 1919, more than one year from the time of the commission of the offense; hence, the misdemeanor under this indictment had been barred by limitation; and a verdict for less than an attempt to commit murder in the first degree would have been equivalent to a verdict of not guilty. 5. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that Milton Lee armed himself with a shot gun at his own home and then went upon the premises of R. A. Loving, where

Lee v. Com., 144 Va. 604, 131 S. E. 212. § 899. Attempt to commit arson.

The court instructs the jury that before you can convict the defendants of the offense charged in the indictment you must believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that they did some act, or acts, towards the commission of the offense charged; and that an attempt to commit a crime can only be made by an actual and ineffectual deed done in pursuance of and in furtherance of a design to commit such crime. And if the jury believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendants combined, on the night on which it is charged the attempt was made to burn the barn, to burn said barn, and that they all assented to it, and a part of them only went to the barn, then those who were absent, knowing with what intent the others went to said barn, and assenting thereto, and that those who went to said barn, went in pursuance of and with the intention of carrying into effect the said combination, and did attempt to commit the offense of burning said barn, and in such attempt did do any act towards the commission of the said offense, but failed in the perpetration of such offense, or were intercepted or prevented from the commission of said offense and the execution of said design, then all persons engaged in said combination, and assenting thereto, are to be regarded as principals. 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 709.

§ 900. Attempt to commit rape. 

1. The court instructs the jury that if you believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that Ethel Garrison is under fifteen years of age (now sixteen), and if you further believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused, Moses Lufty, attempted by force to have sexual intercourse with her, and that he did any overt act toward carrying out that purpose, such as taking hold of her, or throwing her down, then he would be guilty of attempted rape as charged in the indictment in this case. 

Lufty v. Com., 126 Va. 713, 100 S. E. 829. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused, with purpose and intent of committing a rape upon the prosecuting witness, Miss Garber, committed an overt act toward the accomplishment of such purpose which was of such a character apparently adapted to produce the result intended, then they should find the accused guilty of an attempt to commit rape, even though they may further believe that he subsequently voluntarily abandoned his purpose and did no further act toward its accomplishment. 

Hart v. Com., 131 Va. 733, 109 S. E. 582.

See sec. 1451.

§ 901. Attempt to shoot.

The court instructs the jury, that if they acquit the prisoner of the felony charged in the indictment, they cannot convict of an attempt to commit the felony, unless they be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, that the prisoner attempted to shoot Francis M. 

Meadows, as charged in the indictment, and not some other person. 

State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 674.

DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS 

§ 914. Reasonable doubt as to first marriage.

§ 902. Bigamy a statutory offense. 

The common law did not provide for the punishment of a bigamous or polygamous marriage. Therefore, the offense as it exists under Virginia Code, sec. 4538, and West Virginia Code 

61-8-1 (sec. 6056), is purely statutory. These two sections are identical, and read as follows: "Any person being married, who, during the life of the former husband or wife, shall marry another person in this state, or if the marriage with such other person take place out of this state, shall thereafter cohabit with such other person in this state, shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years." 

Ex parte Brinkman, 93 W. Va. 351, 116 S. E. 757. 

1 Bishop's Crim. Law, sec. 502. 

Bishop on Statutory Crimes, sec. 579. 

3 R. C. L., 756. 

7 Corpus Juris, 1158.

$ 904 

BIGAMY § 903. Elements of offense. 

To constitute the crime of bigamy, two elements are absolutely essential: 

1. The first marriage must have been valid, and the marital relation subsisting between the parties thereto at the time the accused entered into the second marriage. 

2. A subsequent or bigamous marriage by accused, which must have taken place within the jurisdiction of the court, or the parties thereto must have cohabited within such jurisdiction. 

Moore v. Com., 9 Leigh 639. 

O'Neal v. Com., 17 Gratt. 582. 

Bird v. Com., 21 Gratt. 800. 

State v. Goodrich, 14 W. Va. 834. 

And in Farewell v. Com., 167 Va. 475, 189 S. E. 321, it is held: "To give local courts jurisdiction of bigamy under the statute, such bigamous marriage must occur within the state, or, if taking place elsewhere, must be followed by cohabitation within the state." § 904. Where bigamous marriage was celebrated in another state.

Under the statutes of both Virginias, if the bigamous marriage takes place out of the state, and the parties thereafter cohabit within the state, the offender is guilty of bigamy in such latter state, and may be tried and punished in the county wherein such cohabitation took place. 

In State v. Goodrich, 14 W. Va. 834, it is held: "Accused cannot be convicted of bigamy in this state if he has not cohabited with his second wife in this state. "And where the indictment charges that the first marriage took place in another state or country, it must be proved satisfactorily to the jury that a valid marriage did take place as stated." 

And in Bird v. Com., 21 Gratt. 800, it is held that where a witness testifies to a marriage in a foreign state, solemnized in the manner usual and customary in such state, by a person duly authorized to celebrate the rites of marriage, and the parties after- 2 CT-6

§ 622 

wards lived together as man and wife, this is as satisfactory evidence of a valid marriage as can be expected or desired; and in such case it is not necessary to prove the laws of such state, or to offer further evidence of a compliance with their provisions. 

905. How first marriage may be proved.

In a prosecution for bigamy the first marriage may be proved: 

1. Where such marriage was celebrated in another State, a copy of the marriage license, with the minister's return thereon duly certified as provided by Virginia Code, secs. 6205 and 6206, and, West Virginia Code 57-1-12 and 13 (secs. 5719, 5720), introduced in evidence. 

State v. Goodrich, 14 W. Va. 834. 

2. By the testimony of the minister who solemnized such marriage; or 

State v. Goodrich, supra. 

Bird v. Com., 21 Gratt. 800. 

3. By the testimony of witnesses who saw such marriage ceremony performed; or 

Warner v. Com., 2 Va. Cas., 95. 

Bird v. Com., supra. 

4. By the admissions, acts and statements of the accused which are competent and sufficient evidence, without producing the marriage record or witness who saw such marriage performed. 

O'Neal v. Com., 17 Gratt. 582. 

Bird v. Com., supra. 

Warner v. Com., supra. 

Womack v. Tankersley, 78 Va. 243. § 906. First marriage may not be proved by reputation and co-habitation. 

In Bird v. Com., 21 Gratt. 806, it was held: "In criminal prosecution and certain civil actions, a valid marriage cannot be proved by reputation and co-habitation.” § 907. Cohabitation not a requisite of offense. 

It is both the general law, and no doubt the law in the Vir-

§ 909 

BIGAMY 

ginias, that cohabitation under the second marriage is not requisite, but the offense is committed when the second marriage is solemnized. 

7 Corpus Juris, 1162. "The crime of bigamy is complete on the second unlawful marriage itself, and needs no act of sexual intercourse to fix the guilt of the defendant. 

It is the unlawful contract which is punished and the crime is complete when the ceremony is completed." * * * 

3 Ruling Case Law, 804. 

§ 908. When divorce is no defense. 

In Corvin v. Com., 131 Va. 649, 108 S. E. 651, the Virginia court holds that a divorce obtained in another state by fraud constitutes no defense to a charge of bigamy. And also that on the question of good faith of accused in obtaining such divorce, the material facts which culminated in his separation and divorce proceedings may be shown. On similar facts, no doubt such will be the holding of the West Virginia court. 

909. Venue of crime. 

Ex parte Brinkman, 93 W. Va. 351, 116 S. E. 757, it is held: "When the second marriage is celebrated within this state, the offense is committed in the county in which such marriage takes place, and in such case the courts of the county in which such second marriage is solemnized alone have jurisdiction to try and punish the offender." Citing, 7 Corpus Juris, 1162. 

3 Ruling Case Law, 804. 

Bishop's Statutory Crimes, 3rd Ed., sec. 586. 

In the opinion in the Brinkman case, it is further said: "In the absence of statute providing otherwise, the offense of bigamy can be prosecuted only in the county in which the unlawful marriage was solemnized. The venue must be laid in that county." Citing, 7 Corpus Juris, 1167. 

State v. Fitzgerald, 75 Mo. 571.

Walls v. The State, 32 Ark. 565.

§ 624 

 Beggs v. The State, 55 Ala. 108. 

Brewer v. The State, 59 Ala. 101.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 912. Marriage in other state must have been valid. 

1. The court instructs the jury that before the jury can find the prisoner guilty, they must be satisfied by the evidence that he was married in New York to Mary Sheridan, and that the marriage was performed under and in accordance with the laws of 

New York; and they must be satisfied by proper evidence what is sufficient to constitute a valid marriage in the State of New York; and the jury may take into consideration the acknowledgments, the confessions and cohabitation of the prisoner with his alleged first wife, if such has been proved, as evidence of a valid marriage in the State of New York. 

O'Neal v. Com., 17 Gratt. 583. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence (in this case), beyond a reasonable doubt, that the prisoner was married in the City of Washington, D. C., to Mary Borden, according to the law prevailing in said city at the time of said marriage; and that afterwards, and during the life of the said 

Mary Borden, and without having been lawfully divorced from the said Mary Borden, he was in the City of Alexandria, state of

§ 626 

Virginia, married to one Henrietta Godwin, according to the law of the State of Virginia, that then they will find the prisoner guilty. And if the jury should not find the facts as stated herein, they will find the prisoner not guilty. 

Bird v. Com., 21 Gratt. 803. § 913. Acts and confessions of prisoner are proper evidence. 

The jury are instructed that the acts, acknowledgments and confessions of a person accused of bigamy is as good evidence and as available and sufficient for his conviction as they would be in any other case. 

O'Neal v. Com., supra.

DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS. 

914. Reasonable doubt as to first marriage.

The court instructs the jury that in order to convict the prisoner, the commonwealth must prove the guilt of the prisoner beyond a reasonable doubt. If, therefore, the jury have a reasonable doubt whether or not the prisoner was lawfully married to Mary Sheridan in the State of New York prior to the alleged marriage with Caroline Moyerhoeffer, they should find the prisoner not guilty. 

O'Neal v. Com., 17 Gratt. 584.

§ 963. Possession of goods from burglarized house. § 964. Property taken under honest claim of ownership. § 965. Entry by tenant not burglary. 

§ 966. Sufficiency of incriminating evidence. 

§ 915. Burglary at common law.

At common law, burglary is the breaking and entering the mansion house of another in the nighttime, with intent to commit some felony within the same, whether the felony be actually committed or not.

Clark v. Com., 25 Gratt. 911. 

State v. Caddle, 35 W. Va. 73, 12 S. E. 1100. 

§ 916. Under Virginia statute. 

The Virginia statute, Code, sec. 4437, closely follows the common-law definition of the offense. It reads: "If any person break and enter the dwelling house of another in the nighttime with intent to commit a felony or larceny therein, he shall be deemed guilty of burglary, though the thing stolen, or intended to be stolen, be of less value than fifty dollars. If any person be guilty of burglary, he shall be punished with death, or, by confinement in the penitentiary not less than five nor more than eighteen years. If any person have in his possession any tools, implements, or outfit, with intent to commit burglary, robbery, or larceny, he shall be deemed guilty of a felony, and be punished by confinement in the penitentiary not less than five nor more than eighteen years."

§ 918 

§ 917. Under West Virginia statute. 

The West Virginia statute, Code 61-3-11 (sec. 5952) has greatly enlarged the common-law offense of burglary, and fixes the punishment there for at confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than fifteen years. In effect, it provides: 

1. That breaking and entering in the nighttime the dwelling house, or an outhouse adjoining thereto or occupied therewith, of another, with intent to commit a felony or any larceny, is burglary. 

2. That entering in the nighttime, without breaking, the dwelling house, or an outhouse adjoining thereto or occupied therewith, of another, with intent to commit a felony or any larceny therein, is burglary. 

3. That breaking and entering in the daytime, the dwelling house, or an outhouse adjoining thereto or occupied therewith, of another, with intent to commit a felony or any larceny therein, is burglary. § 918. Housebreaking, Virginia statute.

In Virginia, housebreaking is defined by Code, secs. 4438 and 

4439. The former reads as follows: 

"If any person in the night enter without breaking or in the daytime break and enter a dwelling house or an outhouse adjoining thereto and occupied therewith or in the nighttime enter without breaking or break and enter either in the daytime or nighttime any office, shop, storehouse, warehouse, banking house or other house, or any ship or vessel or river craft or any railroad car with intent to commit murder, rape, or robbery, he shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than three nor more than fifteen years."

While the latter section provides: "If any person do any of the acts mentioned in the preceding section, with intent to commit larceny, or any felony other than murder, rape, or robbery, he shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years, or, in the discretion of the jury, confined in jail not exceeding twelve months, and fined not exceeding five hundred dollars. * * ""

§ 

630 

§ 919. Same, West Virginia statute. 

1. While improperly included therein, the last paragraph of 

Code 61-3-11 (sec. 5952), provides that entering in the daytime, without breaking, a dwelling house, or an outhouse adjoining thereto or occupied therewith, of another, with intent to commit a felony or any larceny, shall be a felony punished by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years. 

2. Also under Code 61-3-12 (sec. 5953), the breaking and entering, or entering without breaking, of any office, shop, storehouse, warehouse, banking house, or any house or building, other than a dwelling house or outhouse adjoining thereto or occupied therewith, or any railroad or traction car, steamboat, etc., with intent to commit a felony or any larceny, is a felony punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years. 

3. Likewise the breaking and entering, or entering without breaking, any motor car or bus, with intent to commit a felony or any larceny, shall be a misdemeanor, punishable by confinement in jail not less than two nor more than twelve months and a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars. § 920. Breaking may be either actual or constructive. 

In both Virginias it is held that the breaking may be either "actual" or "constructive." Actual breaking involves the application of some force, slight though it may be, whereby the entrance is effected. Merely pushing open the door, turning the key, lifting the latch, or resort to other slight physical force is sufficient to constitute the element of breaking and entering. A constructive breaking is obtained when entrance is obtained by threat of violence, or by fraud, or by conspiracy. 

Hunter v. Com., 7 Gratt. 641. 

Clarke v. Com., 25 Gratt. 912. 

Davis v. Com., 132 Va. 521, 110 S. E. 356. § 921. Dwelling may be temporarily unoccupied. 

In State v. Blair, 112 W. Va. 655, 166 S. E. 369, it is held: "A building suitable for residential purposes, having

§ 924 

been so designated and 'used, being equipped with household furnishings, remains a dwelling house though temporarily unoccupied, if the absence of the householder be with intent to return. Entry of such temporarily unoccupied building, in the nighttime, with or without breaking, with intent to commit a felony or any larceny therein, constitutes burglary." 

See authorities cited in opinion. 

§ 922. Intent, essential element. 

It is generally held that the intent constitutes an essential part of the crime of burglary and must be both alleged and proved. 

Vaughan v. Com., 10 Gratt. 758. 

And in State v. Phillips, 80 W. Va. 752, 93 S. E. 828, it is held: "In the crime of burglary, there are always two intents, one to break and enter, which must be executed, and the other to commit in the building, a theft or other offense, which may be executed or not.' 

See authorities cited in opinion. 

923. Same, how shown in indictment.

In Speers v. Com., 17 Gratt. 573, it is held that the allegation of actual larceny in an indictment for burglary or housebreaking is simply to show the intent to commit a felony therein, which is an essential element of these crimes. § 924. Same, when presumed. 

In State v. Walker, 109 W. Va. 351, 154 S. E. 866, it is held: "Where it is shown that accused broke and entered a dwelling house in the nighttime, and no satisfactory explanation of his conduct appears from evidence offered by him or from the circumstances, it may ordinarily be presumed that he broke and entered with intent to commit larceny, though when detected in the dwelling he had not appropriated any of the householder's belongings." 

See authorities cited in opinion.

§ 632 

§ 925. Possession of stolen goods not a presumption of housebreaking.

The general law as stated in 2 Wharton's Crim. Ev. (10th Ed.), 1509, as follows: "To raise the presumption of housebreaking from the possession of stolen goods, the possession must be personal, must be recent, must be unexplained, and must involve a distinct and conscious assertion of ownership of property by the defendant." 

But in Drinkard v. Com., 163 Va. 1074, 178 S. E. 27-28, this rule is thus stated: "The law in Virginia is well settled that the possession of stolen goods is of itself not even prima facie evidence of housebreaking or burglary." Citing, Walters v. Com., 159 Va. 903, 165 S. E. 495. 

Tyler v. Com., 120 Va. 868, 91 S. E. 172. 

Taliaferro v. Com., 77 Va. 413. 

Walker v. Com., 28 Gratt. 971. 

Gravely v. Com., 86 Va. 400, 10 S. E. 431. 

Porterfield v. Com., 91 Va. 806, 22 S. E. 352. 

Stallard v. Com., 130 Va. 775, 107 S. E. 722. 

Diggs v. Com., 163 Va. 1066, 178 S. E. 6. 

And in State v. Mullett, 94 W. Va. 680, 120 S. E. 75, it is further held: "Where the only evidence adduced to support the charge that defendant entered a store building with intent to steal is that six months after the robbery, part of the stolen goods were found in his possession and part in the possession of his father who lived nearby, a verdict finding defendant guilty as charged must be set aside as without proof to support it." Citing, State v. Littleton, 77 W. Va. 804, 88 S. E. 458. 

State v. Reece, 27 W. Va. 375. 

9 C. J., p. 1081. § 926. Corpus delicti in housebreaking. 

In Drinkard v. Com., 163 Va. 1074, 178 S. E. 25, 28, it is held that the "corpus delicti must be proved before any influence of guilt can arise from the possession of the fruits of crime"; and

§ 928 

"where the charge is breaking and entering with intent to commit larceny, the corpus delicti is the breaking and entering with that intent," and the possession of stolen goods does not give rise to an inference of guilt until the corpus delicti is proved by other evidence. Citing, Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 761, 111 S. E. 468.

But in Drinkard's Case, supra, it is also held that when the accused was in exclusive possession of recently stolen goods, and falsely denied that he had been in possession of them, falsely testified to an attempted alibi or that he had tried to dispose of the stolen goods, such evidence was sufficient to sustain a verdict of guilty of housebreaking. Citing, Branch v. Com., 100 Va. 839, 41 S. E. 862. 

Myers v. Com., supra. 

927. Indictment.

Under Virginia Code, sec. 4439, and West Virginia Code, 613-12 (sec. 5953), the indictment may charge both housebreaking and larceny in one count, and a general verdict is for the major offense of housebreaking. 

Walters v. Com., 159 Va. 905, 165 S. E. 495. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 746, 111 S. E. 463. 

Vaughn v. Com., 17 Gratt. 386. 

Speers v. Com., 17 Gratt. 574.

However, under the Virginia statute burglary consists in breaking and entering the dwelling house of another in the nighttime, and in Com. v. Weldon, 4 Leigh 652, it is held: "In every indictment for burglary it must distinctly and plainly appear that the offense was committed in the nighttime but an indictment omitting to state such time may still be good as an indictment for larceny." § 928. Same, count for larceny may be added.

In both Virginias it is held that to an indictment for burglary or housebreaking, where property has been stolen, may be added a count charging the larceny of such goods. But care should be exercised to designate, describe and state the value of each article

$ 634 

stolen, else the count will be quashed on motion. However, if the first count be good the failure of the second count is of no consequence, as said in State v. Johnson, 111 W. Va. 653, 164 S. E. 

31, it is held: "A count in an indictment charging the felonious breaking and entering into a theater, not a dwelling nor an outhouse adjoining thereto, with intent to steal goods therein, and actual larceny thereof, although that part charging larceny is not drawn with sufficient precision to support a conviction of larceny, is not for that reason bad under Code, 61-3-12 (sec. 5953). As the breaking and entering are charged to have been done with intent to commit larceny, a charge of actual larceny is not necessary and may be rejected as surplusage.' 

State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654. 

State v. Mullett, 94 W. Va. 680, 120 S. E. 75. 

State v. Cooper, 111 W. Va. 225, 161 S. E. 30. 

And in Speers v. Com., 17 Gratt. 570, it is also held: "To such a count (charging housebreaking and larceny) may be added a count for simple larceny of the same goods. 

And the jury may find the prisoner guilty on each count, and fix a several punishment for each offense." See also, Benton v. Com., 91 Va. 728, 21 S. E. 495. 

Clark v. Com., 25 Gratt. 908. § 929. Same, but larceny need not be specifically laid.

It is held in both Virginias that the allegation of larceny is only in aid of the allegation of intent, and need not be laid with the same formality as in an indictment for larceny itself. 

Speers v. Com., 17 Gratt. 570. 

Vaughn v. Com., 17 Gratt. 386. 

Wright v. Com., 82 Va. 183. 

State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654. 

State v. Caddle, 35 W. Va. 73, 12 S. E. 1098. "And although that part of the count charging larceny is bad, and will not support a conviction for larceny, the count is not for that reason bad as a count for burglary." 

State v. McClung, supra. 

State v. Johnson, 111 W. Va. 653, 164 S. E. 31. 

McDaniel v. Com., 165 Va. 709, 181 S. E. 534.

§ 929  

The general law in this regard is summarized from the following excerpts from decided cases: "An indictment which charges a breaking into a house with intent to steal, and the stealing therefrom, is an indictment for housebreaking, and not for larceny; and is good."

§ 930. Same, when charge of larceny should be well laid. 

In State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654, it is said: "But to support a conviction for larceny, the charge of it must be as well laid as in an indictment for larceny." 

And in Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 757, 111 S. E. 463, it is further said: "It is always better, however, to lay the charge of larceny in proper form, to avoid objection in case the prisoner should, as he may, on such a count as this, be found not guilty of the breaking and entering, but guilty of the larceny." 

Vaughn v. Com., 17 Gratt. 386. 

Wright v. Com., 82 Va. 183. "But if an indictment contains sufficient averments to make it a good indictment for the grand larceny the charges in regard to the breaking and entering the storehouse may be treated as surplusage, and a conviction upon the indictment may be sustained." 

State v. Reece, 27 W. Va. 375. § 931. Same, must allege offense to have been "burglariously" committed.

An indictment for burglary must charge the offense to have been "burglariously" committed, else it is fatally defective.

936. Verdict.

In State v. Littleton, 77 W. Va. 807, 88 S. E. 458, it is held: "When a count in an indictment properly alleges both housebreaking and larceny, there my be a conviction of either but not of both; on a general verdict of guilty on such count, the judgment should be for housebreaking and not for larceny." Citing, State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654. 

Speers v. Com., 17 Gratt. 570. 

Benton v. Com., 91 Va. 782, 21 S. E. 495. 

Clark v. Com., 135 Va. 496, 115 S. E. 704. § 937. Same, when count for burglary is bad, and a general verdict. 

In State v. Cottrell, 45 W. Va. 837, 32 S. E. 162, it is held: "A person found guilty by a verdict of a jury, under a bad count for burglary, cannot be sentenced for housebreaking, although the indictment contain a good count charging the latter offense." § 938. Same, when indictment contains one count. 

In Walters v. Com., 159 Va. 903, 165 S. E. 495, it is held: "It is well settled in Virginia that when an indictment contains but one count, charging housebreaking and larceny, and the verdict is a general one of guilty, the verdict will be considered as one for the major offense of housebreaking." 

Speers v. Com., 17 Gratt. 574. 

Vaughn v. Com., 17 Gratt. 386. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 746, 111 S. E. 463. "When an indictment charges both burglary and larceny, the jury could find the accused guilty of either, but a general finding is considered to cover the burglary and not the larceny." 

State v. Williams, 40 W. Va. 271, 21 S. E. 721. 

State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654. 

And in Benton v. Com., 91 Va. 788, 21 S. E. 495, it was held: "If it is desired to punish for both offenses in a case of this kind, there must be inserted in the indictment a sep-

It is the general law that where the indictment contains but one count, charging car-breaking and larceny, and the verdict is a general one of guilty, it is for the major offense of car-breaking.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

949. Elements of offense.

You are instructed that the burden is upon the Commonwealth to prove the guilt of the defendant beyond a reasonable doubt. If you believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, first, that the defendant broke and entered the railroad car with intent to commit larceny therein, as charged in the indictment, you should find him guilty as charged in the indictment; or, second, if you believe, beyond a reasonable doubt, that he stole the goods out of the car without breaking, you should find him guilty of grand larceny, without convicting him of breaking and entering. 

If you have a reasonable doubt of any of those things, you should find them not guilty.

§ 952 

The above instruction is based upon the instruction given in, Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 754, 111 S. E. 463. § 950. Verdict may be based upon first or second counts. as ..)

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant, broke and entered into the storehouse of .... charged in the indictment in this case, with intent to commit larceny therein, then they should find the said defendant guilty as charged in the first count in the indictment; and, if you should believe from the evidence in the case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the said defendant entered said storehouse without breaking, as charged in said indictment, with intent to commit larceny therein, then you should find him guilty as charged in the second count in the said indictment.

This instruction is based upon the language of the indictment. § 951. Breaking and entering, when no larceny is committed.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that the prisoner broke and entered the storehouse of as charged in the indictment, with the intent of committing larceny therein, they should find him guilty, though he may not have been guilty of any larceny therein. 

, State v. Shores, 31 W. Va. 504, 7 S. E. 413. 

§ 952. What constitutes breaking and entering. 

1. The court instructs the jury that there is no necessity in this case to show the absolute separation of the particles of wood, iron, etc., of the storehouse of .. referred to in the indictment or to the door thereof, in order to make the breaking and entering thereof by the prisoner burglary. But if they believe from the evidence (in the case), beyond a reasonable doubt, that 

---

§ 650 

the prisoner raised the latch or pushed open the door of the said storehouse, which was closed, and entered the same with the intent to commit larceny therein, at the time and in the manner charged in the indictment, then the jury should find him guilty. 

, State v. Shores, 31 W. Va. 504, 7 S. E. 413. 

2. The jury are instructed that if from the evidence they should believe that an entry was effected by the prisoner through a door that was open or partially open, that this was in law no breaking. 

But if they should believe from the evidence (beyond a reasonable doubt), that an entry was effected by the prisoner through a door that was so closed that it came within the casing of the door, and to open which required some degree of force. that this constituted in law a breaking, though there was no fastening of any other kind on said door. 

Finch v. Com., 14 Gratt. 643. § 953. Where accused acted alone or with another. 

The court instructs the jury that if you believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant, alone, or with some other person, prior to the finding of the indictment in this case, entered the dwelling house of Shott and White mentioned in the indictment, in the nighttime, with intent to take, steal and carry away any of the property in said dwelling house, then you shall find the defendant guilty as charged in this case. 

State v. Bair, 112 W. Va. 659, 166 S. E. 369.

NOTE: The words in italics are inserted as the better form, and to meet objections raised by counsel for the defense. However, the instruction was approved without such words. § 954. Possession of house is sufficient. 

If the jury believe from the evidence (in this case) that John B. Morrison held the possession of said house at the time alleged in the indictment, and that he used and occupied said house as a dwelling, then, in contemplation of law, said house was the dwelling house of John B. Morrison, although he may have absented

himself therefrom for several months, and although he may have had another dwelling house during the same time. 

State v. Williams, 40 W. Va. 269, 21 S. E. 321. § 955. Possession of house may be actual or constructive.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence (in this case) that the house mentioned in the indictment was in the actual or constructive possession of John B. Morrison, then the ownership (thereof) is properly laid in the said Morrison, although they believe from the evidence that the title to said. property was at the time in W. F. Morrison. 

State v. Williams, supra. § 956. Conviction of larceny may be had on indictment charging burglary. 

1. The jury is instructed that although they should believe that no dwelling house was broken or entered, as alleged in the indictment, yet if they believe from the evidence that the defendant stole and carried away any of the goods of John B. Morrison, as alleged in the indictment, then they should find him guilty of the larceny of said goods. 

State v. Williams, 40 W. Va. 269, 21 S. E. 721. 

2. The jury are instructed that the burden is upon the Commonwealth to prove the guilt of the defendants beyond a reasonable doubt. If you believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, first, that the defendants, or either of them, broke and entered the railroad car with intent to commit larceny therein, you should find them guilty, as charged in the indictment; or, second, if you believe that they stole the goods out of the car without breaking and entering, beyond a reasonable doubt, you should find them guilty of grand larceny, without convicting them of breaking and entering. If you have a reasonable doubt of any of those things you should find them not guilty. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 754, 111 S. E. 463.

The court instructs the jury that if the prisoner broke and entered the storehouse with intent to commit larceny, he is guilty as charged.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the prisoner broke and entered the storehouse of in the nighttime, as charged in the indictment, and was guilty of larceny therein, then he is presumed to have broken and entered said storehouse with the intent to commit larceny therein, and unless this presumption is negatived to the satisfaction of the jury, then they should find the prisoner guilty.

§ 965. Entry by tenant not burglary.

Conversion by public officer, justice of the peace. § 1031. Conversion must have been with felonious intent. § 967. Embezzlement defined.

Embezzlement is not an offense at common law, but is the creature of statute. In State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 149, 52 S. E. 30, Judge Sanders, speaking for the court said: 

It was "Embezzlement is purely a statutory offense. unknown to the common law, and the statute was enacted for the purpose of supplying what were regarded as defects in the common law of larceny, so as to reach and punish for the fraudulent conversion of money or property which could not be reached by the common law. And

$ 968 

EMBEZZLEMENT 

while our statute denominates the offense larceny, and concludes by providing that the person so committing an act of embezzlement shall be deemed guilty of larceny, yet embezzlement is generally regarded as a separate and distinct crime, and is so treated. The distinction between embezzlement and larceny is that embezzlement is the wrongful conversion of property without trespass, or where the original taking and possession is lawful. In order to constitute the offense, it is necessary that the property embezzled should come lawfully into the hands of the party embezzling, and by virtue of the position of trust he occupies to the person whose property he takes." 

State v. Larue, 98 W. Va. 677, 128 S. E. 116. 

Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 803, 35 S. E. 452. 

Pittsnogle v. Com., 91 Va. 808, 22 S. E. 551.. 

Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4870. 

West Virginia Code, 61-3-20 (sec. 5960). 

§ 968. Elements of offense. 

In both Virginias, to sustain a conviction for embezzlement, it is necessary for the state to show: 

1. The trust relation of the person charged, and that he falls within the class of persons named. 

2. That the property or thing claimed to have been embezzled or converted is such property as is embraced in the statute. 

3. That it is the property of another person or corporation. 

4. That it came into the possession, or was placed in the care, of the accused under and by virtue of his office, place, or employment. 

5. That his manner of dealing with or disposing of the property constituted a conversion and appropriation of the same to his own use. 

6. That the embezzlement or fraudulent conversion of the property to his own use was with the intent to deprive the owner of his property. 

State v. Larue, 98 W. Va. 677, 128 S. E. 119. 

State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 149, 52 S. E. 30. 

Pittsnogle v. Com., 91 Va. 808, 22 S. E. 351. 

State v. Smith, 117 W. Va. 598, 186 S. E. 621. 

State v. Cantor, 93 W. Va. 239, 116 S. E. 396. 

State v. Hudson, 93 W. Va. 435, 117 S. E. 122.

State v. Workman, 91 W. Va. 774, 114 S. E. 276.

§ 660 

 § 969. A statutory crime. 

The statutes of both Virginias specifically declare it to be larceny for any agent, clerk or servant, etc., of any firm, person or corporation to embezzle or fraudulently convert to his own use any effects or property of any other person which shall have come into his possession by virtue of his place or employment, and an indictment for larceny is supported by proof of the embezzlement of the property alleged in the indictment to have been stolen. 

State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 633, 84 S. E. 508. 

State v. McClung. 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654. 

Pittsnogle v. Com., 91 Va. 808, 22 S. E. 351. 

Boyd v. Com., 156 Va. 934, 157 S. E. 546. 

Swick v. Bassell, 77 W. Va. 78, 87 S. E. 176.

State v. Workman, 91 W. Va. 771, 114 S. E. 276. 

State v. Cantor, 93 W. Va. 245, 116 S. E. 396. 

State v. Goldstrom, 84 W. Va. 130, 99 S. E. 248. 

State v. Lewis, 69 W. Va. 472, 72 S. E. 478. 

State v. Williams, 68 W. Va. 86, 69 S. E. 474. 

Price v. Com., 21 Gratt. 846. 

Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4451. 

West Virginia Code, 61-3-20 (sec. 5960). § 970. Distinguished from simple larceny. 

In State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 149, 52 S. E. 30, it is said: "The distinction between embezzlement and larceny is that embezzlement is the wrongful conversion of property without trespass, or where the original taking and possession is lawful." § 971. Property which may be subject of. 

The statutes on embezzlement of both Virginias make it an offense to embezzle, among other things, any "property" of any other person. The word "property" as here used has a very broad and flexible meaning, and embraces any species of property "capable of beneficial ownership," and while a "check" is not mentioned in the West Virginia statute it may be the subject of embezzlement.

State v. Fraley, 71 W. Va. 101, 76 S. E. 134.

$ 973 

EMBEZZLEMENT 

Coal Co. v. Tax Com., 59 W. Va. 609, 53 S. E. 928. 

Hulings v. Lumber Co., 38 W. Va. 351, 18 S. E. 620.

Percelle v. Allemong, 22 Gratt. 739. 

Cox v. Boone, 8 W. Va. 506. § 972. Conversion an essential element of offense. 

Conversion is a necessary element of embezzlement, and is defined as the fraudulent appropriation of another's property to one's own use. 

State v. Holley, 115 W. Va. 464, 177 S. E. 302. 

Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 803, 35 S. E. 452. 

And in State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 632, 84 S. E. 510, it is also said :. "An unauthorized assumption and exercise of the right of ownership over goods or personal chattels belonging to another, to the alteration of their condition or the exclusion of the owner's right, amounts to a conversion." 

However, in State v. Hudson, 93 W. Va. 435, 117 S. E. 122, it is held that the word "embezzle," as used in the statute, includes in its meaning a conversion or appropriation to the embezzler's own use; therefore the use of the word "embezzle" in an indictment under the statute contains within itself the charge that the defendant converted the property to his own use. § 973. Where agent embezzles money received at different times. 

In State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 146, 52 S. E. 30, syl. 12, the court held: "On the trial of the charge of embezzlement, proof that the money alleged to have been embezzled by an agent was received in several sums, at different times, and from different persons, during a course of continuous dealing between the agent and his principal, will support a verdict of the jury, finding the aggregate sum as the amount of a single embezzlement."

And in 7 Enc. Pl. & Pr. 447, the law is thus stated: "Where the accused has been guilty of a series of peculations, an indictment charging the embezzlement of the entire amount, and setting out with minute particularity

§ 

662 the circumstances attending the transaction from its commencement to its consummation, is not open to the objection that it charges more than one offense." 

In State v. Wetzel, 75 W. Va. 7, 83 S. E. 68, syl. 5, it is stated: "An indictment charging defendant, the cashier of a bank, with embezzling money belonging to the bank, at divers times, beginning with the said 27th day of April, 1906, and ending with the said .... day of July, 1909,' stating the aggregate amount of such various sums, charges but a single act of embezzlement, and does not contravene the above statute." § 974. Crime may be based on one transaction. 

In State v. Fraley, 71 W. Va. 100, 76 S. E. 134, it is held that the crime of embezzlement is sufficiently established by evidence showing that the agency or service related to but a single transaction of entrusting the property embezzled to the defendant. 

State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 633, 84 S. E. 508. 

State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 146, 52 S. E. 30. 

Keenan v. Scott, 64 W. Va. 137, 61 S. E. 806. § 975. Agency need not be for compensation.

In State v. Fraley, supra, it is held that: "The agency thus established is within the statute on embezzlement whether the contract of agency provides for compensation or not. One may agree to become an agent without compensation, and the relationship be thereby established." held: § 976. Demand for return of property.

In West Virginia, Code 61-3-20 (sec. 5960), provides that failure to restore the embezzled property within thirty days, after proper demand has been made therefor, raises a presumption of guilt; but the accused may rebut such presumption by disproving such facts, or by other competent evidence. 

However, in State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 156, 52 S. E. 30, it is 

66* * ** that a demand and refusal does not of itself, in any case establish fraudulent conversion, or conversion

8 978 

EMBEZZLEMENT 

by a defendant to his own use, but that it is only evidence to go to the jury, upon the question of the defendant's fraudulent conversion." § 977. But demand unnecessary to sustain a conviction. 

In State v. Moyer, supra, it is further held: "In all cases for embezzlement or fraudulent conversion, evidence of demand for a return of the money or property, and its refusal by the defendant, is competent for the purpose of tending to show conversion; but while it is always admissible, yet it is not always necessary." 

State v. Holley, 115 W. Va. 464, 177 S. E. 302. 

§ 978. Intent. 

The animus furandi, or the intent to take and deprive another of his property, is an essential element in the crime of larceny. 

State v. McCoy, 63 W. Va. 69, 59 S. E. 758. 

Johnson v. Com., 24 Gratt. 555.

Jordan's Case, 25 Gratt. 943. 

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 779. 

Whalen v. Com., 90 Va. 544, 19 S. E. 182. 

Jones v. Morris, 97 Va. 43, 33 S. E. 377. 

Page v. Com., 148 Va. 733, 138 S. E. 510.

And criminal intent is also necessary in the crime of embezzlement. In Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 810, 35 S. E. 452, it was held: "There must be a fraudulent purpose to deprive the owner of his property and appropriate the same." See also, Cook v. Darby, 4 Munf. 444. 

Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899. 

Also in Page v. Com., 148 Va. 733, 138 S. E. 510, it is further said: "The most material element of embezzlement is the fraudulent intent of accused." 

And in State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 149, 52 S. E. 30, it is further stated: "A mere detention of money belonging to another, without a fraudulent intent to convert it to the use of the one by whom it is detained, and to deprive that other person

§ 664 

of such property, does not constitute embezzlement." also, State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 632, 84 S. E. 508. 

State v. Smith, 97 W. Va. 313, 125 S. E. 90. 

979. Same, time of formation of.

To be guilty of embezzlement it is not necessary that one should intend at the time he receives the money or property to deprive the owner thereof and to convert the same to his own use. If, after he obtains the same, he conceives the purpose and intent to unlawfully appropriate such money or property to his own use, and does so convert it, within the meaning of the statute, the crime is complete. See 

State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 632, 84 S. E. 508. § 980. Where property is appropriated under a bona fide claim of right.

It is the general rule in both Virginias that if the property alleged to have been embezzled was appropriated under a bona fide claim of right it is not embezzlement. 

Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 803, 35 S. E. 452. 

State v. Flanagan, 48 W. Va. 115, 35 S. E. 862. 

Jones v. Morris, 97 Va. 43, 33 S. E. 377. 

Vaughan v. Lytton, 126 Va. 671, 101 S. E. 865. 

Ambrose v. Com., 129 Va. 763, 106 S. E. 348.

But whether such claim of right is bona fide or only pretended is a question for the jury. 

State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 668, 60 S. E. 785. 

Webb v. Com., 122 Va. 899, 94 S. E. 773.

And the jury have the right to infer such felonious intent from the facts and circumstances of the case. 

Booth v. Com., 4 Gratt. 525. 

Webb v. Com., supra. 

West v. Com., 125 Va. 747, 99 S. E. 654. 

Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899. 

Boyd v. Com., 156 Va. 934, 157 S. E. 546. 

And in Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 803, 35 S. E. 452, it is said: "The conversion of property under a bona fide claim of

§ 983 

EMBEZZLEMENT 

ownership is not embezzlement. To constitute embezzlement there must be a fraudulent intent to deprive the owner of his property." § 981. Scope of evidence to establish or refute intent. 

In Page v. Com., 148 Va. 733, 138 S. E. 510, it is held: "Since the crime of embezzlement depends upon the existence of a fraudulent intent in the mind of the person by whom the money or property is alleged to have been converted, a wide scope is given to the evidence which may be introduced by the State to show a fraudulent or criminal intent, or in behalf of the defense to show the absence thereof." 

Also in State v. Smith, 117 W. Va. 598, 186 S. E. 623, it is held error to reject evidence tending to show good faith on the part of the accused. "Great latitude," said the Court, "is permitted in proving or disproving the element of intent in embezzlement cases." 

State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 146, 52 S. E. 30. 

20 Corpus Juris, 485. § 982. Intention to return property later, no defense. 

In Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899, it was held : "But an intention to return money fraudulently appropriated, will not protect the prisoner from a conviction of embezzlement." 

State v. Camp, 110 W. Va. 444, 158 S. E. 664. 

§ 983. Restoration of property no defense. 

In Robinson v. Com., 104 Va. 888, 52 S. E. 690, it is held: "The restoration of public funds embezzled by an officer cannot relate back so as to efface the prior completed crime." 

State v. Camp, 110 W. Va. 444, 158 S. E. 664.

Embezzlement is larceny, and it is well settled that when a larceny is complete the voluntary abandonment, or restitution of the property by the thief, no matter how soon after the larceny, is no defense.

§ 666 

State v. Goldstrom, 84 W. Va. 129, 99 S. E. 248.

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 779. 

Whalen v. Com., 90 Va. 544, 19 S. E. 182. 

Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899. 

State v. Camp, supra. 

§ 984. Retention of commissions by agent no offense. 

In Page v. Com., 148 Va. 734, 138 S. E. 510, it is held: "An agent or officer is not guilty of embezzlement in retaining a commission or fee which he is entitled to retain out of a fund in his hands. 

But in Virginia (also in West Virginia) such a right will not prevent a conviction where the agent appropriates the entire fund." * * * § 985. Variance, as to amount embezzled.

In a prosecution for the embezzlement of a given sum of money charged in the indictment, it is not necessary to prove the embezzlement of the whole of the sum so charged. 

Robinson v. Com., 104 Va. 891, 52 S. E. 690. 

State v. Moyer, 58 W. Va. 146, 52 S. E. 30. § 986. Same, as to ownership. 

In State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 632, 84 S. E. 508, it is held: "On a trial of one charged with the larceny or embezzlement of goods, proof of actual or constructive possession of such goods by the person alleged in the indictment to be the owner thereof is sufficient.' § 987. Evidence of other crimes, when admissible. 

In State v. Wetzel, 75 W. Va. 8, 83 S. E. 68, it is held: "In a trial for embezzlement, it is proper to admit evidence tending to prove that defendant, the cashier of a bank, forged certain notes for the purpose of falsifying the bank's accounts. Such evidence is admissible on the question of intent to embezzle."

But, the court should limit such evidence, by proper instructions to the jury, to the question of intent only. 

State v. Wetzel, supra.

§ 988 

EMBEZZLEMENT 

And in State v. Cantor, 93 W. Va. 238, 116 S. E. 396, syl. 5, it is held: "As a general rule, where evidence is introduced tending to show a contemporaneous embezzlement by defendant, arising out of the same transaction for which he is indicted, the court should instruct the jury to consider the evidence only for the purpose of showing intent, system or method of the accused, and not to consider it as evidence of another crime, and to carefully limit the evidence to the purposes for which it is admissible; yet, where the circumstances are such that the jury could not possibly apply the evidence to any other purpose than that for which it was admissible, failure to instruct will not be reversible error.

But where such instruction is asked for by the prisoner, it should be given." 

See authorities cited in the opinion. Also, Boyd v. Com., 156 Va. 934, 157 S. E. 546. 

State v. Rush, 108 W. Va. 254, 150 S. E. 740. 

State v. Camp, 110 W. Va. 444, 158 S. E. 623. 

State v. Smith, 117 W. Va. 598, 186 S. E. 623.

But if acts subsequent to that charged in the indictment are to be proved, they must meet the test as stated in State v. Adkins, 109 W. Va. 579, 155 S. E. 669, which is as follows: "The test of the admissibility of evidence of a subsequent offense is, does proof of the subsequent act have some logical connection with and tend to establish the specific crime charged." 

State v. Leatherwood, 112 W. Va. 339, 164 S. E. 295. 

And in Boyd v. Com., supra, it is held: "It is permissible, in cases where the motive, intent, or knowledge, of the accused is involved, to admit evidence of acts, conduct, or declarations which tend to establish such knowledge, intention, or motive of the accused, notwithstanding the fact that this may disclose a different crime in law. "Proof of other crimes is admissible where the other crimes constitute only a part of the general scheme of which the crime is a part.' 99 

§ 988. Civil liability of defendant immaterial. 

In Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899, it is held:

§ 668 

"The fact that accused is civilly liable to the owner of the goods will not affect the question of his criminal responsibility, if he acted with a felonious intent." 

State v. Rush, 108 W. Va. 254, 150 S. E. 740. 

State v. Smith, 117 W. Va. 598, 186 S. E. 623. 

989. Bank records as evidence.

In State v. Frantz, 108 W. Va. 639, 152 S. E. 326, it is held: "An original ledger sheet from the records of a bank showing the account of a depositor may be admitted in evidence to establish overdrafts by the customer." § 990. Embezzlement by county officers of public moneys. 

In State v. Turner, 118 W. Va. 93, 188 S. E. 765, it is held that 

West Virginia Code, 11-7-1 (sec. 751), providing that an assessor who fails to pay over money collected by him within the time fixed by the statute shall be guilty of the embezzlement thereof, is to be construed as stating a prima facie case and not one of conclusive guilt. 

State v. Smith, 117 W. Va. 598, 186 S. E. 624. 

State v. Jackson, 100 W. Va. 543, 131 S. E. 11.

Likewise, the same construction is to be given to Code 59-1-32 (sec. 5849), relating to other county officers. 

State v. Sixo, 77 W. Va. 243, 87 S. E. 267. 

State v. Jackson, supra. 

State v. Turner, supra.

It follows, therefore, that an instruction which tells the jury that if they believe from the evidence that defendant failed to account for and pay over within the time fixed by law, any moneys collected by him, he is guilty of the embezzlement thereof, is erroneous as it precludes the jury from weighing the question of in- 

tent. 

State v. Turner, supra. 

State v. Smith, supra. 

State v. Jackson, supra. 

§ 991. Indictment, form of. 

An indictment for embezzlement may be for simple larceny, or
