for embezzlement only, and West Virginia Code, 62-2-24 (sec. 

6188), provides that the two may be joined as separate counts in the same indictment. The Virginia Code contains no such provision, but such joinder is generally practiced and is recognized by the courts.

State v. Workman, 91 W. Va. 771, 114 S. E. 276. 

State v. Cantor, 93 W. Va. 245, 116 S. E. 396.

However, where the offense is embezzlement and the indictment charges simple larceny only, the Virginia Code, sec. 4451, requires the attorney for the Commonwealth to give defendant, if he demands it, a statement in writing, of what statute he intends to rely upon to ask for conviction. But such demand must be made before the trial begins. 

Boyd v. Com., 156 Va. 934, 157 S. E. 546.

West Virginia has no such statute, but there as in Virginia, the accused may demand a bill of particulars. 

Virginia Code, sec. 6091.

§ 992. Same, essentials of. 

Under the Virginia Code, sec. 4451, and the West Virginia 

Code, 61-3-19 (sec. 5960), an indictment must aver the proper venue and time that defendant did feloniously embezzle, convert to his own use and steal the property embraced in the statute, describing it, and stating its value; that the property belonged to another person, naming him; that it came into defendant's possession or care by virtue of his office, place or employment, which must also be stated; and the indictment must conclude, "against the peace and dignity of the State," or "Commonwealth," in Virginia. 

State v. Cantor, 93 W. Va. 243, 116 S. E. 396. 

And in State v. Hudson, 93 W. Va. 435, 117 S. E. 122, it is held that an indictment for embezzlement, which alleges that defendant (1) feloniously did embezzle, (2) certain moneys, stating the amount and value thereof, (3) belonging to a designated bank, naming it, (4) which moneys then and there were in defendant's 2 CT-9

§ 670 

possession, (5) by virtue of his office of cashier of said bank, (6) with intent to injure and defraud said bank, against the peace and dignity of the State, contains all the elements essential to a valid indictment for the embezzlement of the moneys of the bank. § 993. Same, unnecessary to allege kind of money.

The Virginia Code, sec. 4870, among other things, provides that in an indictment for the embezzlement of money, it is not necessary to specify the particular kind of such money. The clause reads as follows: 

"* * * and it shall be sufficient to allege the embezzlement or fraudulent conversion to be of money, without specifying any particular money, gold, silver, note or security, and such allegation, so far as it regards the description of the property. shall be sustained, if the accused be proved to have embezzled any bullion, money, bank note, or security for money, although the particular species be not proved." 

Holley v. Com., 113 Va. 769, 75 S. E. 88.

And in West Virginia, the revisers' note to Code 61-3-20 (sec. 

5961), says that in order to obviate the effect of the decision in 

State v. Hudson, 93 W. Va. 435, 117 S. E. 122, the following provision, taken from the Massachusetts statute, was added to the section on embezzlement : "And it shall not be necessary to describe in the indictment, or to identify upon the trial, the particular bullion, money, bank note, draft, or security for money which is so taken, converted to his own use: or embezzled by him, etc." § 994. Same, may charge any number of distinct acts. 

The Virginia Code, sec. 4870, and the West Virginia Code, 62-2-5 (sec. 6169), are identical and provide: "In a prosecution against a person accused of embezzling, or fraudulently converting to his own use, bullion, money, bank notes, or other security for money, it shall be lawful, in the same indictment, to charge, and thereon to proceed against the accused, for any number of distinct acts of such embezzlement or fraudulent conversion which

EMBEZZLEMENT 

may have been committed by him within six months from the first to the last of such acts; * * * ""

In neither of the Virginias does the statute define the term "distinct acts" of embezzlement. But in State v. Wetzel, 75 W. Va. 

7, 83 S. E. 68, it is held that where the accused occupied a position of trust (cashier of a bank in this case), and embezzled small sums, taken at various times, the jury might well infer that they were taken in furtherance of, and pursuant to, a preconceived and continuing design to appropriate the same to his own use. 

NOTE: The various separate offenses should be alleged in the indictment as separate counts. § 995. Same, state not required to elect.

In State v. Larue, 98 W. Va. 677, 128 S. E. 116, where the accused was indicted for embezzling certain quantities of cement at divers times, covering a period of about one year. period of about one year. The indictment contained twenty counts, ten counts charging embezzlement followed by a count charging larceny in each instance. The defendant moved the court to require the state to elect on which count it would proceed to trial, and, at the conclusion of the evidence, to elect on which count it would rely for conviction. Both motions were overruled by the trial court, and a general verdict of guilty was returned by the jury. 

HELD: No error; syl. 3, 4 and 5 of this case are as follows:

Syl. 3. "If all the offenses charged in one or more counts of an indictment represent but one continuous transaction, it is well settled in this state (and in Virginia) that they may be so joined as distinct offenses in different counts, and that, where properly joined as distinct offenses, unless they appear on the face of the indictment to involve a different transaction, a motion to quash for misjoinder should be overruled." See- 

State v. Ringer, 84 W. Va. 546, 100 S. E. 413.

State v. Smith, 24 W. Va. 814. 

State v. Shores, 31 W. Va. 491, 7 S. E. 413. 

State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 289, 13 S. E. 654. 

Dowdy v. Com., 9 Gratt. 728, 60 Am. Dec. 314.

Syl. 4. "A joinder as separate counts in one indictment. of several offenses, which, though distinct in point of law,

$ 672 

yet spring out of substantially the same transaction, cannot operate to the legal prejudice of the accused; and he is not entitled as a matter of right in such cases to compel an election." See- 

Van Sickle v. People, 29 Mich. 61, 31 Corpus Juris, 781.

Syl. 5. "On the trial of an indictment for embezzlement, there is no error in the court refusing to compel the prosecution to elect upon what alleged act of embezzlement a conviction will be asked, as embezzlement may, and often does, consist of many acts done in a series of years by virtue of the relations existing between the employer and the employee." See- 

Willis v. State, 134 Ala. 429, 33 So. 226. § 996. Offenses charged must grow out of same transaction.

At page 687 of the opinion in State v. Larue, supra, it is said: "The authorities are quite uniform in maintaining the right of the prosecutor, where offenses arose from the same transaction, to include a number of counts in one indictment variously framed to meet the possible contingencies that may arise in the introduction of the evidence. 

Upon this subject the following pertinent language is used by Wharton: 

66 'Every cautious pleader will insert as many counts as will be necessary to provide for every possible contingency in the evidence, and this the law permits.' 

Beaseley v. People, 89 Ill. 571. 

Com. v. Andrews, 132 Mass. 236. 

State v. Flye, 26 Me. 312. 

State v. Smith, 24 W. Va. 814. See, "In this case the offense charged in the indictment grew out of one continuous transaction, and, upon whichever of the counts the prosecution should proceed, evidence of the entire transaction would be admissible. * * * "We think the state, under such circumstances, may of right insert in the indictment more than one count, in order to meet the possible varying phases of the evidence; and the right to insert separate counts implies a right to support them by testimony, for, without the latter right the former would be of no value.

§ 998 

EMBEZZLEMENT 

"The court in the instant case, by its ruling, submitted all the evidence touching the alleged embezzlement of the property, by defendant, to the jury, and it is not perceived how it could have done otherwise. Embezzlement may and most often does, consist of many acts done, while the fiduciary relation existed between employer and employee. 

The fact that at last disclosed that the employer's property has been embezzled is the crime against which the statute is leveled. In such case, should the prosecution be compelled to elect, it would claim a conviction for only one of the many acts of the series that constitute the corpus delicti; it would be doubtful if a conviction could ever be obtained. The body of the crime consists of many acts done by virtue of the confidential relation existing between the parties. The separate acts may not be susceptible of direct proof, but the aggregate result is, and that is embezzlement." 

§ 997. Venue, 

In State v. Berle, 117 W. Va. 825, 188 S. E. 482, it is held: "As a general rule, in embezzlement prosecutions, the venue must be laid in the county wherein the conversion or misapplication took place. But where the conduct which entered into the embezzlement extended to two or more counties, the state's right of prosecution is not confined to one of them." Citing, State v. Bailey, 50 Ohio St. 636, 36 N. E. 233. 

State v. Gengen, 106 Iowa 711, 77 N. W. 453. 

Rhodes v. Com., 145 Va. 893, 134 S. E. 723. 

And in Rhodes v. Com., supra, it is held: "The formation in one county of the fraudulent intent to appropriate the property to one's use, followed by a conversion of the property, with that intent, in another county, is sufficient to give jurisdiction in the county wherein such intent was formed." 

998. Instructions. 

In State v. DeBerry, 75 W. Va. 633, 84 S. E. 610, it is held: "If on the trial of one charged with larceny or embezzlement of goods, the jury are instructed to find a certain way, all elements necessary to constitute the offense must

§ 674 

be included therein, and particularly the element of intent to steal or embezzle such goods."

W. Larue, having then and there in his possession such bullion, money, bank notes, securities for money and such other effects and property, by virtue of a certain office, place and employment, to-wit: As agent, employee and custodian of and on behalf of the said County Court of Mason County and as such agent, employee and custodian having custody of the said cement and other material belonging to the County Court of Mason County; against the peace and dignity of the State.

§ 1015. Conversion of part of property.

, State v. Larue, supra. § 1019. Restoration of, or payment for property. 

1. The jury are further instructed that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant is guilty of fraudulently converting to his own use the property of the County Court, or any part thereof, as charged in the indictment, then he is guilty of the offense of embezzlement ; and this offense cannot be condoned or effaced by subsequent efforts at atonement nor by any subsequent agreement between the said Larue and the said County Court; and the jury are further instructed that it is no defense that after the conversion of said property or any part thereof the same was restored, or the loss made good by the defendant or others acting in his behalf, or that he has offered or promised to restore the same to the owner thereof, or that the owner has obtained a judgment therefor. So that, when the offense is complete it cannot be relieved against except by the punishment of the defendant for the crime as provided by law; and therefore, the jury further instructed that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant is guilty of fraudulently converting to his own. use the property of the County Court or any part thereof, as charged in the indictment, though the value thereof may not exceed $20, it is the duty of the jury to find the defendant guilty.

EMBEZZLEMENT DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1020. State must prove elements of offense. 

The court instructs the jury that the law does not presume, merely because money has been intrusted to a person or from the fact that he has used some of it to pay himself wages or other expenses of the business in which he is engaged, that he has embezzled it, but the law presumes that he acted in good faith in all of his transactions in respect thereto. Neither is he called upon to show what disposition he has made of such money. But to enable the state to sustain such a charge it devolves upon it to show, beyond all reasonable doubt, the following things, before a conviction can be made:

FIRST: That the person charged with such crime occupied the trust relation alleged in the indictment. 

SECOND: That the property claimed to have been converted to the use of the accused is the property described in the indictment.

THIRD: That it was the property of the Bank of Spencer. 

FOURTH That it came into possession of the accused by reason of his office and employment alleged in the indictment. 

FIFTH: That such property was converted by the accused to his use.

SIXTH That such conversion was with intent to deprive the owner of such property, without any intention of accounting therefor.

And the court instructs you that unless you believe beyond all reasonable doubt from the evidence in this case that each of said six several essentials have been proved against the defendant you shall find him not guilty in this case. 

, State v. Wetzel, 75 W. Va. 7, 83 S. E. 68. . 

§ 1021. Faulty bookkeeping of defendant. 

The court further instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case that the defendant, O. B. Wetzel, in keeping the books of the Bank of Spencer, followed a system of bookkeeping or method of keeping his accounts, that was not in

§ 690 

accordance with the usual system or method followed by banks, the jury cannot draw any inference from such method or system of keeping the books of said bank relating to the guilt or innocence of the accused, unless the jury further believe from the evidence in this case that such method or system was used by said defendant for the purpose of committing fraud; and to draw any inference against the accused from such method or system of keeping the books or accounts of said bank, the jury must further believe from the evidence that the defendant used this system or method of bookkeeping for the purpose of enabling him to carry into effect an intent on his part to deprive the Bank of Spencer, of its property, without any right so to do. 

, State v. Wetzel, supra. § 1022. Entries in books by defendant not confession. 

The court instructs the jury that entries of the defendant O. 

B. Wetzel in the books of account of the Bank of Spencer, which he was required to keep, do not constitute confessions or admissions of guilt, but, are perfectly innocent in themselves; and it is only when these entries are first shown by competent evidence to be false and fraudulent, that any inference, whatever, may be drawn by the jury from such entries against the defendant with reference to the charges against him contained in the indictment found in this case. 

Taken from the record in, State v. Wetzel, supra. § 1023. Overdraft not sufficient.

The court instructs the jury, that although you may believe from the evidence that the defendant overdrew his account with the Bank of Spencer, and that upon a settlement with said bank he would be indebted to it; still that is not sufficient proof alone upon which to base a conviction in this case; and unless you believe from all the evidence in the case beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant overdrew his account with said bank with the intention of not accounting therefor to said bank, then they must find the defendant not guilty.

Taken from the record in, State v. Wetzel, supra. § 1025. Distinction between larceny and embezzlement. 

1. The jury are hereby instructed that in larceny there must be a felonious taking of the property; that in embezzlement there must be a conversion, with a fraudulent intent. So, before you can convict of a larceny in this case you must believe beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant did feloniously take, steal and carry away the goods and chattels mentioned in some count in the indictment, you must believe beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant converted the property described in some count in the indictment to his own use, and that said conversion was felonious; and unless you believe that such conversion was fraudulent and felonious you cannot convict of embezzlement. 

Taken from the record in, State v. Larue, 98 W. Va. 677, 128 S. E. 116. 2. The jury are instructed that in larceny there must be a felonious taking of the property; that in embezzlement there must be a conversion, with a fraudulent intent.

So, before you can convict of a larceny in this case you must believe, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the defendant did feloniously take, steal and carry away the goods and chattels mentioned in some count in the indictment, and before you can convict the defendant of embezzlement, you must believe beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant converted the property de-

§ 692 

scribed in some count in the indictment to his own use, and that said conversion was felonious; and unless you believe that such conversion was fraudulent and felonious, you cannot convict of embezzlement. 

,

State v. Larue, supra. § 1026. Fraudulent intent necessary.

The jury are hereby instructed that the mere conversion of goods mentioned in the indictment to defendant's use after receiving the same by virtue of his agency (if you believe beyond all reasonable doubt that there was such agency), then the failure to turn it over to the County Court does not constitute the offense of embezzlement charged in the indictment, but there must have been in the mind of the defendant, at the time of such conversion, an unlawful, felonious and fraudulent intent to appropriate such goods to the defendant's use and to deprive the County Court of such use thereof absolutely. 

Taken from the record in,

State v. Larue, supra. 

Blashfield on Instructions, sec. 2828. § 1027. Money must have been secured by virtue of position.

The court instructs the jury that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt before she can convict the prisoner of embezzlement under any count in the indictment that the property alleged to have been embezzled, or some part of it, was intrusted to him by the Wytheville Banking and Insurance Company, as its president, and that it came into his possession by virtue of his position, and that he unlawfully, fraudulently, and feloniously disposed of, used, concealed, or embezzled it for his own use and not for the benefit of said company. 

Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 810, 35 S. E. 452. § 1028. Defendant's honesty presumed.

The jury are further instructed by the court that the law presumes every man to be honest in the transaction of business and

§ 1031 EMBEZZLEMENT 

in all the affairs of life and that this presumption goes with him even when he is indicted for a crime, which imputes to him by means of the indictment dishonesty, with reference to the matters charged against him.

And the jury are therefore instructed that when they retire to their room to consider of their verdict in this case, and when they enter upon the consideration of the evidence and the instructions of the court given in this case they are to enter upon such consideration, with the presumption in favor of the accused, that he acted honestly, while acting in his position as cashier of the Bank of Spencer, and that he was innocent of the crime charged to him in the indictment in this case until such presumption of innocence has been overcome beyond all reasonable doubt, by the evidence in the case.

, State v. Wetzel, 75 W. Va. 7, 83 S. E. 68. § 1029. Conversion by officer or agent of corporation.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe the money was borrowed for the use and benefit of the Tailoring Company, and defendant gave the company's receipt therefor, which was accepted by Marich, then they should find the defendant not guilty. 

State v. Cantor, 93 W. Va. 248, 116 S. E. 396. § 1030. Conversion by public officer, justice of the peace. 

The court instructs the jury, that unless they believe from the evidence that the accused knowingly misused or misappropriated, or knowingly disposed of otherwise than in accordance with law, a fine of five dollars, collected by him as justice of the peace of the County of Warwick, which five dollars were funds of the State of Virginia, as alleged in the indictment, then they must find him not guilty. 

Robinson v. Com., 104 Va. 888, 52 S. E. 690. § 1031. Conversion must have been with felonious intent.

The court instructs the jury that before you can convict the prisoner under any count of the indictment against him you must

§ 

694 

believe beyond a reasonable doubt that he feloniously took, appropriated, disposed of, or converted to his own use the property, or some part thereof, therein mentioned—that is, that he did so with a criminal intent, and not under an honest belief that he had a bona fide claim of right to do so. 

Wadley v. Com., 98 Va. 810, 35 S. E. 452. 

NOTE: The above instruction was modified by the trial court by striking therefrom the words: "and not under an honest belief that he had a bona fide claim of right to do so." Held error. 

The court said: "If there was evidence to support the instruction, as asked for, it should have been given. In embezzlement, there must be a fraudulent purpose to deprive the owner of his property and appropriate the same. If property is converted under a bona fide claim of right, the conversion is not embezzlement."

§ 1032. Extortion at common law. 

At common law extortion is a misdemeanor. It may only be committed by public officers; and is a species of malfeasance in office. In 8 R. C. L. p. 293, it is thus defined: "At the common law extortion is defined as the unlawful taking by an officer, by color of his office, of any money or thing of value that is not due him, or more than is due or before it is due."

Another definition, quoted with approval by numerous text writers, is found in State v. Logan, 104 La. 762, 29 So. 336. It reads: "The ordinary meaning of the word extortion is the taking or obtaining of anything from another by means of illegal compulsion or oppressive exaction. But the word has acquired a technical meaning in the common law, and in this sense, may be defined to be the corrupt and unlawful taking by any officer of the law, under color of his office, of any money, or thing of value, that is not due to him, or the corrupt or unlawful taking of any money or thing of value,

$696 

under color of his office, in excess of what is due to him, or before it is due to him.' 

§ 1033. Statutes relating to common-law extortion. 

The Virginia Code, sec. 4514, provides: "If any officer, for performing an official duty for which a fee or compensation is allowed or provided by law, knowingly demand and receive a greater fee or compensation than is so allowed or provided, he shall be fined not exceeding fifty dollars." 

And the West Virginia Code, 61-5-20, (sec. 6018), provides: "If any officer, for performing an official duty for which a fee or compensation is allowed or provided by law, knowingly demand and receive a greater fee or compensation than is so allowed or provided, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and, upon conviction, shall be fined not exceeding fifty dollars." § 1034. Must be committed under color of office.

Not only must common-law extortion be committed by an officer, but it is also essential that the taking of the money or other thing of value be taken under colore officii, i. e., under color of office. Only public officers can do acts colore officii, and color of office means color of official authority. 

In 19 Cyc., p. 38 it is said: "To constitute extortion it is also essential that the taking be under color of office. In other words the one taking the fees must have acted in his official capacity, not as a private individual.” 

And in State v. Mankin, 68 W. Va. 776, 70 S. E. 764, it is held: "An act done under colore officii (color of office) is an act done, not only by an officer, professing to act as such, but also under color of authority to act in and about the particular matter in connection with which it is done." 

Also in State v. Hansford, 43 W. Va. 777, 28 S. E. 791, it is held: "The test of an official act is, was it done colore officii,by color of authority." 

See also 

Wait v. B. & L. Asso., 76 W. Va. 436, 85 S. E. 637.

EXTORTION AND KIDNAPI’ING 

§ 1035 

§ 1035. Indictment for common-law extortion. 

In 19 Cyc., p. 41, it is said: "As extortion can be committed by one only under color of his office, it is necessary to allege an official capacity, and that the act was done under color thereof, and a failure so to do constitutes ground for an arrest of judgment." "It is also necessary that the indictment should designate the services for which the illegal fees were charged. And where the officer is not allowed to charge fees the indictment must allege that no fees were allowed by law." "An evil intent being a necessary element of the act, an indictment must allege the existence of such intent. For this purpose it is sufficient to allege that defendant took the money extorsively' or wilfully and knowingly." 

Also in 8 R. C. L., p. 294, sec. 316, it is also said: "A person cannot be convicted of the crime of extortion under color of office when in fact no such office exists although he purports to act as such officer, but where an office dejure exists a de facto officer holding such office may be guilty of extortion under color of office. A taking of fees under color of office is of the essence of the offense of extortion. The money or thing received must have been claimed or accepted in right of office, and the person paying must have yielded to official authority. Therefore it is not extortion if an officer receives a compensation or fee for services which it was not his official duty to perform. Likewise, a voluntary payment of a greater sum, where a less is due, is not extortion, since the offense supposes that the money is paid unwillingly and by constraint; and the voluntary payment of a fee where none is due is not extortion." 

And on page 318 of the same work, it is further said: "Where it is necessary to charge that the money or other thing of value was corruptly taken, this is sufficiently done by alleging that the fees were "extorsively" taken, although the technical words in an indictmentt for extortion at common law are 'extort' and 'by color of office.' The indictment should be certain in every material allegation or charge; hence it should state the office held by the defendant by color of which he committed the crime, the place where the crime was committed, the exact amount extorted, and whether it was in excess of the lawful fee or where no fee

§ 698 

was chargeable. Where nothing is due it must be averred that nothing was due; and if the charge be for taking more than was due, the indictment must show how much was due."

To the same effect is the statement of the law in 25 Corpus Juris, p. 240, where it is said: "An allegation that fees were taken 'by color of office' is necessary. This allegation must not be merely in the words 'by color of office' without more. It should show further by color of what office the extortionate act was committed, and by express terms, not by implication from the averment of defendant's official capacity. It is not necessary in charging the offense at common law to allege that defendant took the money 'as fees' or 'to his own use' it is sufficient to allege that defendant extorted it by color of office. Under statutory requirements, it has been held necessary to allege that the sum extorted was demanded as a fee for some official duty. "An allegation of the services for which fees were charged is necessary, and the offense, if statutory, must be charged in terms bringing the rendition of the services within the statutory definition. The allegation must be with sufficient certainty to enable the court to conclude from facts stated whether or not the compensation received was other than that authorized or permitted by law. "It is not sufficient to allege generally that defendant took a certain sum, or that he took more than was due, but an allegation should be made of what he ought to have taken and what was the excess; but the amount of the legal charge need not be averred where fixed by law and not varying according to circumstances. Where the fee fixed by law is not certain and unchangeable by circumstances, it is necessary to allege not merely the amount taken, but also the facts by which its legality can be ascertained. Where the taking of illegal fees is for services for which no statutory allowance is made, the fact that no statutory allowance is made must be alleged. Where the amount taken is an aggregate of charges for several items of service. an allegation of the items of service and of the aggregate amount taken but omitting the items of illegal fees taken would seem to be open to the objection that it does not inform the accused as to what items were overcharges and what he must prepare himself to meet."

EXTORTION AND KIDNAPPING § 1037 § 1036. Statutory extortion. 

The statutes of both Virginias have greatly extended the common law offense of extortion, and made it a felony for any person to extort money, property, pecuniary benefit, or any bond, note, etc., by threats of injury to the character, person or property of another person, and in West Virginia such offense extends to threats against the wife or child of such other person. 

The Virginia statute, Code sec. 4406, provides: "If any person threaten injury to the character, person, or property of another person or accuse him of any offense and thereby extort money, property, or pecuniary benefit or any note, bond, or other evidence of debt from him or any other person he shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than three nor more than five years or in the discretion of the jury be confined in jail not exceeding one year and fined not exceeding one thousand dollars." 

The West Virginia statute, Code 61-2-13 (sec. 5928), is somewhat broader than Virginia law. It provides: "If any person threaten injury to the character, person or property of another person, or to the character, person or property of his wife or child, or to accuse him or them or any one of them of any offense, and thereby extort money, pecuniary benefit, or any bond, note or other evidence of debt, he shall be guilty of a felony, and, upon conviction, shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years. And if any person make such threat of injury or accusation of an offense as herein set forth, but fail thereby to extort money, pecuniary benefit, or any bond, note or other evidence of debt, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and, upon conviction, shall be confined in jail not less than two nor more than twelve months and fined not less than fifty nor more than five hundred dollars." 

§ 1037. Indictment for statutory extortion. 

Under the statutes of both Virginias the threat is the gist of the offense of statutory extortion, and without such a threat as stated in the statute there is no such statutory crime. Therefore, the nature and character of the threat, or threats, must be alleged in the indictment, else it is fatally defective and should be quashed on motion, the demurrer thereto sustained, or judgment arrested. But

$700 

an indictment which follows the language of the statute is suffi cient. 

State v. Keiffer, 112 W. Va. 74, 163 S. E. 841. 

§ 1038. Truth of charge no defense. 

Under the statutes of both Virginias the crime is complete when the threats are made and the money or property obtained. The truth of the charge contained in the threats is wholly immaterial. 

The indictment need not aver the falsity of such charge, nor is evidence of its truth admissible as a defense. 

Mitchell v. Com., 75 Va. 856. 

§ 1039. Kidnapping, Virginia statute. 

See Virginia Code, sec. 4407. § 1040. Same, West Virginia statute. 

See West Virginia Code 61-2-14a (sec. 5929).

§ 1049 

FALSE PRETENSES 

§ 1047. False pretenses defined.

It is generally held that the crime of false pretense is the obtaining or taking from any person by false pretense, any money or other property, with the intent to defraud. 

State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 54. 

And in State v. Edwards, 51 W. Va. 224, 41 S. E. 429, it is said: "If the property is delivered with the intention on the part of the owner of parting with it altogether, passing both title and possession, the offense is not larceny but obtaining property by false pretenses." 

§ 1048. Statutes compared. 

Originally, the statutes of the two Virginias on false pretenses were identical, but in comparatively recent years West Virginia has amended her law in some minor particulars. However, by both statutes the offense is made larceny, and the prescribed penalties attach regardless of the amount of money, or the value of the property, so obtained. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4459. 

West Virginia Code, 61-3-24 (sec. 5965). 

§ 1049. Penalty, rule in West Virginia. 

While the offense is made larceny by statute, a specific punishment is prescribed by Code 61-3-24 (sec. 5965),-confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years, or, in the discretion of the court, confinement in jail not more than one year and a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars, and not the punishment for ordinary larceny. 

State v. Grove, 74 W. Va. 702, 82 S. E. 1019. 

State v. Martin, 103 W. Va. 448, 137 S. E. 885. 

In State v. Grove, supra, it is said: "The obtaining of the property of another by false pretense with intent to defraud is by section 23, chapter 145 (now 61-3-24, sec. 5965), a felony, regardless of the value of the property, and the punishment in that section applies to the offense, not the punishment for ordinary

§ 710 

larceny." This case overrules State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 54. 

And in the opinion in this case, page 704, the court further said: "But as the statute now is, the punishment for ordinary larceny is not applicable to larceny by false pretenses.

The latter offense is, by the present statute, of felony grade, whatever the value of the property involved. Formerly it was otherwise. State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 54.

By the enactment of 1891 a significant change was made in section 23, chapter 145. That section was made to read so that the special punishment therein mentioned applies to the provisions thereof, that the obtaining of the property of another by false pretenses shall be deemed larceny, as well as to the other provisions of the section." § 1050. Same, rule in Virginia.

In Virginia the punishment for obtaining by false pretense is the same as that provided in Code sec. 4440 for larceny. But the statute, sec. 4459, further provides that if one "obtain, by any false pretense or token," with intent to defraud, "the signature of any person to a writing, the false making whereof would be forgery, he shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than two nor more than ten years.” 

Dull v. Com., 25 Gratt. 965. 

Trogdon v. Com., 31 Gratt. 862. § 1051. False pretenses distinguished from larceny. 

In State v. Martin, 103′ W. Va. 448, 137 S. E. 885, it is held: "The distinction between the crimes of obtaining by false pretense and larceny lies in the intention with which the owner parts with his property. If the owner in parting with his property intends to invest the accused with the title as well as the possession, the latter has committed the crime of obtaining the property by false pretense. 

But if the intention of the owner is to invest the accused with the mere possession of the property, and the latter with the requisite intent receives it and converts it to his own use, it is larceny." Citing, State v. Edwards, 51 W. Va. 220, 41 S. E. 429. 

25 Corpus Juris, p. 657.

§ 1053 

FALSE PRETENSES § 1052. Elements of offense. 

To constitute the offense of obtaining money or property by false pretenses, four elements must concur: 

1. There must be an intent to defraud. 

2. There must be an actual fraud committed. 

3. False pretenses must be used for the purpose of perpetrating the fraud. 4. The fraud must be accomplished by means of the false pretenses made use of for the purpose; that is, they must be in some degree the cause, if not the controlling and decisive cause, which induced the owner to part with his property. 

Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 567. 

State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 54. 

Hagy v. Com., 168 Va. 663, 190 S. E. 144.

State v. Pishner, 72 W. Va. 603, 78 S. E. 752. 

§ 1053. False pretenses need not be such as would deceive one of ordinary intelligence. 

In Sudnick v. Kohn, 81 W. Va. 492, 94 S. E. 962, it is held: "In order to constitute the offense of obtaining money or property by false pretenses, it is not necessary that the alleged false pretense be such as would deceive one of ordinary intelligence, or as would impose upon one of ordinary prudence or caution. It is sufficient that the representations upon which the money or property is obtained falsely assert the existence or non-existence of a fact, and were made with the intention of procuring the money or property of another."

And in the body of the opinion, page 495, it is further stated: "The law is as much for the protection of those ignorant and illiterate and full of credence as for the astute and incredulous. * * * To hold otherwise would be to say that those who are beneath the average in intelligence and capacity, and who are more credulous or incautious than the average are without the protection of the law, and are the legitimate prey of the knave and charlatan."

$ 712 

§ 1054. Giving worthless check, rule in West Virginia

Under the holding of the West Virginia court the giving of a worthless check, as defined in Code 61-3-39 (sec. 5980), is a false pretense. In State v. Augustine, 114 W. Va. 143, 171 S. E. 

111, it is held: "The giving of a worthless check, or a check which the accused has no reason to suppose will be honored, is, in itself, a false pretense; the giving of such check being a rep resentation, symbol, or token that the accused has money or credit with the drawee, to the amount of its face value." Citing, 25 Corpus Juris 612. 

West Virginia Code, 61-3-24 (sec. 5965). § 1055. Same, check must be protested for nonpay. ment.

In State v. Ambrogio, 103 W. Va. 594, 138 S. E. 322, it is held: "To convict one of violating this section (worthless check law) by issuing and delivering to another for value a check or draft without sufficient funds on deposit with which the same may be paid, it is incumbent upon the State to prove that the check or draft has been protested for nonpayment within a reasonable time and that the defendant has received actual notice of the protest." § 1056. How false pretense may be made. 

In State v. Augustine, 114 W. Va. 145, 171 S. E. 111, it is held: "False representations may be made by acts or conduct as well as by words. In fact they may be made in any of the ways in which ideas may be communicated." § 1057. False pretense must be believed and be the controlling cause.

Other inducements may have combined with the false pretenses to induce the owner to part with his property, but it must appear that, but for the false pretenses, the owner would not have parted

§ 1060 

FALSE PRETENSES 

with his property; that they had the controlling, prevailing influence. 

Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 563. 

Trogdon v. Com., 31 Gratt. 862. 

State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 54. 

And in Fay v. Com., 28 Gratt. 912, it is also held that the false pretenses, either with or without other causes, must have had a decisive influence upon the mind of the owner, so that without this weight he would not have parted with his property. § 1058. Accused may show that representation was true. 

In Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 563, it was held that the gravamen of the offense is that the pretenses are false and if the prisoner can show that representations upon which he obtained the property from the owner are true, he cannot be convicted. § 1059. Intent to defraud must be present.

The accused must have a present intent to defraud, and it must have existed at the time he made the false pretenses by which he obtained the money or property. 

Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 563. 

Trogdon v. Com., 31 Gratt. 862. 

Fay v. Com., 28 Gratt. 912. § 1060. How intent may be shown.

Evidence of other transactions of similar character where not too remote in time or place to throw light upon the intent of the accused in the main transaction, is admissible. But such evidence is only to be considered by the jury as explanatory of such intent and not as proof that the accused has committed other offenses not charged in the indictment. 

Trogdon v. Com., 31 Gratt. 862. 

In State v. Paulian, 120 W. Va. 265, 197 S. E. 728, it is held: "In a prosecution for obtaining money by false pretenses, question of defendant's criminal intent in obtaining excessive change from prosecuting witness was for

§ 714 

jury, where he had obtained excessive change from another by a similar method."

And the remoteness as to time and place is for the court, in its discretion, to determine. 

Trogdon v. Com., supra.

The fraudulent intent is a question of fact to be determined by the jury from all the facts and circumstances of the case. 

State v. Edwards, 51 W. Va. 220, 41 S. E. 429. 

State v. Stonestreet, 112 W. Va. 668, 166 S. E. 378. 

Trogdon v. Com., supra. § 1061. Indictment, may charge false pretense or simple larceny.

It is the settled law in the Virginias that since obtaining by false pretenses is made larceny by statute, the indictment may charge simple larceny or the specific facts of false pretenses. 

Dowdy v. Com., 9 Gratt. 727. 

Leftwich v. Com., 20 Gratt. 716. 

Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 563. 

Fay v. Com., 28 Gratt. 912. 

State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 54. 

State v. Edwards, 51 W. Va. 229, 41 S. E. 429. 

State v. Williams, 68 W. Va. 86, 69 S. E. 474. 

Lewis v. Com., 120 Va. 879, 91 S. E. 174. 

State v. Lilly, 112 W. Va. 232, 164 S. E. 242.

But in whatever form the indictment may be drawn, where the money or property was actually obtained by false pretenses, the state must prove all the essential elements of false pretenses, and if there is wanting in the proof any one of such elements there can be no conviction. 

Anable v. Com., supra. 

Fay v. Com., supra. 

Trogdon v. Com., supra. 

State v. Williams, supra. § 1062. Same, must allege, and state must prove guilty knowledge.

In an indictment for false pretenses it is necessary to aver that

§ 1065 

FALSE PRETENSES 

the accused knew that the pretenses were false, and it is also necessary for the state to prove this fact. 

State v. Hurst, supra. § 1063. Same, must aver, and state must prove fraudulent intent.

Where the indictment is for obtaining goods by false pretenses, it must aver fraudulent intent, and the state must prove it. It is the very gist of the offense. 

Trogdon v. Com., supra. 

State v. Geyer, 44 W. Va. 649, 29 S. E. 1020. 

State v. Edwards, 51 W. Va. 220, 41 S. E. 429. 

However, in State v. Paulian, 120 W. Va. 265, 197 S. E. 729, it is held: "The fraudulent intent is abundantly charged in the opening lines of this indictment by the words 'did fraudulently, designedly * * * pretend.' The word fraudulently' alone implies fraudulent intent." Citing, State v. Probert, 19 N. M. 13, 140 P. 1108. § 1064. Same, joining false pretense count with count for larceny, rule in Virginia. In Anthony v. Com., 88 Va. 847, 14 S. E. 834, it is held proper to join a count for obtaining by false pretenses with a count for larceny in the same indictment. And in Dowdy v. Com., 9 Gratt. 

727, it is further held that the same offense may be charged in several counts for obtaining by false pretenses and larceny, and the indictment will not be quashed nor the prosecutor compelled to elect on which count he will proceed. This is because the Virginia statute, section 4459, defining false pretenses, simply declares the offense to be larceny and does not fix the punishment therefor, but leaves the punishment as fixed by section 4440 for larceny. § 1065. Same, rule in West Virginia.

In West Virginia it is held that the crime of false pretenses

§ 716 

may be charged in the indictment as simple larceny. But the court has not said whether the two offenses may be joined as separate counts in the same indictment. Code, 61-3-13 (sec. 5528), fixes the punishment for grand larceny at not less than one nor more than ten years in the penitentiary. And while Code, 61-3-24 (sec. 5965), make it larceny to obtain goods or money by false pretenses, it also fixes the punishment regardless of the value of such goods or money at not less than one nor more than five years in the penitentiary, or, in the discretion of the court, at confinement in jail not more than one year and a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars. Again, Code 62-2-24 (sec. 6188), provides that "A count for receiving stolen goods or for embezzlement, may be joined with a count for larceny in the same indictment; * *" But there is no such provision with reference to joining a count with a count for false pretenses. Hence it is unsafe to join such counts. The better practice is to either charge the offense as false pretenses or as simple larceny. If the latter, a bill of particulars must be furnished the defendant, if demanded, showing the nature of the transaction and the facts upon which the State will rely for a conviction. 

See sec. 92, etc. § 1066. Where the "money, goods or other property" is of less value than twenty dollars, rule in 

West Virginia. 

Since Code 61-3-24 (sec. 5965), by the punishment prescribed, makes the obtaining of "money, goods or other property," by false pretenses a felony regardless of the value of such goods, it necessarily follows that an indictment for so obtaining such "money, goods or other property" of less value than twenty dollars, must charge it to have been done "feloniously." An indictment for the larceny of such goods, etc., where the value thereof is less than twenty dollars, must also allege the same to have been feloniously stolen. 

State v. Groves, 74 W. Va. 702, 82 S. E. 1019.

§ 1069 

FALSE PRETENSES 

§ 1067. Giving worthless check, rule in West Virginia.

In State v. McGinnis, 116 W. Va. 473, 181 S. E. 820, it is held that where the false pretense is the delivery of a worthless check for more than twenty dollars under Code 61-3-39 (sec. 5980), the indictment must allege the same to have been done "with intent to defraud," and failure so to do renders it utterly void. 

Without such allegation precise proof of all the charges contained in the indictment would not convict the accused of the crime defined in the statute. A verdict of guilty on such an indictment will be set aside although its sufficiency was not challenged in the trial court by motion to quash, demurrer, or motion in arrest of judgment. The same is also true where the check is for less than twenty dollars and a misdemeanor. And this is true notwithstanding Code 62-9-15 (sec. 6277) prescribes a form of indictment and omits the words "with intent to defraud." 

State v. Augustine, 114 W. Va. 143, 171 S. E. 111. § 1068. Instructions, may not go beyond offense charged in indictment. 

In State v. Stonestreet, 112 W. Va. 670, 166 S. E. 378, the instruction, after stating the false pretense charged in the indictment continued in this language, "or made any other false and fraudulent pretenses that were material." This was held error, as it authorized the conviction of the accused upon false representations other than those alleged in the indictment.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1072. Intent to defraud.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence, that the defendant, Gilbert L. Hurst, on the 28th day of

December, 1876, had in his possession, as the property of his wife, Amanda G. Hurst, the single bill mentioned and described in the first four counts of the indictment, and that he, on said day, for the purpose of transferring the same to the witness Benjamin R. Coffman, and, with intent to defraud, represented to him, said Coffman, that there was then due upon said obligation the sum of one hundred and ninety-seven dollars and sixty-eight cents ($197.68), and that, as a part of the means by which he sought to induce said Coffman so to believe, changed a credit endorsed upon said bill or obligation from a credit of $250.00 to a credit of $200.00, and that by such representation the said 

Coffman was induced to take said obligation from said Hurst and paid him therefor the sum of $158.00, and in fact there was only the sum of $144.39 due upon said obligation, and the same. was known to the Hurst, the jury must find him guilty of taking the whole sum of $158.00, though said obligation was then worth $144.39. But if the jury further believe from the evidence,

$ 722 

1111 that said Coffman had previously assigned said obligation to Amanda G. Hurst, wife of the prisoner, for a valuable consideration, and, as an inducement to get her to accept it, had agreed and promised her that if Watkins did not pay her he (Coffman) would take it up; this would negative the idea of an intent to defraud Coffman, so far as the procuring of $144.39, the amount of said obligation, was concerned, and they should find him guilty of taking only $13.61. 

State v. Hurst, 11 W. Va. 57. § 1073. False pretense must have been believed.

The court instructs the jury that they must believe from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the alleged false pretenses were believed by Messrs. Millhiser & Company; that but for them they would not have parted with their property-that is, that they had the prevailing and controlling influence in making Millhiser & Company part with their property. 

Trogdon v. Com., 31 Gratt. 867. § 1074. Aiding and abetting another to obtain by false pretenses. 

1. The jury are instructed that if the jury believe from the evidence that Robert Purdy, Dr. Lewis, or any other persons, at the house of accused, by the use of false pretenses, obtained from one Joseph M. Fowlkes, the sum of $570, the jury cannot find the accused guilty of the larceny alleged in the indictment, unless they are satisfied from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the prisoner was present, aiding and abetting therein, or suffered or permitted the said persons so using the false pretense, to use the said house with knowledge that such persons intended to use said house for the employing of such fraudulent pretense.

But if the prisoner was within easy call, to aid or assist them in their purpose, or in escaping, or in getting rid of, or misleading the person from whom such money was obtained, that is a presence, aiding and abetting, and the prisoner is as guilty as if he were personally present. 

Dull v. Com., 25 Gratt. 976.

The court instructs the jury that before you can find the defendant, guilty in this case, it is incumbent upon the 

State to prove beyond all reasonable doubt the following facts: ........ 9 

1. That the offense charged in the indictment was committed in ... county. ....... 9 

2. That at the time of the transaction between the prisoner and the prosecuting witness, the prisoner intended to defraud the said prosecuting witness. 

3. That there was an actual fraud perpetrated by the prisoner upon the said prosecuting witness. 

4. That false pretenses were used by the prisoner for the purpose of perpetrating said fraud upon the said prosecuting witness. 

5. That the prisoner believed said false pretenses and that the said fraud was accomplished by means of said false pretenses made use of by the prisoner, for that purpose; that is, said false pretenses must have been in some degree the cause, if not the controlling and decisive

§ 1078. Statutes compared. 

Prior to the amendment of 1928 the Virginia statute was the same as the West Virginia law. The latter, Code 61-4-5 (sec. 5995), reads: "If any person forge any writing, other than such as is mentioned in the first and third sections (secs. 5191, 5193)

§ 728 

of this article (which relate to forging of public records and counterfeiting), to the prejudice of another's right, or utter or attempt to employ as true such forged writing, knowing it to be forged, he shall be deemed guilty of a felony, and, upon conviction, shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than two nor more than five years.' 

In 1928, however, Virginia added two important amendments to her statute, Code sec. 4489. The first provides that, in the discretion of the jury, or the court trying the case without a jury, the accused shall be confined in jail not less than six nor more than twelve months; while the second makes it forgery, with like punishment, "to obtain, by false pretense or token, the signature of another person, to any writing, with intent to defraud any other person." 

NOTE: The sections excepted in the Virginia Code likewise refer to the forgery of public records and counterfeiting, and are not treated in this work. § 1079. Offense not defined by statutes.

In neither of the Virginias is the crime of forgery defined by law, and with unimportant statutory modifications the offense remains as at common law. Blackstone defines it as "The fraudulent making or alteration of a writing to the prejudice of another man's rights." In 12 R. C. L., p. 139, it is thus defined: "The false making or material alteration, with intent to defraud, of any writing which, if genuine, might apparently be of legal efficacy or the foundation of a legal liability." § 1080. As defined by the courts.

In Virginia, the appellate court has approved the definition of forgery as stated in Bishop's New Criminal Law, vol. 2, sec. 523, as follows: 

"Forgery is the fraudulent making of a false writing which, if genuine, would be apparently of some legal efficacy." 

Terry v. Com., 87 Va. 673, 13 S. E. 104. 

Gordon v. Com., 100 Va. 829, 41 S. E. 746.

§ 1081 

FORGERY 

And in West Virginia, State v. Lotono, 62 W. Va. 310, 58 S.

E. 621, the offense is thus defined: "Forgery is the false and fraudulent making or altering of an instrument which would, if genuine, apparently impose a legal liability on another or change his legal liability to his prejudice." Citing,

State v. Poindexter, 23 W. Va. 805. 

Also, in State v. Pine, 56 W. Va. 10, 48 S. E. 206, it is further said: "The offense of forgery consists in the false making or altering of a written instrument, to the prejudice of another's rights, and the intent to defraud."

State v. Talip, 90 W. Va. 632, 111 S. E. 601. 

State v. Sotak, 100 W. Va. 652, 131 S. E. 706. 

Barbee v. Amory, 106 W. Va. 507, 146 S. E. 59. 

§ 1081. Nature of instrument forged. 

Under the statutes of both Virginias the making, or material alteration of any writing of apparent legal efficacy, or which may prejudice another's right, or by which another may be defrauded is forgery. 

Powell v. Com., 11 Gratt. 822. 

Terry v. Com., 87 Va. 672, 13 S. E. 104. 

Gordon v. Com., 100 Va. 825, 41 S. E. 746.

The word "forge" used in the statutes has been construed to include (1) the unauthorized filling of blanks in checks, notes, acceptances, and similar instruments of commercial character. (2) The unauthorized endorsement of the name of third persons on the back thereof. (3) The unauthorized alteration of bail bonds in a material way. (4) The unauthorized making or alteration of any other writing of apparent legal efficacy, which may prejudice the rights of another, or by which another may be defrauded. 

State v. Pine, 56 W. Va. 1, 48 S. E. 206. 

Powell v. Com., 11 Gratt. 822. 

State v. Cotts, 49 W. Va. 615, 39 S. E. 605. 

State v. Lotono, 62 W. Va. 310, 58 S. E. 621. 

Terry v. Com., supra. 

Gordon v. Com., supra.

§ 730 

 § 1082. Material alteration of writing is forgery. 

The statutes of the Virginias also make the material alteration or changing of a written instrument forgery, provided it is done with intent to defraud. But such alteration must be material. 

An immaterial alteration, that is, a change which, if true, would not affect the legal liability of the parties in an action on the instrument, would not amount to a forgery. 

Com. v. Linton, 2 Va. Cas. 478. 

State v. Cotts, 49 W. Va. 617, 39 S. E. 605. 

And in State v. Lotono, supra, it is held: "An alteration in an instrument to constitute forgery, must be of a material part thereof; and a material alteration of an instrument is one which makes it speak a language different in legal effect from that which it originally spoke, or which carries with it some change in the rights, interests or obligations of the parties to the writing." Citing, State v. Poindexter, 23 W. Va. 805. 

§ 1083. Materiality of alteration a question of law. 

"The materiality of the alteration is a question of law for the court upon the admissibility of the altered instrument in evidence, and, the alteration being shown, nothing remains for the jury to pass upon." 

State v. Lotono, 62 W. Va. 310, 58 S. E. 621. 

Mfg. Co. v. Watson, 58 W. Va. 189, 52 S. E. 515. 

§ 1084. Changing figures in check not material altera tion.

In State v. Lotono, supra, it is held: "The figures in a check, following the words in the body thereof denoting the sum called for, are not a material part of the instrument, the words being controlling in determining its legal effect." 2 Cyc. 196-211. 

Schryver v. Hawkes, 22 Ohio 308. § 1085. Forgery and uttering, two distinct crimes.

The statutes of both Virginias embrace two separate and dis-

§ 1087 

FORGERY 

tinct crimes: (1) Forgery, and (2) uttering and attempting to employ as true such forged writing. The latter being an offense added by statute to the common-law offense of forgery. 

Dowdy v. Com., 9 Gratt. 732.

Page v. Com., 9 Leigh 683. 

Mowbray v. Com., 11 Leigh 645. 

Johnson v. Com., 102 Va. 927, 46 S. E. 789. 

State v. Cotts, 49 W. Va. 615, 39 S. E. 605. 

State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 124, 132 S. E. 368. This being true, it is apparent that proof of forgery will not sustain a count in the indictment for uttering a forged instrument. 

§ 1086. Uttering defined. 

It has long been held in the Virginias that any assertion or declaration, by word or act, directly or indirectly, that the forged writing is true or genuine, with knowledge that the same is forged, made with the intent to defraud, is an uttering or attempting to employ such writing as true; provided that such assertion or declaration was made in the prosecution of the purpose of obtaining the money mentioned therein. And such assertion, declaration, or act of the accused, or of another in his presence and with his knowledge, or the bringing of a suit on such forged writing, with like knowledge, is an uttering thereof. 

Sands v. Com., 20 Gratt. 800. 

Chahoon v. Com., 20 Gratt. 733. 

State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 123, 132 S. E. 368.

And one who so utters a forged writing is guilty, regardless by whom or when it was actually forged. 

State v. Perry, supra.

But knowledge that the instrument was forged at the time of uttering it, is a necessary element of the crime. 

State v. Campbell, 112 W. Va. 356, 164 S. E. 301. § 1087. Where accused uses a fictitious name. 

In State v. Austin, 93 W. Va. 715, 117 S. E. 607, it is held that where the accused uses a fictitious name without explanation

§ 732 

at the time is in itself a suspicious circumstance that the jury may weigh along with other evidence presented in the case. § 1088. To the prejudice of another's right. 

In State v. Talip, 90 W. Va. 635, 111 S. E. 601, it was held: "The gravamen of the offense at common law, and by our statute, is that the instrument alleged to have been forged must have been to the prejudice of another's rights. * * * It is not essential that the forged instrument be one such that, if genuine, an action might be brought on it. If it could be used as proof in a suit, either against him whose name is forged, or in a suit against any other, whether to sustain a claim made or in defense of one, it is susceptible of forgery. It is not essential to the crime of forgery that actual injury should have resulted, it is sufficient if any one may be, or might have been injured by the instrument." Citing, Powell v. Com., 11 Gratt. 822. 

Terry v. Com., 87 Va. 672, 13 S. E. 104. 

State v. Cotts, 49 W. Va. 615, 39 S. E. 605. 

State v. Boasso, 38 La. Ann. 202.

Arnold v. Cost (Md.), 22 Am. Dec. 302. 

State v. Johnson, 26 Iowa 407. 

See secs. 679 and 689. § 1089. Same, not necessary in indictment. 

In State v. Tingler, 32 W. Va. 546, 9 S. E. 936, it is held: "It is not necessary in an indictment, for forgery and uttering and attempting to employ as true a forged instrument, to allege that the act was 'to the prejudice of another's right;' these words describe or characterize the writing not the act. But it must appear from the description of the writing in indictment, that it is such as might prejudice his right." 

Powell v. Com., 11 Gratt. 822. 

Hendrick v. Com., 5 Leigh 707. 

Murry v. Com., 5 Leigh 720. 

See secs. 664 and 689. § 1090. Same, when unnecessary in an instruction. 

In State v. Blackwell, 102 W. Va. 425, 135 S. E. 393, it is said:

FORGERY 

"Instruction No. 1 for the State directed a verdict of guilty, if the jury found beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant 'forged the name on the check as set out in the indictment.' Counsel contend that this instruction is erroneous because it omits the words, 'to the prejudice of another's right,' * * * The indictment severally charged that the forging and the uttering of the endorsement of Holly Brake were 'to the prejudice of another's rights.' S. E. 919. The indictment was delivered to the jury when it retired to deliberate on its verdict. This contention is therefore not apposite." § 1091. Person intended to be defrauded need not be named.

Neither in an indictment for uttering, nor attempting to employ as true, a forged instrument is it necessary to name the person intended to be defrauded. 

State v. Tingler, supra. 

State v. Henderson, 29 W. Va. 147, 1 S. E. 225. 

State v. Koontz, 31 W. Va. 127, 5 S. E. 328.

This is because of the provisions of West Virginia Code, 62-2-8 (sec. 6172), and Virginia Code, sec. 4873, which read as follows: "Where an intent to injure, defraud, or cheat is required to constitute an offense, it shall be sufficient, in an indictment or accusation therefor, to allege generally an intent to injure, defraud, or cheat, without naming the person intended to be injured, defrauded, or cheated, and it shall be sufficient, and not be deemed a variance, if there appear to be any intent to injure, defraud, or cheat the

United States, or any state, or any county, corporation, officer or person.' 

§ 1092. Meaning of "legal efficacy." 

In Gordon v. Com., 100 Va. 829, 41 S. E. 746, it is held: "The doctrine may be stated generally, that an instrument is one of legal efficacy, within the rules relating to forgery, where by any possibility it may operate to the injury of another." 2 CT-13

§ 734 

10 In Bishop's New Cr. Law, vol. 2, sec. 533, it is stated: 

The false writing must be such as, if true, would be of some real or seeming legal efficacy, since otherwise it has no tendency to defraud; in other words, it must either be in fact, or must appear to be, of legal validity, but it need not have both the appearance and the reality." § 1093. Knowledge and intent necessary to a conviction for uttering forged writing.

To convict one of uttering, or attempting to employ as true, a forged writing, it must be shown that the accused knew at the time that the writing was in fact forged, and that he acted with intent to defraud. 

Sands v. Com., 20 Gratt. 800. 

Chahoon v. Com., 20 Gratt. 733. 

State v. Campbell, 112 W. Va. 356, 164 S. E. 301. 

And in State v. Austin, 93 W. Va. 715, 117 S. E. 607, the court said: "It is too clear for argument that it is not the ultimate prejudice of another's rights which determines the crime, it is sufficient that the false instrument be made with intent to defraud." Citing, 26 C. J., p. 907.

State v. Poindexter, 23 W. Va. 805. 

The intent of the accused to defraud is the essence of the crime and must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, although it need not be an intent to defraud any particular person. The intent is always a question for the jury, and it may be inferred by them from what the accused does and says, and from all the facts and circumstances of the case. 

State v. Austin, supra. 

Underhill Crim. Ev., 3d. sec. 628.

See sec. 677, and cases cited in other chapters on the question of intent. § 1094. How guilty knowledge may be proved.

In Underhill's Criminal Evidence, 3d Ed., sec. 628, it is said: "Guilty knowledge is always material. It must be strictly

§ 1094 FORGERY 

proved, though direct and positive evidence is not required. if, from existing circumstances, it may be inferred that the accused knew the fraudulent character of the transaction."

Upon a count in an indictment charging defendant with uttering a forged instrument knowing it to be forged, his guilty knowledge of the forgery may be proved by the evidence in the case, "or by the fair inferences therefrom." 

Chahoon v. Com., 20 Gratt. 733. 

In State v. Austin, 93 W. Va. 715, 117 S. E. 607, it is said: "It need scarcely be stated that the passing or uttering of the check alleged to be forged is a strong circumstance to be considered as tending to show intention to defraud, and evidence thereof is clearly admissible for that purpose." 

And in Sands v. Com., 20 Gratt. 800, it is held: 

"Any assertion or declaration, by word or act, directly or indirectly, that the forged writing is good, with such knowledge and intent, is an uttering or attempting to employ as true the said writing; provided that such assertion or declaration was made in the prosecution of the purpose of obtaining the money mentioned in said writing.' 

In State v. Poindexter, 23 W. Va. 805, syl. 1, the court said: "If on the trial of a prisoner in a certain county for the forgery of a certain writing alleged to have been committed in that county, it be proved that the said writing was found in the possession of the prisoner in the said county where he had uttered or attempted to utter the same as true, and there be no evidence to show that the forgery of said writing was committed in any other county, the jury from these facts may infer that the forgery of said writing was committed in that county." See also, State v. Tingler, 32 W. Va. 551, 9 S. E. 936. 

Underhill's Crim. Ev. (3d. Ed.), sec. 87.

Also in Underhill's Criminal Evidence, 3d Ed., sec. 630, it is further said: "Proof that a forged writing was delivered to a person for value with an intent to pass it as good, or was used to obtain money or credit, directly or indirectly, is enough to sustain a charge of uttering, without proof of forging it.

§ 

736 It must also be proved that there was a declaration or assertion, either by language or actions, that the signature was valid and the instrument good." 

Chahoon v. Com., 20 Gratt. 733.

Likewise, in Sands v. Com., 20 Gratt. 800, it is further held: "To convict of uttering or attempting to employ as true a forged writing, it must be shown that the accused himself uttered or attempted to employ as true such writing, or was present at the time such forged writing was uttered or attempted to be employed as true by some other person, aiding and assisting such person to utter and employ the same as true; and it must be further shown that the accused at the time knew such writing to be in fact forged, and that such uttering or attempting to employ as true was made or done by him with intent to defraud." 

See also, Chahoon v. Com., supra. 

Wash v. Com., 16 Gratt. 530. 

State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 123, 132 S. E. 368. § 1095. Drunkenness as a defense. 

In State v. Fugate, 103 W. Va. 656, 138 S. E. 318, it is held: "Likewise, the accused may show that he was incapable from intoxication of forming the intent necessary to constitute the crime of forgery." Citing, Cyc. of Ev., vol. 5, p. 62. 

§ 1096. Time of forgery. 

In Gordon v. Com., 100 Va. 825, 41 S. E. 746, where Gordon gave a check for ten dollars to one Hughes and after check passed through the bank, paid, and returned to Gordon cancelled, he inserted therein the words "In full of account to date." Held: 

Such alteration was forgery. 

§ 1097. Invalid writings. 

Writings which are invalid on their face are not subjects of forgery. 

Terry v. Com., 87 Va. 672, 13 S. E. 104.

In State v. Lowry, 42 W. Va. 205, 24 S. E. 561, it is held: "On the trial of a person accused of forgery the alleged forged paper must be produced, or its non-production satisfactorily accounted for, by showing it to be lost, destroyed, or in the hands of the accused or his friends." 

Pendleton v. Com., 4 Leigh 694. § 1099. When other offenses may be shown. 

In Underhill's Criminal Evidence, 3d. Ed., sec. 629, it is said: "Evidence of similar forgeries, or of the possession of forged papers about the same time, is admissible to show a uniform course of acting from which guilty knowledge and criminal intent may be inferred." 

In State v. Lowry, 42 W. Va. 214, 24 S. E. 561, our court held such evidence admissible, but further held: "In a proceeding for uttering forged notes, evidence tending to show that defendant had a questionable connection with another note is properly admitted when it is first shown that such other note is forged and the prisoner is shown to have had some questionable connection therewith." 

Syllabus 5, of the same case states: "It is error to allow one accused of forgery, on trial therefor, to be interrogated as to other similar papers, unless it is first shown that such papers were forged, and the accused had culpable connection therewith." § 1100. Ratification of the forgery. 

In State v. Austin, 93 W. Va. 715-16, 117 S. E. 607, the court said: "No subsequent ratification by the party sought to be injured could in any way mitigate the guilt of the accused. 

So far as the right of the state to pursue and punish the fofger as a criminal is concerned, it is certain that a subsequent ratification by the individual sought to be charged, will be unavailing to defeat it. Any undertaking to sup-

press the crime would policy and void." Citing, 1 Mechem's Agency (2d. Ed.), sec. 360. be contrary to public § 1101. Where forged instrument is in the hands of accused or his friends, rule in West Virginia. 

In State v. Lowry, 42 W. Va. 210, 24 S. E. 561, it is held: "Where the forged instrument is in the hands of the accused or his friends notice to produce it must be given to the accused or his counsel before evidence of its existence, character, and contents is admissible." 

See authorities cited in opinion. § 1102. Same, rule in Virginia.

In Virginia the rule is otherwise. In Powell v. Com., 167 Va. 

558, 189 S. E. 443, the court quotes with approval the following rule from McKnight v. U. S., 115 F. 980, 54 C. C. A. 358: "Nor is it essential to the ends of justice that the accused may be thus called upon to produce evidence of a documentary character. The authorities seem very clear that in such cases, where a criminating document directly bearing upon the issue to be proven is in the possession of the accused, the prosecution may be permitted to show the contents thereof, without notice to the defendant to produce it. As it would be beyond the power of the court to require the accused to criminate himself by the production of the paper as evidence against himself, secondary evidence is admissible to show its contents. As the introduction of secondary evidence of a writing in such instances is founded upon proof showing the original to be in the possession of the defendant, it will ordinarily be in his power to produce it, if he regards it for his interest to do so. The court, as we have seen, cannot compel a defendant in a criminal case to produce an incriminating writing. The notice would therefore be futile as a means of compelling the production of the document, and refusal to comply therewith might work injustice to the defendant in the inferences drawn from its nonproduction." § 1103. Indictment, separate counts. 

In Johnson v. Com., 102 Va. 927, 46 S. E. 789, it is held:

§ 1105 

FORGERY 

"It is well settled that forging and uttering (a forged instrument knowing it to be forged) are separate and distinct offenses. It is equally well settled that each of these offenses may be charged in separate counts of the same indictment.'

Wharton's Criminal Law (8th Ed.), sec. 910. 

Spears v. Com., 17 Gratt. 570. 

Or the offense of forgery and uttering a forged instrument knowing it to be forged, while constituting two separate and distinct crimes may be joined in one count in an indictment. 

In State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 123, 132 S. E. 368, it is held: "An indictment containing one count, which charges that defendant, on a day stated, unlawfully and feloniously forged a certain writing therein fully described, and did then and there feloniously utter and attempt to employ the same as true and genuine, he (the defendant) knowing the same to be forged, with intent to defraud, and against the peace and dignity of the state, is sufficient in law." 

However, at the conclusion of the state's evidence the defense. may require the state to elect the offense on which it will stand for conviction. 

State v. Perry, supra. Citing, State v. Hudson, 93 W. Va. 443, 117 S. E. 125. § 1104. Unnecessary to set out forged writing in indictment.

Both the Virginia Code, sec. 4871, and the West Virginia Code, 62-2-6 (sec. 6170), among other things, provide that in an indictment for forgery or uttering a forged instrument, it shall not be necessary to set forth in the indictment any copy or facsimile thereof. 

Coleman v. Com., 25 Gratt. 866. 

State v. Henderson, 29 W. Va. 147, 1 S. E. 225. § 1105. But such forged writing must be described. 

The last above cited sections of the respective Codes further provide that "it shall be sufficient to describe the same in such manner as would sustain an indictment for stealing such instrument or other thing, supposing it to be the subject of larceny."

§ 740 

In State v. Henderson, supra, it is held: "An indictment for uttering, and attempting to employ as true, a forged writing need not set out the whole writing, but it is sufficient to give its purport and effect." 

Also in State v. Duffield, 49 W. Va. 274, 38 S. E. 577, it is further held: "In a prosecution for forging, or attempting to employ as true any forged instrument, it is sufficient to describe the same in the indictment in such manner as would sustain an indictment for the larceny thereof." 

State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 123, 132 S. E. 368. § 1106. Necessary facts must be set out. 

In State v. Viquesney, 103 W. Va. 392, 137 S. E. 538, it is held: "Every fact necessary to constitute the crime of forgery sought to be charged should be directly and affirmatively alleged in the indictment. No essential element of the offense should be left to intendment, implication or recital." 

State v. Welch, 69 W. Va. 547, 72 S. E. 649. § 1107. When forged writing is set out in full, exactness required.

While, in an indictment for forgery or uttering and attempting to employ as true any forged writing, it is unnecessary to set forth in haec verba the forged writing, yet if the state elects to descend to this unnecessary particularity, it must sustain it by sufficient proof. Thus an indictment for forgery, setting forth the instrument by its tenor, makes every word averred material and calls for proof thereof. 

State v. Jarrell, 73 W. Va. 782, 81 S. E. 523.

§ 1108. Material variance is fatal. 

In State v. Fleshman, 40 W. Va. 726, 22 S. E. 309, it is held that when the prosecution elects to set forth a copy or facsimile of the forged writing in the indictment, and there is a material variance between the copy so set out and the paper offered in evidence, such paper, on motion of the accused, should be excluded from the consideration of the jury. 

State v. Poindexter, 23 W. Va. 812. 

State v. Duffield, 49 W. Va. 274, 38 S. E. 577. 

Burress v. Com., 27 Gratt. 934. 

State v. Fleshman, 40 W. Va. 726, 22 S. E. 309.
