§ 1109. Test of whether variance is material. 

In neither of the Virginias have the courts laid down an absolute test as to what is such a material variance as will exclude the writing when offered in evidence. 

However, differences incident to clerical errors, or misspelling do not constitute a fatal variance.

State v. Poindexter, 23 W. Va. 812. 

State v. Duffield, 49 W. Va. 274, 38 S. E. 577. 

And the difference between the word "account" as set out in the indictment, and the abbreviation "acct." as written in the forged order is immaterial. 

Burress v. Com., 27 Gratt. 934.

Also omission in the indictment of the words "witness Susan 

M. Armstrong" appearing on forged receipt is immaterial. 

State v. Henderson, 29 W. Va. 147, 1 S. E. 225.

But the omission in the indictment of the words "with 6 per cent int. from date" appearing in the forged note is a fatal variance. 

State v. Fleshman, 40 W. Va. 726, 22 S. E. 309.

§ 742 

§ 1110. Endorsement on forged writing need not be stated in indictment. 

In Perkins v. Com., 7 Gratt. 651, it is held: "The indictment charged the forgery of a note and set it out in haec verba, without setting out the endorsements upon the back of it. On the trial when the note was offered in evidence it was objected to on the ground of variance. Held: It was not necessary to set out in the indictment the endorsements upon the note, or any other matter written upon the same paper constituting no part of the note itself; and not entering into the essential description of that instrument."

But when the forged endorsement is charged in the same count which charges the forging of the instrument it is not duplicity or misjoinder. 

Sprouse v. Com., 81 Va. 374. § 1111. Unnecessary to name person intended to be defrauded. 

In State v. Tingler, 32 W. Va. 546, 9 S. E. 937, it is held that under West Virginia Code, 62-2-8 (sec. 6172), an indictment for forgery or uttering and attempting to employ a forged instrument as true, it is unnecessary to name the person intended to be defrauded. And the Virginia Code, sec. 4873, is identical with the 

West Virginia statute. Hence the same is no doubt true in that State. § 1112. Requisites of a charge of uttering. 

In State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 125, 132 S. E. 368, it is held: "In charging the crime of uttering it is only necessary to set out the instrument or its substance, and charge that defendant knowing it to be forged did utter and attempt to employ it as true with intent to defraud. It is not necessary to predicate the charge with an averment that defendant or some other person at a time stated forged the writing with intent to defraud, against the peace and dignity of the State." 

See authorities cited in opinion.

§ 1116 

FORGERY 

§ 1113. Duplicity and misjoinder in indictment.

As a rule the joinder of two or more offenses in one count in an indictment is not permitted. But if the whole transaction be only parts of one fact of endeavor, all the parts may be stated together as one offense. And so, an indictment charging in one count the forgery of a check and of the endorsement thereon, is not liable to the objection of duplicity or misjoinder. 

Sprouse v. Com., 81 Va. 374. 

State v. Perry, 101 W. Va. 123, 132 S. E. 368. 

See sec. 35. § 1114. Forgery of bank check, sufficiency of indictment. 

In State v. Fugate, 103 W. Va. 653, 138 S. E. 318, it is held: "An indictment charging, in effect, that the defendant did forge a certain paper writing, purporting to be a check, and which said forged check, set out in full therein, has all the essential elements of a bank check in common usage for the payment of money, with the usual averment that it was made with the intent to defraud, is good on demurrer. Specific averments of the corporate existence of the bank on which the check is drawn and the character of the party (whether corporation, partnership or individual) to be defrauded are not essential to its validity. "In this case the forged instrument described discloses upon its face that it is capable of being used to defraud." § 1115. Notice of protest attached to forged check.

In State v. Fugate, supra, it is held: "It was error to admit the notice of protest of the check in this case, since it stated on its face that the reason for the protest was that the check was forged." Citing,

W. Va. Const. Art. III, sec. 14. 

8 R. C. L., 89. § 1116. Averments necessary in indictment for forging deed, or release deed. 

See State v. Davis, 87 W. Va. 188, 104 S. E. 484. 

State v. Meadows, 89 W. Va. 467, 109 S. E. 486.

§ 744 

 § 1117. Verdict. 

On an indictment containing two counts, one for forgery and one for uttering a forged instrument knowing it to be forged, the accused may be found guilty and sentenced on both counts; and such sentence may be cumulative. 

Johnson v. Com., 102 Va. 927, 46 S. E. 789. 

State v. Cotts, 49 W. Va. 615, 39 S. E. 605.

But the usual and better practice in such cases is to find a general verdict for the two cognate offenses charged. 

Johnson v. Com., supra. 

§ 1118. Punishment. 

In both Virginias the statutes prescribe the same penalty for both forgery and uttering a forged instrument, not less than two nor more then ten years in the penitentiary. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4489. 

West Virginia Code, 61-4-5 (sec. 5995). 

Johnson v. Com., 102 Va. 927, 46 S. E. 789. 

State v. Cotts, 49 W. Va. 615, 39 S. E. 605. 

See sec. 1078.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

The following six instructions were given by the State in the case of State v. Austin, 93 W. Va. 704, 117 S. E. 607. All of the instructions were objected to, but the objection was stressed only as to Nos. 3 and 7. These were held good. The others appear to be proper. § 1121. If the jury believe defendant forged check described in indictment.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant, McTier Austin, in Mercer County, West Virginia, forged the

FORGERY § 1124 

check described in the indictment in this case, with intent to defraud, then the jury should find the defendant guilty as charged in the indictment. § 1122. If jury believe defendant uttered check.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant, in Mercer County, West Virginia, had in his possession the check described in the indictment in this case, and if they shall further believe from the evidence that said check was forged, and that the defendant at the time he is alleged to have had said check in his possession, knew it was forged, and while having said check in his possession, and knowing it to be forged, the defendant employed and passed said check as true, then the jury should find the defendant guilty as charged in the indictment in this case. § 1123. Uttering forged check is a circumstance showing guilty knowledge.

The court instructs the jury that the mere uttering-that is passing of a forged instrument-is of itself a circumstance tending to show knowledge of its falsity which you may consider in determining the guilt or innocence of this defendant; and if you find from all the evidence in the case that the check described in the indictment in this case was forged, that is falsified, and if you further find from the evidence that it was uttered-that is passed by the defendant, then you have the right to consider these facts in determining whether the defendant knew it was forged at the time it was uttered. § 1124. Proof of forgery need not be direct.

The court instructs the jury that while they must be convinced of the guilt of the defendant, beyond a reasonable doubt, from the evidence in the case, yet the proof need not be direct evidence of persons who saw the check, described in the indictment, forged; the acts constituting the crime may be proved by all the facts and circumstances in the case. 2 CT-14

$ 750 

CRIMINAL TRial in the ViRGINIAS 

§ 1125. Evidence of other forgeries to be considered on question of intent only.

The court instructs the jury that all evidence of any crime, other than that for which the defendant is now on trial, should be considered by them only upon the question of intent, or guilty knowledge of the defendant with respect to the check described in the indictment in this case, upon which the defendant is now being tried, and which charges both forgery and the uttering of a forged check. § 1126. Where defendant represented himself to be another person.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant, McTier Austin, uttered the check described in the indictment in this case that is passed it, in Mercer County, West Virginiaand that said check was forged, and if they further believe from the evidence that at the time he so uttered said check, he represented himself to be Joe Johnson, this fact is a circumstance to be considered by the jury in determining the guilt or innocence of the defendant in this case. § 1127. Forgery of public records.

The jury are instructed that forgery of a public record can only consist in forging those things which the law authorizes or requires to be recorded. But the warrant book of the said sinking fund is such a public record as may be the subject of forgery. 

Coleman v. Com., 25 Gratt. 868. § 1128. Instituting suit on forged writing is attempt to utter.

The court instructs the jury that, the bringing of a suit upon a forged paper, as counsel, for the purpose of recovering the money purporting to be due by such paper, amounts, in law, to an uttering or attempting to employ the same as true; and if the act be done with knowledge of the forgery and intent to defraud,

it is sufficient to complete the offense of uttering and attempting to employ as true the said forged writing. 

Chahoon v. Com., 20 Gratt. 742, as modified by the court on page 795 of the opinion. § 1129. Guilt of accused must be shown beyond reasonable doubt. 

1. The jury are instructed that if from the evidence they are satisfied beyond all reasonable doubt that the prisoner either actually and personally made the alleged forged instrument, or was actually present, aiding, or abetting and assisting some other person to do so, with the felonious intent, as charged in the indictment, when the alleged forged writing was made, they should find him guilty. 

Denis v. Com., 144 Va. 588, 131 S. E. 131.

State v. Sotak, 100 W. Va. 661, 131 S. E. 706. § 1130. Possession of forged writing prima facie evidence of guilt.

The court instructs the jury that, though they ought to be satisfied (beyond a reasonable doubt) that the prisoner either did forge and counterfeit the note (described in the indictment), or act or assist in making, forging and counterfeiting thereof, yet that the prisoner being in possession of this note, as well as the other notes, and plates and ink, found in his possession, was prima facie evidence of his having forged or assisted in forging the note in the indictment mentioned. 

Spencer v. Com., 2 Leigh 753. 

§ 1131. Venue. 

The court instructs the jury they ought to be satisfied that the making and forging, or assisting in making, forging and counterfeiting, was committed in Botetourt (county); but that the prisoner, being first found in possession of the other notes, plates, ink and paper, in the first bill of exceptions mentioned, in Botetourt (county), was prima facie evidence of the fact of his having counterfeited them in Botetourt (county). 

Spencer v. Com., 2 Leigh 753.

DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1132. Questions to be considered by the jury.

The court instructs the jury that the offense of forgery consists in the false making or altering of a written instrument to the prejudice of another's rights and the intent to defraud; that in the case at bar the only two questions arising upon the first count

§ 1133 

FORGERY 

in the indictment and before the jury are (1) did the defendant falsely make the check introduced in evidence, and (2) was the making of the writing done by the defendant with intent to defraud, and that the question of intent need not be inquired into by the jury unless they first believe from the evidence beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant actually made and executed the said check; and the court further instructs the jury that the offense of uttering a forged writing is offering such instrument, knowing it to be forged, with a representation by words or actions, that it is genuine and with an intent to defraud; that in the case at bar the only questions before the jury upon the second count in the indictment are (1) did the defendant offer a forged check with knowledge, at the time, that the same was forged, (2) did the defendant at the time of offering the writing represent by words or actions that it was genuine, (3) was the offering of the writing done with intent to defraud? And the jury are further instructed that if the evidence leaves a reasonable doubt in their minds as to whether the defendant made and executed the said check, then the jury cannot find the defendant guilty on the first count in said indictment, and if the evidence leaves the jury with a reasonable doubt in their minds as to whether the defendant, at the time of offering the said check, knew that it was a forgery and offered same with intent to defraud, then the jury. cannot convict the defendant on the second count in the said indictment, and the defendant must be found not guilty. This instruction is based on 

State v. Pine, 56 W. Va. 10, 48 S. E. 206. See also, Sands v. Com., 20 Gratt. 823. § 1133. Accused must utter or aid another therein with criminal knowledge and intent.

The court instructs the jury that, before you can convict the accused upon the second count in the indictment, the jury must be satisfied from the evidence (beyond all reasonable doubt), that the accused himself uttered or attempted to employ as true the said forged writing, or the forged endorsement, respectively, or was present at the time such forged writing or forged endorsement, respectively, were uttered or attempted to be employed as

§ 754 

true, by some other person, aiding and assisting such other person to utter and employ the same as true; and in either case, that the jury must be further satisfied, from the evidence, that the accused knew at the time that the said forged writing, or the said forged endorsement, respectively, were in fact forged; and that such uttering or attempting to employ as true in either case, were made or done by the accused with the intent charged in the indictment. But the court further instructs the jury that any assertion or declaration, by word or act, directly or indirectly, that the forged writing or endorsement is good, with such knowledge and intent, is an uttering or attempting to employ as true the said writing or endorsement; provided that such assertion or declaration was made in the prosecution of the purpose of obtaining the money mentioned in the said writing.

Sands v. Com., 20 Gratt. 813, as modified by the court on page 823 of the opinion. § 1134. Defendant must have knowledge of the forgery to be guilty of uttering.

The court instructs the jury that even though they may believe from the evidence that the defendant uttered a forged paper, yet unless the State has shown to the jury by evidence sufficiently clear and compelling as to convince the jury beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant, at the time he uttered the writing, had knowledge of the fact that the writing was a forgery and made without authority, the jury must find the defendant not guilty. 

, State v. Austin, 93 W. Va. 704, 117 S. E. 607. § 1135. Reasonable doubt as applicable to forgery and uttering.

§ 1142. Larceny at common law. 

At common law larceny is the taking and carrying away of the personal property of another, against his will or without his consent and with a felonious intent.. 

Richards v. Com., 13 Gratt. 803. 

In Greenleaf's Evidence, larceny is defined:

§ 

760 "The wrongful or fraudulent taking and carrying away by any person of the personal goods of another from any place, with a felonious intent to convert to his (the takers) own use, and make them his property without the consent of the owner."

At common law larceny is distinguished into two kinds, viz., simple larceny, or plain theft unaccompanied with any other atrocious circumstances; and mixed or compound larceny, which also includes in it the aggravation of a taking from one's house or person. Larceny from the person is either by privately stealing, or by open and violent assault, which is robbery. 

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 786. 

In Vaughan v. Lytton, 126 Va. 671, 101 S. E. 865, simple larceny is defined to be: "The wrongful or fraudulent taking of personal goods of some intrinsic value, belonging to another, without his assent, and with the intention to deprive the owner thereof permanently." 

§ 1143. West Virginia statute. 

In West Virginia, Code 61-3-13 (sec. 5954), larceny is not defined, and there is no distinction between simple larceny and larceny from the person, unless the latter is accompanied by such force and fear as to raise the crime to robbery. Hence all larceny not amounting to robbery is simple larceny. 

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 786. 

The statute divides the offense into two classes: (1) Grand larceny, where the value of the stolen property is twenty dollars or more; and (2) petit larceny, where the value of such property is less than twenty dollars. The former is a felony, punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years. The latter is a misdemeanor, punishable by confinement in the county jail not exceeding one year.

West Virginia Code, 61-6-7 (sec. 6033), commonly called the "Red Men's Act," provides for the crime of larceny as the result of a conspiracy. However, it must be observed that this statute contemplates the taking of property by physical force or threats and against the owner's consent, in pursuance of such con-

§ 1145 

LARCENY 

spiracy for that purpose. It does not apply where the property is taken by false pretenses with the owner's consent and without force or threats. 

State v. Porter, 25 W. Va. 685. 

State v. Piscoineri, 68 W. Va. 76, 69 S. E. 375.

NOTE: Under this section the indictment must allege (a) the conspiracy, (b) the actual taking of the property by force or threats, and against the consent of the owner, and (c) that such property was not the property of the conspirators. 

State v. Porter, supra. 

§ 1144. Virginia statute. 

The Virginia statute, Code sec. 4440, makes a distinction between larceny from the person and simple larceny. The former, where the money or other thing taken is of the value of five dol-. lars or more, is a felony-grand larceny-punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years. 

While simple larceny (not from the person) of goods and chattels of the value of fifty dollars or more is also grand larceny, punishable as above stated. And if the thing stolen be of less value than five dollars in the first case or fifty dollars in the second the offense is petit larceny, punishable by confinement in jail not less than ten days nor more than twelve months, or by a fine of not less than five nor more than one hundred dollars or both. Punishment is also provided for the theft of live stock. 

NOTE: Virginia has no statute comparable to the "Red Men's

Act" of West Virginia, discussed in the preceding section. § 1145. Indictment for larceny.

At common law both grand and petit larceny were felonies. 

Neither the statutes of Virginia nor West Virginia define larceny, but simply divide the offense into grand larceny (a felony) and petit larceny (a misdemeanor), according to the value of the property stolen. The West Virginia statute says "if a person commit simple larceny," while the Virginia statute says if any person "steal," or commit "simple larceny," thus adopting the commonlaw definition of larceny. Therefore, prior to the adoption of the

§ 762 

new Code (1931) it was necessary in West Virginia to charge the offense, whether a felony or a misdemeanor, to have been done "feloniously." But Code, 62-9-10 (sec. 6272), now prescribes the form of indictment for grand larceny, and provides that if the offense be "petit larceny, the word 'unlawfully' shall be substituted for the word 'feloniously'."

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 779. 

Hogg's Treatise and Forms, secs. 995, 1029. 

W. Va. Code, 62-9-10 (sec. 6272). 

NOTE: Where the larceny is the result of a conspiracy on the part of defendants, see sec. 1143 for rule in West Virginia. Virginia has no such statute. § 1146. Same, larceny of money, rule in West Virginia.

Under the State's constitution and statutes the common law obtains in West Virginia, except as changed by the constitution or by legislation. At common law an indictment for the larceny of money was required to particularize the kind of money alleged to have been stolen, and this rule has not been changed. Hence it is held that an indictment for the larceny of money which simply states the subject of the larceny as so many dollars, or so many dollars in money, without further particularization as to description is bad on demurrer; nor is such defect cured by the criminal statute of jeofails, Code, 62-2-11 (sec. 6175).

West Virginia Const., Art. VIII, sec. 21. 

Code, 2-1-1 (sec. 22). 

State v. Robison, 109 W. Va. 561, 155 S. E. 649.

In State v. Robison, supra, it is held: "An indictment charging the defendant with the larceny of thirty-five hundred dollars ($3500.00), the property of G. A. Bowyer, is bad on demurrer because of insufficiency of description of the property alleged to have been stolen." 

See numerous authorities cited in opinion.

And this rule also applies to counts for the larceny of money which may be added to indictments for receiving money knowing it to have been stolen, or for obtaining the same by false pretenses.

In State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 729, syl. 3 and 4, it is held: "To constitute the crime of simple larceny, there must have been a felonious taking of the property from the possession of the owner, and the thief must, for an instant at least, have had complete and absolute possession of the stolen property, and that during such possession and control, he must have feloniously removed the same from the place it occupied just before he grasped, seized or laid hold of the same. "Where property has been so feloniously taken from the owner, the slightest removal thereof, by the thief, from the place it occupied, even if it be but a hair's breadth, with intent to steal the same, will complete the offense of simple larceny."

And beginning on page 789 of the opinion it is said: "All the authorities agree in stating that in every larceny, there must be an actual taking, or severance of the

§ 

764 * * goods from the possession of the owner, and this taking must be felonious-animo furandi.' To 'take' an article, signifies to lay hold of, seize or grasp it with the hands or otherwise.' Doing the same act animo furandi, constitutes a felonious taking. * 

But this felonious taking does not constitute the offense of larceny. The property so taken, must also be carried away. It need not be retained in the possession of the thief. Any removal, however slight, of the article is suf- ficient." * * * 

3 S. E. 2d, 530, Also in State v. Nelson, it is held: 

W. Va. "The removal of property from the place it occupies, even a hair's breadth, with intent to steal, is sufficient asportation to constitute the offense of 'larceny'."

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 779. 

§ 1149. Lost property may be subject of larceny.

It is also held that lost property may be the subject of larceny, provided the person finding it knows or has means of knowing the owner, or has reason to believe that the owner may be discovered. But he must intend at the time of finding the property to appropriate it to his own use. 

Tanner v. Com., 14 Gratt. 635. 

Perrin v. Com., 87 Va. 554, 13 S. E. 76. 

And in Hunt v. Com., 13 Gratt. 757, it is held that to constitute larceny of lost property, the person finding it must know or have the means of knowing the owner, or have reason to believe that the owner may be discovered, and he must have intended at the time of finding the property to appropriate it to his own use. See also, Tanner v. Com., supra. 

Perrin v. Com., supra. 

Also in Hutchinson v. Com., 133 Va. 711, 112 S. E. 624, it is held: "The law is that one who receives lost property from the finder directly or through another assumes, in legal contemplation, as to the owner of the property, the relation occupied by the finder, placing himself in the finder's

§ 1152 

LARCENY 

stead; and in such case, whether or not the person receiving the lost property is guilty of larceny must be determined on the same principles that govern in the case of the actual finder. Otherwise, a person knowingly receiving lost property from the finder, who had no intent to steal, with the felonious intent to appropriate it to his own use, escapes punishment." 

§ 1150. Temporary possession of property. 

In State v. Wisman, 111 W. Va. 183, 161 S. E. 437, it is held: "Where one, who has acquired temporary possession of goods from their owner upon a specified condition, ignores the condition and disposes of the goods as if his own, it is a question for the jury whether he obtained possession with intent to steal." 

State v. Edwards, 51 W. Va. 220, 41 S. E. 429. 

36 Corpus Juris, subject Larceny, sec. 140. 

§ 1151. Obtaining property by trick or device. 

It is also held that when possession of property is obtained by means of fraud, trick or device, so as to make the taking felonious, and the taker converts the property to his own use, the offense is common law larceny and a conviction may be had upon a common law indictment for larceny.

It is well settled that when the larceny is complete the voluntary abandonment, or restitution of the property, by the thief, no matter how soon after the larceny, is no defense. 

Shinn v. Com., 32 Gratt. 899.

In State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 672, 60 S. E. 785, it is held: "If a person in good faith take the property of another believing it to be his own, he is not guilty of larceny, even though his claim turn out ultimately to have been unfounded, because of a lack of intent on his part to deprive another of his property." 

State v. Flannagan, 48 W. Va. 115, 35 S. E. 862.

"Facts and circumstances indicating lack of confidence in the claim of right under which property has been taken and carried away, and determination to defeat the adverse claim by putting the property beyond the reach of legal process, such as concealment, disposition or destruction thereof, tend to prove lack of good faith on the part of the taker." § 1154. Intent, or animus furandi, is essential.

The intent, or animus furandi, to take and deprive another of his property, is an essential element in the crime of larceny.

"The animus furandi or intent to steal is the intent of the taker to deprive the owner permanently of his property."

§ 1159. Bill of particulars must be furnished defendant on demand.

West Virginia has no such statute, but the courts have held that Code 56-4-19 (sec. 5574) applies to criminal as well as civil cases, and a bill of particulars must be furnished accused in such cases upon demand. 

See sec. 93. § 1160. Corpus delicti must be proved.

The corpus delicti must be proved before any inference of guilt can arise from the possession of the fruits of crime. Where the charge is merely larceny, the corpus delicti is the larceny of the goods. The possession of stolen goods will not give rise to an inference of guilt until the corpus delicti charged be proved by other evidence. 

Drinkard v. Com., 163 Va. 1074, 178 S. E. 25. § 1161. Joinder of counts in indictment.

In Wolverton v. Com., 75 Va. 909, it is held that an article to be the subject of larceny must be of some value; but it may be worth less than the smallest coin. § 1165. Indictment must allege value of stolen property.

An indictment for larceny must allege, and the state must prove, the value of the goods or thing stolen. The reason for the rule is to distinguish between grand and petit larceny. 

Adams v. Com., 23 Gratt. 949. 

State v. Sparks, 30 W. Va. 101, 3 S. E. 40.

The Virginia statute makes an exception as to bank notes, section 4443, providing that they shall be deemed to be of the value expressed on their face.

§ 772 

In other words, the value of the stolen property must be averred in the indictment and established by the evidence to be equal to, or above, the amount fixed by the statutes to make the crime a felony, else the offense will only be a misdemeanor. 

In State v. Boswell, 107 W. Va. 213, 148 S. E. 1, it is held: "Upon a charge of grand larceny the market value of the thing stolen (if it have a market value) as at the time and place of the theft, must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. "Testimony of a bona fide offer to purchase the thing stolen within a few months of the larceny by one affirmatively shown to possess a fair knowledge of the market value thereof, may be admitted, provided it is shown that the value of the thing stolen did not decline between the time of the offer and the theft." 

See cases cited in opinion. § 1166. Indictment must allege owner of stolen property.

An indictment for larceny must allege that the stolen property belonged to some certain person, or that the owner thereof is to the grand jurors unknown. 

In Barker v. Com., 2 Va. Cas. 122, an indictment for larceny of bank notes was held fatally defective unless it charged the notes were the property of some person therein named, or of some person to the grand jurors unknown, and that such defects. were not cured by the statute of jeofails (our Code, chapter 158, sections 7, 9 and 10).

One who is dead cannot own property. Death terminates his ownership. So an indictment is fatally defective if it alleges the goods stolen to be the property of a deceased person. 

Neither can the indictment allege the ownership of the property stolen to be in the "estate" of a deceased person. The owner-

§ 1169. Description of stolen property. 

The property alleged to have been stolen must be described in the indictment. The rule stated in Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 

563, in this regard, seems to be universally recognized and followed. It reads: "The law of larceny does not require a minute description of the property stolen. The general rule is that it should be described with such certainty as will enable the jury to decide whether the chattel proved to have been stolen is the very same as that upon which the indictment was founded, and show judicially to the court that it could have been the subject matter of the offense charged and enable the defendant to plead his acquittal or conviction to a subsequent indictment relating to the same chattel." 

But in State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 668, 60 S. E. 785, it is further held that in a larceny indictment it is not necessary to describe the stolen goods by reference to any mark or identification by which they can be distinguished from other goods of the same or similar kind. 

State v. Blair, 63 W. Va. 635, 60 S. E. 795. 

§ 1170. Selection of trial jury in larceny case. 

In State v. Dushman, 79 W. Va. 747, 91 S. E. 809, it is held that an employee of the party from whom the goods were stolen is prima facie disqualified to sit as a juror in the trial of one indicted for stealing or buying and receiving property alleged to have been stolen from his employer. 

State v. Davis, 91 W. Va. 241, 112 S. E. 414. 

See sec. 114. § 1171. When others had equal opportunity to commit the larceny. 

In State v. Harden, 117 W. Va. 805, 188 S. E. 377, it is held:

§ 1174 

LARCENY 

"In a prosecution of a series of larcenies in which a number of people, including defendant, had opportunity to engage, the state is required to prove specific larceny against defendant, in the absence of proof, showing conspiracy, but mere opportunity of others to engage in such series will not avail defendant against such proof." § 1172. As a rule evidence of other larcenies inadmissible. 

In Walker v. Com., 1 Leigh 574, it is said: "On trial of an indictment for the larceny of a watch, evidence of another larceny of a cloak, committed by the prisoner, the two acts being wholly distinct and unconnected, is not admissible for any purpose." 

See Chapter on Character. 

§ 1173. Exception to rule. 

In State v. Camp., 110 W. Va. 444, 158 S. E. 664, it is held: "Upon a charge of larceny or embezzlement, other acts of similar character by the accused, so intimately connected with the one under investigation as to indicate a general criminal design or system, are admissible." 

State v. Rush, 108 W. Va. 254, 150 S. E. 740. 

State v. Smith, 119 W. Va. 347, 186 S. E. 623. 

State v. Furr, 121 N. C. 606. 

16 Corpus Juris, p. 603. 

36 Corpus Juris, p. 893. 

See Chapter on Embezzlement.

But the consideration of such evidence by the jury should be restricted by proper instructions from the trial court to the purpose of showing the method, system and intent of the accused. 

State v. Camp, supra. § 1174. Acts and declarations of accused admissible. 

In State v. Baker, 84 W. Va. 151, 99 S. E. 252, syl. 3 and 4, it is held: "Acts and declarations by accused on receipt of stolen. goods, or on his arrest while the goods are in his possession, are parts of the res gestae, and evidence of them is admissible whether it be for or against him."

S 

776 "To constitute the conduct and statement of accused parts of the res gestae, it is not necessary that they should be precisely concurrent with the act charged; it is sufficient if they spring from it and are done and made under circumstances precluding design." 

And in State v. Camp, 110 W. Va. 448, 158 S. E. 664, it is held: "When persons voluntarily pay the value of the stolen goods and the costs of the prosecution, this conduct is evidence of their guilt.” 

See cases cited in opinion. § 1175. Where husband and wife are jointly charged. 

In State v. Buchanan, 111 W. Va. 142, 160 S. E. 920, it is held: "Where a wife is accused of the offense of larceny committed jointly with her husband, and in his presence she will be presumed to have acted under his coercion. 

But if the circumstances show that she was not acting under such coercion, but of her own free will, then she is accountable for her acts." 

State v. McDonie, 96 W. Va. 224, 123 S. E. 405. 

Uhl v. Com., 6 Gratt. 707. 

13 R. C. L. 275. 

See secs. 295, 296 and 1549.

§ 1177. Verdict. 

In both Virginias, upon an indictment for grand larceny the accused may be found guilty of petit larceny. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4921. 

West Virginia Code, 62-3-17 (sec. 6206). § 1178. Same, where indictment charges both housebreaking and larceny. 

In McDaniel v. Com., 165 Va. 709, 181 S. E. 534, it is held : "One charged with housebreaking and larceny may be found guilty of larceny, grand or petit as the case may be. although acquitted of the housebreaking."

§ 1192. Money on prisoner's person when arrested.

The court further instructs the jury that the possession of money by the prisoner, when arrested, cannot be considered as sufficient proof that he stole the same from the firm of Spitzer & Hess, or that he committed the crime charged in the indictment, but if the jury believe from the evidence that the prisoner did have money on his person when arrested, that is a fact which the jury have a right to consider in connection with all the other evidence adduced before them and it is for the jury, upon consideration of the whole of the evidence introduced by the Commonwealth and for the prisoner, to say whether or not the prisoner is guilty of the crime with which he is charged beyond any reasonable doubt. 

Henderson v. Com., 98 Va. 798, 34 S. E. 881. 

1193. Possession of stolen goods, rule in West Virginia.

It is well for trial courts and prosecuting attorneys in West Virginia to observe that our court has never adopted the rule as declared in Price's case, 21 Gratt. 846, with reference to the possession of stolen goods. In that case it was held that, "If property be stolen, and recently thereafter be found in the exclusive possession of the prisoner, then such possession of itself affords sufficient grounds for a presumption of fact that he was the thief; and in order to

§ 1193 

LARCENY 

12 to t

TE 12 th repel the presumption, makes it incumbent on him, on being called on for the purpose, to account for such possession consistent with his innocence." 

The rule in West Virginia is best expressed in the following instructions: 

1. The court instructs the jury that the possession of personal property recently stolen is a circumstance tending to show that the person found in possession of the stolen property is the thief, and the jury may consider it in connection with all the other attending circumstances and facts in proof in the case; and that if the jury believe from all the facts and circumstances in evidence in the case at bar that the Ford Touring Car described in the indictment was stolen on the night of April 22, 1921, and was, on the 23d day of April, 1921, found in the possession of

James Powers, the prisoner now on trial, and the three other men indicted jointly within, for the theft thereof, then they may consider the same in connection with all the other attending circumstances and facts in proof in this case; and if they believe beyond a reasonable doubt from all the facts and circumstances in evidence in the case that James Powers, directly or indirectly participated in the larceny of said car, then they should find him guilty as charged in the indictment in this case. 

State v. Powers, 91 W. Va. 737, 113 S. E. 918. 

State v. Reece, 27 W. Va. 375. 

2. The court instructs the jury that the possession of a stolen. car within a short distance from and within a half hour after the theft, the car then being driven from the place of the theft is a strong circumstance tending to show that the persons found in possession are the thieves, and the jury may consider it in connection with all the other facts and circumstances in proof, although, considered by itself, it would not be prima facie evidence of their guilt. 

State v. Powers, supra, syl. 5. 

3. The court instructs the jury that while the possession of recently stolen property is not of itself even prima facie evidence that the person in whose possession the goods are found is the thief, you are further instructed that the exclusive possession and

§ 788 

control of property recently stolen are circumstances tending to show that the person found in possession is the thief, and the jury may consider them along with all other attending circumstances and facts in the case. 

State v. Heaton, 23 W. Va. 773. 

State v. Reece, 27 W. Va. 375. 

State v. Littleton, 77 W. Va. 804, 88 S. E. 458. 

State v. Ringer, 84 W. Va. 546, 100 S. E. 416. 

State v. Mullett, 94 W. Va. 680, 120 S. E. 77. 

4. The court instructs the jury that the exclusive possession and control of property recently stolen, are circumstances tending to show that the person found in possession is the thief, and the jury may consider them in connection with all the other circumstances and facts in proof. 

State v. Mullett, supra. 

State v. Littleton, supra. 

State v. Reece, supra. 

NOTE: It is also held in the Mullett case that the possession must not be too remote in point of time. Citing, 9 Corpus Juris, p. 1081. 

5. The court instructs the jury that the possession of recently stolen property is a circumstance tending to show that the possessor is the thief and may be considered in connection with all other attending circumstances and facts.

State v. Powers, 91 W. Va. 752, 113 S. E. 912. 

6. The court instructs the jury that possession by defendant of property recently stolen is a circumstance to be considered with all other facts and circumstances. 

State v. Winans, 100 W. Va. 420, 130 S. E. 607. 

7. While given and approved in a civil case, the following instruction clearly states the law of larceny:

The court instructs the jury that to constitute the crime of larceny as charged against the plaintiff, Vinal, it must have been shown, that Vinal with a felonious intent did take, steal and carry away the oil in question from the possession of Core or his agents with intent to convert the said oil to his, Vinal's, own use; and if the said oil was not in the possession or under the

§ 1194 789 

LARCENY 

Egy Fi control of said Core or of his agents, then the removing of said oil by the said Vinal and its conversion to his own use did not constitute larceny; and if the defendants knew that said oil was not in fact in the possession or under the control of the said Core and his agents, when it was removed by Vinal, then such removal did not constitute probable cause for the prosecution of the plaintiff, and the jury may presume that the defendants knew that said oil was not in fact in the possession or under the control of the said Core or his agents when so removed, from the mere existence of the fact, and if it be found by the jury to have existed, unless they prove to the satisfaction of the jury, that they did not know this fact. 

Vinal v. Core, 18 W. Va. 72. 

See secs. 1473 and 1174. 

1194. Same, rule in Virginia.

The rule as expressed in Prices' case, as hereinbefore stated, is still the rule in Virginia. In Stallard v. Com., 130 Va. 775, 107 

S. E. 722, it is further said: "The exclusive possession of money recently stolen, unaccompanied by a reasonable account of how the possession was acquired, creates the presumption that the possessor was the thief." Citing, Porterfield v. Com., 91 Va. 805, 22 S. E. 352-4. 

1. If the property be stolen, and recently thereafter be found in the exclusive possession of the prisoner, then such possession of itself affords sufficient ground for a presumption of fact that he was the thief; and, in order to repel the presumption, makes it incumbent on him, on being called on for the purpose, to account for such possession consistently with his innocence. If he give a reasonable account of it, then it devolves on the Commonwealth to prove that such account is untrue. If he give an unreasonable account of it then it devolves on the prisoner to sustain such account by other evidence. 

Price v. Com., 21 Gratt. 869. 

Branch v. Com., 100 Va. 839, 41 S. E. 862. 

Gravely v. Com., 86 Va. 396, 10 S. E. 431. 

NOTE: What is such a recent possession as raises a presump-

§ 790 

tion against a prisoner, in the meaning of the rule, is a question for the jury, and depends upon the nature of the property and other circumstances of the particular case. See cases cited above. 

2. The court instructs the jury that the possession of recently stolen goods usually creates a presumption of guilt of the larceny of the property, and is a circumstance from which the jury may presume guilt, unless it appears from the evidence that the possession was consistent with the innocence of the accused. 

Jolly v. Com., 136 Va. 765, 118 S. E. 109. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 746, 111 S. E. 463. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if property be stolen and recently thereafter be found in the exclusive possession of the prisoner, then such possession of itself affords sufficient ground for the presumption of fact that he was the thief; and in order to repel the presumption makes it incumbent on him, on being called for the purpose, to account for such possession consistently with his innocence. If he gives a reasonable account of it, then it devolves on the Commonwealth to prove that such account is untrue. If he give an unreasonable account of it, then it devolves on the prisoner to sustain such account by other evidence. 

You are further instructed that the circumstances under which the prisoner is found in possession of such property; the time and place, the conduct of the accused and his account of his possession are all matters for the consideration of the jury. 

Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 482, 124 S. E. 240. 

Price v. Com., 21 Gratt. 849. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond all reasonable doubt that the saddle and bridle owned by H. C. Sivert were stolen, and were recently thereafter found in the exclusive possession of the prisoner, then such possession of itself affords sufficient ground for the presumption of fact that he was the thief, and makes it incumbent on him to account for such possession consistently with his innocence. 

Stallard v. Com., 130 Va. 775, 107 S. E. 722. 

5. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the bonds were stolen property, and that they came into the possession of the defendant,

F § 1196 

LARCENY 

791 18 Lash Hutchinson, in the City of Lynchburg under such circumstances that the defendant must have reasonably known that they were stolen property, and that he took possession of them intending to convert them to his own use or to assist in disposing of them, then they should find the defendant guilty. 

Hutchinson v. Com., 133 Va. 710, 112 S. E. 624. 

6. The court instructs the jury that possession of recently stolen property creates a presumption of guilt of the larceny of the property, and places upon the accused the burden of explaining such possession. 

Jolly v. Com., 136 Va. 765, 118 S. E. 109. 

7. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the property set forth in the indictment belonged to the prosecuting witness, and that said property or any part thereof was stolen and was thereafter found in the exclusive and unexplained possession of the prisoner, then such possession of itself affords sufficient ground for the presumption that the accused was the thief, and makes it incumbent upon him to account for such possession consistently with his innocence. 

Hicks v. Com., 157 Va. 946, 161 S. E. 919.

NOTE: However, it is further held in this case that in addition to the above instruction the jury should be properly instructed on the elements of reasonable doubt and presumption of innocence. § 1195. Same, erroneous instruction.

The following instruction, while correct as an abstract statement of the law in West Virginia, is improper as an instruction: 

The court instructs the jury that the mere possession of stolen goods is not prima facie evidence that the possessor is the thief. 

State v. Littleton. 77 W. Va. 804, 88 S. E. 460. 

State v. Ringer, 84 W. Va. 546, 100 S. E. 416. § 1196. Where goods were not actually found in possession of accused.

tually found in the possession of the accused, yet all of the facts and circumstances which have been introduced in evidence surrounding the whole transaction should be considered by them in arriving at a verdict as to the guilt or innocence of the accused. 

Johnson v. Com., 141 Va. 457, 126 S. E. 5. § 1197. When one charged with burglary may be convicted of larceny.

The jury instructed that although they should believe that no dwelling house was broken or entered, as alleged in the indictment, yet if they believe from the evidence that the defendant stole and carried away any of the goods of John B. Morrison, as alleged in the indictment, then they should find him guilty of the larceny of said goods. 

State v. Williams, 40 W. Va. 269, 21 S. E. 721. 

§ 1198. Intent. 

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the defendant received the automobile mentioned in the indictment from Mrs. Schmoele, the wife of F. J. 

Schmoele, to sell for her under instructions to pay to her the money from the sale, if made, and if not made to return to her the automobile, and not having made the sale he went to Raleigh, North Carolina, where Mrs. Schmoele then was, for the purpose of returning the car, then they must find the defendant not guilty. 

But if they find from the evidence that the defendant received the automobile fraudulently, and was knowingly aiding Mrs. 

Schmoele in permanently depriving her husband of his property, then they should find the defendant guilty; but the jury are further told that in order to convict the accused, they must find him. guilty under the evidence beyond all reasonable doubt. 

Ambrose v. Com., 129 Va. 766, 106 S. E. 348. § 1199. Jury may infer intent.

The court instructs the jury that to warrant a conviction in this case it must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the original taking of the property was felonious; but that the jury

Booth v. Com., 4 Gratt. 526.

The court instructs the jury that the indictment in this case charges the defendant, Edgar Parsons, with having stolen an automobile belonging to John Lyons. Under this indictment, if the evidence so warrants, it is possible for the jury to return any one of three verdicts, namely: 1st, guilty of felony, as charged therein; or 2nd, not guilty of felony as charged in the indictment, but guilty of petit larceny as charged therein; or 3rd, not guilty.

§ 1201. Accused must have had criminal intent at time of taking. 

1. The court instructs the jury that chattels and personal property, when the donor and donee reside together, can only be conveyed by deed or will, and that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that F. J. Schmoele made an oral gift of the automobile in this case to his wife, with whom he was living at the time, it did not operate to pass the title and the property remained that of F. J. Schmoele; but the court further instructs the jury that "intent" is the essence of the crime of larceny, and if they believe that the defendant honestly thought the automobile was the property of Mrs. Schmoele and that she had full right to dispose of the same and receive the proceeds, and that he was not merely aiding her in wrongfully carrying away her husband's property, and that he was without guilty knowledge of any wrongful or illegal purpose on the part of Mrs. Schmoele toward her husband in placing the automobile in his possession, then they should acquit him; but if they believe from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant acted with

dishonest intent in carrying the automobile away, thereby fraudulently contriving to deprive the said F. J. Schmoele permanently of his property, then they should convict him.

The court instructs the jury that the intent of the accused at the time of the taking of the horse in the indictment mentioned is a material fact in this case, and that before they can convict him of the offense charged they must be convinced beyond all reasonable doubt that at the time he took it, he took it intending wholly to deprive the owner of this horse and without an intention to return it. 

Webb v. Com., 122 Va. 903, 94 S. E. 773.

The court instructs the jury that before the possession of stolen property creates even a presumption that the person is a thief, the Commonwealth must prove by the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the possession was personal; that it was exclusive; that it was recent; that it was unexplained, and that it involved a distinct and conscious assertion of property by the defendant. 

Jolly v. Com., 136 Va. 766, 118 S. E. 109.

Hutchinson v. Com., 133 Va. 710, 112 S. E. 624. 

§ 1204. Possession of money. 

The court instructs the jury that the possession of money by the prisoner, when arrested, cannot be considered as sufficient proof that he stole the same from the firm of Spitzer & Hess, or that he committed the crime charged in the indictment, but if the jury believe from the evidence that the prisoner did have money on his person when arrested, that is a fact which the jury have a right to consider in connection with all the other evidence adduced before them, and it is for the jury, upon consideration of the whole of the evidence introduced by the Commonwealth and for the prisoner, to say whether or not the prisoner is guilty of the crime with which he is charged beyond any reasonable doubt. 

Henderson v. Com., 98 Va. 798, 34 S. E. 881.

§ 1209. Statutes compared. 

Under the early common law the offense of mayhem or maiming was a misdemeanor. But an early English statute broadened the offense and made it a felony. The maiming statutes of the Virginias are almost identical. Their purpose is to define and punish as felonies certain acts where it appears that they were done with a felonious intent to maim, disfigure, disable or kill. These statutes create two offenses, malicious wounding and unlawful wounding, both felonies, and they must be charged and tried as such. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4402. 

West Virginia Code, 61-2-9 (sec. 5924). 

Harris v. Com., 150 Va. 580, 142 S. E. 354. 

§ 1210. Offenses included in statutes. 

In State v. Harr, 38 W. Va. 64, 17 S. E. 794, our court said: "The statute, as construed and applied in these cases (the cases cited in the opinion), provides for an offense which it divides into two classes: "1. Malicious shooting, etc., with intent to maim, disfigure, disable or kill, which having the requisite of malice corresponds to murder. "2. Unlawful, but not malicious shooting, etc., with intent aforesaid, which lacking the element of malice corresponds to manslaughter. Both are made felonies by the statute, and both must be so charged in the indictment, and must be tried as such. The discretion given the court to ascertain and fix in the second class a less degree of punishment does not reduce the grade of the crime.' 

3. While not mentioned in the statute, the indictment also includes simple assault and battery. 

Canada v. Com., 22 Gratt. 899.

§ 800 

Hoback v. Com., 28 Gratt. 922. 

Stuart v. Com., 28 Gratt. 950. 

Quillen v. Com., 105 Va. 874, 54 S. E. 333. 

Honaker v. Com., 136 Va. 752, 118 S. E. 85. 

State v. Scaggs, 99 W. Va. 689, 129 S. E. 705. § 1211. Degree of crime, how determined. 

In Harris v. Com., 134 Va. 688, 114 S. E. 597, it is said: "Whether a person indicted under sec. 4402 (West Virginia Code, 61-2-9, sec. 5924) is guilty of malicious shooting with intent to kill depends upon whether, if he had killed the person at whom he shot, instead of only wounding him, he would have been guilty of murder, or would have been guilty of manslaughter, or homicide in self-defense. 

If he would have been guilty of murder had he killed the person at whom he shot, he is guilty of malicious shooting with intent to kill; if he would only have been guilty of manslaughter, then he is guilty of unlawful shooting; and if he shot in self-defense he is not guilty of any offense." 

Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 924. 

Price v. Com., 77 Va. 393. 

Gills v. Com., 141 Va. 445, 126 S. E. 51. 

Drinkard v. Com., 163 Va. 1074, 178 S. E. 25. 

And in Johnson v. Com., 135 Va. 524, 115 S. E. 673, it is also said: "Whether a prisoner on trial for malicious shooting with intent to kill is guilty of that charge depends upon whether, if death had resulted, he would have been guilty of murder —either in the first or second degree, it matters not which." 

NOTE: This principle also applies to the other offenses enumerated in the statute, namely, cutting, stabbing, wounding, or causing bodily injury by any other means. § 1212. Meaning of terms "maim", "disfigure", "disable" and "wound" as used in statutes.

MAIM: Maiming at common law means to violently inflict a bodily injury upon a person so as to make him less able to defend himself or annoy his adversary. 

State v. McDonie, 89 W. Va. 185, 109 S. E. 710. 

4 Blackstone's Com., 206.

MAIMING 

DISFIGURE: In Lee v. Com., 135 Va. 578, 115 S. E. 671, it is held: "The word 'disfigure' as used in the maiming statute * * * means a permanent and not merely a temporary and inconsequential disfigurement." See also, Vawter v. Com., 87 Va. 245, 12 S. E. 339. 

26 Cyc. p. 1600. 

DISABLE: In Vawter v. Com., supra, the court said: "The court instructs the jury that the intent to disable, charged in the indictment, must be understood as a permanent disability, and not merely one which may be temporary." 

WOUND: In State v. Gibson, 67 W. Va. 548, 68 S. E. 295, it is held that to constitute a wound, within the meaning of the terms 'shoot, cut, stab or wound' as used in the statute, an injury must have been inflicted with a weapon, other than any of those with which the human body is provided by nature, and must include a complete parting or solution of the external skin. But in State v. Coontz, 94 W. Va. 59, 117 S. E. 701, it is also held that "Our statute has been broadened somewhat by the use of the terms 'or by any other means cause him bodily injury with intent,' etc. Under a proper indictment, any sort of a bodily injury, inflicted by any means with intent to maim, disfigure, disable or kill, is an offense under the statute, punishable as a malicious wounding, but it is not a technical wounding, and an indictment merely for cutting and wounding does not cover it." § 1213. Same, jury should be properly instructed on meaning of terms.

In both Virginias the words "maim, disfigure, and disable," as used in the statute and charged in the indictment, mean a permanent maiming, disfiguring and disabling, and the defendant is entitled to have the jury so instructed. In fact it is reversible error to refuse such an instruction. 

Vawter v. Com., 87 Va. 245, 12 S. E. 339. 

Lee v. Com., 135 Va. 578, 115 S. E. 671. 

State v. Taylor, 105 W. Va. 298, 142 S. E. 254. 

See sec. 1242.

§ 802 

§ 1214. Intent, must be alleged in indictment.

By reference to the statutes of both Virginias it will be observed that both "malicious wounding" and "unlawful wounding" must be done with intent "to maim, disfigure, disable or kill." Hence an indictment for maiming must charge such intent, or it is not sufficient. 

State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 658. 

Randall v. Com., 24 Gratt. 644. 

Hoback v. Com., 28 Gratt. 922. 

Jones v. Com., 87 Va. 63, 12 S. E. 226. 

Lee v. Com., 135 Va. 578, 115 S. E. 671. 

Williamson v. Com., 165 Va. 750, 181 S. E. 351. 

State v. Davis, 58 W. Va. 94, 51 S. E. 230. § 1215. Same, must be proved.

Under the statutes the crime consists of an act combined with the particular intent "to maim, disfigure, disable or kill." This intent is the very gist of the offense, and without it there can be no conviction; and the burden is on the state to prove such intent the same as any other essential fact in the case, either by direct or circumstantial evidence. 

In Thacker v. Com., 134 Va. 767, 114 S. E. 505, it is held: "The law can presume the intention to commit a certain crime so far as such intention is realized in an act, but not an intention beyond what was so realized. The law does not presume, because an assault was made with a weapon likely to produce death, that it was an assault with the intent to murder. And where it takes a particular intent to constitute a crime, that particular intent must be proved either by direct or circumstantial evidence, which would warrant the inference of the intent with which the act was done. "When a statute makes an offense consist of an act combined with a particular intent, that intent is just as necessary to be proved as the act itself, and must be found as a matter of fact before a conviction can be had; and no intent in law or mere legal presumption, differing from the intent in fact, can be allowed to supply the place of the latter. "To constitute an attempt to commit a crime, an act must be done with the specific intent to commit that particular crime. This specific intent at the time the act is done is

§ 1216 

MAIMING 

essential. To do an act from general malevolence is not an attempt to commit a crime, because there is no specific intent, though the act according to the consequences may amount to a substantive crime. To do an act with intent to commit one crime cannot be an attempt to commit another crime, though it might result in such other crime." 

See also, Hay v. Com., 139 Va. 578, 123 S. E. 333. 

Gills v. Com., 141 Va. 445, 126 S. E. 51. 

Winckler v. Com., 155 Va. 1150, 156 S. E. 364. 

State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 658. § 1216. Same, when presumed.

In maiming it is held that where one shoots and wounds another, or strikes him a violent blow with an instrument, like a knife or other deadly weapon, the law, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, imputes the malicious intent. This is on the theory that one is presumed to intend the natural and probable consequences of his act. 

Murphy v. Com., 23 Gratt. 960. 

Price v. Com., 77 Va. 393. 

Gills v. Com., 141 Va. 445, 126 S. E. 51. 

Drinkard v. Com., 165 Va. 799, 183 S. E. 251.

But there are cases where such malicious intent may not be inferred from defendant's act. In Lee v. Com., 135 Va. 572, 115 S. 

E. 671, it is held: "Men are presumed to intend the natural and probable consequences of their acts, and a permanent disfigurement would be the natural and probable consequence of a violent blow in the face with a sharp instrument like a knife or steel knuckles. "But it cannot be presumed from a blow with the fist that the striker intended to permanently disfigure his adversary." 

Also in State v. Taylor, 105 W. Va. 298, 142 S. E. 254, it is held that the "character of the wound or the permanency of the scar is not the test," nor will the presumption arise from a blow with the fist that the accused "intended to disfigure permanently his adversary, and yet some disfigurement would naturally be expected and would almost necessarily follow from such a blow."

804 

§ 1217. Same, question for jury.

The intent of the prisoner at the time he committed the offense is a question to be determined by the jury from all the facts and circumstances of the case. And to give instructions which eliminate from the consideration of the jury the question of the intent is error. 

Lee v. Com., 135 Va. 578, 115 S. E. 671. 

And in State v. Davis, 58 W. Va. 94, 51 S. E. 230, it is also held: "In the trial of an indictment found under this section for malicious wounding, with intent to maim, disfigure, disable or kill, an instruction at the instance of the state which eliminates from consideration of the jury the intent with which the alleged wounding was done is erroneous." 

Also in State v. Edgell, 94 W. Va. 207, 118 S. E. 144, it is held: "It is always for the jury to determine whether the prisoner had a criminal intention or not. They must take into their consideration all the surrounding facts and circumstances of the case; but they generally infer a man's intention from his acts and words." Citing, Odgers, The Common Law of England, p. 112. 

§ 1218. Same, prisoner may state.

When one is indicted and on trial for shooting another with intent to maim, disfigure, disable and kill, and takes the witness stand in his own defense, it is proper to ask him with what intent he fired the shot. 

Parsons v. Com., 138 Va. 777, 121 S. E. 68. 

State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 658. 

State v. Arrington, 88 W. Va. 154, 106 S. E. 445. 

State v. Panetta, 85 W. Va. 212, 101 S. E. 360. § 1219. Indictment, must charge offense to have been done "feloniously." "Although the statute does not expressly declare the offense therein mentioned to be a felony, it makes it punishable with confinement in the penitentiary, and hence it must be described in the indictment therefor by the term 'feloniously'."

MAIMING 

Randall v. Com., 24 Gratt. 644. 

Trimble v. Com., 2 Va. Cas. 143. 

And in Williamson v. Com., 165 Va. 750, 181 S. E. 351, where the intent was not alleged in the indictment, it is held: "Indictment failing to allege that blow with fist was struck with the specific intent to wound, disfigure, disable, and kill, as required by the statute, held insufficient to support conviction under Maiming Act (Code 1919, sec. 4402)." 

Merritt v. Com., 164 Va. 653, 180 S. E. 395. § 1220. Offense should be charged conjunctively. 

Although the statutes uses the disjunctive, "disable or kill," it is proper to charge the offense conjunctively, "disable and kill." 

Angel v. Com., 2 Va. Cas. 231. § 1221. When weapon must be averred.

When the injury is inflicted by some means other than those stated in the statutes, namely, shooting, stabbing, cutting or wounding, the indictment must specify the means by which it was caused. 

State v. Gibson, 67 W. Va. 548, 68 S. E. 295. 

State v. Coontz, 94 W. Va. 59, 117 S. E. 701. 

State v. Scaggs, 99 W. Va. 689, 129 S. E. 705. 

And in Jones v. Com., 87 Va. 63, 12 S. E. 226, it is held: "An indictment charging that accused made an assault with a stone, and did feloniously, maliciously, and unlawfully beat, wound, ill-treat and cause bodily injury, etc., sufficiently conforms with this section (the maiming statute).' § 1222. When weapon need not be charged.

An indictment which alleges the injury to have been inflicted by maliciously shooting, stabbing, cutting and wounding another need not state the character or kind of weapon used by the defendant. 

Canada v. Com., 22 Gratt. 899. 

Jackson v. Com., 96 Va. 107, 30 S. E. 452. 

State v. Gibson, 67 W. Va. 548, 68 S. E. 295. 

State v. Scaggs, 99 W. Va. 689, 129 S. E. 705.

§ 806 

§ 1223. When indictment not subject to demurrer for failure to specify weapon. 

In State v. Coontz, 94 W. Va. 59, 117 S. E. 701, it is held: "In an indictment for malicious stabbing, cutting and wounding, with intent to maim, disable and kill, it is not subject to demurrer or motion to quash because it fails to specify the instrument with which that injury was inflicted." 

State v. Scaggs, supra. § 1224. When wound is caused by "any other means." 

In State v. Gibson, 67 W. Va. 548, 68 S. E. 295, it is said: "Our statute has been broadened somewhat by the use of the terms or by any means cause him bodily injury with intent, etc.' Under a proper indictment any sort of bodily injury inflicted by any means, with intent to maim, disfigure or kill is an offense under this statute, punishable as a malicious or unlawful wounding, but is not a technical wounding, and an indictment merely for cutting and wounding does not cover it. This addition to the statute does not alter the meaning of its original term. It simply introduces a new offense made up of new elements." 

And in State v. Coontz, 94 W. Va. 59, 117 S. E. 701, it is also held: "Under this section an indictment which charges that the defendant did unlawfully, feloniously and maliciously stab, cut and wound one M. and caused him bodily injury by means of a blow with his fist, with intent him, the said M. then and there to maim, disable and kill, is sufficient, as charge of technical 'wounding,' or a charge of causing bodily injury, with intent to maim, disable and kill." § 1225. Proof of injury must conform to charge in indictment.

In proving the injury the state is confined to the manner alleged in the indictment. Thus an indictment charging malicious cutting and wounding with intent to maim, etc., is not broad enough to admit proof that such injury was inflicted otherwise than by cutting and wounding. 

State v. Gibson, 67 W. Va. 550, 68 S. E. 295.

MAIMING 

§ 1227 § 1226. When other attacks by accused may be shown. 

In Drinkard v. Com., 165 Va. 799, 183 S. E. 251, it is held: "In a prosecution for malicious wounding, assignments of error were grounded upon the admission of testimony showing that just before the shooting accused made an unprovoked attack with a pistol, used as a club, upon a girl, and immediately after the shooting and his arrest, he struck a man. Held: That the testimony was clearly admissible to show the mental attitude of accused immediately preceding and immediately subsequent to the shooting." 

And in Trogdon v. Com., 31 Gratt. 862, it is further said: "There is another class of cases in which it is held permissible to prove other offenses for the purpose of showing the guilty intent of the accused. Thus upon an indictment for maliciously shooting at the prosecutor, it has been held proper to show that the accused had twice shot at the prosecutor on the same day, for the purpose of rebutting the idea of accident, and of establishing the wilful intent. 

See secs. 389, 680, 691 and 1300. § 1227. Instructions must conform to indictment.

Instructions must conform to the charge made in the indictment. 

Thus, where the indictment charged defendant with feloniously and maliciously shooting one "with a certain gun then and there loaded with gunpowder and bullets," it is error to instruct the jury "that if they believe defendant made an assault upon the prosecuting witness with any deadly weapon capable of producing a dangerous wound, etc." 

State v. Best, 91 W. Va. 559, 113 S. E. 919. 

State v. Gibson, 67 W. Va. 550, 68 S. E. 295. 

In State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 658, the defendant was charged in an indictment with "maliciously shooting one Francis Meadows with the intent to maim, disfigure, disable and kill him, etc." The court instructed the jury, "that if they believe from the evidence that the prisoner maliciously shot the prosecuting witness, as charged in the indictment, with intent to maim, disfigure, disable or kill him, or cause him bodily injury, then they should find the prisoner guilty, etc." 

HELD: "The instruction in adding to the words of the statute,

§ 808 · 

'or to cause him bodily injury,' was clearly erroneous. It was an instruction to the jury, that upon an indictment for one offense, they might convict of another and a wholly different offense, etc.” § 1228. Jury may be instructed to acquit of felony and find prisoner guilty of attempt.

Under an indictment for maiming it is not error for the court to instruct the jury that if warranted by the evidence they can acquit the prisoner of the felony and find him guilty of an attempt to commit such felony.

State v. Meadows, 18 W. Va. 658. 

This is true by virtue of West Virginia Code, 62-3-18 (sec. 

6207), Virginia Code, sec. 4922. These two sections are identical, and read as follows: "On an indictment for felony, the jury may find the accused not guilty of the felony, but guilty of an attempt to commit such felony; and a general verdict of not guilty upon such indictment shall be a bar to a subsequent prosecution for an attempt to commit such felony." 

See Chapter XXI, Attempts to Commit Crime. 

§ 1229. Where indictment is insufficient to sustain verdict. 

In Williamson v. Com., 165 Va. 750, 181 S. E. 351, it is held that when the indictment is not sufficient to sustain the verdict, it should be set aside. In this case the charge was maiming under 

Code, sec. 4402, but the indictment did not allege that the blow, with the fist, was struck with intent to wound, disfigure, disable and kill. Held fatal. § 1230. Verdicts that may be returned. 

In the Virginias, under an indictment based upon the maiming statutes, if the evidence warrants, the verdict may be for malicious wounding, unlawful wounding, assault and battery, or not guilty. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4920. 

W. Va. Code, 62-3-16, (sec. 6205). 

Canada v. Com., 22 Gratt. 899.

And in Williams v. Com., 153 Va. 987, 151 S. Verdict to be read in connection with indictment.

In both Virginias it is held that the verdict of the jury shall be read in connection with the indictment, and if otherwise proper it is sufficient when it fails to name the person wounded.

644, where it is said: "A verdict of 'guilty of felonious shooting,' without stating who was shot, etc., is fatally defective; and the appellate court, at the instance of the prisoner, will set aside such verdict, although no motion was made in the court below in arrest of judgment.

§ 810 

§ 1232. Where verdict is for unlawful wounding.

In both Virginias, where the verdict is for unlawful wounding, the accused may not be both sentenced to the penitentiary and fined. 

Under the statutes the fine attaches only where he is sentenced to confinement in jail. However, it is held in Ex Parte Mooney, 26 

W. Va. 36, that where such an illegal sentence is imposed, the remedy of the prisoner is not by habeas corpus, but by application for a writ of error. Under such circumstances the appellate court will simply remand the case for proper judgment on the verdict. 

State v. Coontz, 94 W. Va. 59, 117 S. E. 701.

§ 1237. Where wound is inflicted with dangerous weapon. 

1. The court instructs the jury that even though you may believe from the evidence in this case that no conspiracy existed between the defendant and W. S. Taylor to inflict bodily injury upon the said A. J. Brewster, yet if you believe from the evidence beyond a

§ 812 

reasonable doubt, that the defendant E. J. (Tim) Taylor on the day of September, 1926, maliciously and unlawfully assaulted and beat the prosecuting witness, A. J. Brewster, with a dangerous weapon of any kind, and wounded him with said weapon with intent, then and there to maim, disfigure, disable and kill the said A. J. Brewster, then the jury should find the defendant guilty of malicious wounding as charged in the first count of the indictment in this case; but if the jury believe from the evidence that the act was done unlawfully, but not maliciously, with the intent aforesaid, then the jury should find the defendant guilty of unlawful wounding as charged in the first count in this indictment. 

State v. Taylor, 105 W. Va. 301, 142 S. E. 254.

NOTE: The italicized words, "with the intent aforesaid," are inserted to meet the objections raised by defense counsel, but the instruction was approved without them. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant in this case, during the altercation with Tom Foster, struck the said Foster with a dangerous weapon of any kind, and inflicted with said weapon upon the said Tom Foster a wound, with intent, then and there, unlawfully, maliciously and feloniously to maim, disfigure, disable, or kill the said Foster, then the jury should find the defendant guilty of malicious wounding as charged in the indictment; if the jury believe from the evidence that the act was done unlawfully, but not maliciously, then the jury should find him guilty of unlawful wounding as charged in the indictment. 

State v. Scaggs, 99 W. Va. 692, 129 S. E. 706. § 1238. Where accused asserts self-defense.

The court instructs the jury that where there is a quarrel between two persons, both being in fault, and a combat, as the result of such quarrel, takes place, and one of the combatants is maimed, disfigured or disabled, in order to reduce the offense to maiming, disabling or disfiguring in self defense, the prisoner must prove two things: First, that before Deane was assaulted by the accused, Haywood Lamb, with intent to maim, disfigure, disable and kill him, the accused declined further combat and retreated as far as

§ 1240 813

1 1 he could with safety; and secondly, that he necessarily assaulted the said Deane with the intent to maim, disfigure, disable and kill him in order to preserve his own life or to save himself from great bodily harm. 

Lamb v. Com., 141 Va. 481, 126 S. E. 3. § 1239. Offenses charged in indictment.

The court instructs the jury that under the indictment in this case, if warranted by the evidence, you may find any one of the four following verdicts, to-wit: (1) Malicious wounding; (2) Unlawful wounding; (3) Assault and battery; (4) Not guilty.

You are further instructed that malicious wounding is committed when one person unlawfully, wilfully, feloniously and maliciously wounds another, intending thereby either to maim, disfigure, disable or kill such other. Unlawful wounding is committed when one person wounds another unlawfully, wilfully and feloniously, but not maliciously, intending thereby either to maim, disfigure, disable or kill such other. Assault and battery is any physical injury done to another in an angry, rude or insolent manner. 

You are further instructed that malicious wounding is a felony punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than two nor more than ten years, in the discretion of the court; that unlawful wounding is a felony punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years in the discretion of the court, or by confinement in the county jail not exceeding twelve months, and fined not exceeding five hundred dollars, in the discretion of the court; that assault and battery is a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment in the county jail and fine, either or both, in the discretion of the court. 

Williams v. Com., 153 Va. 987, 151 S. E. 151. § 1240. Where accused provoked difficulty with felonious intent.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the prisoner provoked the combat, or produced the occasion between himself and George Ratliff, in evidence before you, in order to have a pretext to kill the 2 CT-18

said Ratliff, or do him some serious bodily harm, then the prisoner is guilty of malicious wounding as charged in the indictment, as the law is that a person cannot bring on a difficulty with a felonious intent, and then defend his acts done in said difficulty upon the ground that he was acting in self-defense. 

Jackson v. Com., 96 Va. 112, 30 S. E. 452. § 1241. Insulting words do not justify assault.

The court further tells the jury that words, however grievous, will not justify an assault.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case that there was a quarrel between the prisoner and the prosecuting witness, and that both were in fault, and that a combat as a result of such quarrel took place, and that the prisoner during such combat shot and wounded the said prosecuting witness, in order to justify said shooting on the grounds of selfdefense, two things must appear from the evidence and the circumstances of the case, first, that before said shot was fired and the wound inflicted, the prisoner declined further combat and retreated, as far as he could with safety; and secondly, that he necessarily shot and wounded the said prosecuting witness in order to preserve his own life, or to save himself from great bodily harm.
