DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1243. Injury intended must be permanent. 

1. The court instructs the jury that the intent to disable, charged in the indictment, must be understood as of a permanent disability, and not merely one which may be temporary. 

Vawter v. Com., 87 Va. 248, 12 S. E. 339. 

2. The court instructs the jury that the words "maim, disfigure

MAIMING 

§ 1243 1 the and disable" as charged in the indictment mean a permanent maiming, disfiguring, and disabling. 

State v. Taylor, 105 W. Va. 302, 142 S. E. 254.

Held reversible error to refuse this instruction. 

3. The court instructs the jury that the accused cannot be convicted of the felony charged unless you believe he intended to kill, or maim, or disable, or disfigure permanently, the prosecuting witness in this case. 

Lee v. Com., 135 Va. 577, 115 S. E. 671.

Held reversible error to refuse this instruction. 

Drinkard v. Com., 165 Va. 799, 183 S. E. 251. 

State v. Taylor, 105 W. Va. 303, 142 S. E. 254.

The substance of the foregoing instructions may be embodied in one instruction. The following is such an instruction, which the author has given in numerous cases: 

4. The court instructs the jury that the accused in this case cannot be convicted of any felony charged in the indictment herein unless you believe from the evidence beyond all reasonable doubt, (a) that the defendant struck the blow, which injured the prosecuting witness, with the (name the weapon used) introduced in evidence, and (b)' that at the time he struck said blow he did so with the intent either to kill, or permanently maim, disable, or disfigure the said prosecuting witness. And in this connection the court further instructs the jury that the words "maim," disfigure and disable" as used and charged in the indictment in this case mean a permanent maiming, disfigurement, and disabling of the said prosecuting witness, and not such a wound as may be only temporary. 

See authorities above cited.

NOTE: In Vawter's Case it is said that such an instruction is correct as an abstract proposition of law. But in that case there was no certificate of the facts or evidence before the court, and therefore the rejection of the instruction was not held error. But 

Lee's Case, supra, was reversed because the trial court deleted the word "permanently" from the instruction. While in State v. 

Taylor, supra, it was held error to refuse instruction No. 2 above which included the word "permanently."

§ 1248. When defendant should be found guilty of the least offense. 

1. The court instructs the jury that, upon the indictment, they could find the prisoner guilty of the offense therein charged, or done maliciously, with intent to maim, disfigure, disable or kill, and punish him by confinement in the penitentiary not less than two nor more than ten years; or if they believe the acts therein charged were done unlawfully, but not maliciously, with intent aforesaid, the accused could, at their discretion, either be confined in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years, or be confined in jail not exceeding twelve months, and fined not exceeding five hundred dollars; or they might find him guilty of assault and battery, and fine him not exceeding five hundred dollars, and imprisonment at the discretion of the court. 

Canada v. Com., 22 Gratt. 901.

NOTE: In West Virginia the jury does not determine the punishment, and the instruction must be modified accordingly. The punishment is now modified in Virginia, Code sec. 4402, and the instruction must be changed accordingly. 

2. The court instructs the jury that even if you should believe the defendant guilty of one of the offenses charged in the indictment in this case, but have a reasonable doubt as to which one of said offenses he is guilty, you should give the defendant the benefit of such doubt and find him guilty of the least offense to which such doubt attaches. 

3. The jury are instructed that if all the evidence and circumstances of the case warrant such finding, they may find the prisoner guilty of the offense charged in the indictment, or if all the evidence and circumstances of the case warrant such finding, the jury may find the prisoner guilty of part of the offense charged in said indictment, if such part be substantially charged therein, whether such part be a felony or a misdemeanor. That under the indictment in this case the jury might, if warranted under all the evidence and circumstances of the case, find the defendant guilty of assault and battery, in which case the punishment would be a fine or imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, or both fine and imprisonment, in the discretion of the court. 

State v. Donahoo, 22 W. Va. 762.

NOTE: The instruction as stated in the opinion has been modified so as to conform to the present law in West Virginia.

Gills v. Com., 141 Va. 448, 126 S. E. 51.

Every unlawful homicide must be either murder or manslaughter, depending on whether the act was done with malice, express or implied. Likewise, every unlawful homicide is prima facie murder in the second degree, and if the accused would reduce the offense to manslaughter the burden is upon him to prove to the satisfaction of the jury such justification or excuse as will show that the crime was without malice, and therefore only manslaughter. 

Hill v. Com., 2 Gratt. 594. 

Williams v. Com., 128 Va. 698, 104 S. E. 853. 

Bryan v. Com., 131 Va. 709, 109 S. E. 477. 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 516, 94 S. E. 972. 

Sims v. Com., 134 Va. 736, 115 S. E. 382. 

State v. Jones, 20 W. Va. 764. 

See Michie's Digest, vol. 5, p. 410. § 1250. Manslaughter defined.

Manslaughter is usually defined by text writers as any form of unlawful killing not amounting to murder; that is killing without malice. 

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 271, 101 S. E. 450.

Manslaughter is the unlawful killing of another, without malice either express or implied. 

4 Blackstone's Com., 190. 

Vaiden v. Com., 12 Gratt. 717. 

Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 924. 

Briggs v. Com., 82 Va. 554. 

Gills v. Com., 141 Va. 446, 126 S. E. 51.

In Harris v. Com., 134 Va. 694, 114 S. E. 597, it is said: "Every unlawful homicide must be murder or manslaughter. Whether it is murder or manslaughter depends entirely upon whether or not the act was done with malice, express or implied. A reasonable provocation is always necessary to reduce a felonious homicide, committed upon sudden provocation, from murder to manslaughter." § 1251. Manslaughter distinguished from murder. 

In Byrd v. Com., 89 Va. 538, 16 S. E. 727, it is said: "The difference between the crimes of murder and manslaughter consists in this, that manslaughter (when voluntary), arises from the sudden heat of the passions, murder from the wickedness of the heart. Malice aforethought is the grand criterion which distinguishes murder from other killings." 

McWhirt v. Com., 3 Gratt. 594. 

In Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 937-8, it is also said: . "Every unlawful homicide must be either murder or manslaughter; and whether it be one or the other depends alone upon, whether the party who perpetrated the act did it with malice or not-malice either express or implied. 

That one word malice is the touch-stone by which the grade of the offense must be determined. When a homicide is committed in the course of a sudden quarrel or broil, or mutual combat, or upon a sudden provocation, and without any previous grudge, the offense may be murder or manslaughter, according to the circumstances of the case. 

Of which circumstances the most important generally, are the nature and degree of the provocation; the manner in which it was resented; the character of the weapon used for the purpose, and whether it was casually or accidentally at hand, or was prepared for the purpose of doing such an act and carried secretly about the person." 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 519, 94 S. E. 972.

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 271, 101 S. E. 450.

Galford, 87 W. Va. 358, 105 S. E. 237.

 § 1252. Degrees of manslaughter. 

There are two degrees of manslaughter, voluntary and involuntary. The former is a felony in both Virginias, punishable by confinement in the penitentiary from one to five years. In West 

Virginia, the latter is a misdemeanor, punishable by confinement in jail not to exceed one year, or a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars, or both, in the discretion of the court. While in 

Virginia it is also a felony punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years; or, in the discretion of the jury, by a fine of not exceeding one thousand dollars, or by confinement in jail not exceeding one year, or both. 

West Virginia Code, 61-2-4 and 5, secs. 5919, 5920. 

Virginia Code, secs. 4396 and 4397. 

Byrd v. Com., 89 Va. 536, 16 S. E. 727. 

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 271, 101 S. E. 450. 

Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 980, 159 S. E. 222. § 1253. Voluntary manslaughter defined. 

Voluntary manslaughter is the unlawful killing of another without malice actual or implied, upon sudden heat or passion, on reasonable provocation, or in mutual combat. 

McWhirt v. Com., 3 Gratt. 594. 

Byrd v. Com., 89 Va. 538, 16 S. E. 727. 

Dock v. Com., 21 Gratt. 909. 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 703.

Voluntary manslaughter is the intentional, unlawful and felonious, but not deliberate or malicious, taking of life. 

State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 9, 52 S. E. 981. 

State v. Dickey, 48 W. Va. 325, 37 S. E. 695. 

State v. Hobbs, 37 W. Va. 812, 17 S. E. 380. 

State v. Crawford, 66 W. Va. 114, 66 S. E. 110. 

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 271, 101 S. E. 450. 

State v. Murphy, 89 W. Va. 413, 109 S. E. 771. 

State v. Cline, 100 W. Va. 57, 130 S. E. 91. 

State v. Abbott, 103 W. Va. 191, 136 S. E. 861. 

State v. Pusey, 118 W. Va. 95, 188 S. E. 745.

In State v. Pusey, supra, it is further said: "Any unlawful and intentional killing, even by the use of a deadly weapon, when the passion of the slayer is sud-

Involuntary manslaughter is the killing of one accidentally, contrary to the intention of the parties, in the prosecution of some unlawful, but not felonious act; or in the improper performance of a lawful act. 

Souther v. Com., 7 Gratt. 678. 

McWhirt v. Com., 3 Gratt. 594. 

Byrd v. Com., 89 Va. 538, 16 S. E. 727. 

State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 9, 52 S. E. 981.

Manslaughter is involuntary where a homicide is caused by the doing of an unlawful act not amounting to a felony nor likely to endanger life, and without an intention to kill; or where one kills another by doing a lawful act in an unlawful manner. 

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 283, 101 S. E. 450. 

13 R. C. L., 784.

And in involuntary manslaughter there is no premeditation, conspiracy or malice. 

State v. Yoho, 64 W. Va. 251, 61 S. E. 367.

For a further discussion of the law on involuntary manslaughter, see 

State v. Michael, 74 W. Va. 613, 82 S. E. 611.

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 271, 101 S. E. 450. 

State v. McHaffa, 110 W. Va. 266, 157 S. E. 595. 

State v. Thornhill, 111 W. Va. 258, 161 S. E. 431. 

State v. Cassim, 112 W. Va. 92, 163 S. E. 769. 

State v. Tharp, 116 W. Va. 256, 180 S. E. 97. 

§ 1255. Distinction between voluntary and involuntary manslaughter. 

In State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 284, 101 S. E. 450, it is said: "The absence of intention to kill or to commit any unlawful act which might reasonably produce death or great bodily harm is the distinguishing feature between voluntary and involuntary homicide."

§ 824 

Quoted and approved in, State v. McHaffa, 110 W. Va. 269, 157 S. E. 595. 

And in Richardson v. Com., 128 Va. 691, 104 S. E. 788, it is said: "Where a homicide is committed in the course of a sudden quarrel, or mutual combat, or upon a sudden provocation and without any previous grudge, and the killing is from the sudden heat of passion, growing solely out of the quarrel, or combat, or provocation, it is not murder, but is manslaughter only-voluntary manslaughter, if there be no further provocation; and involuntary manslaughter if the killing be done in the commission of some lawful act, such as in justifiable self-defense." 

1256. Whether malice exists. 

1. Whether there is any evidence of the existence of malice is a question for the court to decide in giving or refusing instructions. 

2. Whether there is sufficient evidence to sustain a finding of the existence of malice is a question for the jury. 

3. Whether there is sufficient evidence of the existence of malice to sustain a verdict (based on the existence of malice) is a question for the court on a motion for a new trial. 

State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 3, 52 S. E. 981. 

State v. Michael, 74 W. Va. 621, 82 S. E. 611.

In the absence of malice a homicide is of no higher grade than voluntary manslaughter. 

State v. Galford, 87 W. Va. 358, 105 S. E. 237. 

Harris v. Com., 134 Va. 688, 114 S. E. 597.

And whether an unlawful homicide is murder or manslaughter depends upon the intent. 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 519, 94 S. E. 972. § 1257. Killing in hot blood. 

In State v. Galford, 87 W. Va. 358, 105 S. E. 237, it is held: "A sudden intentional killing with a deadly weapon, by one who is not in any way at fault, in immediate resentment of a palpably gross provocation, is prima facie a kill-

§ 1259 

MANSLAUGHTER 

ing in heat of blood, and, therefore, an offense of no higher degree than voluntary manslaughter." And, Brown v. Com., 86 Va. 473, 10 S. E. 475. 

State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 1, 52 S. E. 981. 

66* * * when in such case the evidence discloses that no time intervened between the giving of the provocation and the act of killing, within which passion could have subsided and reason regained its dominion, and the fatal act itself was not attended by circumstances of extreme cruelty and inhumanity, nor preceded by conduct from which malice can be inferred, a conviction of murder in the second degree should be set aside and a new trial awarded." 

State v. Clifford, supra. 

State v. Galford, supra. § 1258. Provocation necessary to reduce homicide to manslaughter.

It is the general rule that reasonable provocation is always necessary to reduce a felonious homicide, committed upon sudden provocation, from the degree of murder which is presumed to that of manslaughter; and this is especially true where the offense is committed with a deadly weapon. 

Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 924. 

Richardson v. Com., 128 Va. 691, 114 S. E. 788. 

Harris v. Com., 134 Va. 688, 114 S. E. 597. 

Hannah v. Com., 153 Va. 863, 149 S. E. 419. 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 516, 94 S. E. 972. § 1259. From what provocation must arise.

It is also held that the provocation relied on can arise only from a physical injury inflicted or attempted. In other words to constitute such provocation there must be some actual affray, some physical encounter which excites passion. 

State v. Murphy, 89 W. Va. 421, 109 S. E. 771.

Also, for a full discussion of an assault as a provocation for a homicide, see 

State v. Hatfield, '48 W. Va. 561, 37 S. E. 626.

§ 826 

§ 1260. Burden on accused to prove provocation.

In the early case of State v. Jones, 20 W. Va. 767, the rule is stated that whoever would shelter himself under the plea of provocation, must prove the same to the satisfaction of the jury; the presumption of law is against him, until this presumption is repelled by contrary evidence. This rule has not been changed by later decisions. 

§ 1261. Degree of provocation necessary. 

In Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 981, 159 S. E. 222, it is held: "Slight provocation does not suffice to reduce murder to manslaughter." 

Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 924. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 289. 

Richardson v. Com., 128 Va. 691, 104 S. E. 788. 

Hannah v. Com., 153 Va. 863, 149 S. E. 419. 

Mosby v. Com., 168 Va. 688, 190 S. E. 152. 

And in Jacobs v. Com., 132 Va. 681, 111 S. E. 90, it is held that provocation cannot be relied upon to reduce murder in the second degree to manslaughter, unless the provocation received so aroused the anger of the accused as to temporarily affect his reason and self-control. 

Also in Minor's Synopsis of Criminal Law, p. 46, it is said: "* * * the provocation, in order to extenuate homicide to manslaughter, must be such as to have actually excited strong passion, so as to have temporarily unsettled the reason. 

Honesty v. Com., supra. 

Mosby v. Com., supra. 

Jacobs v. Com., supra. 

Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 993, 159 S. E. 222. § 1262. Passion and provocation must concur.

It is the general rule that to reduce an unlawful homicide from murder to manslaughter, the provocation and passion relied on must have concurred. In other words, provocation without pas-

§ 1264 

MANSLAUGHTER 

sion, or passion without provocation, will not suffice. Both must co-exist and concur to reduce the offense to manslaughter. 

Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 924. 

And in Minor's Synopsis of Criminal Law, p. 46, it is said: "Adequate provocation and ungovernable passion must concur." 

Also, in Mosby v. Com., 168 Va. 688, 190 S. E. 154, it is held: "Provocation without passion or passion without provocation will not do; both must concur to reduce the offense to the grade of manslaughter." 

Read v. Com., supra. 

Jacobs v. Com., 132 Va. 681, 111 S. E. 90. 

Harris v. Com., 134 Va. 694, 114 S. E. 597. 

And in Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 981, 159 S. E. 222, it is held: "Both passion and adequate provocation must co-exist before murder is reduced to manslaughter, and the passion must grow solely out of the provocation." § 1263. Accused must not have brought about the provocation. 

In Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 993, 159 S. E. 222, it is held: "Provocation cannot avail and self-defense cannot avail where the accused has wrongfully occasioned the necessity for the homicide." 

Vaiden v. Com., 12 Gratt. 717. 

Carr v. Com., 134 Va. 656, 114 S. E. 791. § 1264. Where "cooling time" intervenes.

It is the general rule that if sufficient time has elapsed between the provocation and the homicide for the passion to cool, the killing is murder, not manslaughter. And whether sufficient time has intervened for the blood to cool so as to reduce the killing to manslaughter is a question for the jury. This rule also applies where the provocation is great. 

State v. Morrison, 49 W. Va. 210, 38 S. E. 481. 

State v. Beaty, 51 W. Va. 232, 41 S. E. 434.

§ 828 

Watson v. Com., 87 Va. 608, 13 S. E. 22. 

Mosby v. Com., 168 Va. 688, 190 S. E. 154. 

§ 1265. Test in such cases. 

It is the general rule that the test of whether the killing was from the sudden heat of passion caused by adequate provocation is found in the nature and the degree of the provocation and the manner in which it was resented. 

Richardson v. Com., 128 Va. 691, 104 S. E. 788. 

Davidson v. Com., 167 Va. 451, 187 S. E. 437. § 1266. Rule applies even when deadly weapon is used. 

In State v. Pusey, 118 W. Va. 95, 188 S. E. 746, it is held: "Any unlawful and intentional killing, even by the use of a deadly weapon, when the passion of the slayer is suddenly aroused upon some great provocation, is voluntary manslaughter, not murder.' 

State v. Michael, 74 W. Va. 613, 82 S. E. 613. 

§ 1267. Insulting words not sufficient provocation to reduce homicide from murder to manslaughter. 

Words alone, however insulting or contemptuous, are never a sufficient provocation, where a deadly weapon is used, to reduce homicide from murder to manslaughter. 

Read v. Com., 22 Gratt. 924. 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 679. 

State v. Douglas, 28 W. Va. 297. 

McCoy v. Com., 133 Va. 731, 112 S. E. 704. 

Reynolds v. Com., 133 Va. 760, 112 S. E. 707. 

Sims v. Com., 134 Va. 736, 115 S. E. 382. 

State v. Crawford, 66 W. Va. 114, 66 S. E. 110. 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 516, 94 S. E. 972. 

State v. Lemon, 84 W. Va. 33, 99 S. E. 263. 

Allen v. U. S., 164 U. S. 497. 

State v. Snider, 81 W. Va. 522, 94 S. E. 981. 

And in Harris v. Com., 134 Va. 694, 114 S. E. 597, it is said: "Words alone, however insulting or contemptuous, are never sufficient provocation, where a deadly weapon is used, to have that effect. In order to reduce the offense,

1269 

MANSLAUGHTER 

it is necessary that there should be a reasonable provocation which produces a sudden passion, under the influence of which the offense is committed. Provocation without passion, or passion without provocation, will not do; but both must concur to reduce the offense to the grade of manslaughter." 

Also, in Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 993, 159 S. E. 222, it is further held: "Neither sharp words, nor abusive language, is sufficient to reduce a homicide from murder to manslaughter." 

Reynolds v. Com., supra. 

Sims v. Com., supra. 

And in State v. Cline, 100 W. Va. 63, 130 S. E. 91, it is held: "* * * where a homicide has been committed with a deadly weapon, proof of mere words, however opproprious, is not enough to purge the crime of malice and reduce it to manslaughter." 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 516, 94 S. E. 972. 

State v. Murphy, 89 W. Va. 413, 109 S. E. 771. 

Mosby v. Com., 168 Va. 688, 190 S. E. 152. 

See secs. 1301 and 1335. § 1268. Where homicide is result of sudden affray. 

In State v. Cassim, 112 W. Va. 97, 163′ S. E. 769, it is held: "If, on a sudden affray, a fight is begun without deadly weapons, and one of them uses a deadly weapon in the heat of blood and kills the other, it is manslaughter only." 

See authorities cited in opinion. 

Also sec. 1296. § 1269. Where killing is result of mutual combat.

Where the defendant and deceased were actually engaged in combat, during the heat of which the former dealt the blow which caused the death of the latter, such killing is manslaughter only. 

King v. Com., 2 Va. Cas. 78. 

Watson v. Com., 87 Va. 608, 13 S. E. 22. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 848, 38 S. E. 184. 

And in State v. Taylor, 57 W. Va. 241, 50 S. E. 247, it is held: "Where two persons engage in sudden combat, and 2 CT-19

§  

830 by w after they become heated thereby, one of them seizes a deadly weapon, or uses one in his hands, having no intention to use it when the combat commenced, and slays his adversary, his offense is manslaughter only. That a deadly weapon was used, under such circumstances without the knowledge of the deceased, is not conclusive. The mere possession of a deadly weapon when the combat began, however, is not sufficient to show an intent to take an unfair advantage by using it in the fight. If the accused did not intend to use the weapon when the fight began, but used it in the heat of passion aroused by the fight, the killing is only manslaughter. It is a question of intent to be determined by the jury from all the facts and evidence in the case. If there was a fixed purpose to do bodily harm, without killing, and death resulted, it was murder in the second degree. If there was a sudden, impulsive killing, due to passion suddenly aroused, furor brevis, it was manslaughter, although there was intent to kill. If there was a fixed, deliberate and sedate purpose to kill, usually termed specific intent to take life, wilful, deliberate and premeditated, although in the course of mutual combat the offense is murder in the first degree." * * 

See authorities cited in opinion. 

§ 1270. Accidental killing. 

The defense of accidental killing is a denial of criminal intent, and imposes on the state the burden of proving such intent beyond a reasonable doubt, and accused need not sustain such defense by a preponderance of testimony. 

State v. Cross, 42 W. Va. 253, 24 S. E. 996. 

State v. Graham, 94 W. Va. 68, 117 S. E. 699. 

Smith v. Com., 155 Va. 1111, 156 S. E. 580. § 1271. Where death is the result of criminal carelessness. 

In State v. Legg, 59 W. Va. 331, 53 S. E. 545, it is said: "One killing another by mere careless use of a deadly weapon commits only manslaughter. And as to what constitutes criminal carelessness is a question of law for the court."

§ 1274 

MANSLAUGHTER 

§ 1272. Instructions that may be requested in manslaughter.

One tried for murder, if the evidence justify, may ask for an instruction on the theory of manslaughter and also on the theory of self-defense. These defenses are not necessarily inconsistent 

State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 1, 52 S. E. 981. 

State v. Crawford, 66 W. Va. 114, 66 S. E. 110. 

State v. Galford, 87 W. Va. 358, 105 S. E. 237.

And where it is justified by the evidence, it is reversible error to refuse such instructions. 

State v. Alderson, 74 W. Va. 732-3, 82 S. E. 1021. § 1273. When error to refuse instructions on manslaughter.

Where there is evidence tending to show that the crime was committed in hot blood it is error to give an instruction omitting the element of manslaughter. 

State v. Taylor, 57 W. Va. 228, 50 S. E. 247. 

State v. Michael, 74 W. Va. 621, 82 S. E. 611. 

And in Tucker v. Com., 159 Va. 1048, 167 S. E. 253, it is held: "It is held by the Federal courts and the majority of the State courts that if the evidence introduced by the prosecution establishes murder and the evidence in behalf of the accused, if believed, establishes justifiable or excusable homicide, a refusal of the trial court to give an instruction on manslaughter is reversible error." 

See the authorities cited in opinion. § 1274. When not error to refuse instructions on manslaughter. 

In Bell v. Com., 167 Va. 526, 189 S. E. 448, it is held no error to refuse to instruct the jury on the law of manslaughter, where, if the evidence is to be believed, the accused was guilty of firstdegree murder. Said the Virginia Court in its opinion: "It is perfectly true that a jury has the power to return a verdict of involuntary manslaughter in a case where first-degree murder is shown beyond controversy, and

$832 

such a verdict should be confirmed for this reason: The accused could not be retried for murder because he has been cleared of that charge by the verdict of manslaughter, and if the verdict for manslaughter be not permitted to stand, he could not be punished at all. "The jury has the power to return such a verdict in such a case, but not the right; and a court should not intimate by its instructions that it might return a verdict which it had no right to return." Citing, Burton, etc. v. Com., 108 Va. 892, 62 S. E. 376. 

State v. Woodrow, 58 W. Va. 527, 52 S. E. 545.

The reason assigned for this holding is that "Instructions containing statements of abstracts principles should never be given unless they find support in the evidence." 

§ 1275. Verdict. 

Under Virginia Code, sec. 4920, and West Virginia Code, 623-16 (sec. 6205), on an indictment for felonious homicide, the jury may find the accused not guilty of the felony, but guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The application of the law to the facts is in the discretion of the jury. 

Burton v. Com., 108 Va. 892, 62 S. E. 376.

But a verdict finding defendant guilty of manslaughter, without specifying whether "voluntary" or "involuntary" is void for uncertainty, except as to its findings in favor of accused. 

State v. Vineyard, 85 W. Va. 293, 101 S. E. 440. 

State v. Lutz, 85 W. Va. 330, 101 S. E. 434.

West Virginia Code, 62-9-4 (sec. 6266), prescribes the form of indictment for manslaughter. Follow the general form in sec.

§ 1278. Voluntary manslaughter defined. 

1. The court instructs the jury that voluntary manslaughter is where the act causing death is committed in the heat of sudden passion caused by provocation; and they are further instructed that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant, in the heat of sudden passion, caused by provocation, killed the said James Tanner at the time and place alleged in the indictment, they should find the defendant guilty of voluntary manslaughter, unless they further believe from the evidence that the defendant believed and had reason to believe, that the blow which resulted in James Tanner's death was necessary to protect his own life, or protect himself from great bodily harm, and that the necessity of inflicting said blow was not brought about by the defendant's own conduct. 

State v. Dickey, 48 W. Va. 326, 37 S. E. 695. 

2. The court instructs the jury that manslaughter is when a person feloniously and unlawfully, but without malice, kills another; and is divided into two classes:

Voluntary manslaughter is the unlawful killing of another

$ 834 

But without malice in a sudden quarrel, or in heat of blood. it is not every killing in the heat of blood, or upon sudden quarrel, which is voluntary manslaughter. In order to be so, it must be done without malice, such as I have defined; for the existence or want of malice is the distinction between murder and manslaughter. Involuntary manslaughter is when one in the performance of an unlawful act kills another by accident. 

Whitehurst v. Com., 79 Va. 559. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the prisoner killed Philpot on a sudden quarrel without malice prepense, then such killing is manslaughter. 

Sims v. Com., 134 Va. 755, 115 S. E. 382. § 1279. Involuntary manslaughter defined. 

The court instructs the jury that involuntary manslaughter is the unlawful killing of a human being without malice, either express or implied, and without intent to kill or inflict the injury causing death, committed accidentally in the commission of some unlawful act not felonious. The court, therefore instructs the jury that if they shall believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that on December 24, 1923, the defendant, Sam Nelson, in or on the side of the public road at or near Nelly's Ford, Nelson County, Virginia, shot off a pistol (which is an unlawful act), without any intent of injuring Thomas Martin Coleman, and without any malice, express or implied, and that the said Thomas Martin Coleman was struck by one of the bullets discharged from said pistol in the hands of the defendant, Sam Nelson, and that by reason thereof the said Thomas Martin Coleman was killed, then they should find the defendant, Sam Nelson, guilty of involuntary manslaughter, * and punish him as set out in another instruction. 

Nelson v. Com., 143 Va. 588, 130 S. E. 389.

as the jury does not fix the punishment in that State.

§ 1280. Distinction between voluntary manslaughter and second degree murder.

The court instructs the jury that if they shall find from the evidence that the killing was done without malice-in the heat of passion, in a sudden brawl, on a sufficient provocation—such killing amounts to voluntary manslaughter only; if, however, they find that the killing was done in the heat of passion, but on slight and insufficient provocation, such killing may amount to murder in the second degree. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 289. § 1281. Voluntary and involuntary manslaughter distinguished. 

1. The court instructs the jury that voluntary manslaughter is the unlawful killing of a human being in heat of blood and sudden passion, upon adequate provocation, and not from malice. 

And involuntary manslaughter is the unintentional killing of a human being in connection with the doing of an unlawful act. 

Reynolds v. Com., 133 Va. 770, 112 S. E. 707. 

2. If the jury believe from the evidence that the deceased and the prisoner were engaged in a sudden and mutual combat, in which no weapon dangerous in itself was used, and during the progress of the fight the prisoner struck the deceased an ordinary blow or blows with his fist or feet, without any intention either to kill the deceased or to do him any great bodily harm, but to repel his attack; and that the death of the deceased was caused thereby accidentally and apart from the prisoner's intention, then the prisoner is guilty of involuntary manslaughter. If, however, though no weapon dangerous in itself was used, but only the fists and feet, yet if the jury are satisfied from the evidence that the manner of inflicting the blows was cruel and unusual and exceeded in number and violence what was necessary to repel the deceased, and the deceased died of such beating, then the prisoner is guilty of voluntary manslaughter. 3. 

Bull v. Com., 14 Gratt. 617.

The court instructs the jury that manslaughter is when a

Da person feloniously and unlawfully, but without malice, kills another; and it is divided into two classes:

Voluntary manslaughter is the unlawful killing of another without malice in a sudden quarrel, or in the heat of blood. But it is not every killing in the heat of blood, or upon sudden quarrel, which is voluntary manslaughter. In order to be so, it must be done without malice, such as I have defined * ; for the existence or want of malice is the distinction between murder and manslaughter. Involuntary manslaughter is when one in the performance of an unlawful act kills another by accident. 

Whitehurst v. Com., 79 Va. 559.

§ 1282. Provocation as a defense. 

1. No provocation whatever can render a homicide justifiable, or even excusable. The lowest grade to which it can reduce homicide is manslaughter; and, if the prisoner killed the deceased suddenly, without any, or without considerable, provocation, the law implies malice, and the killing is murder. 

Hodges v. Com., 89 Va. 271, 15 S. E. 513. 

2. The court instructs the jury that to sustain provocation as a defense to murder in the first degree, it must be shown that the prisoner, at the time of the fatal shooting (blow), was deprived of the power of self-control by the provocation which he had received; and in deciding the question whether this was or was not the case, regard must be had to the character of the provocation, to the nature of the act by which death was caused-to the time which elapsed between the provocation, and the act which caused death-to the prisoner's conduct during the interval, and to all the circumstances tending to show the state of his mind at the time he committed the act. 

Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 363, 18 S. E. 440. 

Litton v. Com., 101 Va. 850, 44 S. E. 923. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 825, 36 S. E. 399. 

Jackson v. Com., 98 Va. 849, 36 S. E. 487. 

Hodges v. Com., supra. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 292.

§ 1283

3. The court instructs the jury that to sustain provocation as a defense to murder in the first degree, it must be shown that the prisoner, at the time of the fatal shooting, was deprived of the power of self-control by the provocation he had received; and in deciding the question whether this was or was not the case, regard must be had to the character of the provocation, and the act by which death was caused, to the time which elapsed between the provocation, and the act which caused death, to the prisoner's conduct during the interval, and to all circumstances tending to show the state of his mind at the time he committed the act. 

Green v. Com., 122 Va. 870, 94 S. E. 940.

The court instructs the jury that to sustain provocation as a defense to murder in the first degree, it must be shown that the prisoner, at the time the fatal shot was fired, was deprived of the power of self-control by the provocation which he had received, and in deciding the question of whether this was, or was not, the case, regard must be had to the character of the provocation, the nature of the act by which death was caused, to the time which elapsed between provocation and the act which caused death, to the offender's conduct during the interval, and all the circumstances tending to show the state of mind of the accused at the time he committed the act. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 825, 36 S. E. 399. § 1283. Where killing is result of sudden quarrel or mutual combat. 

1. If the jury believe from the evidence that the deceased and the prisoner were engaged in a sudden and mutual combat, in which no weapon dangerous in itself was used, and during the progress of the fight the prisoner struck the deceased an ordinary blow or blows with his fist or feet, without any intention either to kill the deceased or to do him any great bodily harm, but to repel his attack; and that the death of the deceased was caused thereby accidentally and apart from the prisoner's intention, then the prisoner is guilty of involuntary manslaughter. If, however, though no weapon dangerous in itself was used, but only the fists and feet, yet if the jury are satisfied from the evidence that

the manner of inflicting the blows was cruel and unusual, and exceeded in number and violence what was necessary to repel the deceased, and the deceased died of such beating, then the prisoner is guilty of voluntary manslaughter.

But if the jury shall upon the whole evidence, entertain a reasonable doubt that the deceased came to his death by violence inflicted by the prisoner at the bar, then they must acquit him. 

Bull v. Com., 14 Gratt. 616-7. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the deceased and the prisoner were engaged in a sudden and mutual combat, in which no weapon dangerous in itself was used, and during the progress of the fight the prisoner struck the deceased an ordinary blow or blows with his fists or feet, without any intention, either to kill the deceased or to do him any great bodily harm, but to repel his attack, and that the death of the deceased was caused thereby, accidentally and apart from the prisoner's intention, then the prisoner is guilty of involuntary manslaughter. 

Bull v. Com., supra. 

NOTE: Where the prisoner is indicted for murder, under proper evidence, this instruction should be given by the defense. § 1284. What defense must show to reduce manslaughter to killing in self-defense. 

1. The court instructs the jury that where death ensues on sudden provocation or quarrel, without malice aforethought, the killing is manslaughter. To reduce the offense to killing in selfdefense the accused must prove two things, to-wit: (1) That before the mortal blow was given he declined further combat, and retreated as far as he could with safety, and (2) that he killed the deceased through the necessity of preserving his own life or to save himself from great bodily harm. 

Vaiden v. Com., 12 Gratt. 717. 

Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 360, 18 S. E. 440. 

2. The court instructs the jury that where death ensues on a sudden provocation, or sudden quarrel, without malice, the kill-

1. The court instructs the jury that even if they should believe from the evidence that offensive or insulting words had been spoken or published by the deceased of and concerning the prisoner, however grievous, still they alone can in no manner justify or excuse the killing of the deceased by the prisoner. 

Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 363, 18 S. E. 440. 

2. The court further instructs the jury that mere words, however insulting or opprobrious they may be, will neither justify nor excuse the person to whom such words are addressed, to commit even an assault upon the person using such words, and that as a matter of law, where a homicide has been committed with a deadly weapon, proof of mere words, however insulting or opprobrious, is not a sufficient provocation to purge the crime of malice and reduce it to manslaughter. 

And the jury is instructed that if they find from the evidence, in this case that the defendant, Harry Porter, armed with a deadly weapon, shot and killed the deceased, Charles Golden Jordan, because of such insulting or opprobrious words only, then the defendant, Harry Porter, is guilty of murder, unless you find from

§ 840 

all the evidence, in this case, that the said defendant is entitled to acquittal on the ground of self-defense. 

, State v. Porter, 98 W. Va. 390, 127 S. E. 393. 

State v. Crawford, 66 W. Va. 114, 66 S. E. 110. 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 516, 94 S. E. 972. 

State v. Lemon, 84 W. Va. 33, 99 S. E. 263. 

3. The court instructs the jury that, upon the evidence in this case, they cannot convict the accused of murder, either in the first or second degree, but may convict of either voluntary or involuntary manslaughter. If the jury believe from the evidence that the accused threw a rock at Zach Lewis, Jr., striking him upon the head and causing his death, then they may convict the accused of voluntary manslaughter, unless they believe that the throwing of the rock at said Lewis was necessary to repel an assault which threatened death or great bodily harm, or unless said Byrd had reasonable ground for believing, and did believe, that the throwing of said rock was necessary to repel said assault. No mere words, however insulting, are sufficient to justify a resort to force. To justify the accused in exercising force, it must have been to repel force—that is, an actual assault upon him—and necessary, or in good faith believed by the accused to be necessary, to repel such assault. 

Byrd v. Com., 89 Va. 541, 16 S. E. 727. 

4. The court tells the jury that words, howsoever grievous, cannot justify taking life, nor will they reduce the grade of homicide below murder or excuse the same. 

McCoy v. Com., 133 Va. 736, 112 S. E. 704. 

5. The court further tells the jury that words, however grievous, will not justify an assault. 

McCoy v. Com., 125 Va. 775, 99 S. E. 644.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the prisoner committed the homicide charged in the indictment in the heat of passion, excited by a reasonable provocation which caused him to do the act without premeditation and yet which was insufficient to deprive him of the power of self-control, in that case he is guilty of murder in the second degree, but if the provocation which he received was such as to reasonably deprive him of the power of self-control at the time the homicide was committed, then they should find him not guilty of murder but of manslaughter. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 825, 36 S. E. 399. case.

NOTE: The above instruction was offered in Reed v. Com., supra, and rejected because not applicable to the evidence in that On page 827 of the opinion it is stated that the instruction was approved in Hodges v. Com., 89 Va. 265, 15 S. E. 513, because applicable to the facts in that case. In Reed v. Com., supra, page 825, the following instruction was given in lieu of the above and held good. 

3. The court instructs the jury that to sustain provocation as a defense to murder in the first degree, it must be shown that the prisoner at the time of the fatal shot, was deprived of the power of self-control by the provocation which he had received, and in deciding the question whether this was or was not the case, regard must be had to the character of the provocation, the nature of the act by which death was caused, to the time which elapsed between the provocation and the act which caused death, to the offender's

$ 842 

11 conduct during the interval, and all the circumstances tending to show the state of his mind at the time he committed the act. 

Reed v. Com., supra. § 1287. Verdicts and punishment for manslaughter in 

West Virginia. 

The court instructs the jury that under the indictment in this case, if warranted by the evidence, you may find any one of the following verdicts: 

1. Voluntary manslaughter. 

2. Involuntary manslaughter. 

3. Not guilty.

That voluntary manslaughter is where one person kills another unlawfully, without malice, but under sudden excitement and heat of passion caused by reasonable provocation; that involuntary manslaughter is where one person, while engaged in an unlawful act, unintentionally causes the death of another, or when engaged in a lawful act negligently causes the death of another person. 

The court further tells the jury that voluntary manslaughter is punishable by confinement in the penitentiary of this state not less than one, nor more than five years, in the discretion of the court; that involuntary manslaughter is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine, or by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, or by both fine and imprisonment, in the discretion of the court. 

NOTE: In State v. Lutz, 85 W. Va. 330, 101 S. E. 434, it was held that assault and battery is not charged in our statutory form of indictment for murder, and it is error to instruct the jury that they may find such verdict. Same holding in State v. Vineyard, 85 W. Va. 293, 101 S. E. 440.

§ 1288. Where killing was result of defendant being assaulted by deceased.

The court instructs the jury that although you may believe from the evidence in this case that the defendant gave to the deceased the knife wound that caused his death, and though you

§ 1289 

MANSLAUGHTER 

3 further believe that it was done with a dangerous and deadly weapon, yet if you also believe from the evidence that he, the defendant, acted from sudden passion brought about by being assaulted, struck and beaten by the deceased without fault on the part of defendant, and after he had declined to engage in a fight with deceased, and that defendant in so wounding the deceased was not actuated by antecedent malice, then you cannot presume malice from the mere fact alone that the killing was done with a deadly weapon. 

State v. Donahue, 79 W. Va. 266, 90 S. E. 834. § 1289. Where killing was result of sudden quarrel or mutual combat, upon provocation. 1. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case that on the day Lee Palmer was killed, and before he was killed, the prisoner and one Mike Sullivan went to the machine shops referred to in the evidence, and that the prisoner went there at the request of said Sullivan, as detailed in the evidence, and that after the prisoner got to the said machine shops he became engaged in a quarrel with the said Palmer, which resulted in a fight between them, and that while engaged in said quarrel and fight the said Palmer and the prisoner were excited, angry, and their passions were aroused, and that in said fight, while the prisoner was excited, angry and his passions aroused, he shot and killed the said Palmer, they cannot find the prisoner guilty of anything higher than voluntary manslaughter. 

State v. Dodds, 54 W. Va. 294, 46 S. E. 288. 

2. The court instructs the jury that although they may not believe from the evidence in this case that the defendant shot and killed the deceased in self-defense, yet, if it appears from the evidence that the killing was not because of any grudge or malice, but was done in the course of a sudden quarrel, in mutual combat, upon sudden provocation, and that the provocation was more than slight, then you cannot find the defendant guilty of any higher offense than voluntary manslaughter, which is punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than five years. 

Reynolds v. Com., 133 Va. 770, 112 S. E. 707.

§ 1290. Surmise as to cause of death not sufficient. 

The court instructs the jury that it is not sufficient for them to surmise that the licks struck by Roush might or possibly or probably did result in the death (of the deceased), but that they must believe from all the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, that the death was the actual result of the blows, before they can find the defendant guilty of involuntary manslaughter (in this case).

§ 1291. Murder in the Virginias. 

In both Virginias murder is divided into first and second degrees. The statutes declare that murder by poison, lying in wait, imprisonment, starving, or by any wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing, or in the commission of, or attempt to commit arson, rape, robbery, or burglary, is murder in the first degree. 

All other murder is murder in the second degree.

Virginia Code, sec. 4393. 

West Virginia Code, 61-2-1 (sec. 5916). 

Every malicious homicide is murder. If, in addition, the killing be wilful, deliberate and premeditated it is murder in the first degree. The distinction between murder in the first and second degrees turns upon whether the killing was wilful, deliberate and premeditated, and the intent of the accused at the time of the homicide. Where the killing is accomplished by means other than those enumerated in the statutes as constituting murder in the first degree, proof must be adduced by the state to satisfy the jury that the death of the party slain was the ultimate result which the concurring will, deliberation and premeditation of the attempt sought. 

McDaniel v. Com., 77 Va. 281. 

Williams v. Com., 128 Va. 698, 104 S. E. 853. 

Sims v. Com., 134 Va. 736, 115 S. E. 382. 

§ 1292. Corpus delicti. 

The corpus delicti in cases of felonious homicide consists of two fundamental facts: (1) The death; and (2) the existence of a criminal agency as the cause thereof. The former must be proved either by direct testimony, or by presumptive evidence of the strongest kind, which is clearly satisfactory to the jury, and convinces them beyond a reasonable doubt; but the latter may be established by circumstantial evidence or by presumptive reasoning upon the facts and circumstances of the case. But the cor-

§ 848 

pus delicti must be established by clear, full and convincing evidence. 

Smith v. Com., 21 Gratt. 809. 

Hatchett v. Com., 76 Va. 1026. 

Dean v. Com., 32 Gratt. 912. 

Russell v. Com., 78 Va. 400. 

Sutton v. Com., 85 Va. 128, 7 S. E. 323.

State v. Flanagan, 26 W. Va. 116. 

State v. Parsons, 39 W. Va. 464, 19 S. E. 876. 

State v. Merrill, 72 W. Va. 500, 78 S. E. 699. 

State v. Toney, 98 W. Va. 236, 127 S. E. 35. 

State v. Roush, 95 W. Va. 143, 120 S. E. 304, and cases therein cited. 

State v. Gilfillen, 96 W. Va. 660, 123 S. E. 578. 

State v. Beale, 104 W. Va. 631, 141 S. E. 7. 

Hamilton v. Com., 163 Va. 1098, 177 S. E. 847. 

State v. Koontz, 117 W. Va. 35, 183 S. E. 680. 

And in Terry v. Com., 171 Va. 505, 198 S. E. 911, it is said: "In every prosecution for the commission of a homicide, the corpus delicti has two components: death as the result, and the criminal agency of another as the means.' 

And in State v. Lucas, 103 W. Va. 743, 138 S. E. 393, it is held: 

"All elements constituting the corpus delicti in a homicide case may be proved by circumstantial evidence which convinces the jury beyond a reasonable doubt that the crime charged was committed." See also, Terry v. Com., supra. 

Smith v. Com., 21 Gratt. 809. 

Nicholas v. Com., 91 Va. 750, 21 S. E. 367. 

Cochran v. Com., 122 Va. 801, 94 S. E. 329. 

Dean v. Com., 32 Gratt. 912. 

See sec. 141. For instruction, see sec. 1530. 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 679. § 1293. Presumption of murder in the second degree.

In the Virginias every unlawful homicide is presumed in law to be murder in the second degree, that is to have been done with malice. To elevate the crime to murder in the first degree the state must, in addition, show that it was done deliberately; but whether the offense be murder of the first or second degree, mal-

§ 1294 

MURDER 

ice either express or implied must appear. There can be no murder of either degree without it. 

State v. Cain, 20 W. Va. 679.

State v. Douglas, 28 W. Va. 297. 

Hannah v. Com., 153 Va. 863, 149 S. E. 419. 

Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 980, 159 S. E. 222. 

Puckett v. Com., 157 Va. 800, 160 S. E. 19. 

But in Litton v. Com., 101 Va. 833, 44 S. E. 923, it is held: 66* * * where the commonwealth has proven the commission of a homicide, and has pointed out the accused as the criminal agent, then it may rest its case, and, unless the accused shows circumstances or justification, excuse, or alleviation, a verdict of murder in the second degree will be warranted." 

Puckett v. Com., supra. 

Adams v. Com., 163 Va. 1053, 178 S. E. 32. 

For additional authorities, see 

Michie's Digest, vol. 5, p. 410, sec. 81.

It is also the general rule that if the accused would reduce the homicide to manslaughter or excusable homicide, the burden of proof is on him to overcome the presumption of murder in the second degree arising from the killing by introducing evidence sufficient to raise a reasonable doubt in the minds of the jury as to whether the offense is murder in the second degree. However, in establishing this fact the accused is entitled to the benefit of the evidence for the state as well as his own. 

State v. Jones, 20 W. Va. 764. 

Willis v. Com., 32 Gratt. 929. 

State v. Trail, 59 W. Va. 175, 53 S. E. 17. 

State v. White, 81 W. Va. 516, 94 S. E. 972. 

Watson v. Com., 85 Va. 867, 9 S. E. 418. 

Jacobs v. Com., 132 Va. 681, 111 S. E. 90. 

Sims v. Com., 134 Va. 736, 115 S. E. 382. 

For additional authorities see, Michie's Digest, vol. 5, p. 410, sec. 81. § 1294. Same, exceptions to the rule.

There are two recognized exceptions to the above stated rule that every unlawful homicide is presumed to be murder in the second degree. In State v. Cross, 42 W. Va. 258, 24 S. E. 996, it

§ 850 

is held that the rule does not apply where the defense is accidental killing. To the same effect is the holding in State v. Graham, 94 

W. Va. 68, 117 S. E. 699. Also in State v. Vineyard, 81 W. 

Va. 102, 93 S. E. 1034, it is held not to apply where accused is under fourteen years of age. In State v. Cross, supra, it is said: "Accidental killing is not such matter of defense as throws on the accused the burden of proving it by a preponderance of evidence. It is the duty of the state to allege and prove that the killing, though done with a deadly weapon, was intentional or wilful. In the absence of all proof, when the killing is shown to have been wilful or intentional the presumption of malice at once arises; but when the evidence, taken as a whole, raises a reasonable doubt in the minds of the jury as to whether the killing was accidental or intentional, they must acquit the accused, for the reason that the state has failed to sustain its case. 

In other words, 'if, on the whole evidence, the jury are left in reasonable doubt as to the intent of the defendant, they cannot convict of the crime.' "The circuit court erroneously put the question of accidental killing in the same category with wilful killing, where some matter such as self-defense or provocation is asserted by way of mitigation, excuse, or justification. In such cases the burden is on the accused to establish his defense by a preponderance of evidence. But the claim that the killing was accidental goes to the very gist of the charge, and denies all criminal intent, and throws on the prosecution the burden of proving such intent beyond a reasonable doubt." § 1295. Degree of murder is a question for the jury. 

It is the general rule that whether a particular homicide is murder in the first or second degree is a question for the determination of the jury; and the verdict must specify the degree of the crime of which accused is convicted or it is erroneous and will be set aside. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4919.

West Virginia Code. 62-3-15 (sec. 6204). 

Com. v. Williamson, 2 Va. Cas. 211. 

Briggs v. Com., 82 Va. 564. 

State v. Welch, 36 W. Va. 690, 15 S. E. 419. 

State v. Morrison, 49 W. Va. 210, 38 S. E. 481.

§ 1296 

MURDER 

State v. Hill, 81 W. Va. 676, 95 S. E. 21. 

For additional authorities see, Michie's Digest, vol. 5, p. 472, sec. 178. 

In State v. Hamrick, 112 W. Va. 158, 163 S. E. 868, it is held: "On a trial of one accused of murder, the jury are ordinarily the judges of the degree of the crime." 

State v. Banks, 99 W. Va. 711, 129 S. E. 715. 

Moreover, West Virginia Code, 62-3-15 (sec. 6204), and Virginia Code, sec. 4919, provide: "If a person indicted for murder be found by the jury guilty thereof, they shall in their verdict find whether he is guilty of murder in the first or second degree, etc." 

And a verdict finding the defendant "guilty of murder as charged in the indictment," and not fixing the degree of murder is fatally defective, and will be set aside. 

State v. McCoy, 95 W. Va. 274, 120 S. E. 597. 

State v. May, 62 W. Va. 129, 57 S. E. 366. 

Com. v. Williamson, 2 Va. Cas. 211. § 1296. Homicide as result of sudden fight, when retreat is necessary. 

In Ballard v. Com., 156 Va. 1004, 159 S. E. 222, it is held: "If a sudden fight is brought on without malice or intention, the accused, if at fault, must retreat as far as he safely can, but having done so and in good faith abandoned the fight, may kill his adversary, if he cannot in any other way preserve his life or save himself from great bodily harm." 

Vaiden v. Com., 12 Gratt. 717. 

Jackson v. Com., 96 Va. 107, 30 S. E. 452. 

McCoy v. Com., 125 Va. 771, 99 S. E. 646. 

Dodson v. Com., 159 Va. 976, 167 S. E. 260. 

See sec. 1268. 

And in Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 368, 18 S. E. 440, it is said: "It is a principle of the criminal law that, where death ensues on a sudden provocation or sudden quarrel, without malice prepense, the killing is manslaughter, and in order to reduce the killing to self-defense, the accused must prove two things- viz.: (1) That before the mortal blow

§ 852 

was given, he declined further combat and retreated as far as he could with safety; and (2) that he killed the deceased through the necessity of preserving his own life, or that there was reasonable ground to believe that the killing was necessary to preserve his own life, or save himself from great bodily harm." 

Quoted with approval in 

Jackson v. Com., 98 Va. 851, 36 S. E. 487. § 1297. Same, when retreat is unnecessary.

But where the fight is brought on without fault on the part of the accused, his retreat is not necessary. In such a case, where a homicide follows, it is held to be justifiable as distinguished from excusable. 

Jackson v. Com., supra.

For a more complete discussion on this point, see 

Michie's Digest, vol. 5, p. 404, sec. 68. § 1298. Justifiable and excusable homicide. 

For the distinction between justifiable and excusable homicide, see sec. 679. 

§ 1299. Evidence of previous conduct of the deceased. 

In State v. Shelton, 116 W. Va. 75, 178 S. E. 663, it is held: "In a murder prosecution, defendant had the right to present evidence in chronological sequence showing deceased's intoxicated condition and line of conduct for several hours prior to receiving the fatal injury as a basis for showing the alleged necessity for killing deceased in self-defense."

Likewise, all conversations or inquiries had or made by accused immediately before the homicide concerning the deceased or his movements, are admissible. 

Sutton v. Com., 85 Va. 128, 7 S. E. 323. 

Mohler v. Com., 132 Va. 713, 111 S. E. 454. 

State v. Price, 92 W. Va. 542, 115 S. E. 393.

And previous difficulties between accused and deceased and the circumstances thereof, are admissible. 

Poindexter v. Com., 33 Gratt. 766.

§ 1300 MURDER 

Hodges v. Com., 89 Va. 265, 15 S. E. 513.

Carr v. Com., 134 Va. 656, 114 S. E. 791. 

State v. Prater, 52 W. Va. 132, 43 S. E. 230. 

Also previous attempts on the part of accused to take the life of the deceased are competent evidence on the question of deliberation and premeditation, as well as to show felonious intent. 

Nicholas v. Com., 91 Va. 741, 21 S. E. 364. 

Taylor v. Com., 90 Va. 109, 17 S. E. 812. 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 667, 115 S. E. 543.

In other words the general rule is that all circumstances leading up to the homicide, and which tend to show the manner in which it was committed are admissible to prove or rebut malice. Likewise, evidences of occurrences immediately preceding the homicide, showing proximity, opportunity and motive, and directly connected in time and circumstance with the crime are admissible. And this is true although such evidence may tend to prove the commission of a distinct offense. 

Mendum v. Com., 6 Rand. 704. 

Reynolds v. Com., 133 Va. 760, 112 S. E. 707. 

Martin v. Com., 143 Va. 479, 129 S. E. 348. 

Mercer v. Com., 150 Va. 588, 142 S. E. 369. 

And in State v. Young, 82 W. Va. 718, 97 S. E. 134, it is held: "Upon the trial of one charged with murder, it is proper for the state to show the whole transaction culminating in the murder, even though this involves proof that the accused committed an assault upon another in his efforts to accomplish the death of his victim." 

See numerous authorities cited in the opinion. Also 

Williams v. Com., 128 Va. 698, 104 S. E. 853. 

Seymour v. Com., 133 Va. 775, 112 S. E. 806.

But proof of other homicides, having no connection with the one for which the defendant is on trial, is irrelevant and inadmissible. 

State v. Sheppard, 49 W. Va. 599, 39 S. E. 676. 

§ 1300. Same, when specific acts of violence or miscon duct by deceased may be shown.

In a trial for homicide, where the accused relies upon self-de-

§ 854 

fense, and there is appreciable evidence to support his theory, he may prove the reputation of deceased as a dangerous and quarrelsome man, and if he has personal knowledge of specific instances of unwarranted violence by deceased against other persons he may testify thereto, in addition to testifying to the general reputation of the deceased in that regard; but it is not error to refuse to permit him to testify of what he has heard, concerning such specific acts of violence, from others, unless such acts are so closely connected with the homicide as to be a part of the res gestae. 

State v. Hardin, 91 W. Va. 149, 112 S. E. 401. 

State v. Walker, 92 W. Va. 499, 115 S. E. 443. 

State v. Porter, 98 W. Va. 390, 127 S. E. 386. 

State v. Waldron, 71 W. Va. 5, 75 S. E. 558. 

State v. McCausland, 82 W. Va. 525, 96 S. E. 938. 

But in Harrison v. Com., 79 Va. 374, the Virginia court said: "As a general rule it may be stated that in a trial for homicide evidence is admissible, in behalf of the prisoner under a plea of self-defense, of the character of the deceased, to show that he was dangerous, fussy and quarrelsome. But this seems to be true only where the evidence as to this main fact is contradictory and does not conclusively show that the defendant was solely in fault." 

Rasnake v. Com., 135 Va. 677, 115 S. E. 543. 

See secs. 389, 680, and 691. § 1301. Insulting words only will not reduce homicide to manslaughter. 

In State v. Cline, 100 W. Va. 63, 130 S. E. 91, it is held: 

66* * * where a homicide has been committed with a deadly weapon, proof of mere words, however insulting and opprobrious, is not enough to purge the crime of malice and reduce it to manslaughter.'

State v. Murphy, 89 W. Va. 413, 109 S. E. 771.

And in Adams v. Com., 163 Va. 1053, 178 S. E. 31, it is said: "Vile as the epithet was that Leebrick employed, it af-

forded no legal excuse to the accused to assault him and was not in law such a provocation as justified the killing." 

See secs. 581, 686 and 1267. § 1302. Capacity to commit crime is a question for the jury. 

In State v. Vineyard, 85 W. Va. 294, 101 S. E. 440, it is held: "Capacity to commit a crime is a question to be determined by the jury from the age, appearance and conduct of the accused, both at the time of the commission of the offense charged and at the time of trial, wherefore the trial court may properly refuse to direct a verdict of acquittal, on the ground of independent, direct and express evidence of such capacity." 

State v. Williams, 40 W. Va. 268, 21 S. E. 721. § 1303. Evidence respecting deceased's children, improper. 

In State v. McCausland, 82 W. Va. 526, 96 S. E. 938, it is held: "Upon the trial of one charged with murder it is improper to admit evidence showing the number of the dead man's children and their ages, when the family of such deceased party is in nowise connected with the difficulty which resulted in his death." § 1304. When adultery of wife will reduce homicide by husband to manslaughter. 

In State v. Cline, 100 W. Va. 63, 130 S. E. 91, it is held: "If a husband detects his wife in the act of adultery there is sufficient provocation to reduce the homicide to manslaughter if he immediately kills either the wife or her paramour, provided that the killing is due to passion aroused by the provocation and not to revenge or malice. 

In many cases it is held or said that he must see them together under circumstances reasonably leading him to believe that they are or have been so engaged, and not kill merely upon information of past adultery." Citing, 29 Corpus Juris, p. 1142, sec. 125.

§ 1305. Homicide in resisting an unlawful arrest.

(* * * 

In State v. Lutz, 85 W. Va. 336-7, 101 S. E. 434, it is held: the law is that one may take life in resisting an unlawful arrest, if he believes and has reasonable grounds to believe it is necessary for him to do so to save his own life or his person from great bodily harm." 

State v. Clark, 64 W. Va. 625, 63 S. E. 402. 

State v. Donahue, 79 W. Va. 260, 90 S. E. 834. 

§ 1306. Flight of accused. 

In State v. Thornhill, 111 W. Va. 263, 161 S. E. 431, it is held that evidence of escape and flight of accused is only a circumstance which may be considered by the jury as tending to prove his guilt. But the accused has the right to show that such flight was attributable to reasons other than consciousness of guilt. 

Anderson v. Com., 100 Va. 860, 42 S. E. 865. 

Wharton's Crim. Ev., vol. 2, p. 1494.

But the fact that defendant while confined in jail had an opportunity to escape and declined to do so, is not admissible. 

State v. Bickle, 53 W. Va. 597, 45 S. E. 917.

NOTE: While the flight of the accused is a proper subject for argument before a jury, the safer practice is for the State not to offer an instruction thereon.

State v. Schilansky, 105 W. Va. 553, 143 S. E. 307. 

§ 1307. Where accused simply evades arrest. 

In State v. Justice, 107 W. Va. 491, 148 S. E. 843, it is held: "Where accused evades arrest, it is proper to show the circumstances surrounding his subsequent apprehension, as well as to show who was in company with him at the time of his arrest." Citing, 16 Corpus Juris, 551, 553.

But the accused may explain such evasion by any competent evidence. 

Hines v. Com., 136 Va. 728, 117 S. E. 843.

§ 1308. Duty of trial court to instruct the jury with reference to punishment in first degree murder. 

In State v. Chaney, 117 W. Va. 605, 186 S. E. 607, it is held: "It is the duty of the trial court, in prosecutions for murder, to inform the jury, without request, of their authority under Code, 62-3-15 (sec. 6204), to determine whether the accused, if found guilty of murder in the first degree, shall be punished by death or confinement in the penitentiary for life."

NOTE: This case specifically overrules State v. Cobbs, 40 W. 

Va. 718, 22 S. E. 310, and State v. Beatty, 51 W. Va. 232, 41 S. 

E. 434, in so far as they are in conflict therewith.

And failure of the trial court to so instruct the jury is reversible error. 

State v. Goins, 120 W. Va. 605, 199 S. E. 875. § 1309. Instructions, when not error to refuse on degree of crime lower than murder in first degree. 

In State v. Stephenson, 114 W. Va. 458, 172 S. E. 533, it is held: "Where the evidence in a murder prosecution does not admit of any other conclusion than of murder in the first degree, an instruction on a lesser grade of the offense charged, need not be granted." 

Thornton v. Com., 24 Gratt. 657, and cases cited in opinion. § 1310. When not error to instruct jury on manslaughter. 

See Chapter on Manslaughter, sec. 1274. § 1311. Verdicts that may be returned upon statutory form of indictment for murder.

Where the evidence warrants, there may be a verdict of murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, voluntary manslaughter, involuntary manslaughter, or not guilty. In West 

Virginia it is held that such indictment does not charge assault and battery, and an instruction which includes that offense among the verdicts which may be returned by the jury is erroneous. The same is no doubt true of the statutory form in Virginia.

State v. Lutz, 85 W. Va. 338, 101 S. E. 434. 

State v. Vineyard, 85 W. Va. 296, 101 S. E. 440. 

§ 1312. Indictment. 

For many years the West Virginia statute, Code 62-3-3 (sec. 

6265), has prescribed a form of indictment for murder; and in 

1930 a short statutory form was prescribed by the Virginia Legislature, Code sec. 4865. And in Hurd v. Com., 159 Va. 880, 165

S. E. 536, it is said that the object of the statute is to eliminate the excessive verbiage used in the old common-law forms and to substitute there for a short, simple statement of the offense charged, and such indictment will sustain a verdict of murder in the first degree, second degree, voluntary manslaughter or involuntary manslaughter. See also, Bausell v. Com., 165 Va. 669, 181 S. E. 453. 

Marwell v. Com., 167 Va. 490, 187 S. E. 506.

§ 1315 

MURDER STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1315. Murder in first degree. 

1. The court instructs the jury that murder is distinguished by the law of Virginia (same in West Virginia) as murder in the first degree and murder in the second degree. And you are further instructed that murder by poison, lying in wait, imprisonment, starving, or any wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing, or killing in the commission of, or in the attempt to commit arson, rape, robbery, or burglary, is murder in the first degree; and that all other murder is murder in the second degree. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 291. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 852, 38 S. E. 184. 

McCue v. Com., 103 Va. 915, 49 S. E. 623. 

Wright v. Com., 109 Va. 848, 65 S. E. 19. 

Spencer v. Com., 143 Va. 533, 129 S. E. 351. 

2. The court instructs the jury, that murder in the first degree is any wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing with malice aforethought. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 826, 36 S. E. 399. 

Wright v. Com., 109 Va. 848, 65 S. E. 19. 

3. The court instructs the jury that they could find the defendant guilty of murder in the first degree, if they found him guilty of wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing, and further believed that defendant had proved no extenuating circumstances or none appeared from the case made out by the State. 

State v. Weisengoff, 85 W. Va. 287, 101 S. E. 450. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that Hite killed Bowers in the manner charged in the indictment, wilfully, deliberately, and premeditatedly, then they will find Hite guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Hite v. Com., 96 Va. 491, 31 S. E. 895. 

5. The court instructs the jury, that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that Elijah Wright wilfully, deliberately, maliciously and premeditatedly shot and killed William Sifers, he is guilty of murder in the first degree and the jury should so find. 

Wright v. Com., 109 Va. 849, 65 S. E. 19.

§ 860 

6. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence, to the exclusion of all reasonable doubt, that the prisoner wilfully, deliberately, and premeditatedly shot and killed the deceased, Enos B. Hylton, in this county, then they should find him guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Hall v. Com., 89 Va. 178, 15 S. E. 517. 

7. To constitute murder in the first degree the prisoner must have been incited to the killing by malice, and the killing must have been a wilful, deliberate, and premeditated act on the part of the prisoner; that is to say, he must have willed, deliberated, and premeditated that he should kill the deceased or do him some serious bodily injury, the necessary result of which would be his death, and from which he died. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 291. 

Horton v. Com., 99 Va. 852, 38 S. E. 184. 

Hodges v. Com., 89 Va. 271, 15 S. E. 513. 

8. To constitute murder in the first degree the prisoner must have been incited to the killing by malice, and the killing must have been wilful, deliberate, and premeditated that is to say, that the prisoner must have willed, deliberated, and premeditated that he should kill the deceased, and then must have killed him. 

Watson v. Com., 87 Va. 608, 13 S. E. 22. 

9. To constitute murder in the first degree, the prisoner must have been incited to the killing by malice, and the killing must have been a wilful, deliberate, and premeditated act on the part of the prisoner; that is to say, he must have willed, deliberated, and premeditated that he should kill the deceased or do him some serious bodily injury, the necessary results of which would be his death, and from which he died; and, to constitute a wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing, it is not necessary that the intent to kill should exist for any particular length of time prior to the actual killing. It is only necessary that such intention should come into existence for the first time at the time of such killing or any time previously. 

Muscoe v. Com., 86 Va. 451, 16 S. E. 534. 

10. The jury are instructed that every wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing, without provocation or excuse, is murder in

§ 1315 

MURDER 

the first degree, and that on a charge of murder, malice is presumed from the fact of the killing. When the killing is proved and is unaccompanied with circumstances of palliation, the burden of disproving malice is on the prisoner. 

Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 363, 18 S. E. 440. 

11. To constitute murder in the first degree, the prisoner must have been incited to the killing by malice, and the killing must have been wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing on the part of the prisoner; but a mortal wound, given with a deadly weapon, in the previous possession of the slayer, without any, or upon slight provocation, is prima facie wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing, and throws upon the accused the necessity of proving extenuating circumstances. 

Hodges v. Com., 89 Va. 271, 15 S. E. 513. 

12. The court instructs the jury that deliberation and premeditation are essential to murder in the first degree, and before the prisoner can be lawfully convicted of murder in the first degree the evidence must be sufficient to establish beyond all reasonable doubt that the killing was deliberate and premeditated. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 817, 36 S. E. 399. 

13. The court instructs the jury that whoever kills a human being with malice aforethought, is guilty of murder. That a murder which is perpetrated by poison, lying in wait or any other kind of wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing, is murder in the first degree. 

State v. Abbott, 64 W. Va. 412, 62 S. E. 693. 

McCue v. Com., 103 Va. 870, 49 S. E. 623. 

14. The court instructs the jury that murder by poison, lying in wait, imprisonment, starving, or any wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing, or in the commission or attempt to commit arson, rape, robbery or burglary is murder of the first degree. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4393. 

West Virginia Code, 61-2-1 (sec. 5916). 

State v. Abbott, supra. 

Harrison v. Com., 79 Va. 377. 

15. The court further instructs the jury that if you believe 2 CT-21

from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant, Joe Corey, wilfully, deliberately and premeditatedly shot and killed Mrs. Katherine Ghiz, you should find him guilty of murder in the first degree. 

State v. Corey, 114 W. Va. 118, 171 S. E. 117. 

16. The court instructs the jury that murder in the first degree is any wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing of one human being by another with malice; murder in the second degree is such killing with malice but without being wilful, deliberate and premeditated. 

Adams v. Com., 163 Va. 1053, 178 S. E. 31.

County of Raleigh, State of West Virginia, with a deadly weapon did feloniously, wilfully, maliciously, deliberately, premeditatedly and unlawfully did kill James Griffith, then it is the duty of the jury under the law to find the prisoner guilty of murder of the first degree.

State v. Worley, supra.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant, Elijah Wright, said in the hearing of William Sifers that "Bill Sifers has been trying to agg up a racket all day," and that the said William Sifers said to him "you are a liar," and that the said defendant replied that "you are another," and immediately began to advance on the deceased with a knife in his hand, and that the deceased told him to stop and shot in the ground near the defendant for the purpose of preventing the defendant from mȧking an assault upon him with said knife, and that the defendant thereupon forcibly disarmed the deceased, and after he had so disarmed him then and there wilfully, deliberately, maliciously, and premeditatedly shot and killed the said William Sifers as is charged in the indictment, he is guilty of murder in the first degree, and the jury should so find. 

Wright v. Com., 109 Va. 849, 65 S. E. 19. 

20. The court instructs the jury that if they believe beyond all reasonable doubt that the defendant wilfully, deliberately and premeditatedly with malice aforethought, struck the deceased with a stone on the head, from which he died, without justification, excuse, palliation or alleviation, the defendant was guilty of murder in the first degree; and that there was no particular period during which it was necessary that malice should have existed or the defendant should have contemplated the killing. 

State v. Wilson, 95 W. Va. 530, 121 S. E. 726. 

1316. Killing by one who is a trespasser.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the prisoner went to the store of the deceased for the purpose of killing him, and was abusive and denunciatory towards the deceased in his own store, and that deceased ordered him out and he refused to go, whereupon deceased, to compel him to go, used only the necessary force against the prisoner, who thereupon fatally shot deceased, the conduct of the prisoner made him a trespasser, and the fact that the deceased, thus provoked

§ 864 

by the prisoner, did use such force, did not justify or excuse the prisoner in killing him, as it was the duty of the prisoner to leave the store when so ordered by the deceased, and he was bound to submit to such force as was necessary to make him go; and if, while such force was being applied, he killed the deceased with a deadly weapon, it was murder. 

Gaines v. Com., 88 Va. 692, 14 S. E. 375. § 1317. Murder by poison.

The court instructs the jury that when one kills another by poison, malice is presumed from the use of poison. 

Whitehurst v. Com., 79 Va. 558. 

§ 1318. Murder in the commission of rape. 

1. The court instructs the jury that murder in the commission of or in the attempt to commit rape is murder in the first degree. 

State v. Beale, 104 W. Va. 630, 141 S. E. 7. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from all the evidence in the case beyond a reasonable doubt that the deceased came to her death as a result of an injury or injuries inflicted upon her by the defendant, or by defendant and Levi Lane, or by either of them, while they were acting together and in concert in committing or attempting to commit the act of rape upon the person of the deceased, then the defendant was guilty of murder in the first degree. 

State v. Beale, supra. § 1319. Murder in the commission of, or attempt to commit robbery. 

1. The court instructs the jury that to constitute murder in the first degree, the prisoner must have been incited to the killing by malice, and the killing must have been wilful, deliberate, and premeditated killing on the part of the prisoner; but, if the jury believe from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the prisoner killed the deceased in the attempt or commission of robbery

Robertson v. Com., 1 Va. Dec. 856.
