The court instructs the jury that under the law of this state, murder in the commission of, or attempt to commit robbery is murder in the first degree, and if the jury believe from the evidence in this case, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the deceased, Buck Williams, was murdered by the defendant, while he, the defendant, was engaged in committing or attempting to commit a robbery upon the said Buck Williams, then you should find the defendant guilty of murder of the first degree. 

, State v. Williams, 98 W. Va. 466, 127 S. E. 320.

Referred to in the opinion as instruction No. 1.

West Virginia Code, 61-2-1 (sec. 5916). § 1320. Murder in execution of purpose to do bodily injury.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the prisoner killed the deceased in execution of a malicious purpose to do the deceased a serious personal hurt, by wounding or beating him, the offense is murder. 

Bristow v. Com., 15 Gratt. 642. 

Gray v. Com., 92 Va. 773, 22 S. E. 858. § 1321. Design to kill previously formed. 

1. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the

§ 866 

evidence, that the prisoner, Charles Jackson, assailed the deceased, and a combat ensued, and in such combat the prisoner killed the deceased, and if they shall further believe that the first assault was made by the prisoner upon the deceased with a preconceived design to kill or to inflict great bodily harm, then the malice of the first assault, notwithstanding the violence with which it was returned, communicates itself to the last act of the prisoner, and the killing is murder. 

Jackson v. Com., 98 Va. 849, 36 S. E. 487. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case that the prisoner armed himself with a loaded pistol and that, after having so armed himself, he sought the said Moffett and put himself in the way of said Moffett so as to have an opportunity of killing said Moffett in case he should attack him, and that the said Moffett afterward, while unarmed, did make an assault upon the prisoner, and the prisoner killed in pursuance of a previously formed design, then such killing is murder in the first degree. 

Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 363, 18 S. E. 440. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that on the night on which the deceased was killed the prisoner had a formed design to kill the deceased and had threatened to kill him, and that afterward on the said night they met and a fight occurred between them, and that the prisoner was armed with a loaded pistol and willingly entered the said fight with the intent to kill the said Moffett in the said fight, and did, in pursuance of the said design, during the said fight, shoot the said Moffett, giving him a mortal wound, from which he died, as charged in the indictment, then such killing is murder in the first degree. 

Clark v. Com., supra.

1. If the jury believe from the evidence that previous to the time of killing there was a grudge on the part of the prisoner toward the deceased; that the prisoner had previously declared his purpose to kill the deceased if the deceased interfered with him, and that he killed the deceased because and in pursuance of such declared purpose on the aforesaid grudge, then such killing was wilful, deliberate, and premeditated, and is murder in the first degree. 

Bristow v. Com., 15 Gratt. 641. 

2. If the jury believe from the evidence that, previous to the time of the killing, there was a grudge on the part of the prisoner toward the deceased; that the prisoner had previously declared that this grudge must be settled; and that he killed the deceased because of this aforesaid grudge, then such killing was wilful, deliberate, and premeditated, and is murder in the first degree. 

Gray v. Com., 92 Va. 773, 22 S. E. 858. 

3. If the jury believe from the evidence that previous to the time of killing there was a grudge on the part of the prisoner toward the deceased, that the prisoner had previously declared his purpose to kill the deceased or inflict upon the deceased a serious personal hurt if the deceased interfered with him, and that he killed the deceased because of, and in pursuance of such declared purpose on the grudge aforesaid, then such killing was wilful, deliberate, and premeditated, and is murder in the first degree. 

Stapleton v. Com., 123 Va. 827, 96 S. E. 801.

Watson v. Com., 87 Va. 620, 13 S. E. 22.

§ 1324. Cooling time. 

1. Mealey v. Com., 135 Va. 595, 115 S. E. 528. § 1325. Length of time required for premeditation. 

1. The jury are instructed that, to constitute murder in the first degree with reference to this case, there must be a premeditated, or previously formed design to kill, but it is not necessary that this premeditated design to kill should have existed for any particular length of time. It is only necessary that it should be a course determinately fixed on, before the act done, and not brought about by provocation at the time of the act, or so recently before, as not to give time for reflection; neither is it necessary to prove this formed design by positive evidence; like every other fact it may be established by circumstantial evidence, which, beyond rational doubt, convinces the minds of the jury that this previous determination to kill did in fact exist. If the prisoner, as he approached the deceased, and when he first came in view of him, at the distance of about fifty yards, then formed the design, and came to the determination to kill the deceased, and in pursuance of this design, walked in a quick pace, the said distance of fifty yards, and killed the deceased, without any provocation then received, it was murder in the first degree. 

Whiteford v. Com., 6 Rand. 722. 

2. The court instructs the jury that, in respect to the premeditation required to be proved to make out a case of murder in the first degree, it is not necessary for the Commonwealth to prove that the design to kill existed for a particular length of time prior to the homicide, but it is sufficient if it should appear that at the

1. The court instructs the jury that to constitute a killing murder in the second degree, it must appear from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the killing was done from malice -that is, from a wicked and depraved heart. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 289. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if the killing of a human being be malicious but not wilful, deliberate and premeditated, then such killing is murder in the second degree. 

Sims v. Com., 134 Va. 752, 115 S. E. 382.

Hite v. Com., 96 Va. 491, 31 S. E. 895. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that there had been a disagreement between the accused and the deceased, and that upon a previous occasion he had beaten and choked her and that upon the evening of the homicide there

was a personal difficulty in the course of which the deceased choked the accused and that she ran out of the kitchen and secured a gun and returned to the kitchen and shot the deceased when he was sitting at the table eating his supper, then if there had existed no previous design to take the life of the accused the killing was murder of the second degree, and they should convict and fix the punishment at not less than five nor more than twenty years in the State prison. Provided you believe the killing was not done in the heat of blood upon a sudden quarrel and mutual combat. 

Mealey v. Com., 135 Va. 593, 115 S. E. 528.

NOTE: In West Virginia the italicized words should be omitted, as the jury does not fix the punishment. § 1327. Homicide presumed to be murder in second degree.

In considering instructions upon this presumption it is well to keep in mind two exceptions to the rule: First, it is held in State v. Cross, 42 W. Va. 258-9, 24 S. E. 996, that no such presumption arises where the defense is accidental killing; second, it is held in State v. Vineyard, 81 W. Va. 102, 93 S. E. 1034, that such an instruction is inapplicable where the accused is under the age of fourteen years. In other words, such instructions are applicable only "where some matter such as self-defense or provocation is asserted by way of mitigation, excuse, or justification." 

State v. Graham, 94 W. Va. 68, 117 S. E. 699.

"This (instruction) is carried into point two of the syllabus of the case (State v. Hobbs, supra) and is, we think, correct."

However, it is our opinion that there should be added to this instruction the following:

And in arriving at a verdict in this case as to the degree of guilt, if any, the jury should take into consideration all the evidence and circumstances in the case, that given both for the state and the defendant.

In State v. Sauls, 97 W. Va. 194, 124 S. E. 670, the following instruction was held improper:

The court instructs the jury that where a homicide is proved the presumption is that it is murder in the second degree. 

In the opinion in the case the court said: "The presumption to which the trial court refers is not a presumption of law, but one of fact, depending for its applicability upon the circumstances of the particular case. 

While it may be that where, as in the case at bar, (Sauls case), the killing is admittedly intentional and committed with a deadly weapon, there is a proper presumption of fact that the killing is murder in the second degree, nevertheless, to lay down a rule that any homicide, however it may come about, whether by accident, negligence or intention, is presumably murder in the second degree, we regard as violative of ordinary reason. Homicide is not necessarily murder, and the two should not be confused. The instruction as given is abstract and too comprehensive, and we do not approve it." Citing, * * * 

Wharton on Homicide, 3d Ed., sec. 147. See also, State v. Stanley, 112 W. Va. 313, 164 S. E. 254. 

These cases overrule State v. Dodds, 54 W. Va. 289, 46 S. E. 

228, wherein it is said: "Under our statute every homicide is prima facie murder in the second degree." 

State v. Galford, 87 W. Va. 366, 105 S. E. 237.

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 825, 36 S. E. 399. § 1332. Killing in heat of passion caused by provocation. 

1. If the jury believe from the evidence that the prisoner killed the deceased without deliberation or premeditation in a fit of jealous rage produced by disclosures made to the prisoner by the deceased and which the prisoner in good faith believed, then the jury cannot find the prisoner guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Reed v. Com., supra. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if at the time of the homicide the prisoner's state of mind caused by passion, anger, or rage, was such as that a reasonable doubt could exist as to his having acted deliberately and with premeditation they cannot find him guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Reed v. Com., supra.

Reed v. Com., supra.

State v. Long, 88 W. Va. 682, 108 S. E. 279. § 1337. Possession of deceased's goods by one accused of his murder.

The court instructs the jury that while the exclusive possession of stolen goods, which were in the possession of the deceased at the time of his death, is, of itself, not even prima facie evidence of the murder of the deceased by the party so in possession of such goods, yet, such possession is a most material circumstance to be considered by the jury, and where, in addition to such possession, other inculpatory circumstances are proved, such, for example, as the refusal of the accused to give any account, or his giving a false account of how he came by the goods, such proof, if they believe from the evidence it has been proven, will warrant

§ 886 

a conviction of murder. In other words, there should be some evidence of guilty conduct, besides the bare possession of the stolen property, before the presumption of murder is superadded to that of larceny, but extrinsic facts and circumstances may constitute such additional evidence. But it is for the jury, under all the circumstances of the case, to determine the value of such refusal, or false account, as evidence. 

Elmoe v. Com., 132 Va. 533, 110 S. E. 257. § 1338. Degree of murder must be found by jury.

The court instructs the jury that, if they find the prisoner guilty (of murder) as charged in the indictment, they shall further find whether he is guilty of murder in the first or second degree. If they find him guilty of murder in the first degree, they may, in their discretion, further find that he (the prisoner) be punished by confinement in the penitentiary; and if such further finding be not added to such verdict, the judgment thereupon rendered by the court will be that the prisoner be punished with death, and if such further finding is added, the judgment thereupon rendered by the court will be that the prisoner be confined in the penitentiary during his life. If the jury find the prisoner guilty of murder in the second degree, as charged in the indictment, the punishment imposed upon the prisoner will be confinement in the penitentiary not less than five nor more than eighteen years. 

State v. Hatfield, 48 W. Va. 573, 37 S. E. 631. 

State v. Staley, 45 W. Va. 792, 32 S. E. 200. 

State v. Clark, 51 W. Va. 462, 41 S. E. 206.

NOTE: In Staley's Case it was held that this instruction does not express the opinion of the court as to the weight and sufficiency of the evidence. § 1341. Killing wife's paramour. 

1. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the deceased and defendant's wife had been guilty of adulterous acts, that the prisoner had been informed of such acts, and that the prisoner believed them to be true, yet if the acts were in fact true, and believed by the prisoner to be true, the law would not justify or excuse the prisoner in seeking the deceased and killing him, if the jury believe from the evidence that he did so. 

State v. Bailey, 103 W. Va. 613, 138 S. E. 202. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from all the evidence that the adulterous acts on the part of deceased were true, that the prisoner was informed thereof and believed them to be true, yet if they further believe beyond a reasonable doubt

§ 888 

that the prisoner then made up his mind to kill the deceased out of a spirit of revenge, and went to the church as detailed to carry out his intent, and there, being sane and normal at the time, did without provocation, wilfully, deliberately and with premeditation, kill the deceased, then they should find him guilty of murder in the first degree. 

State v. Bailey, supra. § 1342. Verdicts under West Virginia statutory indictment. 

1. The court instructs the jury that one of five verdicts may be found under the indictment in this case, if the evidence in the case so warrant: (1) murder in the first degree, (2) murder in the second degree, (3) voluntary manslaughter, (4) involuntary manslaughter and (5) not guilty.

The court further instructs the jury that murder in the first degree is when one person kills another person unlawfully, wilfully, maliciously, deliberately and premeditatedly; that murder in the second degree is when one person kills another person unlawfully and maliciously, but not deliberately; that voluntary manslaughter is when a person unlawfully kills another person without malice, but under sudden excitement and heat of passion; that involuntary manslaughter is where one person while engaged in an unlawful act, unintentionally causes the death of another person, or when engaged in a lawful act negligently causes the death of another person.

The court further instructs the jury that murder in the first degree is punishable by death, or confinement in the penitentiary of this State for life, as the jury shall find in their verdict; that murder in the second degree is punishable by confinement in the penitentiary of this State not less than five nor more than eighteen years in the discretion of the court; that voluntary manslaughter is punishable by confinement in the penitentiary of this State not less than one nor more than five years in the discretion of the court; that involuntary manslaughter is a misdemeanor and punishable by imprisonment in the county jail or fine or by both, in the discretion of the court.

1. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the prisoner, Charles Amos Long, armed with a revolver, sought the deceased Clement Jefferson Long, with a view of provoking a difficulty with him, or with intent of having an affray with him, for the purpose of killing him, and a difficulty ensued, he cannot without some proof of a voluntary change of conduct or action on his part excuse the killing of the deceased, Clement Jefferson Long, upon the ground that the deceased, Clement Jefferson Long, struck him first with his mace, and that the revolver in the hands of said Charles Amos Long was accidentally discharged; for the law will not hold him guiltless, who by seeking a combat and continuing therein brings upon himself the very thing out of which the accident grew; accidental killing wholly to be excused from all guilt must be caused in the doing by some lawful act. 

State v. Long, 88 W. Va. 684, 108 S. E. 279.

§ 1345. Intent to kill need not exist for any particular length of time.

The court instructs the jury that to constitute a wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing, constituting murder of the first degree, it is not necessary that an intention to kill should exist for any particular length of time prior to the actual killing; it is only necessary that said intention should come into existence for the first time at the time of such killing or at any time previous. 

State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 14, 52 S. E. 981. 

Mosby v. Com., 168 Va. 688, 190 S. E. 154. 

Wright v. Com., 33 Gratt. 893. 

Whiteford v. Com., 6 Rand. 721.

DEFENSE INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1346. Murder in first degree. 

1. The court instructs the jury that to constitute murder in the first degree the evidence must clearly and distinctly prove, beyond any reasonable doubt, that the prisoner was not only incited to the killing of the deceased by malice, and desperate wickedness of heart, but such killing must have been a wilful, deliberate, and premeditated act on the part of the prisoner; in other words, at the time of the killing the prisoner must have distinctly understood what he willed and intended to do; he must have also reflected, and deliberated, and premeditated that he would kill the deceased, or do him some serious bodily injury, the probable result of which would be death. And if there be a reasonable doubt whether he had willed, and deliberated, and premeditated to kill the deceased, or do him some serious bodily injury, which would probably occasion his death, they ought not to find him guilty of murder in the first degree. 

Honesty v. Com., 81 Va. 289. 

2. The court instructs the jury that deliberation and premeditation are essential to murder in the first degree, and before the prisoner can be lawfully convicted of murder in the first degree the evidence must be sufficient to establish beyond all reasonable doubt that the killing was deliberate and premeditated. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 828, 36 S. E. 399.

§ 892 

3. The court instructs the jury that before you can find the defendant guilty of murder in the first degree you must believe from the evidence that the killing of Dr. Harris was wilful, deliberate and premeditated and with malice aforethought, and was the result of cool, deliberate judgment, and previous malignity of heart, without justification, excuse, palliation or alleviation. 

State v. Manns, 48 W. Va. 485, 37 S. E. 613. 

§ 1347. Premeditation and deliberation. 

1. The court instructs the jury that in order for the killing to embrace the necessary elements of premeditation and deliberation there must have been on the part of the prisoner a formed design and intention to kill, in execution of which the homicide was committed. 

Reed v. Com., 98 Va. 828, 36 S. E. 399. 

2. The court instructs the jury that in order for the killing to come within the meaning of the terms, "premeditation and deliberation" used in the statute, the mind of the accused must have been sufficiently composed, calm and undisturbed as to admit of reflection and consideration in forming the design to kill, and if they believe from the evidence that at the time of the homicide the accused was so drunk and excited that his mind was not in that condition then they cannot find him guilty of murder in the first degree.

§ 1351. Killing by one while engaged in a lawful act. 

The court instructs the jury that if they believe that the accused was in the discharge of a lawful duty, engaged in a lawful act, he need not retreat but may repel force by force, if need be, to the extent of slaying his adversaries. This is justifiable selfdefense. 

Mercer v. Com., 150 Va. 597, 142 S. E. 369. § 1352. Killing by one while resisting lawful arrest. 

The court instructs the jury that although they may believe from the evidence that the deceased at the time he was shot was attempting to arrest the accused, yet if they further believe from the evidence that in making such attempt he shot at the accused, and thereupon, because of said shooting at the accused by the deceased, the accused believing himself in imminent danger of being killed or sustaining great bodily injury, and being without fault in provoking the affray, returned the fire and killed the deceased, * * * such killing was not murder, notwithstanding the jury may believe from the evidence that the accused had previously threatened to kill any one who might attempt to arrest him. 

Looney v. Com., 115 Va. 931, 78 S. E. 625. § 1353. Killing by one while resisting unlawful arrest. 

The court instructs the jury that when an officer attempts to arrest a person charged with a felony and uses more force than is reasonably necessary to make the arrest, the officer himself becomes a wrongdoer and the person whose arrest is sought, if himself without fault, can resist such excessive force and even kill the officer if necessary to preserve his own life (or to save himself from great bodily harm). 

Palmer v. Com., 143' Va. 602, 130 S. E. 398. § 1354. Killing during sudden quarrel.

§ 1363. Cooling time. 

If the jury should believe from the evidence that the deceased had made, a few hours previously to the homicide, a violent assault upon the prisoner, and had inflicted a severe blow and wound upon his cheek, which rendered him unconscious for a time, and that before he had fully recovered his mental faculties and was still in the heat of passion and smarting under the influence of said assault, and when under all the circumstances surrounding him and in view of his condition from being struck the blow in the meadow a sufficient time had not intervened for his blood to cool and (for reason) to resume her sway in allaying his resentment, the deceased passed along the public road near the prisoner's home, armed with a pistol, and the prisoner fired upon the deceased and killed him, the court instructs the jury that they cannot find him guilty of a higher grade of offense than manslaughter, even though they may believe from the evidence that the accused, after the assault in the meadow, did not have reasonable ground to believe that he was in imminent danger of death or great bodily harm at the hands of the deceased, and even though they may believe that, under all the circumstances, he was not justifiable in getting his gun and going down the road to await the approach of deceased.

, Litton v. Com., 101 Va. 850, 44 S. E. 923.

State must prove witness was sworn by competent authority. § 1367. Perjury at common law.

At common law perjury is the wilful and false swearing of one to whom an oath is legally administered, in a proceeding authorized by law, touching any material matter or thing. 

Conner v. Com., 2 Va. Cas. 30. 

Com. v. Stockley, 10 Leigh 678. 

Thomas v. Com., 2 Rob. 795.

§ 902 

And in Fitch v. Com., 92 Va. 828, 24 S. E. 272, it is said: "Perjury at common law is defined to be a wilful false oath by one who, being lawfully required to depose the truth in any judicial proceeding, swears absolutely in a matter material to the point in question, whether he believed it The oath must be administered by one having legal authority to do so, and in a judicial proceeding before a tribunal that has jurisdiction to try it; otherwise, the testimony given under the oath, although false, does not constitute the crime of perjury." or not. * * * 

§ 1368. Under Virginia statute. 

The Virginia statute, Code sec. 4493, thus defines perjury: "If any person, to whom an oath is lawfully administered on any occasion, wilfully swear falsely on such occasion touching any material matter or thing, or if a person falsely make oath that any other person is twenty-one years of age, in order to obtain a marriage license for such other person, he shall be guilty of perjury.' 

And the next succeeding section, 4494, prescribes the punishment for both perjury and subornation of perjury. It reads as follows: 

"If any person commit or procure another person to commit perjury, he shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years; or, in the discretion of the jury, be confined in jail not exceeding one year, or fined not exceeding one thousand dollars, or both." 

Robinson v. Com., 165 Va. 876, 183 S. E. 257. 

§ 1369. Under West Virginia statute. 

The West Virginia Code, 61-5-1, 2 and 3 (secs. 5999, 6000 and 

6001), creates three offenses, namely, perjury, subornation of perjury and false swearing. The first two are felonies, and each is punishable by confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than ten years. While false swearing is a misdemeanor and punishable by a fine of not more than one thousand dollars, and, in the discretion of the court, confinement in jail not more than one year.

§ 1371 

 § 1370. Elements necessary to constitute offense. 

At common law and under the statutes of both Virginias, four elements are necessary to constitute the crime of perjury: 

1. The oath must be wilful, that is, the false qath must be taken deliberately and advisedly; for if it be occasioned by surprise or inadvertence, or a mistake of the true meaning of the question it will not be perjury. 

2. The oath must be false, but it is immaterial whether the fact, which is sworn to, be in itself true or false, for however true the things sworn to may happen to prove, yet if it were not known to be so at the time by him who swears to it, his offense is as great as if it had been false. 

3. The oath must be taken before competent legal authority, that is, it must be taken before some court or person legally authorized to administer it; and the court or person before whom it is taken, must be acting under the authority of law upon the subject matter to which the false oath relates. 

4. The thing sworn to must be material to the issue being tried, or the point in question; for if it be wholly foreign from the purpose, or altogether immaterial, not tending to aggravate or extenuate damages, nor likely to induce a jury to give readier credit to the substantial part of the evidence or thing sworn to, it cannot amount to perjury, because it is in such a case, merely idle and insignificant. However, if the false oath has any tendency, however slight, to prove or disprove the matter in issue, however uncircumstantially, it will amount to perjury. 

Mayo's Guide, pages 501-2. 

State v. Berkeley, 41 W. Va. 455, 23 S. E. 609. 

Crump v. Com., 75 Va. 922. 

Rhodes v. Com., 78 Va. 692. 

Com. v. Pickering, 8 Gratt. 629. 

Thomas v. Com., 2 Rob. 795. 

Fitch v. Com., 92 Va. 824, 24 S. E. 272. § 1371. False statement must have been material. 

It is the general rule that to convict one of perjury, the alleged false statement must have been material in the judicial proceeding in which it is proved to have been made. 

Com. v. Roach, 1 Gratt. 561.

$904 

 Com. v. Pickering, 8 Gratt. 629. 

Crump v. Com., 75 Va. 922. 

Rhodes v. Com., 78 Va. 692. 

Stofer v. State, 3 W. Va. 689. 

Fitch v. Com., 92 Va. 824, 24 S. E. 272. § 1372. Want of cause for belief in truth of testimony may be perjury. 

In State v. Berkeley, 41 W. Va. 458, 23 S. E. 609, it is held: "It is perjury where one swears wilfully and corruptly to a matter which he, according to his own lights, has no probable cause for believing, since a man is guilty of perjury if he knowingly and wilfully swears to a particular fact without knowing at the time the assertion is true, supposing his purpose is corrupt. Hence it is a good assignment of perjury that the defendant swore that he 'thought' or 'believed' a certain fact, whereas in truth and in fact he thought and believed the contrary, and had no probable grounds for what he swore. It has just been seen that falsity consists in knowingly affirming a condition without probable cause. Here we must again accept a position so often vindicated in these pages that probable cause must be estimated, not from the jury's standpoint, nor from the judge's, but from the defendant's. On the other hand, the fact sworn to may have been true; but, if the defendant swore to it wilfully and corruptly, not knowing it to be true, or not having probable cause, according to his own lights, for believing it to be true, he is guilty, as stated in the last section, of perjury. On the other hand, if he swears honestly to a fact or belief, with probable cause, according to his own lights, for the truth of his belief, he is not guilty of perjury, though his oath was untrue. Hence it is admissible to prove reception of such information by the defendant as gave him probable ground for his oath. One commits perjury where he swears falsely to a matter, the truth of which, though he believed, yet he had no probable cause for believing, and might with little trouble have ascertained the fact." * * "On the other hand, if he swears honestly to a fact or belief, with probable cause, according to his own lights, for the truth of his belief, he is not guilty of perjury, though his oath was untrue. Hence it is admissible to prove reception of such information by the defendant as gave him probable ground for his oath."

§ 1374 

 § 1373. The indictment. 

In West Virginia, the indictment must conform to the provisions of Code 62-2-4 (sec. 6168), which reads: 

"In an indictment or accusation of perjury or subornation of perjury, it shall be sufficient to state the substance of the offense charged against the accused, in what court or by whom the oath was administered which is charged to have been falsely taken, and to make an averment that such court or person had competent authority to administer the same, together with the proper averments to falsify the matter wherein the perjury is assigned, without setting forth any part of any record or proceeding at law or equity, or the commission or authority of the court or person before whom the perjury was committed; but nothing herein shall be construed to allow, without the consent of the accused, a part only of the record, proceeding or writing to be given in evidence on the trial of such indictment or accusation.' § 1374. Same, must aver materiality and falsity of statement. 

In State v. Aley, 94 W. Va. 529, 119 S. E. 549, it is held that an indictment for perjury which fails to allege that the defendant wilfully and falsely swore to certain statements touching a material matter or thing in the charging part thereof, is bad on demurrer. 

And it is also held that the charging part of such indictment must include the essential elements of the offense, viz., that the oath was lawful, that it was taken before one authorized by law to administer it, that the statements made were wilfully false, and that such false testimony was material to the matter or thing in issue. 

Thomas v. Com., 2 Rob. 795. 

Fitch v. Com., 92 Va. 824, 24 S. E. 272. 

Stofer v. State, 3 W. Va. 689.

Com. v. Roach, 1 Gratt. 561. 

Com. v. Williamson, 4 Gratt. 554. 

It was the law in Virginia before the 1919 revision of the Code, hereinafter referred to, and is now the law in West Virginia, that an indictment for perjury must charge: 

1. The taking of the oath. 

2. Its substance. 

3. The time of taking

§ 906 

4. The authority of the officer to administer.

5. Materiality of testimony. 

6. Its falsity. 

Rhodes v. Com., 78 Va. 692. 

Fitch v. Com., 92 Va. 824, 24 S. E. 272.

But in an indictment for perjury it is not necessary to aver that the defendant swore positively and absolutely. It is sufficient where one swears as he believes, thinks, or remembers to negative the fact he so believed, thought or remembered. 

Fitch v. Com., supra.

And in State v. Aley, supra, the court, quoting from Bishop's 

Crim. Proc., sec. 901, said: "The elements of this offense to be charged in the allegation are: 1. A judicial proceeding or course of justice. 

2. The defendant having been sworn to give evidence therein. 3. His testimony. 4. Its falsity. 5. Its materiality. 

And in State v. Lake, 107 W. Va. 124, 147 S. E. 473, it is also said: "It is vital in a trial of an indictment for perjury that the evidence given by defendant in a former judicial proceeding and alleged to have been wilfully false, should show that such evidence so given by defendant was material to the issue in the trial." Citing, State v. Aley, supra. 

And in Fitch v. Com., supra, it is further said: "It should appear on the face of the indictment that the false testimony was material to the matter in issue, but it is not necessary to set forth all the circumstances which render it material. Its materiality may be expressly averred, or the facts which show its materiality may be set out in the indictment.” 

And in State v. Aley, supra, it is said: "An indictment for perjury which fails to positively allege the materiality of the testimony alleged to have been sworn to, in the charging part of the indictment, and fails to set forth facts showing its materiality, is bad on demurrer." 

And in syl. 3, it is further stated: "The facts constituting the offense of perjury must be averred directly, positively and with certainty, and not by way of inference, argument or legal conclusions."

§ 1378 

Shunt with § 1375. Same, how materiality may be shown. 

In State v. Lake, 107 W. Va. 126, 147 S. E. 473, it is said: "It is quite generally held that the materiality of the testimony alleged to be false may be charged in either of two ways: First, by a direct averment of materiality, or, second, by setting forth the facts from which the materiality is made apparent or necessarily inferred." Citing, Wharton's Crim. Proc. (10th Ed.) p. 1552, sec. 1096. 

Bishop's New Crim. Proc., vol. 3, sec. 921. 

Chitty on Crim. Law, vol. 2, 307. § 1376. Same, joinder of counts.

In West Virginia, under Code 62-2-24 (sec. 6188), a count for false swearing may be joined with a count for perjury in the same indictment. 

State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 104. § 1377. Same, omission of the word "falsely," rule in 

West Virginia.

The omission of the word "falsely" from the charging part of the indictment renders it defective both at common law and under the West Virginia statutes.

State v. Aley, 94 W. Va. 529, 119 S. E. 549. 

§ 1378. Same, rule in Virginia.

The above was formerly true in Virginia. But the revisers of the Code (1919), to cure the defect in the law as disclosed in 

Fitch's Case, supra, added the following sentence to section 4869: "A distinct allegation, averment or statement in any part of the indictment, that the defendant did corruptly swear falsely, or did on the occasion mentioned in the indictment, commit wilful perjury, shall be a sufficient allegation of the falsity of the oath alleged to have been taken.' 

In one of his addresses on the new (Virginia) Code, with reference to this addition, Judge Burks said: "The last sentence is new, and the object of it is to meet the objection to the indictment sustained in Fitch's Case,

§ 908 

92 Va. 824, 24 S. E. 272; while not intending to criticise the holding in that case, it would seem that the former law was defective in not providing for a contingency which there arose. The defendant had a fair and impartial trial, but because the charge of the falsity of the oath was contained in the concluding part of the indictment instead of the charging part, the court felt compelled to give him a new trial." 

Hence, in Virginia, it is no longer necessary to use the word "falsely" in the charging part of the indictment, but it is still necessary in West Virginia. 

State v. Aley, supra.

In State v. Aley, supra, syl. 1, it is said: "In an indictment for perjury, under our statute, which fails to allege that the defendant wilfully and 'falsely' swore to certain statements touching a material matter or thing in the charging part of the indictment, is bad on demurrer." § 1379. Same, allegations as to time when offense was committed.

Virginia Code, sec. 4875, and West Virginia Code, 62-2-10 (sec. 

6174), among other things, provide: "No indictment * * * shall be quashed or deemed invalid * * * for omitting to state, or stating imperfectly, the time at which the offense was committed, when time is not of the essence of the offense." 

And in Mundy v. Com., 161 Va. 1049, 171 S. E. 691, it is said: "Time is no more the essence of subornation of perjury than it is of perjury itself. Hence both crimes are within the provisions of Code, sec. 4875, (W. Va. Code 62-2-10, sec. 6174), * * The charge of perjury was not based on any record or written instrument, but upon the oral testimony, and in plain language informed the accused of the occasion and in what specific proceeding the alleged perjury was committed. Time is not the essence of perjury, and when the crime charged consists of false testimony given ore tenus there is no sound reason to require more specific allegations of time than is required in charging the commission of other felonies in which time is not essential. 

Where the charge of perjury is not founded upon any record or written evidence, proof of the precise day stated in the indictment is not material."

Rhodes v. Com., 78 Va. 696. 

Stofer v. State, 3 W. Va. 689. § 1380. Subornation of perjury defined. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4494, defines subornation of perjury as the procuring of another person to commit perjury. While in West 

Virginia, Code 61-5-1 (sec. 5999), it is defined as the inducing or procuring another person to testify falsely in a trial for a felony concerning a material matter or thing. 

And in Mundy v. Com., 161 Va. 1049, 171 S. E. 691, it is said: "Subornation of perjury consists in procuring or instigating another to commit the crime of perjury, * * * 22 

§ 1381. Trial of suborner of perjury. 

Subornation of perjury is a separate and distinct offense from perjury, and the suborner and the perjurer are separately prosecuted. And while the offense is accessorial in its nature, the suborner may be tried and convicted although the perjurer himself has not been convicted of the perjury. 

Mundy v. Com., 161 Va. 1061, 171 S. E. 691.

But in all such cases it is necessary for the state to prove that perjury was actually committed in the first instance by the perjurer. 

Mundy v. Com., supra. 

However, in Maybush v. Com., 29 Gratt. 857, accused was convicted of subornation of perjury and judgment rendered against him. Later, at the same term, the alleged perjurer was tried for the perjury and acquitted. Maybush then moved for a new trial, which was denied. The appellate reversed the lower court, and held that if the alleged perjurer was not guilty, Maybush could not be guilty of the subornation. 2 CT-24

§ 910 

§ 1382.

Evidence necessary to convict of perjury or subornation. 

In Greenleaf on Evidence, vol. 2, sec. 257, it is said: "In proof of the crime of perjury it was formerly held that two witnesses were necessary because otherwise there would be nothing more than the oath of one man against another upon which the jury could not safely convict. But this strictness has long since been relaxed, the true principle of the rule being merely that the evidence must be something more than sufficient to counterbalance the oath of the prisoner and the legal presumption of innocence. 

The oath of the opposing witness therefore will not avail unless it is corroborated by other independent circumstances."

However, this rule does not obtain in either of the Virginias. In 

Mundy v. Com., 161 Va. 1049, 171 S. E. 691, it is held: "Where there is a charge of subornation of perjury the Commonwealth must establish the fact that perjury has been committed, by at least two witnesses, or by one witness and strong corroborating circumstances, and while the uncorroborated testimony of the perjurer is sufficient to establish the element of suborning, the jury should be instructed to scrutinize such evidence with care and caution as is done in cases involving the testimony of accomplices." 

And in State v. Miller, 24 W. Va. 807, it is further said: * * * "We doubt whether the rule that prevails in other states on this subject is the rule here. 

The rule that to convict of perjury, one witness and corroborating circumstances are required is obviously founded on the fact, as the defendant has made his statement, the falsity of which is in issue, under the sanctity of an oath, the law raises a legal presumption that it is true, and the defendant at common law not being permitted to testify, in his own behalf, this presumption of the truth of the statement and the good character of the defendant continues, until it is removed by evidence, and that the oath of the prosecuting witness is entitled to no more weight than that of the defendant made before the prosecution was instituted, and that therefore no man should under such circumstances be convicted of an infamous offense, and to authorize such conviction, the evidence of the prosecuting witness should be corroborated. But when the statute permits the defend-

§ 1383 

ant to be sworn before the jury in his own defense, as it does in our state in such case, and he avails himself of the right and is examined as a witness in his own behalf, the reason for the rule is gone, and the jury then is the sole judge of the weight to be given to his evidence, and the legal presumption of the truth of his statements previously made is removed, and the manner of the witness in giving his evidence may be sufficient corroboration of the evidence of the prosecuting witness. Like any other case under such circumstances, the jury would be the exclusive judge of the credit to be given to the witnesses, and if they find him guilty, this court could not on well settled principles disturb the verdict." "QUERY: What would be the power of this court over a verdict of a jury finding a person guilty of perjury, who was not sworn in his own behalf, and where there was no corroboration of the testimony of the prosecuting witness is not decided in this case."

Perjury may be committed under such a variety of circumstances as to make it impossible to set out a form of indictment applicable to every case, but the forms here given may be modified to suit any case likely to arise.

GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1386. Accused must have knowledge of the falsity of his testimony. 

1. The court instructs the jury that the falsity of the statement must be known to the witness when he testified, and he must testify to the same wilfully and corruptly, and a false statement is not

§ 916 

wilfully made unless the witness purposely made the same with knowledge of its falsity. 

Blashfield's Instructions, vol. 3, sec. 5676. 

2. The court instructs the jury that a false statement, purposely made, cannot be said to have been corruptly made, if made by or through surprise, mistake, inadvertence, or while the witness was in such a state of mind on account of physical or mental suffering that he believed in good faith that such facts were in fact true, although false. 

Blashfield's Instructions, vol. 3, sec. 5677. § 1387. Where no reasonable grounds exist for believing statements to be true.

The jury are instructed, that while false swearing, under an honest belief that the statements are true, is not perjury, still, the jury are to determine, from all the evidence in the case, whether such honest belief existed; and if the jury believe, from the evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the defendant swore falsely, as charged in the indictment, and that he had no reasonable grounds for believing his statements to be true, and did not honestly and in good faith believe them to be true, then he is guilty of perjury. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3257. § 1388. Testimony alleged in indictment must be proved. 

1. The jury are further instructed, that while it is incumbent upon the state, in order to warrant a conviction, to prove, as one of the material averments in the indictment, that the defendant did testify to one or more of the statements of testimony contained in the indictment, still, it is not necessary that they should be proved in the precise words alleged; it is sufficient if they are, substantially, proved in language and effect as therein stated. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3260. 

2. The state is not required to prove that the defendant testified before the grand jury in the precise words alleged in the indictment. Upon that point it is sufficient if the state proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant in testifying before the grand

§ 1389  

Same purple ade by tness suffe true he tilli he fak th jury made the statements in language, effect and meaning substantially as they are alleged in the indictment. 

Blashfield's Instructions, vol. 3, page 3597, No. 7. § 1389. Materiality of alleged false testimony must be shown. 

1. The jury are further instructed, that among the material averments in the indictment is the statement, that whether the said defendant had bought the horse therein referred to of A. B. and paid $100.00 for it in cash at the time, became a material question on said trial; and to warrant a conviction in this case, the fact of such materiality must be established to the satisfaction of the jury, beyond a reasonable doubt; and if, after a careful consideration of all the evidence, and in view of the principles of law given you in these instructions, you entertain any reasonable doubts as to whether the fact above stated did become material on said trial, you should find the defendant not guilty. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3262. 

2. The jury are instructed, as a matter of law, that to render testimony material in a case it is not necessary that it should bear directly upon the main issue in the case; it is sufficient if it is material to any question arising upon the trial, and such as, if it were true, might properly influence the justice or the jury before whom the case is being tried in any matter affecting the rights of the parties. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3263. 

3. That the true test of whether the alleged testimony of the defendant was material on said trial is this: Was it of such a character that, if true, it should properly influence the action of the justice or the jury on the trial in any matter affecting the rights of the parties to that suit; and if the jury find, from the evidence, that the alleged testimony could not properly influence the action of the justice, or jury, in any matter affecting the rights of the parties to the suit, then it is wholly immaterial whether it was true or false, and the jury should find the defendant not guilty. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3264.

§ 918 

§ 1390. When one witness is sufficient to establish perjury.

The court instructs the jury that as to each and all of the material averments in the indictments, except the allegation of the falsity of the testimony therein stated and set forth, they may be proved by the testimony of one witness alone; provided, the jury are satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt, of the truth thereof by the testimony of such witness; and as regards proving the falsity of such testimony, the court instructs the jury, that while that fact cannot be established by the testimony of one witness alone, it is not absolutely necessary that it be established by the testimony of two witnesses; it may be proved by the testimony of one witness. and other corroborating facts or circumstances corroborating such witness; provided the jury are satisfied, beyond a reasonable doubt, from the testimony of such witness, and such corroborating facts and circumstances, that such testimony was false in fact. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3259. § 1391. State must prove witness was sworn by competent authority. 

1. That to authorize a conviction in this case it must appear, among other things, that the defendant was sworn, as a witness, before giving his alleged testimony; and this must be proved, beyond a reasonable doubt; and if the jury entertain any reasonable doubt as to whether the defendant was sworn, in the usual manner before testifying, the jury should find the defendant not guilty. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3256. 

2. The jury are further instructed, that, while it is necessary for the prosecution, in order to warrant a conviction for perjury, to show that the person administering the oath was authorized, by law, to administer oaths, still, if it be shown, by the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, that the oath was administered by a person who was then an acting justice of the peace in and for the county where the oath was administered, this is sufficient evidence of his authority to administer the oath. 

Sackett's Instructions, vol. 2, sec. 3265.

§ 1393 RAPE ​Virgini 2 of § 1392. At common law.

At common law, rape is defined as the having of unlawful carnal knowledge by a man of a woman, forcibly and against her will. 

State v. Fudge, 96 W. Va. 110, 122 S. E. 519. 

King v. Com., 165 Va. 843, 183 S. E. 187. 

Mings v. Com., 85 Va. 638, 8 S. E. 474. 

Givins v. Com., 29 Gratt. 830. 

Bishop's Crim. Law (9th Ed.), p. 824. 

22 R. C. L. p. 1171. 

And in King v. Com., 165 Va. 843, 183 S. E. 189, it is said: "To constitute rape other than statutory rape, there must be unlawful, carnal knowledge by a man of a woman, forcibly and against her will. It is thus seen that there must appear three facts: (a) Carnal knowledge; (b) force; (c) against the will of the woman, before there can be rape. 

§ 1393. Force an essential element.

Except in statutory rape, where the female is under the age of consent (sixteen years in both Virginias), force is an essential element of the crime of rape both at common law and under the statutes of the Virginias. In Mings v. Com., supra it is said: "Rape is commonly defined to be the unlawful carnal knowledge of a woman by a man, forcibly and against her will. The crime, however, really consists in the ravishment of a woman without her consent; and the question, therefore, always is, was the woman willing or unwilling." 

And in Buzzard v. Com., 134 Va. 651, 114 S. E. 664, it is said: And "Force, actual or constructive, is essential to the crime of rape, and there is no force where the female is legally capable of giving her consent, and does so." 

And in Jordan v. Com., 169 Va. 898, 194 S. E. 719, it is held: "To constitute rape, act charged must have been committed by force and against victim's will or there must be some array or show of force or intention to use force, if necessary to overcome victim's will, but force, whether actual or constructive, must be sufficient to overcome resistance." "To constitute rape by force and violence, victim's op-

§ 

922 position must be evidenced by protest, which may be by words or acts, and her resistance, if she is of the age of consent, of sound mind and without physical disability, should be by acts reasonably appropriate to her strength and opportunities." 

See cases cited in opinion. 

§ 1394. West Virginia statute. 

In West Virginia, Code 61-2-15 (sec.

5930), rape is defined as follows: 

"If any male person carnally know a female person, not his wife, against her will by force, or if any male person over the age of sixteen years carnally know a female person of previous chaste character, not his wife, under that age, he shall be deemed guilty of a felony, and, upon conviction, shall be punished with death or with confinement in the penitentiary for life, in the discretion of the court, or if the jury add to its verdict a recommendation for mercy, with confinement in the penitentiary for not less than five nor more than twenty years: Provided, That this section shall not apply to any male person under sixteen years of age who carnally knows a female over twelve years of age with her free consent. Any female person over the age sixteen years who shall carnally know any male person, not her husband, under that age shall be guilty. of a misdemeanor, and upon conviction, shall be confined in the county jail not less than two nor more than six months."

The revision of this statute in the 1931 Code makes drastic changes in the law respecting statutory rape. Under the old law carnal knowledge of a female under the age of sixteen years was rape, regardless of the previous chaste character of the prosecutrix. 

But under the present law such act is no longer rape unless the female was "of previous chaste character." Moreover, it will be observed that under the act it is no offense for a boy under the age of sixteen years to have intercourse with a girl over twelve years of age with her free consent. 

§ 1395. Virginia statute. 

In Virginia Code sec. 4414, defines rape as follows: 

"If any person carnally know a female of sixteen years of age or more against her will, by force, or carnally know

But if such female child be between the ages of fourteen and sixteen years and not an inmate or pupil of such institutions hereinbefore mentioned, and consents to the carnal knowledge, the punishment shall be confinement in the penitentiary not less than one nor more than twenty years.'

§ 1396. Indictment, may follow the statutory language, or the common-law form.

The courts of both Virginias hold that the statutes on the subject are merely declaratory of the common law, and an indictment for the crime of rape may follow the language of the statutes, or be in the common-law form. 

31 Corpus Juris, 712. 

Bishop's Statutory Crimes (3rd Ed.), p. 181. 

Bishop's New Crim. Proc. (2nd Ed.), secs. 97, 549. 

State v. Fudge, 96 W. Va. 109, 122 S. E. 519. 

State v. Schilansky, 105 W. Va. 549, 143 S. E. 307.

And it is likewise held in both Virginias that where an indictment for rape is in the usual form, and in the words of the statute defining the offense, or is, in substance, sufficiently specific to put the prisoner fairly upon trial for the offense therein charged, it will generally be held sufficient. 

Smith v. Com., 85 Va. 924, 9 S. E. 148. 

Mitchell v. Com., 89 Va. 826, 17 S. E. 480. 

State v. Michael, 37 W. Va. 565, 16 S. E. 803. § 1397. Same, for attempted rape.

With reference to prosecutrix, the West Virginia statute uses the words "not his wife," which are not required at common law. 

In State v. Fudge, 96 W. Va. 109, 122 S. E. 519, it is held that the indictment should have been quashed for failure to aver that the prosecutrix, Myrtle Fudge, was not the wife of the accusedher name and the name of the accused being the same. However, it is further held that this "averment need not be made in specific terms, if from the language of the indictment it may reasonably be inferred." - " 

State v. Digman, W. Va. 5 S. E. 2d 113. 

And in State v. Schilansky, 105 W. Va. 549, 143 S. E. 307, it is further held: 

"The statute does not change the (common-law) nature of the offense. And where it may reasonably be inferred that no marital relation exists, as by the names of the parties, no injustice is done the accused, for he may show such relationship by evidence." 

However, West Virginia's new Code, 62-9-7 (sec. 6269) prescribes a form of indictment for rape which includes the allegation that the prosecutrix is not the wife of the accused. Hence it is possible that the words "not his wife" are now essential. At least it is the safer practice to include them.

But this prescribed form of an indictment is fatally defective for the reason that it fails to charge that the crime was accomplished "by force," an essential element of the offense both at common law and by Code 61-2-15 (sec. 5930). Hence after the words "against her will," in the statutory form, the pleader must insert the words "and by force." This view is sustained in Scott v. 

Harshbarger, 116 W. Va. 300, 180 S. E. 187, which involved the

Same, use of the word "ravish" in.

The use of the word "ravish" in an indictment is unnecessary where the female is under the age of consent. 

Lufty v. Com., 126 Va. 710, 100 S. E. 829.

But the use of the word is essential where the female is over the age of consent. In Christian v. Com., 23 Gratt. 954, it is held: “In an indictment for an attempt to commit rape, it is necessary to describe the crime of rape in the terms in which that offense could only be described, and without the insertion of the word "ravish" it will be fatally defective even after verdict." See also, State v. Michael, 37 W. Va. 565, 16 S. E. 803. § 1402. Same, where indictment is in two counts. 

It is held in Virginia that an indictment for statutory rape may be in two counts, one charging rape upon a female under sixteen years without force, the other by force. Nor will the prosecution be required to elect on which count it will ask for conviction. This

It is thus seen that there must appear three facts: (a) Carnal knowledge; (b) force; (c) against the will of the woman, before there can be

§ 1404. Carnal knowledge defined. 

In King v. Com., supra, carnal knowledge is thus defined: "Carnal knowledge means sexual intercourse and is complete upon proof of penetration of the female organ by the male organ, however slight." § 1405. Consent of female, question for jury. 

In Mings v. Com., 85 Va. 638, 8 S. E. 474, it is held: "Hence, it is for the jury to determine upon all the facts and circumstances of each particular case whether the woman, upon whom the crime of rape is charged to have been committed, consented or not." be 1406. Penetration necessary to constitute rape. 

Penetration is an essential element of the crime of rape. It must proven the same as any other fact in the case. 

Bailey v. Com., 82 Va. 107. 

State v. Brady, 104 W. Va. 523, 140 S. E. 546. 

But in King v. Com., 165 Va. 843, 183 S. E. 187, it is held: "Carnal knowledge means sexual intercourse and is complete upon proof of penetration of female organ by male organ, however slight."

§ 928 

And in proving penetration the words of the prosecutrix must be given their ordinary meaning. In King v. Com., 165 Va. 843, 183 S. In both cases it was held that there was sufficient proof of penetration. § 1407. Unnecessary to show emission.

In Com. v. Thomas, 1 Va. Cas. 307, it was held that penetration without emission, was sufficient to constitute the crime of rape. § 1408. May be committed upon unchaste woman. 

It is well recognized that the crime of rape may be committed as well upon an unchaste woman, or a common prostitute, as upon any other woman. But want of chastity may be shown as rendering it more probable that she consented. 

Christian v. Com., 23 Gratt. 954.

State v. Martin, 102 W. Va. 107, 134 S. E. 599. § 1409. Moral character of prosecutrix may be attacked by defense.

It is both the general law and the rule in the Virginias that evidence of the moral character of the prosecutrix in a trial for rape is admissible on the question of her probable consent, as it is more likely that a prostitute would consent to the act than a previously chaste woman. But such evidence is not admissible in a simple attack upon her credibility as a witness.

And in State v. Kittle, 85 W. Va. 116, 101 S. E. 70, the general rule in this regard is thus stated: "In a prosecution for rape where the defendant admits having illicit connection with the prosecutrix, but swears she consented, evidence of her previous character for chastity is material upon the principal issue. "Where in a trial for rape the defendant admits having sexual intercourse with the prosecutrix but swears she consented to the act, and there is evidence tending to prove that, prior to the commission of the alleged crime, she was a prostitute receiving the embraces of other men promiscuously, and she is asked on cross-examination whether she did not, on prior occasions designated and within a month or two before the alleged offense, have illicit connection with certain other men and she denies it, evidence of the facts denied are admissible as tending to prove her consent."

While in the opinion the court further said: "We understand very readily how it would be a collateral matter if the question is asked only for the purpose of laying a foundation for impeaching the prosecutrix for truth and veracity. The question is allowable on cross-examination of the prosecutrix because her previous character for chastity or unchastity is a material fact bearing on the material issue, whether or not she consented.”

In Fry v. Com., 163 Va. 1085, 177 S. And in Vance v. Com., supra., the Virginia court further said: "This court is not required to believe the statement of the prosecutrix. It is very improbable that any offense was committed against her. We are not required to believe that which is contrary to human experience and which we know to be incredible. We are not compelled to accept as true what in the nature of things could not have occurred in the manner and under the circumstances narrated."

§ 1421. Where defense is impotency. 

In State v. Friend, 100 W. Va. 180, 130 S. E. 102, it is held : "Where evidence has gone to the jury, in a trial for rape, sufficient to show that the accused at the time of the alleged offense was afflicted with a malady rendering him impotent and not able to copulate, it is error to refuse an instruction telling the jury they may take into consideration the probability of his lack of desire for sexual intercourse, and give it such weight as, under the evidence, they may think proper. "A physician who has qualified as an expert and who has formed an opinion from a physical examination of the genital organs of a male then afflicted with orchitis, regarding his ability or inability to copulate, may express that opinion in his evidence to the jury. "The evidence of the wife of such male so afflicted, to the effect that he has not and could not copulate with her although they slept together, for more than a year, is competent on the issue of his guilt of statutory rape alleged to have been committed within that time; and to refuse to admit her testimony in that regard is reversible error." § 1422. Depositions in rape cases.

The Virginia statute, Code sec. 4415, provides that in a trial for rape the deposition of the assaulted female may be taken and read as evidence in behalf of the Commonwealth at the trial of the accused.

However, West Virginia has no such statute, and the prosecutrix is required to be present and testify as a witness, or her evidence is lost to the state. § 1423. Force necessary in attempt.

To sustain a charge of an attempt to commit rape there must be evidence of force, or of an intention on the part of the accused to use force in the perpetration of the offense if it should become necessary to overcome the will of his victim.

§ 1424. Elements of attempt. 

In order to constitute the crime of attempt to commit rape two elements are essential: 

1. The intent to commit the crime, (and this may be inferred from the conduct, declarations, threats and circumstances). 

2. The doing of some act by the accused toward the consummation of the crime. And that act must reach far enough toward the accomplishment of the desired result to amount to the commencement of the consummation. 

Hicks v. Com., 86 Va. 223, 9 S. E. 1024. 

Glover v. Com., 86 Va. 382, 10 S. E. 420. 

Cunningham v. Com., 88 Va. 37, 13 S. E. 309: 

Christian v. Com., 23 Gratt. 954. 

Com. v. Clark, 6 Gratt. 675. 

Com. v. Fields, 4 Leigh 648. 

Lufty v. Com., 126 Va. 707, 100 S. E. 829. 

Hart v. Com., 131 Va. 726, 109 S. E. 582. 

In State v. Coram, 116 W. Va. 492, 182 S. E. 83, it was said: “Assault with intent to rape is a specific crime consisting of an intent to have the male sexual organ penetrate that of the female, at least to some extent, and of an overt act in pursuance of that intent which fails; intent to produce emissio seminis and actual production thereof through external contact with the female, without intent to penetrate, does not constitute such crime." 

And in the same case it is further held: "Intent to rape cannot depend on mere speculation, but must be clearly shown." 

§ 1425. Instructions on attempt. 

In a prosecution for an attempt to commit rape it is reversible error to fail to instruct the jury that accused may, should the evidence warrant, be found guilty of assault, which is a lesser offense. 

In Richards v. Com., 161 Va. 1037, 171 S. E. 525, it is held:

§ 

936 "In a prosecution for attempted rape, failure to instruct jury that accused might be found guilty of lesser offense than attempted rape held reversible error."

NOTE: The same rule will likewise apply in a prosecution for rape. § 1426. Prosecutrix may testify as to her age. 

In State v. Spielman, 105 W. Va. 370, 142 S. E. 523, it is held that in a trial for statutory rape, the uncontradicted evidence of the prosecutrix as to her age is admissible for what it is worth. 

See cases cited in opinion. 

But in Dotson v. Com., 170 Va. 630, 196 S. E. 623, it is held that birth records of another state or of the U. S. Bureau of Census are inadmissible unless properly authenticated. § 1427. That infant misrepresents her age is no defense.

In Lawrence v. Com., supra, it is held that the fact that the female misrepresents her age and consents to the act is no defense, even though accused has reasonable cause to believe that she is over the statutory age. 

Rainey v. Com., supra. § 1428. Verdict for attempt.

In Cates v. Com., 111 Va. 839, 69 S. E. 520, it is held that under the Virginia statute on attempts a person indicted for rape may be found not guilty of rape, but guilty of an attempt to commit rape; and that a verdict of guilty of an attempt to commit rape is an acquittal of the offense of rape, and if such verdict be set aside, the accused cannot on a second trial, be convicted of rape, as this is a higher offense.

NOTE: The same is true in West Virginia under the statute on attempts. 

And in State v. Collins, 108 W. Va. 98, 150 S. E. 369, it is further held: "Where a defendant in an indictment is charged with the commission of rape, he may be convicted of an attempt

§ 1430 RAPE to commit the offense, such attempt being included in, or a part of, the offense charged, by virtue of Code 62-3-18 (sec. 6207). "On a conviction for an attempt to commit rape, this Court will not set aside the verdict on the ground that there was no evidence to support it, if there was sufficient evidence to warrant a conviction of rape." Citing, State v. Prater, 52 W. Va. 132, 43 S. E. 230. 

§ 1429. Force unnecessary in statutory rape. 

In both Virginias the age of consent is sixteen years. Under that a female cannot legally consent to the act of sexual intercourse, and constructive force is present, even though she does in fact consent. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4414. 

West Virginia Code, 61-2-15 (sec. 5930). 

Rainey v. Com., 169 Va. 892, 193 S. E. 501. 

Buzzard v. Com., 134 Va. 641, 114 S. E. 664.

Givens v. Com., 29 Gratt. 830. 

Lawrence v. Com., 30 Gratt. 845. 

State v. Driver, 88 Va. 479, 107 S. E. 189. 

And in Addington v. Com., 161 Va. 975, 170 S. E. 566, it is held: "To sustain a conviction of rape where the victim is under the age of sixteen years, it is not necessary to establish that it was accomplished by actual force. It is rape to carnally know a female child under the age of sixteen whether it be with or without actual force, because under that age she cannot legally consent and constructive force is present.' 

Rainey v. Com., 169 Va. 892, 193 S. E. 501. 

§ 1430. Issues involved in statutory rape, rule in Virginia. 

Prior to 1931 the statutes of the Virginias on this subject were almost identical. During that time the West Virginia Court decided State v. Spielman, 105 W. Va. 370, 142 S. E. 523, wherein it is said that in such a prosecution two issues are involved: First, was there sufficient penetration to constitute the offense; and sec-

§ 938 

ond, was the female under the age of consent, sixteen years. 

These are still the only issues in Virginia. But in Dotson v. 

Com., 170 Va. 630, 196 S. E. 623, it is held that prior acts of unchaste conduct may be shown in mitigation of punishment. It is also held in Dotson's Case, supra, that "In a prosecution for rape of a girl under age of consent, evidence that prosecutrix had made statements that another man was responsible for her pregnancy, but she had decided to 'law' defendant for. ulterior motives, was admissible as corroborating defendant's testimony denying relations with prosecutrix and as showing improper motives for prosecution, where testimony of prosecutrix was the only direct evidence of defendant's guilt." 

See authorities cited in opinion. § 1431. Same, rule in West Virginia.

Spielman's Case, supra, was decided in 1928, prior to the adoption of the 1931 Code, which added a third important issue in West Virginia, namely, "the previous chaste character" of the prosecutrix. If she was not of such character at the time of the offense, the accused is not guilty under the statute. 

Must the previous chaste character of the prosecutrix be alleged in the indictment and proved at the trial? The appellate court has not passed on this question. But such character goes to the very gist of the offense, and therefore it must be alleged in the indictment and established by proof. 

In State v. Tenney, 117 W. Va. 342, 185 S. E. 469, it is said: "Where the exception or proviso does not appear in the enacting clause creating the offense, the general rule is that the indictment need not negative such exception or proviso." 

See authorities cited in opinion. 

Also in State v. Fudge, 96 W. Va. 111, 122 S. E. 519, it is said: "It is generally held, under a statute limiting in its enacting clause the offense of rape to a female who is not the wife of the perpetrator, as in this case, that an indictment therefor should negative the marriage relation between the parties. 

See authorities cited in opinion. 

---

§ 1431 

RAPE 

And in State v. Tapit, 52 W. Va. 473, 44 S. E. 232, it is held that the true rule is as follows: "The true rule is that only those exceptions need be negatived in an indictment under a statute which are a part of the description of the offense. Where the description of the offense is in general terms, and the exceptions are such as permit certain persons, under certain circumstances, to do the thing forbidden, such exceptions need not be set out negatively, but the defendant on the trial may excuse himself from the charge by showing himself within the provisions of one or more of the exceptions."

But these rules cannot apply to statutory rape under the present statute which restricts the offense to a female of "previous chaste character," because the exception or proviso in the statute was inserted by the revisers of the Code, and there is no "enacting clause" to the statute.

Therefore, it seems reasonable that the indictment must allege the "previous chaste character" of the prosecutrix, and that the same must be established by proof at the trial. The latter may be done by simply asking the prosecutrix whether she had had sexual intercourse with any man prior to her relations with the accused. 

The defendant may attack the "previous chaste character" of the prosecutrix (1) by showing her general reputation for unchastity in the community where she resides, and (2) by showing one or more specific acts of unchastity or sexual intercourse with other men prior to his alleged relations with her. 

Underhill's Crim. Ev. (4th Ed.) sec. 676, p. 1276, and cases cited.

Again, Code 62-29 (sec. 6173), provides: "All allegations unnecessary to be proved may be omitted in any indictment or other accusation." The converse of this statute is equally true, and all allegations necessary to be proved may not be omitted from any indictment. It being necessary to prove that the prosecutrix was of "previous chaste character" makes it necessary for the indictment to so allege. 

And in Ruling Case Law, vol. 22, pp. 1190-1, under the title

Rape, this provision of the statute is thus interpreted: "The term of previous chaste character' in a statute means the same in law as in morals. It describes a condi-

§ 

940 tion of sexual purity, and means a female who has never submitted herself to the sexual embrace of man, and who still retains her virginal chastity. A woman to be unchaste, within the statutory meaning, need not be of notorious lewd and lascivious habits. The object of these being to protect virtuous maidens it is held that it is not a crime thereunder to have intercourse with a woman within the prescribed age who has theretofore had sexual intercourse, and that the fact that she was first deprived of her virginity by the prisoner does not strengthen the state's case; but such prior unchastity is a complete defense, provided such prior act was not punishable in the jurisdiction and at the time the act charged was committed; though one who performs several acts of intercourse with a previously chaste child, within a few weeks, in the same county, cannot defeat a prosecution for statutory rape in which the state relies on one of the later acts, on the theory that at the time of its commission the child was not chaste, and therefore the offense did not come within the statutory definition of the crime, which makes the previous chaste character of the child an element of the offense." Citing, State v. Kelly, 245 Mo. 489, 150 S. W. 1057, 43 L. R. A. (NS) 476 and note. 

Bailey v. State, 57 Neb. 706, 78 N. W. 284, 73 A. S. R. 540. 

State v. Dacke, 59 Wash. 238, 109 Pac. 1050, 30 L. R. 

A. (NS) 173. 

State v. Sargent, 62 Wash. 692, 114 Pac. 868, 35 L. R. 

A. (NS) 173.

NOTE: Attention is called to State v. Ray, to be heard by West 

Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals, January 16, 1940, upon a demurrer to an indictment for statutory rape which failed to allege that prosecutrix was of "previous chaste character." § 1432. Same, attempt to commit. 

In Rainey v. Com., 169 Va. 892, 193 S. E. 501, it is held: "In a prosecution for attempt to commit statutory rape, evidence showing that accused committed overt acts amounting to more than mere preparation to commit crime, sufficiently showed an attempt."

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1442. Rape defined, etc. 

1. The Court instructs the jury that rape is having sexual intercourse with a woman against her will by force. Before the jury will be warranted in convicting the accused on a charge of rape, they must be satisfied from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the act of sexual intercourse was accomplished by force and against the will of the prosecutrix, and, considering under the evidence, the time, the place, the relative physical strength and endurance of the prosecutrix and the accused, the whole situation as it confronted her, and all the circumstances in the case, it must ap-

§ 946 

pear from the evidence, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the prosecutrix resisted her assailant by every means at her command until she was overcome by his superior strength. And, if the jury entertain a reasonable doubt as to whether she did so resist, then such doubt is decisive and the jury should find that the crime has not been committed. 

, State v. Wilson, 74 W. Va. 772, 83 S. E. 44. 

Given by the court. 

2. The court instructs the jury that rape is the carnal knowledge of a female, forcibly and against her will; and where personal violence and force is used to overcome her will and the defendant has sexual intercourse with her, then the law considers such carnal knowledge as having been forcibly had and against the will of the female; if at the time the man had carnal knowledge of the female her mind was overpowered by fear induced by the man, and therefore she made no resistance it is rape; and if the female was incapable of resistance through fear, or if resistance was entirely useless, there might be rape even if no resistance was in fact made. 

Taken from the record in both, State v. Kittle, 85 W. Va. 116, 101 S. E. 76. 

Referred to in opinion as instruction No. 4. 

State v. Golden, 90 W. Va. 496, 111 S. E. 320. 

3. The court instructs the jury that rape is the having of sexual intercourse with a woman against her will by force. Before the jury will be warranted in convicting the accused on a charge of rape, they must be satisfied from the evidence beyond all reasonable doubt that the act of sexual intercourse was accomplished by force and against the will of the prosecutrix and, considering under the evidence the time, the place, the relative physical strength, and endurance of the prosecutrix and the accused, the whole situation as it confronted her, and all the circumstances of the case, it must appear from the evidence beyond all reasonable doubt that the prosecutrix resisted her assailant by every means at her command until she was overcome by his superior strength. you

And, if believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant in company with Olaf Martin went to the home of Nina Paugh, the prosecutrix, on or about the

State v. Wamsley, 109 W. Va. 576, 156 S. E. 75.

§ 1443. Elements of statutory rape. 

1. The court instructs the jury that if it believes from the evidence (in this case) beyond a reasonable doubt that John Barker, the accused, is a male person over the age of sixteen years, and it further believes from the evidence in this case, beyond a reasonable doubt, that he had sexual intercourse with Mary A. Galliher, and they further believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that said Mary A. , State v. Barker, 92 W. Va. 583, 115 S. E. 421.
