1444. Penetration necessary.

The court instructs the jury that in order to constitute the crime of rape there must be some degree of penetration of the female organ by the male genital organ, but any penetration, however

§ 1446 

RAPE 

slight, of the labia of the pedenum of the female is all that is necessary. 

State v. Brady, 104 W. Va. 533, 140 S. E. 546. § 1445. Force must be used.

The court instructs the jury that in order to constitute the offense of rape, force must be used. It is a necessary ingredient of the crime; and that force must be such as may reasonably be supposed adequate to overcome the physical resistance of the woman upon whom the rape is charged to have been committed, taking into consideration the relative strength of the parties and other circumstances of the case, such as making outcries and giving alarm. 

Mings v. Com., 85 Va. 639-640, 8 S. E. 474. 

State v. Hull, 45 W. Va. 767, 32 S..E. 240. § 1446. Woman required to resist to utmost. 

1. The court instructs the jury that the law requires a woman assaulted by a man with intent to commit rape, to resist him to the utmost, and (if) she fails to resist to the utmost and sexual intercourse is had with her because of her failure to resist to the utmost, then the jury cannot convict of rape. But, in considering whether a woman so assaulted resisted to the utmost, the jury may take into consideration, as shown by evidence in the case, the time, the place, the relative physical strength and endurance of the woman and her assailant, the whole situation as it confronted her, and all the circumstances in the case; and so considered, the jury must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the woman did, in good faith, resist her assailant to the utmost of her ability, under all the circumstances, and that she did, in fact and in good faith, withhold her consent to the act of sexual intercourse. 

And the court further instructs the jury that a mere statement of the prosecutrix that she did resist to the utmost is not sufficient to show such resistance, but the jury must judge whether or not she did make such resistance, from the details of facts of such resistance as shown by the evidence. 

, State v. Wilson, supra. 

Given by the court.

§ 950 

2. The court instructs the jury that to constitute the crime of rape, if it be upon a woman capable, in the eyes of the law, of consenting to sexual intercourse, the act must be committed by force and against her will, and that the commission of said act must be resisted by the woman, and that the force and resistance by the woman must be more than mere verbal expressions, but there must be the exercise of every means or faculty within the woman's power to resist penetration, under the circumstances, and that the persistence in such resistance must continue until such offense is consummated, and if the jury believe, from the evidence in this case, that the prosecutrix, even though they may believe that Andrew Brady was the person who actually made the alleged assault, did not make such resistance as herein described and explained, then they cannot find the defendant guilty. 

State v. Brady, 104 W. Va. 534, 140 S. E. 546. § 1447. Determining whether force was used.

§ 1455. The issue in the case. 

The court instructs the jury that the issue in this case is not whether the entire statement made by the accused on the stand is true, or otherwise, but the sole issue is whether or not the accused raped Miss Turner by force and against her will. Therefore, upon their consideration of the case, even should the jury disbelieve any part or all of the evidence of the accused, still, if upon the whole evidence in the case they entertain a reasonable doubt of his guilt on the charge of rape, it is their duty to acquit him of such charge. 

, State v. Wilson, 74 W. Va. 772, 83 S. E. 44. § 1456. Jury must believe intercourse was had by force.

That before there can be any conviction in this case under the indictment, the jury must find beyond a reasonable doubt, such as defined in Instruction No. 2, all of the essential elements of rape, that is to say, that the defendant had sexual intercourse with Miss Turner by force and against her will and consent. 

Every one of these elements are essential and each one of them must be established by the state beyond a reasonable doubt, the court telling the jury that although they may believe from the evidence that the defendant had sexual intercourse with Miss Turner, without force or against her will and consent, he is not guilty of the crime charged in the indictment and the jury should acquit him of the charge contained in the indictment.

§ 1469. Statutes compared. 

Prior to the adoption of the 1931 Code, the West Virginia statute on receiving stolen goods was the same as the Virginia law. 

The latter, Code sec. 4448, is as follows: "If any person buy or receive from another person, or

§ 1469 

aid in concealing any stolen goods or other thing, knowing the same to have been stolen, he shall be deemed guilty of larceny thereof, and may be proceeded against, although the principal offender be not convicted."

The new West Virginia statute, Code 61-3-18 (sec. 5959), the changes being in italics, is as follows: "If any person buy or receive from another person, or aid in concealing, or transfer to a person other than the owner thereof, any stolen goods or other thing of value, which he knows or has reason to believe has been stolen, he shall be deemed guilty of the larceny thereof, and may be prosecuted although the principal offender be not convicted."

The italicized words in the above quoted West Virginia statute show the present difference between it and the Virginia law. 

Under the latter (which is West Virginia's old law) there is but one way by which the offense may be committed, namely, the receiving or aiding in concealing stolen goods knowing them to have been stolen. While under the present West Virginia statute (1931 Code) there are two ways by which the offense may be committed: (1) By receiving stolen goods, etc., knowing them to have been stolen; and (2) by receiving stolen goods, etc., with reason to believe that they had been stolen. 

State v. Lewis, 117 W. Va. 670, 187 S. E. 316.

The case of State v. Lewis, supra, was reversed because the indictment was drawn under the old statute, and charged defendant with receiving the goods "well knowing" them "to have been unlawfully and feloniously stolen," while the trial court instructed the jury to convict defendant if they believed beyond a reasonable doubt that the goods were stolen and that they came into his possession under such circumstances as that he knew or had cause to believe they were stolen. “In other words, the indictment charged but one offense, and the instruction of the court included both; and accused could not be convicted on a statement of facts not charged in the indictment."

Attention is called to the dissenting and concurring opinions filed in this case. 

State v. Lewis, 117 W. Va. 670, 187 S. E. 728. 

State v. Lewis, 117 W. Va. 728, 188 S. E. 473.

§ 966 

 § 1470. A statutory offense. 

At common law, the receiving of stolen goods, knowing them to have been stolen, was a distinct substantive offense. But under the statutes of both Virginias it is a specific statutory crime, and the statutes are construed strictly. The crime consists of one person receiving "from another person" the stolen goods (in bad faith), knowing (or, in West Virginia, having reason to believe) them to be stolen. Thus two persons are contemplated by the statutes: (1) The original thief, or a successor in criminal possession of the goods; and (2) a person to whom that possession is transferred. And where the state fails to show any concert of action between the defendant and the thief who stole the goods, or a former wrongful possessor thereof, nor proof from which such concert of action or connection can legitimately be inferred, no conviction can be had under the statutes. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4448. 

West Virginia Code, 61-3-18 (sec. 5959). 

Wharton's Crim. Law (12th Ed.), sec. 1229. 

State v. Smith, 98 W. Va. 188, 126 S. E. 703. 

State v. Fowler, 117 W. Va. 761, 188 S. E. 137. 

State v. Lewis, 117 W. Va. 670, 187 S. E. 316. 

State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 104. 

Thus, as said in Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 475, 124 S. E. 237, the crime of receiving stolen goods, knowing them to have been stolen, is deemed larceny merely by reason of the statutes making it so. 

Dowdy v. Com., 9 Gratt. 727. 

Price v. Com., 21 Gratt. 846. 

Hey v. Com., 32 Gratt. 946. 

State v. Hill, 52 W. Va. 302, 43 S. E. 160. 

State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 131, 99 S. E. 248. § 1471. Necessary elements of the offense, rule in Virginia.

To warrant a conviction for receiving stolen goods in Virginia, the Commonwealth must establish the following elements of the offense: 

1. The proper venue of the crime.

§ 1472 

1. 

2. That the goods had been stolen from some person other than the defendant. 

3. That the accused bought or received them from another person, or aided in concealing them after they were stolen. 

4. That at the time he so bought, received, or aided in concealing them, he knew they had been stolen. 5. 6. 

That he so bought, received, or aided in concealing them, malo animo, i. e., with dishonest intent. 

That the goods he so bought, received, or aided in concealing were the identical goods, or some part thereof, which are alleged to have been stolen from the owner. 

Hey v. Com., 32 Gratt. 947. 

Patterson v. Com., 165 Va. 736, 181 S. E. 282.

The elements of the offense as set out in State v. Lewis, 69 W. 

Va. 479, 72 S. E. 478, are here modified to conform to West Virginia's new statute: 

1. The proper venue of the crime. i. e., that the offense occurred in the county alleged in the indictment. 

2. That the goods described in the indictment and evidence had been previously stolen by some person other than the defendant. 

3. That the accused bought, or received the goods from another person, or aided in concealing them, or transferred the same to some person other than the owner thereof. 

4. That at the time he so bought, or received the goods, or aided in concealing them, or transferred them to some person other than the owner thereof, he (a) knew, or (b) had reason to believe they had been stolen. 

5. That he so bought, or received such goods, or aided in concealing them, or transferred them to such other person, with dishonest intent. 

6. That the goods he so bought, or received, or aided in concealing, or transferred were the identical goods, or some part thereof, which are alleged in the indictment to have been stolen from the owner thereof.

§ 1473. Presumption arising from the possession of stolen goods, rule in Virginia. 

In Porterfield v. Com., 91 Va. 801, 22 S. E. 352, it is held: "The exclusive possession of goods shortly after they have been stolen raises a presumption of fact that the possessor is the thief, unless, when called on for the purpose he can account for such possession consistently with his innocence." Affirming the holding in, Price v. Com., 21 Gratt. 846. 

But, in Taliaferro v. Com., 77 Va. 411, the Virginia court said: * * * "It has never been decided in this state that such possession is even prima facie evidence of guilt in cases of burglary and housebreaking. 

And that, even in cases of simple larceny, in order to raise the presumption of guilt from the possession of the stolen goods, it is necessary that they be found in the exclusive possession and subject to the exclusive control of the accused." 

West v. Com., 125 Va. 747, 99 S. E. 654. 

Stallard v. Com., 130 Va. 769, 107 S. E. 722. 

And in Walters v. Com., 159 Va. 907, 165 S. E. 495, it is said that it is well settled in Virginia that the possession of stolen goods is, of itself, not even prima facie evidence of housebreaking or burglary. Citing, Tyler v. Com., 120 Va. 870, 91 S. E. 172.

§ 1474 § 1474. Same, rule in West Virginia.

The rule stated in Price v. Com., 21 Gratt. 846, has never been adopted in West Virginia. In State v. Littleton, 77 W. Va. 807, 88 S. E. 460, it is held: "But this court has in express terms disapproved the Price Case. * * * It is now well settled in this state that the possession of stolen goods is not of itself prima facie evidence that the person in possession is the thief, but finding such goods recently after the offense is committed, in the exclusive possession and control of the accused, is a circumstance which may be submitted to the jury with other evidence. 

State v. Ringer, 84 W. Va. 546, 100 S. E. 416. 

State v. Mullet, 94 W. Va. 680, 120 S. E. 77. 

State v. Powers, 91 W. Va. 737, 113 S. E. 918. 

State v. Heaton, 23 W. Va. 773. 

State v. Livingston, 110 W. Va. 24, 156 S. E. 842. 

And in State v. Littleton, 108 W. Va. 494, 151 S. E. 713, syl. 

4, the first Littleton Case is approved as follows: 

"The possession of stolen goods is not of itself even prima facie evidence that the person in whose possession the stolen goods are found, is the thief, or that he is guilty of breaking and entering the house from which the goods were stolen; but the exclusive possession and control of property recently stolen, are circumstances tending to show that the person found in possession is the thief, and the jury may consider them in connection with all other circumstances and facts in proof." Citing, State v. Heaton, 23 W. Va. 773. 

State v. Reece, 27 W. Va. 375. 

State v. Ringer, supra. 

State v. Powers, supra. 

State v. Mullett, supra. 

See also, State v. Livingston, 110 W. Va. 24, 156 S. F. 842. 

However, in State v. Reece, supra, it is held: "The possession of stolen goods is a circumstance tending to show that the person found in the possession is the thief, and the jury may consider it in connection with all the other attending circumstances and facts in proof, but of itself it is not prima facie evidence of guilt."

§ 

970 

Also in State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 135-6, 99 S. E. 248, it is further held that such possession "is at least proper to be considered by the jury in connection with other evidence and circumstances appearing on the trial, among them conduct and declarations of the defendant which are inconsistent with his claim of innocence." 

§ 1475. Constructive possession. 

In Longman v. Com., 167 Va. 461, 188 S. E. 145, it is said: "While reception of stolen goods by the accused must be substantially proven, actual physical handling by him is not necessary. It is well settled that constructive possession is sufficient." Citing, 53 C. J., p. 505. 

Wharton's Crim. Law (12th Ed.), p, 1553, sec. 1238. 

And in the still later case of Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 488, 124 S. E. 237, it is also said: "When goods are shown to have been stolen, recent possession of them is evidence against the possessor, tending to show a guilty receiving by him." § 1476. Knowledge that goods were stolen is essential. 

In Judge Hatcher's dissenting opinion in State v. Lewis, 117 

W. Va. 670, 187 S. E. 728, are bought together the numerous authorities supporting the following statement of the general law with respect to guilty knowledge: "In all cases, knowledge at the time the goods are received that they have been stolen is absolutely essential; but knowledge may be inferred from the circumstances, and is sufficiently shown if the circumstances proven are such as must have made the recipient believe they were stolen. * * * It is not necessary for the state to prove that the defendant had personal knowledge of the larceny in the sense that he was present as a witness thereof. It was sufficient if the facts and circumstances known to him were sufficient to satisfy him or cause him to believe the goods were stolen. In such cases belief is tantamount to knowledge within the meaning of the statute and such is the uniform holding of the courts.” 

See cases cited in dissenting opinion. Also

ゴル ​§ 1476 971 

State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 133, 99 S. E. 248. 

State v. Hill, 52 W. Va. 302, 43 S. E. 160. 

State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 104. 

State v. Mounts, 120 W. Va. 661, 200 S. E. 53. 

And in Longman v. Com., 167 Va. 461, 188 S. E. 144, it is held: The guilty knowledge essential to a conviction for receiving stolen goods may be shown by circumstances, and evidence that accused had purchased similar goods from the alleged thief on other occasions is admissible for two purposes: (1) To show a course of dealing between the thief and the accused; and (2) to show accused's criminal intent. Citing, 17 R. C. L., p. 85, sec. 92. 

And in State v. Manstoff, 118 W. Va. 214, 189 S. E. 700, it is further said: "The possession of stolen property, alone, is not sufficient to convict the accused of knowledge of the theft; but such possession may, with all other evidence and circumstances in the case, be considered by the jury." Citing, State v. Lewis, 117 W. Va. 670, 187 S. E. 315. 

State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 129, 99 S. E. 248. 

53 C. J., 536. 

Further, in State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 106, the West Virginia Court laid down the rule that where the person charged with receiving or secreting stolen goods is operating a legitimate business (a pawn shop in this case), it must be brought home to him that the seller of goods was the thief or that the property had been stolen.

Also in State v. Goldstrohm, supra, it is held: "Upon the trial of an indictment for buying or receiving stolen property, knowing it to have been stolen, such knowledge is an essential element of the offense, and, as bearing upon that question, evidence of the conduct and statements of defendant in reference to the stolen property in his possession and explanatory of the reason and character of such possession, if made while such possession continues, and especially if offered at a time when he is first called upon by the circumstances of the case to make such explanation, is admissible both for and against him." 

See numerous authorities cited in opinion.

§ 972 

And in State v. Mounts, 120 W. Va. 661, 200 S. E. 55, it is said: "The element of knowledge, or reason to believe, the property bought or received was stolen cannot rest on mere suspicion. The evidence must show beyond a reasonable doubt that accused, when he received the goods, either knew, or had reason to believe, the goods had been stolen." Citing, 17 R. C. L., 85, sec. 92. 

53 Corpus Juris, p. 535. 

State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 104.

State v. Goldstrohm, supra. 

Also in State v. Baker, 84 W. Va. 151, 99 S. E. 252, it is further said: "Acts and declarations by accused on receipt of stolen goods, or on his arrest, while the goods are still in his possession, are parts of the res gestae, and evidence of them is admissible whether it be for or against him." § 1477. Guilty knowledge may be shown by circumstantial evidence.

In State v. Mounts, 120 W. Va. 661, 200 S. E. 55, it is held that the necessary element of guilty knowledge "may be established by circumstantial, as well as by direct, evidence." But "When circumstantial evidence is relied on, the accused is entitled to an acquittal unless the fact of guilt is proven to the actual exclusion of every reasonable hypothesis of innocence." Citing, State v. Hunter, 103 W. Va. 377, 137 S. E. 534. 

State v. Johnson, 104 W. Va. 586, 140 S. E. 532. 

State v. Kapp, 109 W. Va. 487, 155 S. E. 537. 

17 R. C. L., 85, sec. 92. 

53 Corpus Juris, 536. 

§ 1478. Inadequacy of consideration. 

The inadequacy of the amount paid for stolen goods is a circumstance to be considered on the issue of guilty knowledge, but is not of itself necessarily controlling. 

State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 104.

§ 1482 

And in State v. Mounts, 120 W. Va. 661, 200 S. E. 55, it is held: 

"Guilty knowledge cannot be inferred merely from the inadequacy of the price paid for the property.' And this "applies with like force to the element 'having reason to believe' the goods to have been stolen." § 1479. Goods bought and sold on open market.

On the trial of one for receiving stolen goods, evidence to show that such goods were bought and sold in the same market by and from individuals, mining companies, and manufacturing companies, and its merchandise commonly on the market, is properly admissible on the question of the guilty knowledge of the accused and the bona fides of the transaction. 

State v. Duschman, 79 W. Va. 747, 91 S. E. 809. 

Watts v. State, 5 W. Va. 532. § 1480. Other purchases from same thief may be shown. 

In Longman v. Com., 167 Va. 461, 188 S. E. 144, it is held: "Evidence that accused had purchased other goods from alleged thief on other occasions, is admissible to show course of dealing between them and intent of accused to receive goods." § 1481. Guilty knowledge is a question for the jury.

It is universally held that guilty knowledge is always a question for the jury to determine from all the evidence in the case. 

State v. Hill, 52 W. Va. 300, 43 S. E. 160. 

State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 129, 99 S. E. 248. § 1482. Character of accused an important factor. 

In Patterson v. Com., 165 Va. 734, 181 S. E. 281, it is held that when the evidence of the Commonwealth was weighed along with the good reputation of the accused, which in a doubtful case deserves great consideration, the proof adduced failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. 

Hey v. Com., 32 Gratt. 947.

See Chapter on Character.

$974 

 § 1483. Restoration of property no defense. 

In State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 133, 99 S. E. 248, it is held: "It is well settled that when a larceny is complete the voluntary abandonment of the property by the thief, no matter how soon after the larceny, is no defense. * *

Hence if it can be established that defendant bought and received the goods * * * knowing them to havs been stolen, the offense was complete from that moment, and the voluntary return thereof to the owner is no defense." 

State v. Chambers, 22 W. Va. 779. 

Whalen v. Com., 90 Va. 554, 19 S. E. 182. § 1484. Subsequent payment for property, no defense. 

In State v. Camp, 110 W. Va. 448, 158 S. E. 664, it is held: "When persons accused of larceny voluntarily pay the value of stolen goods and the costs of prosecution, their conduct is evidence of their guilt. * * * In cases involving larceny such evidence is valuable as showing the conduct of the accused immediately after the larceny which has a legal tendency to connect him with the crime." Citing, 36 Corpus Juris, 893. 

State v. Furr, 121 N. C. 606. 

1485. When evidence of other offenses is admissible. 

In State v. Baker, 84 W. Va. 151, 99 S. E. 252, it is held: "On the trial of one charged with receiving stolen goods, evidence that he received other stolen goods, knowingly or ignorantly, either prior or subsequent to the time of the offense charged, is admissible to prove a scienter, provided such other collateral acts are not too remote in point of time." 

State v. Ringer, 84 W. Va. 550, 100 S. E. 413. 

Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 475, 124 S. E. 237. 

Longman v. Com., 167 Va. 461, 188 S. E. 144. § 1486. Corpus delicti. 

In Drinkard v. Com., 163 Va. 1074, 178 S. E. 28, it is held that the "corpus delicti must be proved before any inference of

$1487 

guilt can arise from the possession of the fruits of crime; and "where the charge is larceny, the corpus delicti is the larceny of the goods," and the possession of stolen goods does not give rise to an inference of guilt until the corpus delicti is proved by other evidence. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 761, 111 S. E. 468.

But it is also held in Drinkard's Case, supra, that where the accused was in exclusive possession of recently stolen goods, and had falsely denied that he had been in possession thereof, and falsely testified to an attempted alibi, or that he had tried to dispose of the stolen goods, such evidence was sufficient to sustain a verdict of guilty of larceny. Citing, Branch v. Com., 100 Va. 839, 41 S. E. 862. 

Myers v. Com., supra. 

§ 1487. Indictment. 

In both Virginias, the offense of receiving stolen goods is made larceny by statute, and the accused may be convicted upon an indictment charging larceny only. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4448.

West Virginia Code, 61-3-18 (sec. 5959). 

Wood v. Com., 163 Va. 1118, 177 S. E. 911. 

Clark v. Com., 135 Va. 490, 115 S. E. 704. 

Stapleton v. Com., 140 Va. 475, 124 S. E. 237. 

Benton v. Com., 91 Va. 782, 21 S. E. 495. 

Anthony v. Com., 88 Va. 847, 14 S. E. 834. 

Mitchell v. Com., 93 Va. 775, 20 S. E. 892.

But in all cases where the indictment charges simple larceny, the accused is entitled to a bill of particulars, or statement in writing, from the attorney for the state of what he intends to rely upon for conviction. 

Hutchinson v. Com., 133 Va. 710, 112 S. E. 624.

The indictment may also contain two counts, one for receiving stolen goods under the statute, and another for the larceny of the goods. The allegations of actual larceny not being necessary, but being inserted merely in aid of intent, need not be made with the same formality as a count for larceny alone. If one

§ 976 

count be good, a general demurrer to the indictment should be overruled, and upon a general verdict of guilty, sentence should be on the good count.

Anable v. Com., 24 Gratt. 563. 

State v. Cartright, 20 W. Va. 32. 

State v. Caddle, 35 W. Va. 73, 12 S. E. 1098. 

State v. McClung, 35 W. Va. 280, 13 S. E. 654.

State v. Cooper, 111 W. Va. 256, 161 S. E. 30. 

State v. Wallace, 118 W. Va. 127, 189 S. E. 106.

And such indictment must allege the name of the person or persons from whom the stolen goods were bought or received, or that such goods were bought or received from a person or persons unknown to the grand jury. 

State v. Smith, 98 W. Va. 185, 126 S. E. 703. 

§ 1488. Description of property. 

While the property must be described in an indictment for receiving stolen goods, it is not necessary to describe such goods by reference to any mark or identification by which they can be distinguished from other goods of the same or similar kind. 

State v. Blair, 63 W. Va. 635, 60 S. E. 795. 

State v. Bailey, 63 W. Va. 668, 60 S. E. 785. 

State v. Lewis, 117 W. Va. 670, 187 S. E. 317. § 1489. Where the receiving of stolen money is charged, rule in West Virginia.

Where the indictment is for the receiving of stolen money, it must conform to the common-law requirements of such offense. 

See secs. 1146, 1147 and 1180.

STATE'S INSTRUCTIONS. 

§ 1492. Receiving stolen goods knowing them to have been stolen. 

1. If the jury believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the bonds were stolen property and that they came into the possession of the defendant, Lash Hutchinson, in the city of Lynchburg under such circumstances that the defendant must reasonably have known that they were stolen property, and that he took possession of them intending to convert them to his own use or to assist in disposing of them, then the jury should find the defendant guilty. 

Hutchinson v. Com., 133 Va. 717, 112 S. E. 624. 

2. The court instructs the jury that before they can convict the accused they must believe beyond a reasonable doubt, first, that the Commonwealth has proved that the Liberty Bonds involved were previously stolen and were the property of the First National Bank; secondly, that the accused received them in the city of Lynchburg; thirdly, that at the time he received the said bonds he knew they had been stolen; which knowledge may be inferred from all the circumstances known to the accused prior to and at the time of receiving said bonds; and, fourthly, that he received the said bonds with a dishonest intent, and unless the jury believe that the Commonwealth has proved each of these four elements beyond a reasonable doubt, they must acquit the accused. 

Hutchinson v. Com., supra. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the property set forth in the indictment belonged to the prosecuting witness, and that said property or any part thereof was stolen and was thereafter found in the exclusive and unexplained possession of the prisoner, then such possession of itself affords sufficient ground for the presumption that the accused was the thief and makes it incumbent

§ 980 

upon him to account for such possession consistently with his innocence. 

Hicks v. Com., 157 Va. 946, 161 S. E. 919. 

4. The court instructs the jury that the possession of recently stolen goods usually creates a presumption of guilt of the larceny of the property, and is a circumstance from which the jury may presume guilt, unless it appears from the evidence that the possession was consistent with the innocence of the accused. 

Jolly v. Com., 136 Va. 765, 118 S. E. 109. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 746, 111 S. E. 463. 

5. The court instructs the jury that the possession of recently stolen property creates a presumption of guilt of the larceny of the property, and places upon the accused the burden of explaining such possession. 

In Jolly v. Com., 136 Va. 765, 118 S. E. 109, the court said that the above instruction embodied a correct principle, citing 

Porterfield v. Com., 91 Va. 805, 22 S. E. 352.

NOTE: In West Virginia these instructions must be modified to conform to the law as stated in sec. 1474.

§ 1493. Elements necessary for state to prove, rule in Virginia.

The court instructs the jury that before you can find the defendant guilty in this case, it is incumbent upon the Commonwealth to prove beyond all reasonable doubt:

First: That the offense charged in the indictment was committed in 

County (or corporation as the case may be).

Second: That the goods described in the indictment and mentioned in the evidence in this case had been previously stolen by some person other than the defendant. 

Third: That the accused received said goods from another person. 

Fourth: That at the time he received said goods he knew they had been stolen.

Fifth: That he so received the said goods, or aided in concealing them, with a dishonest intent.

§ 1497. Robbery defined. 

The crime of robbery is not defined by statute in either of the Virginias, and the elements of the offense remain as at common law. Hence in these states robbery "is the felonious and forcible taking from the person of another of goods or money to any value, by violence or by putting such person in fear. The gravaman being attack or assault on the person, the force employed, and terror caused.” 

State v. Alvis, 116 W. Va. 326, 180 S. E. 257.

§ 1498 

ROBBERY §0 

State v. Fulks, 114 W. Va. 785, 173 S. E. 888. 

State v. McCoy, 63 W. Va. 70, 59 S. E. 758. 

State v. McAllister, 65 W. Va. 97, 63 S. E. 758.

State v. Williams, 98 W. Va. 464, 127 S. E. 320. 

State v. Hackle, 110 W. Va. 485, 158 S. E. 708. 

Maxwell v. Com., 165 Va. 860, 183 S. E. 452. 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 326. 

23 R. C. L., 1139. 

And in Houston v. Com., 87 Va. 257, 12 S. E. 387, robbery is thus defined: "To constitute this offense there must be (1) violence, but it need only be slight, for anything which calls out resistance is sufficient; or, what will answer in place of actual violence, there must be such demonstrations as put the person robbed in fear. The demonstrations or fear must be of a physical nature, with the single exception that, if one parts with his goods through fear of a threatened charge of sodomy, the taking is robbery. There must therefore be (2) a larceny embracing the same elements as a simple larceny; and (3) the taking must be from what is technically called the 'person,' the meaning of which expression is not that it must necessarily be from the actual contact of the person, but it is sufficient if it is from the personal protection and presence." 

Quoted with approval in Maxwell v. Com., 165 Va. 860, 183 S. E. 454, and in Fleming v. Com., 170 Va. 636, 196 

S. E. 697. 

Also, in State v. Hackle, supra, it is said: It "Robbery is an aggravated larceny, a taking of something of value from another by putting him in fear. is a compound of an offense against property and the person. Robbery with a dangerous weapon is regarded as a more serious crime than when committed without a weapon; and our statute fixes the minimum punishment for armed robbery at ten years' confinement, without a maximum; but if the robbery be not so committed, the minimum is five years."

Jordan v. Com., 25 Gratt. 943. 

Butts v. Com., 145 Va. 800, 133 S. E. 764. 

Jones v. Com., 172 Va. 615, 1 S. E. 2d 300. 

1498. Statutes compared. 

Formerly the Virginia and West Virginia statutes on robbery

§ 986 

were identical, except as to the penalties prescribed. The Virginia statute, sec. 4405, reads as follows: "If any person commit robbery by partial strangulation, or suffocation, or by striking or beating, or by other violence to the person, or by the threat or presenting of firearms, or other deadly weapon or instrumentality whatsoever, he shall be punished with death, or by confinement in the penitentiary for life, or for any term not less than eight years. If any person commit a robbery in any other mode, or by any other means, he shall be confined in the penitentiary not less than five nor more than ten years." 

In West Virginia, the 1939 legislature reenacted Code 61-2-12 (sec. 5927). In the main, however, it is similar to the Virginia statute, except as to the penalties prescribed. If the offense is committed in any manner specified in the first sentence of the statute, the punishment is confinement in the penitentiary "not less than ten years." When committed "by any other mode or means," the punishment is confinement in the penitentiary “not less than five years."

This section adds a specific penalty for robbing or attempting to rob any bank, and fixes the penalty at confinement in the penitentiary not less than ten nor more than twenty years. A like penalty is prescribed for assaulting or putting in jeopardy the life of any person by the use of a dangerous weapon while robbing or attempting to rob any such bank.

Acts of the Legislature, 1939, chapter 28. § 1499. No statutory robbery in the Virginias.

Since these statutes do not define robbery, there is no such thing in either of the Virginias as "statutory robbery." In Houston v. Com., 87 Va. 261, 12 S. E. 385, it is held: "In Virginia (and in West Virginia) there is no such thing as statutory robbery. The offense of robbery was not created by the statute, but was at a very early period, and still is, a common-law offense, and was adopted by us at the formation of our state government, with the great body of the common law then adopted, and the crime, with its common law definition, has remained unchanged. The statute above quoted does no more, and was intended to

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 326.

1500. Common-law elements of robbery. 

In Houston v. Com., 87 Va. 264, 12 S. E. 385, it is held that the following common-law elements must exist before the offense is robbery: "To constitute this offense (robbery), there must be, 1st, violence, but it need only be slight, for anything which calls out resistance is sufficient, or what will answer in place of actual violence, there must be such demonstrations as put the person robbed in fear. The demonstration or fear must be of a physical nature, with the single exception, that, if one parts with his goods through fear of a threatened charge of sodomy, the taking is robbery. 

There must, therefore, be 2d, a larceny, embracing the same elements as simple larceny; and 3d, the taking must be from what is technically called the 'person'; the meaning of which expression is, not that it must necessarily be from the actual contact of the person, but it is sufficient if it is from the personal protection and presence. Robbery is a mere compound larceny, consisting of simple larceny and an assault, intended by one or more of the cir-

§ 988 

cumstances of aggravation expressed in the first clause of our act; the second clause thereof, with which we have no concern here, being with respect to robbery committed in any other mode,' or, by any 'other means,' and for which a different punishment is prescribed." 

State v. Alvis, 116 W. Va. 326, 180 S. E. 257. 

Maxwell v. Com., 165 Va. 860, 183 S. E. 452. 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 326. 

Flemming v. Com., 170 Va. 636, 196 S. E. 696. 

And in State v. McCoy, 63 W. Va. 73, 59 S. E. 758, a fourth element is stated:

The animus furandi, or the intent to take and deprive another of his property. Citing,

Jordan v. Com., 25 Gratt. 943. 

Also in Ayers v. Com., 157 Va. 899, 161 S. E. 888, it is said: "At common law, robbery is * * * 'the taking, with intent to deprive the owner permanently, of personal property, from his person or in his presence, against his will, by violence or intimidation.' 

Green v. Com., 133 Va. 695, 112 S. E. 563. 

Brookman v. Com., 151 Va. 522, 145 S. E. 358. 

State v. Worthington, 109 W. Va. 449, 155 S. E. 313. 

Jones v. Com., 172 Va. 615, 1 S. E. (2d) 300. 

§ 1501. When offense is complete. 

In Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 326, it is held: "Before the crime of robbery is complete it must appear that the property was taken into possession by the robber; that the taking was with felonious intent; that the property was taken from the person or in the presence of the actual or constructive owner; that it was against the will of the owner; and finally, that it was taken from the owner by violence or by putting him in fear." § 1502. Robber must have been in possession of property taken.

By the term "taking" is meant that the robber must have been in actual possession of the property taken, and the offense is not actually completed without such possession.

§ 1505 

ROBBERY 

HEL 1. 1 

State v. McAllister, 65 W. Va. 97, 63 S. E. 758. 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 326. § 1503. Robbery distinguished from larceny.

Robbery is an offense against the person, and is the felonious and forcible taking from the person of another, of goods or money of any value, by violence or by putting in fear. The gravamen is the attack or assault upon the person the force employed and terror caused. The value of the money or other property taken from the person of the victim is not material. 

Larceny is an offense against property, and the gravamen is the taking of a thing of value without the consent of the owner and with intent on the part of the taker to convert it to his use. The character and value of the thing taken is of prime importance, for, by such means, the identification of the article taken is made certain and the grade of the offense established. 

State v. Fulks, 114 W. Va. 785, 173 S. E. 888. 

State v. Alvis, 116 W. Va. 326, 180 S. E. 257. 

State v. McAllister, 65 W. Va. 97, 63 S. E. 758. 

Maxwell v. Com., 165 Va. 860, 183 S. E. 452. 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 326. 

§ 1504. Intent necessary. 

In Jordan v. Com., 25 Gratt. 943, it is held that to constitute the crime of robbery it is not necessary that the accused should intend to appropriate the property taken to his own use. If he intended to deprive the owner of his property, it is sufficient. 

State v. McCoy, 63 W. Va. 73, 59 S. E. 758. 

Ayers v. Com., 157 Va. 899, 161 S. E. 888. 

Green v. Com., 133 Va. 695, 112 S. E. 563. 

Brookman v. Com., 151 Va. 522, 145 S. E. 358. 

State v. Worthington, 109 W. Va. 449, 155 S. E. 313. 

Jones v. Com., 172 Va. 615, 1 S. E. (2d) 300. 

§ 1505. Intent explained. 

The intent must be with reference to the property described in the indictment; and it is not necessary that accused should in- 2 CT-29

tend to appropriate the property taken to his own use. If he intended to deprive the owner thereof, it is sufficient. 

Jordan v. Com., 25 Gratt. 943. § 1506. Time when intent must exist. 

In State v. Morris, 96 W. Va. 292, 122 S. E. 914, it is held: "To constitute the crime of robbery in this case the intent to steal, take and carry away the pistol must have existed in the minds of the accused at the time the prosecuting witness was disarmed; any subsequent appropriation or carrying away of the pistol, although illegal, does not make it robbery." 

State v. McCoy, 63 W. Va. 69, 59 S. E. 758. 

Jordan v. Com., 25 Gratt. 943.

See authorities cited in opinion. § 1508. When property is taken under claim of right. 

When violence is used to obtain possession of property with a felonious intent, it will none the less amount to robbery because the thief has recourse to some colorable or specious pretense or claim of right, to effect his purpose. 

Parrish v. Com., 81 Va. 11. Citing, 1 Russell on Crimes, 876.

§ 1511 

ROBBERY § 1509. How motive may be shown. 

Where a murder is committed in the commission of a robbery, testimony to the effect that the accused was without money immediately before the homicide and that he was seen with considerable money a few hours after the time that the crime was committed, is admissible as not only tending to connect the accused directly with the commission of the murder, but also to disclose a motive for its commission. 

State v. Williams, 98 W. Va. 465, 127 S. E. 320. § 1510. Conspiracy to commit robbery.

Conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons by some concerted action to commit an offense, and applies to the crime of robbery. But to be convicted, the accused must have conspired to rob a person. 

Virginia Code, sec. 4483b. 

West Virginia Code, 61-6-7 (sec. 6033). 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 328. § 1511. Essential allegations in indictment. 

Under the statutes of both Virginias the manner of the taking of the property in robbery is in the alternative: (1) It may be through violence, or (2) through intimidation. But allegations of both force and intimidation are unnecessary in the indictment, since the allegation of either is sufficient. 

State v. Fulks, 114 W. Va. 785, 173 S. E. 888. 

State v. Alvis, 116 W. Va. 326, 180 S. E. 257.

While the statutes of both Virginia and West Virginia, hereinbefore cited, state several alternative ways of committing robbery, including "violence to the person." However, it is well to consult the numerous authorities cited in the foregoing cases. 

In Houston v. Com., 87 Va. 257, 12 S. E. 385, it is held that robbery under the Virginia statute (same as the West Virginia statute) differs in no respect from the common-law offense. 

Hence if the indictment is good at common law, it is good under

$992 

the statutes of both states. At common law it is sufficient to charge that the accused at a stated time and place "in and upon one (name of victim) feloniously did make an assault, and him the said (name of victim) in bodily fear did then and there feloniously put, and one, etc. (setting out the things of taken and their value as in simple larceny), of the moneys, goods, and chattels of the said B., then and there feloniously and violently did steal, take, and carry away, against the peace and dignity of the Commonwealth of Virginia." 

§ 1512. Ownership of property taken. 

In Booth v. Com., 165 Va. 794, 183 S. E. 257, it is held that an indictment for robbery which alleges ownership in a certain person, will be sustained by proof that such person is the agent or bailee of the true owner, or has, in behalf of the owner, the control, care and management of the property taken. 

1513. Description and value of property taken.

It is generally held that the indictment must describe the property alleged to have been taken. But where its description is unknown, its lack may be supplied by an allegation that a description of the property is to the grand jurors unknown. However, no specific value of the property taken need be averred, but it must appear from the indictment that the property had some value. 

State v. Alvis, 116 W. Va. 326, 180 S. E. 257. 

And in State v. Fulks, 114 W. Va. 785, 173 S. E. 888, it is held: "A robbery indictment describing the property as 'certain bank notes, the description and denomination thereof being unknown to said grand jurors, of the value of eight hundred dollars,' held sufficient."

And such description was held sufficient where the evidence established the taking of currency and coin. 

See also, State v. Jackson, 26 W. Va. 250. 

54 Corpus Juris, p. 1036.

 § 1521. Robbery by conspirators. 

The court instructs the jury that before they can find the defendant (name him), guilty as charged in the indictment, they must believe beyond all reasonable doubt that he entered into a conspiracy and confederation with (name other or other participants), or any one of them, for the purpose of robbing the prosecuting witness (name him), and in pursuance of such conspiracy the said prosecuting witness (name him), was robbed, as charged in the indictment, and that such belief must be founded upon the evidence adduced before them in the trial of this case. 

State v. Roberts, 50 W. Va. 427, 40 S. E. 484. § 1522. Attempt to commit robbery.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the driver, Morris, parted with possession of the truck and its contents willingly and in accordance with a previous plan to which he was a party, and not because of any force exercised by the defendant or any other person, and not because he, the said Morris, was put in fear by the defendant or any other person, then they must find the defendant not guilty of an attempt to commit robbery. 

Falden v. Com., 167 Va. 542, 189 S. E. 331.

NOTE: In this case the indictment charged three defendants jointly with the offense. Where only one person is so charged, the words "or any other person" should be omitted. 

§ 1523. Aiding and abetting robbery. 

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence in this case beyond a reasonable doubt that Barney Cleaves robbed the prosecuting witness, William Meyers, as charged in the indictment, and that the prisoner, Henry Houston, was present aiding and abetting him therein, then the prisoner is guilty as principal in the second degree, although you may further believe that the prisoner neither beat nor struck the said William Meyers, or that the prisoner after the robbing moved any portion of the goods and articles carried away by the said Carney Cleaves, as the "fruits of said crime."

AUTREFOIS, ACQUIT AND CONVICT 

§ 1571. Previous trial for same offense. 

§ 1525. Unanimity of verdict, rule in West Virginia. 

It is the rule in West Virginia that an accused is entitled to an instruction on the unanimity of the jury in arriving at a verdict. 

The decisions are somwhat confused as to the proper wording of such instruction, but they agree that it should not be couched in language that will invite the jury to disagree. 

Beginning with State v. Joseph, 100 W. Va. 213, 130 S. E. 

451, the Supreme Court began to enforce a more rigid rule with respect to such instructions. In that case, for the first time, it was held that it must embrace the following four points of consideration by the jury: (1) The evidence in the case, (2) the instructions of the court, (3) the argument of counsel, and (4) consultation among their fellow jurors. On page 221 of the opinion it is said: "This court has held in a number of cases that the accused in a criminal case is entitled to have the jury told that, if any juror has a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the accused, after hearing the evidence, receiving the instructions of the court, listening to the arguments of counsel, and consulting with his fellow jurors, such juror should not agree to a conviction."

The holding in this case has been approved in the following later cases: 

State v. Sibert, 113 W. Va. 717, 169 S. E. 412.

$1002 

Emery v. West Penn Co., 111 W. Va. 699, 163 S. E. 620. 

Robertson v. Hobson, 114 W. Va. 236, 171 S. E. 745.

And in the still later case of State v. Manstoff, 118 W. Va. 

214, 189 S. E. 698, with reference to last two above cited cases, Judge Fox said: "These were civil cases, but it is quite apparent that this court has sought to find a way to express its disapproval of instructions of the nature of those under consideration, which may tend to invite obduracy or disagreement on the part of the jury, while adhering to the holding that juries should, upon request, be instructed in every case that their verdict must be unanimous, and the individual views of jurors fully recognized.'

Hence it is apparent that the prior holdings of the court in approving instructions which omit one or more of the four elements, as above set out, are overruled, and particularly the following cases: 

State v. Wisman, 94 W. Va. 224, 118 S. E. 139. 

State v. McKinney, 88 W. Va. 400, 106 S. E. 894. 

State v. Edgell, 94 W. Va. 198, 118 S. E. 144. 

State v. Noble, 96 W. Va. 432, 123 S. E. 237. 

State v. Warrick, 96 W. Va: 723, 123 S. E. 799. 

State v. Fugate, 103 W. Va. 658, 138 S. E. 318. 

State v. Brady, 104 W. Va. 535, 140 S. E. 546.

From a consideration of the later cases on the subject, an instruction in substantially the following language is suggested as being correct: 

1. The court instructs the jury that upon the trial of a criminal case by a jury the law contemplates the concurrence of twelve minds in the conclusion of guilt before a conviction can be had. 

Each individual juror must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the defendant's guilt before he can rightly, under his oath, consent to a verdict of guilty. Each juror should feel the responsibility resting upon him as a member of the jury, and should realize that his own mind must be convinced beyond all reasonable doubt of the defendant's guilt before he can consent to a verdict of guilty. Therefore, if any individual juror, after having duly considered the evidence in the case, the instructions of

§ 1003 

MISCELLANEOUS INSTRUCTIONS 

It the court, the arguments of counsel, and consulting with his fellow jurors, should entertain a reasonable doubt of defendant's guilt, it is his duty not to surrender his own convictions simply because all, or some, of the other jurors entertain a different opinion. 

2. The court further instructs the jury that before they can find the defendant guilty as charged in the indictment in this case, that each and every one of the jurors must be convinced by all the evidence in the case, beyond all reasonable doubt, that the accused is guilty as charged in the indictment; that it is the duty of every juror to consider all the evidence in the case, the instructions of the court, the argument of counsel, and the argument of his fellow jurors; that no juror should give up or surrender his own opinion simply because the other jurors are of a different opinion; and that no juror entertaining a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the defendant should join in a verdict of guilty. 

, State v. Joseph, 100 W. Va. 213, 130 S. E. 451. 

3. The court instructs the jury that no juror should yield a conscientious opinion deliberately formed after a full and fair investigation of the case, and the jury is further instructed that the jury room is no place for pride of opinion or stubbornness, but that it is the duty of the jurors to discuss the evidence in a spirit of fairness and candor with each other and with open minds, and to give careful consideration to the views of their fellows, and if it can be done without a sacrifice of conscientious convictions, agree upon a verdict. 

State v. Koski, 100 W. Va. 98, 130 S. E. 101.

However, either of the following instructions have been held a sufficient substitute for an instruction on the unanimity of the verdict: 

4. The court instructs the jury that the defendant is presumed to be innocent of any offense charged in the indictment against him, and that such presumption is not a mere form of law to be disregarded by the jury, but it is their duty to cling to such presumption until they are driven from it by such evidence and circumstances as convince the jury, and each member thereof, of the

§ 1004 

guilt of said defendant of the offense charged in the indictment beyond all reasonable doubt. 

State v. McKinney, 88 W. Va. 400, 106 S. E. 904. 

5. The court instructs the jury that the law presumes that the defendant, Samuel Manstoff, is innocent of the crime charged against him in the indictment in this case, and that such presumption follows him throughout every step of the trial; that it is incumbent upon the state to establish the prisoner's guilt by proof so clear and convincing and satisfactory in its nature as to convince the jury of his guilt beyond all reasonable doubt; that before the jury can find the defendant guilty in this case they must believe and be satisfied from the evidence in the case beyond all reasonable doubt that he is guilty; that if the jury, or any member thereof, after having carefully weighed and considered all the evidence in the case, should entertain a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the defendant they cannot return a verdict of guilty. 

State v. Manstoff, 118 W. Va. 214, 189 S. E. 702. § 1526. Same, rule in Virginia.

The giving of an instruction on the unanimity of the verdict is discouraged in Virginia. The controlling rule is stated in Sims v. 

Com., 134 Va. 757, 115 S. E. 389, as follows: "The instruction might probably, with propriety, have been given, but it embodies principles so well understood by every one and so fully covered by the oath of each juror that its refusal cannot be deemed error. 

No juror should ever yield a conscientious opinion deliberately formed after a full and fair investigation of the case, as to the guilt or innocence of the accused, but jurors should not be invited to disagree if they can. When such an instruction is given the jury should be further instructed. that the jury room is no place for pride of opinion or obstinacy, but that it is the duty of the jurors to discuss the evidence in a spirit of fairness and candor with each other, and with open minds to give careful consideration to the views of their fellows, and, if it can be done without a sacrifice of conscientious convictions, agree upon a verdict. By such means and such only, in a body where unanimity is required, can safe and just results be attained, and without them trial by jury, instead of being an essen-

§ 1528 

MISCELLANEOUS INSTRUCTIONS 

tial aid in the administration of justice, would be a most effective obstacle to it." 

Scott v. Com., 143 Va. 510, 129 S. E. 360. 

Peoples v. Com., 147 Va. 692, 137 S. E. 603. 

Nelson v. Com., 153 Va. 909, 150 S. E. 407. 

Smith v. Com., 168 Va. 703, 190 S. E. 95.

However, where an instruction on the unanimity of the verdict is denied, we suggest the use of Instruction No. 1, in the preceding section, with the addition of a second paragraph in the following language, so as to conform to the holding in Sims' Case, supra.

And in this connection the jury is further instructed that the jury room is no place for pride of opinion or obstinacy, and it is the duty of the jurors to discuss the evidence in a spirit of fairness and candor with each other, and with open minds to give careful consideration to the views of their fellow jurors, and, if it can be done without a sacrifice of conscientious convictions, agree upon a verdict. 

NOTE: The Virginia rule is based upon sound principles of public policy, and it is probable that the West Virginia Court eventually will adopt it. In fact the above addition to the instruction was approved by the latter court as a separate instruction (No. 3 in preceding sec.), in State v. Koski, 100 W. Va. 98, 130 S. E. 101. § 1527.  § 1531. Distinction between civil and criminal cases. 

The court instructs the jury that a distinction is to be noted between civil and criminal cases in respect to the degree or quantity of evidence necessary to justify the jury in finding their verdict for the state. In civil cases their duty is to weigh the evidence carefully and find for the party in whose favor the evidence preponderates, although it be not free from reasonable doubt; but in criminal trials the party accused is entitled to the benefit of the legal presumption in favor of innocence which, in doubtful cases, is always sufficient to turn the scale in his favor. 

It is, therefore, a rule of criminal law that the guilt of the accused must be fully proved beyond all reasonable doubt; neither a mere preponderance of evidence or any weight of preponderant evidence is sufficient for the purpose unless it generate full belief of the fact to the exclusion of all reasonable doubt. The persuasion of guilt based upon the evidence in a criminal case must rise above mere suspicion or even the highest degree of mere probability and ought to amount to a moral certainty, or such a moral certainty as convinces the minds of the jury as reasonable men beyond all reasonable doubt. And this degree of conviction only exists when the facts proved coincide with, and are legally sufficient to establish the truth of the hypothesis assumed, namely, the guilt of the party accused, and are inconsistent with any other hypothesis. It is not enough that the evidence goes to show his guilt to warrant his conviction, but unless the jury believe from the evidence that the guilt of the defendant, is inconsistent with any other hypothesis, they should find the defendant, not guilty. 

, State v. Gebhart, 70 W. Va. 232, 73 S. E. 964. 

Based upon Greenleaf's Ev., vol. 3, sec. 29.

§ 1536. Where wound was aggravated by unskillful medical treatment.

If the jury believe from the evidence that the prisoner wilfully inflicted upon the deceased a dangerous wound, one that was calculated to endanger and destroy life, and that death ensued therefrom within a year and a day, the prisoner is none the less responsible for the result, although it may appear that the deceased might have recovered but for the aggravation of the wound by unskillful or improper treatment. 

Clark v. Com., 90 Va. 363, 18 S. E. 440.

§ 1537. Moral certainty defined. 

The court instructs the jury that, moral certainty is that full and complete assurance which admits of no defense and induces a sound mind to act without doubt upon the conclusion to which it naturally and reasonably leads. 

Kibler v. Com., 94 Va. 813, 26 S. E. 858. 

§ 1538. Moral certainty sufficient. 

It is not essential to proof of guilt by circumstantial evidence that the facts and circumstances established should produce on the minds of the jury absolute and demonstrative certainty, but it is sufficient if they produce moral certainty of the commission of the offense charged, to the exclusion of reasonable doubt. 

Nicholas v. Com., 91 Va. 751, 21 S. E. 364. 

§ 1539. Detectives as witnesses. 

The court instructs the jury that the testimony of a paid detective, who invites the commission of crime in order to detect the commission thereof, is of a kind with that of a person in interest, and should be scrutinized closely and received with great caution. 

Walker v. Com., 132 Va. 823, 111 S. E. 274. 

§ 1540. Objections of counsel not evidence. 

The court instructs the jury that the matter of objecting to the introduction of testimony by counsel in this case and the arguments made in connection therewith are questions of law addressed solely to the court and should not be considered by the jury in any respect whatever, and furthermore, the rulings of the court and the language adopted by the court in his rulings should not be considered by the jury for any purpose in arriving at a verdict as to the guilt or innocence of the accused, as it is the province of the court to pass upon the introduction of testi-

§ 1012 

mony that may be objected to by counsel in the course of the trial, and it is the duty of the jury to consider the weight and credibility of the testimony permitted by the court to be introduced, and the jury should be very careful in arriving at their verdict not to take into consideration for any purpose any testimony not permitted by the court to go to the jury where the same was ruled out upon objection by counsel or without objection, or in any wise held by the court to be improper for them to consider. 

, State v. Huffman, 69 W. Va. 770, 73 S. E. 292. 

§ 1541. Flight of accused. 

It is error to instruct the jury that the flight of the accused after the commission the crime raises a presumption of guilt. 

However, instructions on this subject couched in the following language are unobjectionable: 

1. The court instructs the jury that in determining the question of the guilt or innocence of the accused, you may take into consideration the flight of the prisoner after the commission of the crime, if the same is proven, along with all the other facts and circumstances introduced in evidence in the case. 

Jenkins v. Com., 132 Va. 692, 111 S. E. 101. 

Chandler v. Com., 135 Va. 486, 115 S. E. 703. 

2. The court instructs the jury that the fact that the defendant ran when approached by the officer is only a circumstance and should be cautiously considered by the jury together with all the facts and circumstances shown in the case. 

Duty v. Com., 137 Va. 762, 119 S. E. 62.

For a full discussion of this subject see, Hickory v. U. S., 160 U. S. 408, 40 L. Ed. 474. § 1542. State police have authority to make arrests.

EF 1 officer in making an arrest of an alleged offender, after he peaceably submits, to acquaint the party he proposes to arrest with the nature and character of the accusation of the alleged crime for which he is going to arrest him, unless the offense be committed in the presence of the officer, and, unless the jury shall believe from the evidence that such crime was committed in the presence of the officer when he attempted to make the arrest, or that said officer apprised the plaintiff of a felony charge against him, then, in such circumstances, the said plaintiff had the right to use such reasonable force as was necessary to prevent the arrest, and the officer had no right to shoot the plaintiff to prevent his escape. 

Bourne v. Richardson, 133 Va. 457, 113 S. E. 893. § 1555. Arrest for violation of city ordinance.

The court instructs the jury that under ordinance LV of the 

Charter of the City of Grafton, Taylor County, W. Va., a city police officer has no authority to make an arrest, and place in jail one suspected of violating said ordinance, without a warrant, and if the jury believe from the evidence that the deceased, J. E. 

B. Phillips, arrested the defendant, without authority of law, the jury are instructed in considering their verdict to give this fact such weight as is due it. 

State v. Lutz, 85 W. Va. 346, 101 S. E. 434. 

§ 1556. What constitutes lewdness and lasciviousness. 

The court instructs the jury that in order for a person to be guilty of open or public lewdness and lasciviousness it is not necessary that the act itself be committed in public or in the presence of other persons. It is sufficient if the act is done in such a manner or under such circumstances as necessarily to become public or generally known in the neighborhood. 

Johnson v. Com., 152 Va. 968, 146 S. E. 289. § 1557. Where evidence contravenes physical laws and human experience.

The following instruction has been formulated from the general law as stated in the cases cited below:

§ 1020 

The court instructs the jury that testimony which is in direct contravention of physical laws or human experience, is necessarily deemed incredible, and the jury is not compelled to accept as true that which in the very nature of things could not have occurred in the manner and under the circumstances detailed in the testimony; and if you believe from all the evidence and circumstances of this case that it was physically impossible and contrary to the nature of things for the defendant, who weighs 265 pounds, to have struck and hit the prosecuting witness, who weighs 135 pounds, upon the head with the rock drill introduced in evidence, which weighs 8 pounds, is 32 inches long and 14 inches in diameter, in the manner and under the circumstances and with no more effect than is testified to by the said prosecuting witness, both as to his head and the straw hat which he wore at the time the blow is alleged to have been struck, then you may disregard such testimony, or give to it such weight, not inconsistent with the physical facts in evidence or human experience, as you may, from all the facts and circumstances in evidence, deem it entitled to receive.

NOTE: The above instruction was formulated by the author, based on the decided cases, and given in an important case. It correctly states the law. See 

Boxley v. Com., 24 Gratt. 649. 

Ry. Co. v. Strickler 118 Va. 153, 86 S. E. 824. 

Grinnell v. Com., 157 Va. 915, 161 S. E. 888.

§ 1559. Venue or place of trial. 

1. The court instructs the jury that you cannot convict the accused for receiving stolen goods, nor for larceny, even though you may believe that he has been proven guilty, beyond all reasonable doubt, unless you further believe that he has committed the crime within the city of Hopewell, or within one mile of the corporate limits. 

Jolly v. Com., 136 Va. 767, 118 S. E. 109. 

2. The court instructs the jury that you cannot consider any of the acts of the defendant alleged to have taken place around. 

Disputants, and to fix upon him the commission of a crime there, in the county of Prince George. 

Jolly v. Com., supra. 

3. The court instructs the jury that the venue or place where the alleged crime is charged as having occurred is a material allegation, and unless the Commonwealth has proven, beyond all reasonable doubt that the alleged crime was consummated in the city of Hopewell, or within one mile of the corporate limits of the city, you must find the defendant not guilty. 

Jolly v. Com., supra. 

4. The court instructs the jury that if from the evidence they believe that the offense named in the presentment was committed not in Calhoun County but in Roane County, the jury must find 2 CT-31

§ 1022 

the defendant not guilty, even though they believe the evidence proves, that the offense was committed within one hundred yards of the county line of Calhoun County. 

State v. Lowe, 21 W. Va. 795. § 1560. Court does not intimate opinion on evidence. 

The court instructs the jury that no instruction or remark of the court was to be taken as intimating an opinion on the evidence of facts. 

State v. Detwilder, 60 W. Va. 586, 55 S. E. 654. § 1561. Duty of jury to consider all evidence. 

The court instucts the jury that they should consider all the testimony offered on behalf of the State and on behalf of the defendant in arriving at a proper verdict in the case. 

State v. Gillispie, 63 W. Va. 153, 59 S. E. 957. § 1562. Infant's capacity to commit crime. 

The court instructs the jury that to establish capacity to commit crime in a person over seven and under fourteen years of age, it is not necessary that any witness shall state that he has such capacity, but the same may be shown to exist by the appearance and general conduct of the accused, and by his testimony as a witness before the jury. 

State v. Williams, 40 W. Va. 269, 21 S. E. 721. § 1563. Another guilty agent need not be pointed out. 

1. The court instructs the jury that the failure of the evidence to disclose any other criminal agent than the accused is not a circumstance which may be considered by the jury in determining whether or not he is guilty of the crime wherewith he is charged. 

The prisoner is presumed to be innocent until his guilt is established, and he is not to be prejudiced by the inability of the Commonwealth to point to any other criminal agent; nor is he called upon to vindicate his own innocence by naming the guilty agent. 

McCue v. Com., 103 Va. 917, 49 S. E. 623. 

Jessie v. Com., 112 Va. 891, 71 S. E. 612.

§ 1564 

MISCELLANEOUS INSTRUCTIONS 

2. The court instructs the jury that, notwithstanding the fact that A. H. Karnes was present at the time Mrs. J. B. Kelly was shot and killed, he is not to be prejudiced by the inability of the Commonwealth to point out any other criminal agent or person who committed the crime, nor is A. H. Karnes called upon to vindicate his own innocence by naming, or identifying, the guilty man, but he rests secure in the presumption of innocence until proof is adduced which establishes the fact beyond all reasonable doubt that he actually shot and killed the deceased, Mrs. J. B. 

Kelly, and if the Commonwealth has failed to prove by clear, distinct and reliable evidence beyond all reasonable doubt that he shot and killed the deceased, the law requires the jury to find him not guilty. ! 

Karnes v. Com., 125 Va. 768, 99 S. E. 562.

NOTE: In Jessie v. Com., 112 Va. 887, 71 S. E. 612, it is held: "Where there is no evidence tending to implicate any person other than the accused in the crime charged, and there is testimony as to his guilt, it is not error to refuse instructions similar to the last two above given." 

See also, Stine v. Com., 162 Va. 856, 174 S. E. 758, and cases therein cited.

SEDUCTION. 

In West Virginia seduction is not recognized as a crime, but under Virginia Code, sec. 4410, the seduction of a female of previous chaste character, under promise of marriage, is a felony. 

The following are the leading instructions on the subject: 

§ 1564. What constitutes seduction. 

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the prosecutrix was an unmarried female of previous chaste character at the time of her alleged seduction, and that she was seduced by the prisoner by having illicit connection with her under promise of marriage, they should find him guilty. 

Barker v. Com., 90 Va. 822, 20 S. E. 776.

$ 1024 

§ 1565. Chastity of prosecutrix.

The court instructs the jury that although they may believe from the evidence beyond a reasonable doubt that the prisoner had illicit connection with the prosecutrix under promise of marriage, and may have thought at the time that she was a female of previous chaste character, yet they must find him not guilty if they believe she was unchaste at the time of said seduction. 

Barker v. Com., 90 Va. 823, 20 S. E. 776. § 1566. Woman over twenty-one.

The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the testimony in the case that the said Julia F. Hodges was, at the time of the said alleged seduction, more than twenty-one years of age; that she was then residing with the defendant, and not with the plaintiff, under a contract made with the defendant by her to render him service in his own house for twelve months, for a consideration agreed by the plaintiff to be paid to said Julia F. 

Hodges, for her own use; and that such contract was made after the said Julia F. Hodges had attained the age of twenty-one years, they must find for the defendant. 

Lee v. Hodges, 13 Gratt. 727. § 1567. Uncorroborated testimony of prosecutrix insufficient.

The court instructs the jury that the facts of the promise of marriage and the seduction cannot be proved by the unsupported testimony of the said Berta Puryear, but there must be some corroborating evidence in addition to hers to support said facts of the promise of marriage and the seduction. 

Mills v. Com., 93 Va. 817, 22 S. E. 863. § 1568. Such testimony must be substantiated by surrounding facts and circumstances. 

1. The court instructs the jury that while they cannot convict the accused on the uncorroborated testimony of the prosecutrix, Katy L. Yates, yet if the admissions of the accused and othe:

I § 1025 

MISCELLANEOUS INSTRUCTIONS 

surrounding circumstances substantiate her testimony so as to satisfy their minds of the truth of her statements, then this is sufficient. 

Atkins v. Com., 132 Va. 507, 110 S. E. 379. 

2. The court instructs the jury that the accused cannot be convicted upon the testimony of the female seduced unsupported by other testimony. Without undertaking to indicate the precise amount of corroborating testimony, which in this case would be sufficient, the court tells the jury that it must be evidence which does not emanate from the mouth of the seduced female, that it must not rest wholly upon her credibility, but must be such evidence as adds to, strengthens, confirms and corroborates her. 

Atkins v. Com., supra. 

§ 1569. Compromise no bar to prosecution. 

The court instructs the jury that no compromise between the prosecutrix and the prisoner, or any one else, could bar a prosecution by the Commonwealth for the crime charged in the indictment. 

Barker v. Com., 90 Va. 822, 20 S. E. 776. 

§ 1570. Time of seduction immaterial. 

The court instructs the jury that the exact time of the seduction is never material in a prosecution for the offense, and that it is not, therefore, essential that the prosecutrix should be corroborated as to the exact date. And the court further instructs the jury that if they should believe from the evidence that the seduction of an illicit connection of the prisoner with the prosecutrix took place within the statutory period of two years prior to the finding of the indictment by the grand jury, they must find the prisoner guilty. 

Shaver v. Com., 151 Va. 547, 145 S. E. 377.

AUTREFOIS, ACQUIT AND CONVICT. 

§ 1571. Previous trial for same offense. 

1. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the

§ 1026 

evidence that the offense for which the prisoner is now arraigned is another and distinct, and not the same offense for which he has been heretofore tried and acquitted, then they must find against the prisoner upon the issue joined.

Page v. Com., 27 Gratt. 966. 

2. The court instructs the jury that if they believe that the evidence necessary to support a conviction on the present indictment would also have supported a conviction in the previous trial, then they must find that he has been heretofore acquitted of the same offense. But if the jury, from the evidence, believe that the prisoner, on the former trial, was tried for a separate and distinct offense, occurring at a separate and distinct time, involving a separate and distinct act, then the jury may find for the Commonwealth on the issue joined. 

Page v. Com., supra. 

3. The court instructs the jury that if they believe from the evidence that the house named in the first count of the indictment, for the burning of which the prisoner was arraigned and tried at the February term of the court, is not the same house nor the same burning charged in the indictment upon which he now stands arraigned, then they must find against the prisoner on the issue joined. And it makes no difference that the offenses charged in the indictments are described as the burnings of the dwelling house of Francis G. Ruffin, if the jury believe that in reality distinct houses and distinct burnings are referred to in the two indictments. 

Page v. Com., supra.

§ 1572. General form of indictment, West Virginia stat ute. 

The West Virginia Code, 62-9-1 (sec. 6263), prescribes the following general form for all indictments:

STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA, COUNTY OF 

To-WIT: 

The grand jurors of the State of West Virginia, in and for the body of the county of ........, and now attending said court, upon their oaths present* (here describe the offense), against the peace and dignity of the State. 

Found upon the evidence of duly sworn in open court to testify the truth and sent before the grand jury this the ......day of 19... (Signed) ··9 

Prosecuting Attorney.

§ 1028 

The statute also requires all indictments to be signed on the reverse side by the foreman of the grand jury, and attested by the prosecuting attorney.

See sec. 4. 

NOTE: The italicized words, "and now attending said court," are not required by the statute, but they are inserted as the better form. 

§ 1573. General form of indictment, Virginia. 

The Virginia Code does not prescribe a general form of indictment, but the following is sufficient: 

COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA, 

COUNTY (OR CITY) OF 

To-WIT: 

The grand jurors of the Commonwealth of Virginia, in and for the body of the county (or city) of and now attending the

Court of said county (or city), upon their oaths present (here describe the offense), against the peace and dignity of the Commonwealth. 

§ 1574. Additional counts. 

Where more than one count is desired in the indictment they may be added in the following language:

SECOND COUNT 

And the grand jurors aforesaid, upon their oaths aforesaid do further present that on the day and year aforesaid, in the county (or city) aforesaid, the said A. B. did (here set forth the offense as another offense), against the peace and dignity of the State (or Commonwealth).

In the following forms follow the general form for the respective state, as above set out, to the asterisk, and continue with the proper allegation.

§ 1585. For attempting to bribe an arbitrator. 

That on the 28th day of January, 1876, a certain cause in which Boyd E. Lusk was plaintiff and Drury Halsey was defendant, was pending and undetermined in the county court of said county, and that at the January term of said court, on the 28th day of January, 1876, by agreement of parties, the matters in controversy in said cause were submitted to the arbitration and award of Martin G.
