§ 1593a. Bills and certificates of exceptions are of statu tory origin.

At common law a writ of error did not lie for errors in law not appearing on the face of the record. And our modern practice of resorting to bills or certificates of exceptions to bring into the record matters not appearing on the face thereof is purely statutory. In Virginia this practice is governed by Code, secs. 6252 and 6253, and in West Virginia it is controlled by Code, 56-6-35 and 36 (secs. 5669 and 5670). In the main these statutes are very similar.

Taliaferro v. Franklin, 1 Gratt. 332. 

Roanoke v. Karn, 80 Va. 589. 

Dryden v. Swinburne, 20 W. Va. 89. 

Ratliff v. Meadows, 116 Va. 975, 83 S. E. 395. 

§ 1594. Bills of exceptions, summary of Virginia statute. 

Briefly the Virginia statute relating to bills of exceptions provides: 

1. They shall state fairly the truth of what opinions of the trial court were objected to, and to which exceptions were taken during the trial, and are to be relied upon in the appellate court. 

2. They shall be tendered to the trial judge for his signature,

1045 § 1595 

EF 

ST 

either in term or vacation, (a) at any time before final judgment is entered, or (b) within sixty days from the time at which the final judgment was entered. 

3. The trial judge may sign such bills within the sixty days, or he may take an additional ten days to consider and sign them, but he shall sign them within seventy days from the day on which the final judgment was entered. 

4. In addition to signing such bills, the trial judge shall endorse thereon the date on which they were tendered to him. 

5. Before the trial judge may sign such bills it must appear that the Commonwealth's attorney has had reasonable notice in writing of the time and place they are to be tendered. 

6. When such bills have been signed and dated by the trial judge as aforesaid, they shall be forthwith delivered or transmitted to the clerk of the court in which the case is pending. 

7. With the strict compliance of the above provisions all bills of exceptions shall become a part of the record of the case. 

8. The statute applies to criminal as well as civil cases. 

§ 1595. Same, summary of West Virginia statute. 

The West Virginia statute, Code 56-6-35 (sec. 5669), is more liberal in scope than the Virginia law. It provides: 

1. Bills of exceptions shall state fairly the truth of what actions or opinions of the trial court were objected to and to which exceptions were taken during the trial, and are to be relied upon in the appellate court. 

2. They may be tendered to the trial judge for his signature in term or vacation at any time before final judgment is entered, or within sixty days after the adjournment of the term at which such judgment is entered. 

3. The trial judge may, by an order entered of record, extend the time within which such bills of exceptions may be tendered, signed and certified beyond the prescribed sixty days. 

4. If the action or opinion of the trial court be upon any question involving the evidence or any part thereof, either upon a motion for a new trial or otherwise, the court shall certify all the evidence touching the question, and the judge shall sign any such bill of exceptions, and it shall be made a part of the record

$1596

1046 in the case, and the whole of the evidence so certified shall be considered by the court of appeals, both upon application for and hearing of the writ of error or supersedeas. 

5. One convicted may avail himself of any error appearing on the record, by which he is prejudiced, without obtaining a formal bill of exceptions, provided he objects or excepts on the record to the action of the trial court complained of, and provided it is such a matter as can be considered without a formal bill of exceptions. 

6. In all cases an objection noted on the record shall have the same effect as if followed by a formal exception to the ruling of the court thereon, and no exception shall be necessary in order to permit the party objecting to avail himself thereof. 

7. If such bills of exceptions be signed by the judge in vacation, he shall certify the same to the clerk of the court, who shall enter such certification upon the order book of such court, and any such bill of exceptions so made in vacation shall be a part of the record and have the same effect as if made in term. 

8. If any judge refuse to sign such bill of exceptions, he may be compelled to do so by the court of appeals by mandamus. 

§ 1596. Certificates in lieu of bills of exceptions. 

The Virginia Code, sec. 6253, and the West Virginia Code, 56-6-36 (sec. 5670), provide for certificates in lieu of bills of exceptions. These statutes are very similar, and provide a less complicated method of making exceptions and objections a part of the record than is provided by formal bills of exceptions. The statutes are explicit, and all necessary forms are set out therein. 

However, the time and manner of tendering such certificates and signature of the trial judge are the same as required for bills of exceptions. 

§ 1597. Statutes are mandatory. 

In both Virginias the statutes relating to bills of exceptions and certificates in lieu thereof are mandatory, and strict compliance therewith is necessary to a consideration of a appellate court. For it is a general rule that the evidence heard, case by the the objections and exceptions thereto, and the exceptions to the

§ 1598 

ID rulings of the court during the trial, will not be considered upon a writ of error unless the same have been made a part of the record by proper bills of exceptions or certificates. The appellant assumes the burden of showing error, and the appellate court will not reverse the judgment of an inferior court unless error affirmatively appears upon the face of the record. Nor will such error be presumed, since all the presumptions are in favor of the correctness of the judgment. This rule makes it necessary for all evidence, the rulings of the trial court court, and all proceedings had and taken upon the trial to be properly made a part of the record, and so brought before the reviewing court. 

Griffith v. Corrothers, 42 W. Va. 59, 24 S. E. 569. 

Craft v. Mann, 46 W. Va. 478, 33 S. E. 260. 

Ketterman v. Ry. Co., 48 W. Va. 606, 37 S. E. 683. 

Wells v. Smith, 49 W. Va. 78, 38 S. E. 547. 

State v. Blair, 63 W. Va. 635, 60 S. E. 795. 

Hall v. Shelton, 93 W. Va. 592, 116 S. E. 12. 

Ry. Co. v. Shott, 92 W. Va. 34, 22 S. E. 811. 

Standard v. Wilson, 110 Va. 650, 66 S. E. 772. 

§ 1598. Rules of Virginia Supreme Court respecting bills or certificates of exceptions.

Rule XXIV of the Virginia Supreme Court respecting bills or certificates of exceptions is as follows: 

It shall not hereafter be necessary to incorporate in any bill or certificate of exception in any action of law, motion, criminal case, common-law or statutory proceeding, issue out of chancery or issue devisavit vel non-(a) any stenographic or other copy or report of testimony and other incidents of the trial therein, which is presented to the trial court or judge before or within sixty days after the final judgment, or order, and which is signed by the judge before or within seventy days after final judgment, or order, and lodged with the clerk of that court; (b) any plea, replication, or subsequent pleading, though rejected when tendered or thereafter stricken out; or (c) any depositions, affidavits, contracts in writing, instructions granted or refused, or any other writings, which were presented to the trial court; but such reports together with all such pleadings and documents which are lodged with the clerk of the trial court and shown by the record,

§ 1048 

or by such authenticated copy or report of testimony and other incidents of the trial, to have been before the trial court shall be deemed parts of the record in that court; and all questions properly raised, as required by Rule XXII, and all rulings thereon which, by the record or by such authenticated copy or report, are shown to have been excepted to, the grounds of such exception being also thereby shown with reasonable certainty, shall be subject to review in this court. (Code, section 5960.) (Effective 

June 16, 1930.) 

And in Nethers v. Nethers, 160 Va. 340, 168 S. E. 428, it is held that this Rule is not in conflict with the statutes. 

§ 1599. Rules of West Virginia Supreme Court relating to bills or certificates of exceptions.

The West Virginia Supreme Court has not revised its Rules since certificates in lieu of bills of exceptions were authorized by the 1931 Code. However, the existing Rules apply to certificates as well as bills of exceptions. They read: 

1. OFFICE AND CONTENTS. It is the office of a bill of ex ceptions to point out errors committed by the court during the progress of the trial. The bill or bills should contain only a concise statement of the facts necessary to present the points intended to be relied on as grounds of error, or only so much of the evidence as may appear necessary to present fairly the rulings of the court to which exceptions are taken. 

No bill of exceptions should contain matter irrelevant or unnecessary to the presentation of the question intended to be raised. 

2. POINTS MUST BE CLEARLY STATED. It is the duty of the exceptor to see that the points and objections on which he relies are correctly and clearly stated, so as to show plainly that an erroneous ruling was made to his prejudice, and should not leave that fact to appear merely by inference or conjecture. 

3. RULINGS ON EVIDENCE OR INSTRUCTION. 

An excep- tion to the admission or rejection of evidence or to the granting or refusal of instructions to the jury, should state so much of the evidence or facts proven as may be necessary to show the relevancy or irrelevancy of such evidence or the pertinency or imperti-

§ 1601 

nency of such instruction. The judge of the trial court should require all unnecessary matter to be stricken out before signing a bill of exceptions. $1600. Necessity for bills or certificates of exceptions.

It is the general rule that the errors or supposed errors of the trial court in its rulings during the trial will not be considered by the appellate on a writ of error unless they are objected or excepted to when made, and proper bills or certificates of exceptions taken. And this rule applies to rulings on a motion for a change of venue and the affidavits, exhibits and evidence introduced and heard in support thereof; to motion for a continuance and the evidence and affidavits in its support; to special pleas; to the evidence taken at the trial; to documentary evidence offered and rejected; and in Virginia to the instructions, but not in West 

Virginia. These subjects are discussed separately in subsequent sections. 

Tracy v. Coal Co., 57 W. Va. 587, 50 S. E. 825. 

State v. Banks, 61 W. Va. 9, 55 S. E. 739. 

State v. Stutler, 61 W. Va. 28, 55 S. E. 906. 

McKenzie v. Mackall, 85 W. Va. 391, 102 S. E. 118. 

Hall v. Shelton, 93 W. Va. 592, 116 S. E. 12. 

Moorefield v. Lewis, 96 W. Va. 112, 123 S. E. 564. 

Newberry v. Williams, 89 Va. 298, 15 S. E. 865. 

Ry. Co. v. Shott, 92 Va. 34, 22 S. E. 811. 

Land Co. v. Obenchain, 92 Va. 130, 22 S. E. 876. 

Nor may bills or certificates of exceptions be dispensed with, even though counsel may agree so to do and so stipulate in writings. 

Ry. Co. v. Shott, 92 Va. 34, 22 S. E. 811. 

Kibler v. Com., 94 Va. 804, 26 S. E. 858. 

§ 1601. Purpose of bills or certificates of exceptions. 

The purpose of bills or certificates of exceptions is to exhibit the errors or supposed errors of the trial court in the record. In 

Penix v. Grafton, 86 W. Va. 278, 103 S. E. 106, it is said: "The purpose of a bill of exceptions is to exhibit the supposed mistakes of the trial court which do not appear upon the record, and which cannot otherwise be brought

§ 1050 

before an appellate court for review and correction if erroneous." 

Milling Co. v. Milling Co., 78 W. Va. 314, 88 S. E. 1079. 

Mineral Co. v. Camden, 106 Va. 663, 56 S. E. 561. "The object of the institution of bills of exception was to enable a party to spread upon the record the matters that occurred at the trial." 

U. S. Co. v. Camden, etc., 106 Va. 666, 56 S. E. 561. "It is the office of a bill of exceptions to set forth a specific and definite allegation of error, and so much of the evidence as is necessary to a clear apprehension of the propriety or impropriety of the ruling made by the court, and if it fails to do this the exception will prove unavailing. Two or more objections may be saved by the same bill, provided they are distinctly set forth with the necessary circumstantiality, and not confused with one another. 

But the better practice is to take a separate bill for each objection." 

Holleran v. Meisel, 91 Va. 143, 21 S. E. 658. "The office of a bill of exception is to call the attention. of the court to some specific matter as to which error is claimed, and when the exceptant relies upon the bill of exceptions he must show by means of it the error complained of clearly and affirmatively; and in order to have relief he must further show that such error was to his prejudice." 

State v. Tucker, 52 W. Va. 421, 44 S. E. 427. 

Brown v. Hall, 85 Va. 146, 7 S. E. 182. 

Cobb v. Com., 125 Va. 941, 146 S. E. 270. 

Mill Co. v. Products Corp., 161 Va. 651, 171 S. E. 681. 

Virginia, etc. v. Coleman, 164 Va. 230, 178 S. E. 908. 

§ 1602. Essentials of bills or certificates of exceptions. 

To avail in the appellate court bills or certificates of exceptions must (1) be drawn so as to distinctly present the ruling objected to, (2) signed by the trial judge, and (3) dated so as to show that they were presented within the time fixed by the statute. 

But the judge's official designation is unnecessary, his signature alone is sufficient. 

See authorities cited in, Michie's Digest, vol. 4, p. 339, sec. 68.

§ 1603 1051 

30 151 202 375 Nor may such bills or certificates of exceptions be superseded by a certificate of the court clerk (or the reporter) as to what transpired during the progress of the trial. It is the province of the trial court, not the clerk (or reporter), to sign the bills of exceptions, or grant a certificate of the evidence or facts. 

Little v. Com., 141 Va. 532, 127 S. E. 164. 

§ 1603. Bills or certificates of exceptions must be signed by trial judge.

All bills or certificates of exceptions must be signed by the trial judge, that is, the judge who presided at the trial, whether regular or special, else they cannot be considered by the appellate court. 

Duckworth v. Stalnaker, 68 W. Va. 197, 69 S. E. 850. 

State v. Goldstrohm, 84 W. Va. 129, 99 S. E. 248. 

Coal Co. v. Cecil, 94 W. Va. 116, 117 S. E. 697. 

State v. Christian, 101 W. Va. 579, 133 S. E. 329. 

Blackwood Coal Co. v. James, 107 Va. 656, 60 S. E. 90. 

Colby v. Reams, 109 Va. 308, 63 S. E. 1009. 

In State v. Stevenson, 64 W. Va. 392, 62 S. E. 688, it is held: "It is reversible error for a regular judge, pending the trial of a cause begun and continued before a special judge duly elected to preside in the absence of such regular judge, on making his appearance at the same term, to assume jurisdiction thereof, proceed with the trial, and pronounce judgment therein.' 

Also in Carper v. Cook, 39 W. Va. 346, 19 S. E. 380, it is further held: * * * "A judge selected to try a certain case, who does try such case, becomes the court with regard to such case for all purposes and may sign bills of exception therein within thirty (now sixty) days after the adjournment of the term at which the trial is had, in all respects as though he were the regular judge of such court." 

And the convening of another term of court before the expiration of the statutory period in which bills or certificates of exceptions are to be tendered in nowise interferes with the jurisdiction of the trial judge to complete the record. 

Jacobs v. Williams, 67 W. Va. 377, 67 S. E. 1113. 

Hall v. Shelton, 93 W. Va. 596, 116 S. E. 12.

§ 1052 

 § 1604. Time when bills or certificates of exceptions must be tendered, rule in Virginia.

The Virginia Code, secs. 6252 and 6253, require all bills or certificates of exceptions to be tendered to the trial judge for his signature, either in term or vacation, within sixty days from the date on which final judgment was rendered, regardless of when the term of court adjourned, and the day on which the final judgment was rendered is to be counted as one of the days. But the judge may take an additional ten days for examination thereof and to affix his signature.

The authority of the judge to receive and sign bills or certificates of exceptions is derived from the statutes, and may be exercised only in accordance with their provisions. He has no power to extend the time, nor may such time be extended by agreement of counsel. And where tendered and signed after the expiration of such statutory period they form no part of the record in the case. 

Virginia, etc. v. Iron Co., 98 Va. 700, 37 S. E. 280. 

Colby v. Reams, 109 Va. 309, 63 S. E. 1009. 

Peanut Co. v. Wilson, 110 Va. 650, 66 S. E. 772. 

Southall v. Evans, 114 Va. 461, 76 S. E. 929. 

Moore v. Harrison, 114 Va. 424, 76 S. E. 920. 

Ratliff v. Meadows, 116 Va. 979, 83 S. E. 395. 

Conaway v. Com., 118 Va. 792, 88 S. E. 75. 

Bragg v. Justus, 129 Va. 354, 106 S. E. 335. 

Harley v. Com., 131 Va. 664, 108 S. E. 648. 

Dailey v. Com., 132 Va. 621, 111 S. E. 111. 

James v. Com., 133 Va. 723, 112 S. E. 761. 

Kelly v. Trehy, 133 Va. 160, 112 S. E. 757. 

Thrift v. Com., 133 Va. 800, 112 S. E. 770. 

Sorros v. Com., 133 Va. 798, 112 S. E. 771. 

Portner v. Portner, 133 Va. 251, 112 S. E. 762. 

Pembroke v. Com., 139 Va. 270, 123 S. E. 334. 

Curleson v. Com., 150 Va. 602, 143 S. E. 696. 

Ringstaff v. Ins. Co., 164 Va. 196, 179 S. E. 66. § 1605. Same, rule in West Virginia. 

The West Virginia Code, 56-6-35, 36 (secs. 5669 and 5670) require all bills and certificates of exceptions to be tendered and signed within sixty days after the adjournment of the term of

§ 1607 

court at which final judgment is entered. But the trial judge may by an order entered of record extend the time within which such bills or certificates may be tendered beyond the prescribed period of sixty days. However, unless such extension order is entered within the sixty days, the trial judge is without authority to receive or sign such bills or certificates of exceptions when tendered after the expiration of sixty days; and if presented and signed after the expiration of such period they constitute no part of the record in the case.

Jordan v. Jordan, 48 W. Va. 600, 37 S. E. 566. 

State v. Strayer, 58 W. Va. 676, 52 S. E. 862. 

Crowe v. Corp., 62 W. Va. 91, 57 S. E. 330.

§ 1606. Notice to opposing counsel, rule in Virginia. 

The Virginia Code, sec. 6252, provides that before the trial judge may sign bills or certificates of exceptions it must appear that the commonwealth's attorney has had reasonable notice in writing of the time when and place where they are to be presented or tendered to such judge. This provision is mandatory and must be strictly complied with. Otherwise such bills or certificates will not be considered by the appellate court. 

Schols v. Ins. Co., 145 Va. 694, 134 S. E. 729. 

Harrison v. Com., 159 Va. 986, 167 S. E. 251. 

Mill Co. v. Phos. Corp., 161 Va. 642, 171 S. E. 681. 

Nachman v. Bank, 161 Va. 576, 171 S. E. 676. 

Virginia, etc. v. Coleman, 164 Va. 230, 178 S. E. 908. § 1607. Same, rule in West Virginia.

In West Virginia there is no such statute, and no notice to the prosecuting attorney of the time and place of presentation of bills or certificates of exceptions to the trial judge is necessary. 2 CT-33

$ 1054 

§ 1608. When trial judge fails to sign bills or certificates of exceptions within statutory time.

In both Virginias it is held that where bills or certificates of exceptions have been tendered to the trial judge for his signature within the statutory period, the failure of such judge to sign the same does not deprive the party of his rights. 

In Conaway v. Com., 118 Va. 792, 88 S. E. 75, it is held: "Proper bills of exception tendered to the judge within the time prescribed by law are valid though not signed by him till after the expiration of such (statutory) time, or if he die, though signed by his successor in office, after the expiration of such time. If tendered in time but not signed, the signature may be compelled by mandamus after the expiration of the time prescribed by law for tendering such bills. A party who has done everything required of him by law to perfect his bill of exception will not be deprived of his rights by the failure of the judge to sign the bill." 

This case overrules Anderson v. Com., 105 Va. 533, 54 S. E. 

305. See also, Mitchell v. Com., 140 Va. 572, 125 S. E. 311. 

And in State v. Berle, 117 W. Va. 825, 188 S. E. 481, it is also held: "The fact that the certificate of evidence was not signed by trial judge within sixty days after adjournment of the term held not to require dismissal of writ of error where certificate was prepared and called to the judge's attention within the required time, although not then signed for reasons not the fault of the judge.' 99 § 1609. Duty of trial judge when bills or certificates do not fairly state the truth.

When the bills or certificates of exceptions do not fairly state the truth, the judge may not simply refuse to sign them. He must go further, and with the aid of counsel settle the bills or certificates, and, when settled, sign them. In Page v. Clopton, 30 

Gratt. 427, it is held: "If the bill presented is not truthful and fair, the judge should alter it, making it such, or suggest what alterations

§ 1612 

should be made, where such alterations can be made in the draft; or, when necessary, he may require it to be redrafted in accordance with such suggestions; for he is not bound to sign a bill that is not true." 

Douglas v. Loomis, 5 W. Va. 542.

Poteet v. County, 30 W. Va. 58, 3 S. E. 97. 

Collins v. Christian, 92 Va. 731, 24 S. E. 472. 

Cummings v. Armstrong, 34 W. Va. 1, 11 S. E. 742. 

Bailey Lum. Co. v. Ward, 109 W. Va. 57, 152 S. E. 862. § 1610. Evidence must be transcribed when bills or certificates are signed. 

In Tracy v. Coal Co., 57 Va. 587, 50 S. E. 825, it is held: "* * * at the time the bill is signed, the evidence must be actually transcribed, and, unless it is attached to the bill, it must bear some mark of identification, such as is required in making any other paper or document a part of such bill." 

McKendree v. Shelton, 51 W. Va. 516, 41 S. E. 909.

Parr v. Currence, 58 W. Va. 523, 52 S. E. 496. 

State v. Strayer, 58 W. Va. 676, 52 S. E. 862.

State v. Coal Co., 109 W. Va. 559, 155 S. E. 667. 

Tracy v. Coal Co., 57 W. Va. 587, 50 S. E. 825. § 1611. Exceptions based upon overruling a motion for a continuance.

Where a motion for a continuance is supported by affidavits or oral evidence, or both, such affidavits and evidence must be made a part of the record by a formal bill or certificate of exceptions. 

Otherwise advantage thereof may not be had in the appellate court. 

Queen v. Westfall, 86 W. Va. 298, 103 S. E. 115. § 1612. Exceptions based upon the rejection of special pleas.

Where a special plea is tendered and rejected by the trial court, or a demurrer sustained thereto, it must be made a part of the record by a proper bill or certificate of exception. Otherwise it is not available in the appellate court.

§ 

1056 

 White v. Toncray, 9 Leigh 347. 

King v. Burdette, 12 W. Va. 688. 

Lawrence v. Com., 86 Va. 573, 10 S. E. 840. 

Fry v. Lesslie, 87 Va. 269, 12 S. E. 671. 

Leary v. Briggs, 114 Va. 411, 76 S. E. 907. 

Bank v. Ashworth, 122 Va. 170, 94 S. E. 469.

But if such plea is made a part of the record by an order of the court, which shows that its rejection was excepted to, the appellate court will review the action of the lower court although no formal bill or certificate of exception was taken. 

Sweeney v. Baker, 13 W. Va. 160. 

King v. Burdette, supra. 

Roanoke, etc. v. Hickson, 80 Va. 589. 

State v. Wetzel, 75 W. Va. 20, 83 S. E. 68.

Such order, however, must fully identify the plea which it purports to bring into the record as fully and completely as the requirements of a bill or certificate of exceptions. 

Queen v. Westfall, 86 W. Va. 298, 103 S. E. 115. § 1613. Exceptions based upon the rejection of proper evidence, or the admission of improper evidence. 

It is the general rule that a party complaining of the rejection of proffered evidence, or the admission of improper evidence, must state the facts in his bill or certificate of exceptions from which it will appear affirmatively to the appellate court that the evidence was improper. Where the rejected evidence is oral the record must show what the witness would have said; if documentary, the documents themselves must be made a part of the record. Otherwise the appellate court cannot determine whether the complaining party has been prejudiced. 

Johnson v. Jennings, 10 Gratt. 1. 

Beirne v. Rosser, 26 Gratt. 537. 

Jackson v. Com., 98 Va. 845, 36 S. E. 487. 

Myers v. Com., 132 Va. 746, 111 S. E. 463. 

Burgess v. Com., 136 Va. 697, 118 S. E. 273. 

Halstead v. Horton, 38 W. Va. 727, 18 S. E. 953. 

Sesler v. Coal Co., 51 W. Va. 318, 41 S. E. 216. 

Oil Co. v. Bartlett, 62 W. Va. 700, 59 S. E. 634.

State v. Farley, 78 W. Va. 471, 89 S. E. 738.

In Triplett v. Bank, 121 Va. 189, 92 S. E. 897, it is held: "The refusal of the trial court to permit a witness to answer a question will not be considered on appeal when the expected answer is not given, as the appellate court cannot determine its materiality." 

Nease v. Capehart, 15 W. Va. 299.

And in Levine v. Lynchburg, 156 Va. 1007, 159 S. E. 95, it is said: "A judgment will not be reversed because evidence has been excluded or rejected by the trial court, unless its materiality is made to appear. In order to show that the trial court erred in rejecting an offer of evidence, or in excluding evidence, the bills of exceptions must show the materiality of the evidence tendered. Where a question is asked, and the witness is not permitted to answer, the bill of exceptions must show what the party offering the evidence expected or proposed to prove by him. If the witness is permitted to answer, and the answer is excluded, it should show what the answer was. This is necessary because it may be that the witness had no knowledge upon the subject, or what he knew was irrelevant or immaterial. 

A judgment will not be reversed because evidence has been excluded or rejected by the trial court unless its materiality is made to appear." 99

Also Guyandotte, etc. v. Virginia, etc., 94 W. Va. 308, 118 S. 

E. 512, it is held: "Errors in the rulings of the trial court upon admission and rejection of evidence are deemed to have been waived if they are not made grounds of the motion for a new trial, nor subjects of special bills of exceptions showing the evidence and ruling of the court thereon." Citing, Bartlett v. Bank, 77 W. Va. 329, 87 S. E. 444. 

Parr v. Howell, 74 W. Va. 413, 82 S. E. 126.

And in the same case the court, quoting from Ireland v. Smith, 73 W. Va. 755, 81 S. E. 542, further said: "During the trial the court overruled the defendants' motion to exclude certain testimony, but there is no formal bill of exception specially calling our attention to that error, nor does it appear that the trial court's attention was called to it on the motion for a new trial. Apparently the only ground offered in support of the motion for a new trial is that the verdict was contrary to law and evidence. Not having called the lower court's attention to the error now complained of in one of the above ways, under the rule long established by this court, the error will be treated as waived." See cases cited in opinion. 

And also quoting from State v. Henaghan, 73 W. Va. 706, 81 

S. E. 539, it is further said: "This court does not consider, and will treat as waived, a claim that evidence was improperly admitted over objection and exception, unless by bill of exceptions attention is directed to the evidence complained of. A bill of exceptions making all the evidence in the case part of the record will not avail, though therein is noted the introduction of such evidence and the objection and exception thereto, unless the record discloses reliance on such objection in support of a motion for a new trial." 

Elec. Co. v. Lake, 105 Va. 311, 54 S. E. 328.

not certified or in any manner made part of the record, will be dismissed, as improvidently awarded." 

Griffith v. Corrothers, 42 W. Va. 59, 24 S. E. 569.

And in Virginia it is further held that bills or certificates of exceptions relating to evidence, either received or rejected, must incorporate the specific evidence relied upon; that the appellate court cannot be burdened with a search through the stenographer's report to ascertain what objections have been made to the reception or rejection of evidence and the rulings of the court thereon. If they are relied on such alleged errors must be made parts of the record by proper bills of exceptions. Otherwise they will be deemed waived.

§ 1614. How materiality of rejected evidence may be shown. 

Where evidence is offered and rejected or excluded by the trial court, counsel should avouch the record so as to show what such evidence would have been. This may be done by having the witness answer the question or questions out of the hearing of the jury, or by counsel simply stating in the record what the witness would say were he permitted to answer the question. 

In Davis v. Lumber Co., 85 W. Va. 191, 101 S. E. 447, it is held: 

66* * * This materiality may be shown by allowing the witness to answer the question in the absence of the jury (for the benefit of the record) or by (counsel) stating in the record the answer the witness is expected to make."

§ 

1060 

Lord v. Henderson, 65 W. Va. 321, 64 S. E. 134. 

Delmar, etc. v. Bartlett, 62 W. Va. 700, 59 S. E. 634. 

In State v. Clifford, 59 W. Va. 11, 52 S. E. 981, it is said: "To make such an error cause of reversal, it is only necessary that the relevancy and materiality of the evidence offered shall appear. When this is not disclosed by the nature of the question, it is necessary that it be made to appear in some other way, and this is usually done by statements of counsel, showing what he expects to prove and how it becomes relevant to the issue." 

See cases cited in opinion. Also, Jones v. Com., 135 Va. 550, 115 S. E. 378. 

And in State v. Price, 92 W. Va. 543, 115 S. E. 393, it is held: "The refusal of the trial court to permit a question to be answered, cannot properly be made the basis of an assignment of error, unless it appears from the bill of exceptions that the answer which would have been given to the question is material to the party offering the evidence, and this materiality may be shown by allowing the witness to answer the question in the absence of the jury, or by stating in the record the answer the witness is expected to make." 

But such bill or certificate of exception, in addition to the question or questions asked and the avouched answer or answers, must contain enough of the preceding evidence to give the appellate court a clear understanding of the propriety or impropriety of the ruling of the trial court, or it is fatally defective. 

Jacobs v. Warthen, 115 Va. 571, 80 S. E. 113. 

Powers v. Hamilton, 117 Va. 810, 86 S. E. 98. 

Burton v. Seifert & Co., 108 Va. 338, 61 S. E. 933. 

Railway v. Ward, 119 Va. 334, 89 S. E. 140. 

Coleman v. Com., 84 Va. 7, 3 S. E. 878. § 1615. Exceptions based upon rejection of records or documentary evidence.

Where records or documents are offered in evidence and rejected, such records or documents themselves must be made a part of the record by proper bills or certificates of exceptions, else the appellate court cannot see whether the complaining party has been prejudiced.

§ 1617 

Delmar, etc. v. Bartlett, 62 W. Va. 700, 59 S. E. 634.

§ 1616. Exceptions based upon the giving or refusing of instructions, rule in Virginia. 

In Virginia the instructions, whether given or refused, are no part of the record unless made so by proper bills or certificates of exceptions in accordance with the statutes. In Ry. Co. v. 

Chandler, 129 Va. 695, 106 S. E. 684, it is held: * * "The instructions are no part of the record unless made so by a bill of exceptions or certificate in accordance with the statutory requirements on that subject. *

In- structions which are not certified by the judge of the trial court within the period of sixty days fixed by the statute (secs. 6252-6253, Code) cannot be made a part of the record under the provision of this section." 

Mitchell v. Com., 93 Va. 775, 20 S. E. 892. 

Newport Co. v. Lake, 105 Va. 311, 54 S. E. 328. 

K. of C. v. Burroughs, 107 Va. 671, 60 S. E. 40. 

Little v. Com., 141 Va. 523, 127 S. E. 164.

And all instructions must be certified, else it cannot be said that the refusal of the trial court to give a certain instruction is reversible error, because the instruction in question may have been covered by some other instruction that was given. 

Harris v. Com., 133' Va. 700, 112 S. E. 753. § 1617. Same, rule in West Virginia.

In West Virginia no bills or certificates of exceptions are necessary to make instructions, whether given or refused, a part of the record. Code 56-6-20 (sec. 5654) provides: "All instructions given shall be read by the court to the jury as the action and ruling of the court, without reference to or disclosing the party by whom they may have been prayed. Every instruction or charge in writing read

§ 1062 

to the jury and every instruction or charge in writing prayed by any party and refused by the court, provided, in either case, that such instruction or charge have a notation thereon showing the action of the court with reference thereto over the signature of the judge, together with the objections and exceptions thereto, endorsed thereon, be a part of the record in the case and shall be included and copied in any transcript of the record without the formality of a bill of exceptions or any formal certification * * * " 

§ 1618. When bills or certificates of exceptions are necessary, rule in Virginia.

In Virginia it is a rule of practice, recognized by the appellate court, that errors apparent on the face of the record will be noticed though no bills or certificates of exceptions have been taken. 

Strange v. Strange, 76 Va. 240. 

Nutt v. Summers, 78 Va. 164. 

Cralle v. Cralle, 84 Va. 202, 6 S. E. 12. 

Trust Co. v. Com., 151 Va. 883, 141 S. E. 825, 145 S.

E. 326. § 1619. Same, rule in West Virginia.

In West Virginia, however, Virginia's rule of practice has been written into the statutes. Code, 56-6-35 (sec. 5669) provides: "Any party may avail himself of any error appearing on the record, by which he is prejudiced, without obtaining a formal bill of exceptions, provided he objects or excepts on the record to the action of the court complained of, and provided it is such a matter as can be considered without a formal bill of exceptions." 

And it is held that this language means "without filing a bill of exceptions." But an objection or exception is necessary, although a formal bill of exceptions thereto is dispensed with. 

Perry v. Horn, 22 W. Va. 381. 

Sweeney v. Baker, 13 W. Va. 158. 

Danks v. Rhodeheaver, 26 W. Va. 274. 

Hughes v. Frum, 41 W. Va. 452, 23 S. E. 604. 

Gilmer v. Sydenstricker, 42 W. Va. 52, 24 S. E. 566. 

Jones v. Harmer, 60 W. Va. 479, 55 S. E. 657. 

Milling Co. v. Milling Co., 78 W. Va. 314, 88 S. E. 1079.

§ 1620 

7 1 Also where the stenographic report of the evidence taken at the trial is made a part of the certificate of evidence upon a motion for a new trial, and it shows objections or exceptions to questions or evidence and rulings of the court thereon, and the particular question or evidence complained of is specified distinctly in such motion for a new trial, or in an assignment of error, or in brief of counsel, so that the appellate court can readily and safely find the particular question or evidence to which the exceptions relate, it will consider the matter objected or excepted to, though there is no formal bill of exceptions thereto; but such matter will not be considered without such specification, even though such report of evidence notes such objections and exceptions.

State v. Bingham, 42 W. Va. 234, 24 S. E. 883. § 1620. What constitutes the record in the absence of bills or certificates of exceptions.

In the absence of any bills or certificates of exceptions, the record in a criminal case consists of the following: 

1. The indictment. 

2. The order showing the finding and recordation of the indictment. 

3. The award of jury process. 

4. The demurrer and motion to quash. 

5. The order empaneling and swearing the jury. 

6. The plea. 

7. The issue. 

8. The instructions given and refused in West Virginia, but not so in Virginia. 

9. The verdict. 

10. Motion to set aside a verdict of guilty and grant prisoner a new trial, and the reasons therefor should be set out in the order. 

11. Asking prisoner why sentence should not now be passed upon him. 

12. The judgment.

§ 

1064 

13. Any other matter or procedure had in the course of the trial sufficiently set out and identified in the orders of the court.

To become a part of the record so as to be considered by the appellate court all other matters must be made so by proper bills or certificates of exceptions. 

§ 1621. Reporter's transcript of evidence not a part of record.

It is the general rule that the evidence taken down by an official stenographer, transcribed and certified by him as a true and correct transcript of the evidence is not a part of the record, and can only be made such by a proper bill of exceptions. 

Tracy v. Carver, etc., 57 W. Va. 587, 50 S. E. 825. 

Dudley v. Barrett, 58 W. Va. 235, 52 S. E. 100. 

Bond v. Fire Ins. Co., 77 W. Va. 736, 88 S. E. 389. 

Milling Co. v. Milling Co., 78 W. Va. 314, 88 S. E. 1079. 

Hall v. Shelton, 93 W. Va. 592, 116 S. E. 12. 

Coal Co. v. Cecil, 94 W. Va. 116, 117 S. E. 697. 

Conley v. Thompson, 99 W. Va. 627, 129 S. E. 397. 

Sheppard v. Ins. Co., 108 W. Va. 569, 151 S. E. 846. 

§ 1622. Skeleton bills or certificates of exceptions. 

In Conley v. Thompson, 99 W. Va. 623, 129 S. E. 397, it is held: "What is familiarly known as a skeleton bill of exceptions, that is, a bill which provides for the subsequent copying by the clerk into it, and as a part of it, some paper or document is allowed, yet to make such a bill valid and complete, these rules must be regarded: (1) The bill in referring to such paper or document must purport to incorporate it into, and make it a part of, the bill. (2) The document must itself at the time of the signature of the bill be in existence, written out and complete. (3) It must be annexed to the bill, and referred to as annexed; or it must be so marked by letter, number, or other means of identification as to leave no doubt, when found in the record, that it is the one referred to in the bill; and these means of identification must be obvious to

§ 1624 

all, so that anyone examining the record can know what document or paper is to be inserted, or after its insertion, that the clerk has made no mistake." Citing, Tracy v. Carver, etc., 57 W. Va. 587, 50 S. E. 825. 

Thornton v. Com., 113 Va. 736, 73 S. E. 481.

Parr v. Currence, 58 W. Va. 523, 52 S. E. 496. 

Sims v. Capper, 133 Va. 278, 112 S. E. 676. 

Reynolds v. Com., 135 Va. 722, 115 S. E. 514. 

§ 1623. One bill or certificate of exceptions may refer to another.

It is also held that one bill or certificate of exceptions may refer to another, provided the latter is sufficiently identified; and the bill or certificate so referred to may be considered on questions presented in the former. 

State v. Legg, 59 W. Va. 315, 53 S. E. 545. 

Marshall v. Stalnaker, 70 W. Va. 394, 74 S. E. 48. 

Arnold v. Hawkins, 79 W. Va. 205, 90 S. E. 678. 

Bernard v. Com., 134 Va. 613, 114 S. E. 563. § 1624. Bills or certificates of exceptions not subject to amendment. 

In Tracy v. Coal Co., 57 W. Va. 592, 50 S. E. 825, it is said: "The authorities upon this point are greatly in conflict. 

Our statutes provide that bills of exception must be taken during the term at which the final judgment is rendered, or within thirty days thereafter, and this Court has held, in 

State v. McGlumphy, 37 W. Va. 805, 17 S. E. 315, and 

Jordan v. Jordan, 48 W. Va. 600, 37 S. E. 556, where a bill of exceptions was taken after the expiration of thirty days, that it could not be treated as a part of the record; and while all courts have the inherent power to correct clerical errors and misprisons in their records, yet we cannot subscribe to the doctrine that after the right to take a bill of exception is barred by the statute, and after the parties, in due course of the proceeding, have, both in law and in fact, been dismissed from the court, that a court or judge can enter any further order in the case, judicially acting upon the rights of the parties." See cases cited in opinion.

§ 1066 

§ 1625. Bills or certificates need not be recorded.

When the trial judge, either in term or vacation, signs the bills or certificates of exceptions and so certifies, it is not necessary that the clerk should spread them as a whole, or any part thereof, upon the order book. 

Bank v. Wetzel, 58 W. Va. 1, 50 S. E. 886. 

See authorities cited in next succeeding section. 

§ 1626. Order of trial court necessary to make bills or certificates of exceptions a part of record.

It is the general rule that although bills or certificates of exceptions be made up and signed by the trial judge within the statutory time, they are not properly a part of the record so as to be considered by the appellate court unless the judge has within such time certified them to the clerk of the court by a certificate or an order to be recorded in the order book under the caption of the case. However, the fact that the certificate or order of the judge does not reach the clerk, or is not recorded by him within the statutory time, will not vitiate the bills or certificates of exceptions. But the certificate or order must be recorded in the order book and a copy thereof appear in the transcript of the record to make such bills or certificates a part thereof. 

Craft v. Mann, 46 W. Va. 478, 33 S. E. 260. 

Ketterman v. Ry. Co., 48 W. Va. 606, 37 S. E. 683. 

Wells v. Smith, 49 W. Va. 79, 38 S. E. 547. 

Bank v. Wetzel, 58 W. Va. 1, 50 S. E. 886. 

Jones v. Harmer, 60 W. Va. 479, 55 S. E. 657. 

State v. Blair, 63 W. Va. 635, 60 S. E. 795. 

Supply Co. v. Irwin, 64 W. Va. 55, 60 S. E. 990. 

Shepherd v, Ex. Co., 65 W. Va. 602, 64 S. E. 720. 

State v. Yoes, 67 W. Va. 546, 68 S. E. 181. 

DeFroscia v. Ry. Co., 68 W. Va. 136, 69 S. E. 1008. 

Miller v. Starcher, 86 W. Va. 90, 102 S. E. 809. 

Penix v. Grafton, 86 W. Va. 278, 103 S. E. 106. 

Hall v. Shelton, 93 W. Va. 592, 116 S. E. 12. 

But in State v. Thornhill, 111 W. Va. 259, 161 S. E. 431, the order making the bills of exceptions was signed by the trial judge within the statutory period, but was "inadvertently not spread upon the order book." A nunc pro tunc order of the trial judge

§ 1627 

making such bills of exception a part of the record was filed with the appellate court. The court held this could be done, and said: “An order can be entered nunc pro tunc to make a record of what was previously done by the court although not then entered, but where the court has wholly omitted to make an order which it might or ought to have made, it cannot afterwards be entered nunc pro tunc." Citing, Payne v. Riggs, 80 W. Va. 57, 92 S. E. 133. 

Tracy v. Coal Co., 57 W. Va. 592, 50 S. E. 825. 

Cameron v. Cameron, 105 W. Va. 621, 143 S. E. 349.

Supply Co. v. Coal Co., 110 W. Va. 560, 158 S. E. 907. 

State v. McGlumphy, 37 W. Va. 805, 17 S. E. 315. 

Jordan v. Jordan, 48 W. Va. 600, 32 S. E. 1022.

FORMS OF BILLS OF EXCEPTIONS. 

Forms for certificates of exceptions are set out in the respective Codes of Virginia and West Virginia, and it is unnecessary to repeat them here. However, since the statutes do not prescribe forms for bills of exceptions, a few are included as a guide and may be modified to meet any situation likely to arise. Of course, each bill must be headed with the style of the case. In West Virginia the plaintiff is "State of West Virginia," while in Virginia it is "Commonwealth of Virginia." § 1627. But the better form is to incorporate in one bill of exceptions all instructions given by the state, offered by the defense and given, those offered by the defense and modified by the court and given, as well as those offered by the defense and refused. The appellate court then has the advantage of having before it in connected form all the instructions and the action of the trial court with reference thereto.

A paragraph may be added excepting to the action of the trial court in giving instructions on its own motion over the objection of defendant; and also where the trial court gives instructions without first submitting them to counsel for defendant.

§ 1638. Order of circuit court filing petition for a writ of error from an inferior court.

Under the present West Virginia Constitution, where the trial is had in a court other than a circuit court an application for a writ of error must first be made to the circuit court of the county before such application may be made to the Supreme Court of Appeals. (Caption as in sec. 1635.)

This day came the defendant in the above styled cause, by counsel, and tendered and asked leave to file his duly verified written petition praying that a writ of error and supersedeas may be

§ 1082 

granted him herein, and that the judgment of conviction be reviewed, the verdict of the jury set aside, and a new trial awarded him, which said petition is accompanied by a transcript of the evidence heard at the trial of said cause, and his several bills of exceptions numbered from 1 to inclusive, which leave is granted. And it is therefore ordered that said petition, with the accompanying papers identified as aforesaid, be and the same is hereby accordingly filed. 

See note to sec. 189. § 1639. Order of circuit court rejecting petition for writ of error from conviction in inferior court. (Caption as in sec. 1634.)

on, sentencing your petitioner to confinement in the State Penitentiary at Moundsville, West Virginia for the term and period of .... years, to which action and ruling of the court, your petitioner duly excepted. 

(Such other facts may be inserted as are pertinent to the case.)

ASSIGNMENT OF ERRORS. 

Your petitioner says that in the trial of this case certain errors were committed by the trial court to his prejudice, to which he makes the following assignment: 

1. Because the trial court erred in overruling defendant's motion for a continuance. 

2. Because the trial court erred in refusing to sustain defendant's motion to quash the indictment in this case. 

3. Because the trial court erred in refusing to sustain defendant's demurrer to said indictment. 

4. Because the trial court erred in admitting and allowing to go to the jury, over the objections and exception of the defendant, certain improper, incompetent and irrelevant evidence offered by the state, as will appear from the Bills of Exception herein. 

5. Because the trial court erred, at the conclusion of the state's evidence, in refusing to direct a verdict of not guilty, on motion of the defendant. 

6. Because the trial court erred in refusing to admit and allow to go to the jury, over the objections and exceptions of the defendant, certain competent and relevant testimony offered by your petitioner, as will appear from the Bills of Exception herein. 

7. Because the trial court erred in giving to the jury, in writing, improper instructions at the instance of and on motion of the State, as will appear from the Bills of Exception herein. 

8. Because the trial court erred in refusing to give to the jury proper instructions offered and requested by the defendant, in writing, over the objections and exception of your petitioner, as will appear from the Bills of Exception herein. 

9. Because the trial court erred in modifying and giving as modified proper instructions in writing, offered and requested by

§ 1640 

the defendant, over the objections and exception of your petitioner, as will appear from the Bills of Exception herein. 

10. Because the trial court erred in refusing to set aside the verdict of the jury, on motion of the defendant, as contrary to the law and the evidence, and to award your petitioner a new trial. 

11. Because the trial court erred in overruling your petitioner's motion in arrest of judgment. 

12. Because the trial court erred in entering judgment against your petitioner and sentencing him to confinement in the State Penitentiary at Moundsville, West Virginia, at hard labor, for the term and period of ... years. 

13. Because the trial court committed other errors which are apparent on the face of the record, which are to be hereafter assigned. 

(Additional errors may be assigned, or any of the above omitted, as the facts warrant.)

Therefore, because of the reasons and errors hereinbefore specifically assigned, and for other errors apparent on the face of the record, to be hereafter assigned, committed by the trial court to his prejudice, your petitioner prays that a writ of error and supersedeas to said judgment may be granted him, and that said judgment may be reviewed, said verdict set aside and a new trial awarded your petitioner and this case be remanded for a new trial in accordance with the laws of this state, as defined by the opinion of Your Honors to be expressed in this case. And as in duty bound, he will ever pray, etc.

§ 1641. For failure to prepare grand jury list at proper time. (Caption as in sec. 1635.)

And the said defendant, C. D., in his own proper person comes and defends the wrong and injury, when, etc., and for plea says that the indictment herein against him was not made or found by a grand jury of the State of West Virginia, in and for the body of the said County of then and there attending the circuit court of said county, because he says that the jury commissioners of the circuit court of 

County, West

Virginia, did not, at the levy term of the county court of said. 

County, in the year 19.., nor at any other time when required by the circuit court of said county, or the Judge thereof, in vacation, prepare a list of not less than one hundred nor more than two hundred qualified persons of their county, for grand jury service; that the grand jurors who found and returned the indictment herein against this defendant were not drawn or selected from any list of names prepared by the said jury commissioners of the circuit court of 

County, West Virginia, for grand jury service and that the said indictment returned herein against this defendant was not found or returned by a grand 

---

§ 1088 

jury selected or drawn from a list of persons duly and legally selected by said jury commissioners to serve as such grand jurors. And this the said defendant is ready to verify.

Whereupon the said defendant prays the judgment of the Court on said indictment and that the same may be abated and quashed. 

C. D., Defendant. (Add verification as sec. 1634.)

NOTE: In both Virginias it is held that the appropriate way to put in issue the validity of an indictment because of the improper constitution of the grand jury which returned it is by plea in abatement. 

Com. v. Carter, 2 Va. Cas. 319. 

Com. v. Cherry, 2 Va. Cas. 20. 

Kerby v. Com., 7 Leigh 747. 

Com. v. St. Clair, 1 Gratt. 556. 

State v. Young, 82 W. Va. 714, 97 S. E. 134. 

State v. Cook, 81 W. Va. 686, 95 S. E. 792. 

And in State v. Young, 82 W. Va. 714, 97 S. E. 134, it is held that a paper styled a "Motion to Quash" and filed in time for a plea in abatement will be treated as such plea. 

See secs. 78 to 81, inclusive. § 1642. That grand jury was improperly selected. (Caption as in sec. 1635.)

And the said defendant, C. D., in his own proper person, comes and defends the wrong and injury, when, etc., and for plea says that the indictment herein against him was not made or found by a grand jury of the State of West Virginia, in and for the body of the said County of then and there attending the cir-

cuit court of said County, and properly constituted under the law, because he says that he, the said defendant herein, is a colored person of African descent, commonly known as a Negro, and that the jury commissioners of said County, whose duty it is under the law to select persons from whom the grand jury which found the indictment in this case against said defendant were taken, selected no persons of color, or of African descent, commonly known as 

Negroes, but on the contrary excluded from their list of persons so selected for grand jury service in said County all persons of color, or of African descent, commonly known as Negroes, solely because of their race and color; and that the grand jury which found and returned the indictment herein against this said defendant was composed exclusively of persons of the white race, and all persons of color, or of African descent, commonly called Negroes, were excluded therefrom solely because of their race and color; that the colored race, or persons of African descent, commonly called Negroes, constitutes one-eighth of the entire population of said

County, a very large number of whom are persons of good moral character, who have never been convicted of a felony or any scandalous offense, and who were bona fide citizens of the State of West Virginia, and the said County of for at least one year immediately preceding the preparation of the grand jury list from which the grand jury which found and returned the indictment herein were drawn and selected, and who were not officeholders under the laws of the United States or of the said State of West Virginia, (add any other qualification which the statutes of Virginia may prescribe), and who were otherwise in every respect qualified to act and serve as grand jurors, and that all such colored persons, or persons of African descent, commonly known as Negroes, were excluded from serving as grand jurors, and were excluded from serving on the grand jury which found and returned the indictment herein against this defendant solely on the ground of their race and color, all which denied to this defendant the equal protection of the laws, and by reason of such discrimination this defendant was and has been denied and deprived of a sacred right guaranteed to him by the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of this State.

§ 1092 

Wherefore, the said defendant prays judgment of the court on said indictment and that the same may be abated and quashed. (Add verification as in sec. 1634.) See

State v. McClelland, 85 W. Va. 289, 101 S. E. 472. 

Younge v. U. S. (W. Va.), 242 Fed. 788.

NOTE: It is usually held that a plea in abatement raising objections to the manner of organizing the grand jury, or to the qualifications of grand jurors, is waived by pleading the general issue alone. 

Early v. Com., 86 Va. 921, 11 S. E. 795.

H. was not a constable in the said county. And this the said J. S. prays may be inquired of by the country. 

§ 1659. To plea of misnomer. 

(Caption as in sec. 1635.)

And hereupon J. S., prosecuting attorney (Commonwealth's attorney in Virginia), who prosecutes for the said State (or Commonwealth) in this behalf, says, that the said indictment, by reason of anything by the said C. D. (using name which defendant claims in his plea) in his said plea alleged, ought not to be quashed; because he says that the said C. D. long before and at the time of the preferring of the said indictment, was and still is known as well by the name of A. B. (the name which the indictment give him) as by the name C. D., to-wit, in the said County of ... and this the said J. S. prays may be inquired into by the country. ...... 

§ 1660. To plea to jurisdiction. 

(Caption as in sec. 1635.)

And hereupon J. S., prosecuting attorney (or Commonwealth's

§ 1661 

attorney in Virginia), who prosecutes for the said State (or Commonwealth) in this behalf, says, that notwithstanding anything by the said C. D. in pleading alleged, this court ought not to be precluded from taking cognizance of the indictment aforesaid; because he says that (here set out the facts relied on, and if it is new matter add the verification; if not, the conclusion is to the country; thus), and this the said J. S. for the said State (or Commonwealth) is ready to verify (or, prays may be inquired into by the country). Wherefore he prays judgment, and that the said C. D. may answer to the said indictment. 

§ 1661. Plea of nolo contendere. 

(Caption as in sec. 1635.)

And the said C. D. in his own proper person comes into court here, and, having heard the said indictment read, says, by permission of the court here, that he will not contend with the said State (or Commonwealth in Virginia), and here he puts himself upon the clemency of the court. 2 CT-36

Appendix Treason Treason, either against the United States or a State, is not a felony, but a crime of a higher grade. Hence it is not considered in this work. However, from an historical standpoint, we here append the indictment against Frank Keeney, and others, for treason against the State of West Virginia in the celebrated "Miners' March" in 1921.

STATE OF WEST VIRGINIA, COUNTY OF LOGAN. 

To-wit: 

In the Circuit Court of Logan County: 

The grand jurors of the State of West Virginia, in and for the body of the County of Logan, upon their oaths present that 

Frank Keeney (and others) of Kanawha, Boone and Raleigh 

Counties, West Virginia, on the ...... .... day of August, 1921, they, the said Frank Keeney (and others) being persons then and there abiding within the State of West Virginia, and deriving protection from the laws of said State, and then and there owing allegiance and fidelity to the said State, and being then and there members and citizens thereof, not regarding their duties of their said allegiance and fidelity, but wickedly devising and intending the peace and tranquility of the said State, to disturb and destroy, on the of August, 1921, at Marmet, Kanawha County, West Virginia, and at the City of Charleston in said Kanawha County, West Virginia, did then and there unlawfully, maliciously and traitorously conspire, to levy war against the State of West Virginia; and to fulfill and effect the said traitorous compassings, intentions and conspirings of them the said 

Frank Keeney (and others), they, the said Frank Keeney (and others) aforesaid, that is to say on the of 

August, 1921, and on the 

of September, 1921, at Marmet in said Kanawha County with Mose Adkins (and others) and with a great multitude of other persons, whose names are to the jurors aforesaid as yet unknown, to the number of from eight to ten thousand, armed and arrayed in a warlike 

---

manner, that is to say, with machine guns, high power rifles, military rifles, pistols and revolvers and other warlike weapons, ammunition and supplies, as well offensive as defensive, being then and there unlawfully, maliciously and traitorously assembled and gathered together, did falsely, maliciously and traitorously assemble, combine, conspire and join themselves together against the said State, and then and there with force and arms, did wickedly, falsely, maliciously and traitorously and in a warlike and hostile manner, array and dispose themselves against the said State, and then and there on the day and dates above mentioned in pursuance of such malicious and traitorous intentions, conspirings and purposes they the said Frank Keeney (and others) with the said Mose Adkins (and others), and the said other persons to the jurors aforesaid unknown, so as aforesaid traitorously assembled, armed and arrayed, in manner aforesaid, most wickedly, maliciously and traitorously did ordain, and prepare and levy war against the said State, contrary to their duties of the allegiance of the said Frank Keeney (and others); and that the said Frank Keeney (and others) did then and there in pursuance of such their malicious and traitorous intentions, conspirings and purposes march in battle or military array to Blair, Logan County and to other places in said Logan County and did then and there wickedly, maliciously and traitorously and within the jurisdiction of this court on the days of August, 1921 and on the days of September, 1921, did engage in a series of battles with the military forces of the State of West Virginia, and with other forces who were then and there acting under the control and direction of the Chief Executive, the Governor of the State of West Virginia, and the said military forces of the State of West Virginia, who were then and there defending the said State of West Virginia and the people of Logan County and Mingo County of said State, from the invasion of said armed forces so maliciously and traitorously assembled, and then and there engaging in war as aforesaid, all with the malicious, wicked and traitorous intentions on the part of the said Frank Keeney (and others) to invade Logan and Mingo Counties of said State and by force, violence, murder and open warfare to deprive the people residing within said counties and mem- ...

Morgan, acting under and in pursuance of the Constitution and laws of the State of West Virginia, proclaimed, by proclamations duly and lawfully issued, martial law in the County of Mingo in said State," which proclamation is in words and figures following, to-wit: (Here were inserted two official proclamations of the Governor of West Virginia, declaring martial law in Mingo County, West Virginia.)

That after martial law was so proclaimed as aforesaid, and after the military forces of the State of West Virginia occupied said Mingo County under and in pursuance of said martial law proclamation, a large number of persons residing within the miltary zone of said Mingo County, West Virginia, were duly arrested and incarcerated in the jail of Mingo County, West Virginia, charged with violations of law and violations of the Governor's proclamation aforesaid, that on the ...... day of August, 1921, while martial law was still in full force and effect and while a large number of persons who had been so arrested and who were being duly and legally held as prisoners in said jail of

. 

Mingo County, West Virginia, the said Frank Keeney (and others), being then and there abiding in Kanawha, Boone and Raleigh Counties, of the said State of West Virginia, and deriving protection from the laws of said State, and then and there owing allegiance and fidelity to the said state, and being then and there citizens and members thereof, not regarding their duty of their said allegiance and fidelity, but wickedly devising and intending the peace and tranquility of the said State to disturb and destroy, and in opposition to the laws of said State; wickedly devising and intending to prevent by force, violence and open warfare the execution of the laws of the State of West Virginia, and especially to prevent by the means aforesaid, the existence and continuance of martial law in said Mingo County, and to destroy such martial law in said county, and nullify the proclamations of the Governor proclaiming martial law therein, and to wrongfully, unlawfully and traitorously release from the jail of said Mingo County by such force, violence and open warfare, the prisoners then and there being duly held as aforesaid, on the day of August, 1921, at Marmet, Kanawha County, West Virginia, did then and there unlawfully, maliciously and traitorously conspire to levy war against the said State of West Virginia; and to fulfill and bring to effect the said traitorous compassings, intentions and conspirings of them the said Frank Keeney (and others), they, the said Frank Keeney (and others) afterwards, that is to say, on the …….. day of August, 1921, and the ...... days of September, 1921, at Marmet, in the said Kanawha County, West Virginia, with Mose Adkins (and others) and with a great multitude of other persons, whose names are to the jurors aforesaid as yet unknown, to the number of from eight to ten thousand, armed and arrayed in a warlike manner, that is to say with machine guns, high power rifles, military rifles, revolvers, and other warlike weapons, ammunition and supplies, as well offensive as defensive, being then and there unlawfully, maliciously, and traitorously assembled and gathered together, did falsely, maliciously and traitorously assemble, combine, conspire and join themselves together against the said State, and then and there, with force and arms, did wickedly, falsely, maliciously and traitorously, and in a warlike and hostile manner ......

August, 1921, and the days of September, 1921, engage in a series of battles with the military forces of the State of West Virginia and with other forces who were then and there acting under the direction and control of the said military forces of the said state, all of whom were then and there fighting in behalf of the said State of West Virginia and were then and there defending said Logan and Mingo Counties from further invasion by said army so maliciously and traitorously assembled and fighting as aforesaid, and they the said Frank Keeney (and others) did then and there on the day and dates aforesaid, wickedly, maliciously and traitorously arrest or cause to be arrested and apprehended by said army so traitorously assembled by them, a number of officials or officers of the law of said Logan County, and held them, the said officers or officials, as prisoners of war for a period of days, and on the ..... day of .... 1921, they the said Frank Keeney (and others) wickedly, maliciously and traitorously, while said battles were being fought as aforesaid, killed or murdered or caused to be killed or murdered, by the army so traitorously assembled by them one J. C. Gore a deputy sheriff of the said County of Logan and wounded certain other persons who were then and there per- 

.... 

---

forming military duties under the military forces of the said state, with the wicked, malicious and traitorous intent and purpose of them, the said Frank Keeny (and others), by force and arms and open warfare, traitorously to take possession of the counties of Logan and Mingo in said State and prevent the execution of the laws of said State in said counties and to deprive the people of said counties abiding therein of the protection afforded by the laws of said State, and especially to destroy the effect and existence of martial law in said Mingo County and to nullify the proclamations of the Chief Executive, the Governor of said State proclaiming martial law in said Mingo County as aforesaid, and further to wickedly, maliciously and traitorously release the prisoners duly held in jail in said Mingo County for the violation of law and for the violation of the martial law proclamations as aforesaid, contrary to the duty of their said allegiance and fidelity, against the peace and dignity of the State. 

NOTE: One of the defendants named in this indictment was tried, and a demurrer on the ground that the indictment failed to charge the acts to have been done feloniously was overruled by the trial court. Defendant was acquitted.
